papers.title: Cup and Cap Topological Neural Network
papers.abstract: Topological Deep Learning (TDL) is designed to learn features associated not only with nodes but also with edges, triangles and higher dimensional simplices. However, most TDL approaches, being based on boundary operators and Hodge Laplacians, have the limitation that features and signals cannot be lifted or lowered across more than one dimension per layer. To overcome this limitation, in this work, we propose the adoption of the cup and cap products. Specifically, we formulate the Cup and Cap Topological Neural Network (CCNN), a topological deep learning architecture designed to learn node-based variables (or 0-cochains) by taking into account their many-body interactions (e.g. triangles) present in the data. We validate CCNN by assessing its performance on the TopoBench datasets, demonstrating its competitive performance with respect to other simplicial complex neural networks.
papers.summary: Topological Deep Learning (TDL) methods built on boundary operators and Hodge Laplacians can only lift or lower features by one dimension per layer. The `Cup and Cap Topological Neural Network` (`CCNN`) instead uses cup and cap products to learn node-level variables (0-cochains) while accounting for many-body interactions such as triangles. On the `TopoBench` datasets it is reported to be **competitive with other simplicial complex neural networks**.

papers.title: To predict or to persist: how decoherence shapes learning in a spin-qubit quantum reservoir
papers.abstract: In this work we investigate how dephasing and the choice of measured observables affect learning in a simulated six-qubit spin chain with Markovian dissipation and exact expectation-value readout. For externally driven nonlinear autoregressive moving-average signals, combining single- and two-qubit observables gives better predictions than a population-only readout at comparable polynomial feature counts. Most of the configurations we tested become more accurate than a reference with relaxation and dephasing disabled, most strongly at $T_2=1\,\mu$s, where total memory capacity drops, and still at $T_2=5$-$10\,\mu$s, where memory is only redistributed across delays. For autonomous generation, we train the readout with scheduled sampling and iterative dataset aggregation to expose it to states reached under its own feedback. We do not find a clear systematic dependence of limit-cycle persistence on coherence across the reservoir ensemble. For chaotic forecasting, in contrast, prediction horizons at $T_2=1\,\mu$s shorten in all 10 reservoir realizations relative to that reference. For the noise-driven strange non-chaotic attractor, the model produces a smooth, approximately closed orbit, and neither captures the target's scatter nor follows its trajectory pointwise. We conclude that, within this simulated reservoir, the impact of coherence depends strongly on the task.
papers.summary: A simulated six-qubit spin chain with Markovian dissipation is used as a quantum reservoir to study how dephasing and the choice of measured observables affect learning. For externally driven nonlinear autoregressive moving-average signals, combining single- and two-qubit observables beats a population-only readout, and most tested configurations become more accurate than a reference with relaxation and dephasing disabled, most strongly at a T2 of 1 microsecond. For chaotic forecasting, however, **prediction horizons at a T2 of 1 microsecond shorten in all 10 reservoir realizations**, and no clear dependence of limit-cycle persistence on coherence is found. The authors conclude that, within this simulated reservoir, the impact of coherence depends strongly on the task.

papers.title: Grid Cells as Spectral Successor Features: A Reusable Basis for Continual Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Continual reinforcement learning requires agents to adapt when the task changes while reusing what they know about the environment. Successor features separate dynamics from task-specific reward, but their effectiveness depends on the choice of base features. Taking the identification of entorhinal grid cells with eigenvectors of the successor representation as a design principle, we build this basis from eigenvectors of the transition matrix of a fixed reference policy. With such a basis, the successor features at a state-action pair are a linear combination of the base features at that same pair, which is not true in general, and the coefficients are known in closed form: each successor feature is its base feature multiplied by $\theta_i = 1/(1-\gamma\lambda_i)$, where $\lambda_i$ is its eigenvalue. The long-term return is thus predicted from the same features as the immediate reward, no successor-feature network or replay buffer is needed, and adapting to a new task reduces to a linear regression on the reward. The agent acts greedily on the action values of the reference policy, which is one step of policy improvement over it and suffices to reach a single goal. In a two-goal gridworld, with the uniform random walk as reference policy, whose eigenvectors are the low-frequency Laplacian eigenvectors, agents built this way maintain near-maximal return across every change of goal, whereas SimpleSF and DQN lose most of their return at each change.
papers.summary: Continual reinforcement learning needs agents that adapt to a changed task while reusing what they know about the environment, and successor features only help if the base features are well chosen. Following the identification of entorhinal grid cells with eigenvectors of the successor representation, the base features are built from eigenvectors of a fixed reference policy's transition matrix, so each successor feature is just its base feature scaled by 1/(1 - gamma*lambda), with lambda its eigenvalue. This removes the successor-feature network and replay buffer, and adapting to a new task reduces to a linear regression on the reward. In a two-goal gridworld these agents **maintain near-maximal return across every change of goal**, whereas `SimpleSF` and `DQN` lose most of their return at each change.

papers.title: SDG: State-Dependent Gating at Chunk Boundaries for Linear Attention
papers.abstract: Recent gated linear attention models use state-independent gates, computed from token representations without directly reading the recurrent memory. This design supports efficient chunkwise computation: sequences are divided into chunks of consecutive tokens, with parallel computation within each chunk. However, the same token representation produces the same gate, even when the layer stores different information. We introduce State-Dependent Gating (SDG), which computes element-wise gates from the change in memory over a chunk and applies them at the chunk boundary. This provides state feedback for forgetting while preserving parallel computation within each chunk. We develop fused kernels for Gated DeltaNet, Kimi Delta Attention, Gated DeltaNet-2, and Mamba-3. Our theoretical analysis quantifies the potential reconstruction benefits of state-dependent, element-wise gating under a signal--noise model. We also show that boundary decay is an element-wise ridge proximal step when the gate is held fixed. Empirical evaluation of 1.3B linear attention and hybrid models trained on 100B tokens shows improvements across language modeling, commonsense reasoning, synthetic and real-world retrieval, and long-context understanding. These results demonstrate that SDG is an effective approach to enhancing existing linear attention models.
papers.summary: Gated linear attention models compute their gates from token representations alone, so the same token yields the same gate regardless of what the recurrent memory currently stores. State-Dependent Gating (`SDG`) computes element-wise gates from the change in memory over a chunk and applies them at the chunk boundary, adding state feedback for forgetting while keeping parallel computation inside each chunk. Fused kernels are provided for `Gated DeltaNet`, `Kimi Delta Attention`, `Gated DeltaNet-2`, and `Mamba-3`, alongside a theoretical analysis of reconstruction benefits under a signal-noise model. On **1.3B-parameter linear attention and hybrid models trained on 100B tokens**, it improves language modeling, commonsense reasoning, retrieval, and long-context understanding.

papers.title: VerifiQuant: Governance-by-Execution for Financial LLM Workflows
papers.abstract: Large language models embedded in financial workflows fail most dangerously by emitting confident, well-formatted but wrong numbers with no signal distinguishing them from correct ones. We argue that the central deployment problem is governability: a system must determine when a question supports a numeric answer and when it should instead clarify, intercept, or refuse. We present VerifiQuant, a governance-by-execution framework that packages financial logic into inference contracts and evaluates each query through an executable diagnostic funnel before deterministic computation. This separation makes computation, clarification, and refusal structured and auditable while keeping financial arithmetic outside the language model. Against matched retrieval-and-execution baselines, and within a declared contract library, the principal benefit is not higher accuracy on well-posed questions but safer behavior when an input does not justify a number. When it finds no applicable contract, it says so instead of guessing. Coverage sweeps and failure analysis put a price on this boundary: safety is bought with coverage rather than with accuracy, and residual failures remain attributable to specific runtime frontiers.
papers.summary: Large language models in financial workflows can emit confident, well-formatted but wrong numbers with nothing to distinguish them from correct ones. `VerifiQuant` packages financial logic into inference contracts and passes each query through an executable diagnostic funnel before deterministic computation, keeping arithmetic outside the language model and making clarification and refusal structured and auditable. Against matched retrieval-and-execution baselines, and within a declared contract library, the main benefit is **safer behavior when an input does not justify a number, not higher accuracy on well-posed questions**. Coverage sweeps show this safety is paid for with coverage, not accuracy.

papers.title: Distributional Deep Hedging
papers.abstract: Deep hedging learns a hedging strategy by optimising a risk preference over a neural-network policy. The preference is fixed before training, so each new preference requires a new policy and, in actor-critic methods, a new critic. We propose distributional deep hedging, in which the distribution of the hedging profit and loss is learned through its quantiles and the risk preference is applied afterwards, as a weight on those quantiles. We characterise the preferences that admit this representation, which include expected shortfall and its mixtures, and show that the entropic utility is computed from the same quantiles. At the current policy, each of these preferences is bounded below by an expected utility with the same gradient. This bound reduces risk-sensitive hedging to a sequence of risk-neutral problems, from which we derive policy-search and actor-critic algorithms. In numerical experiments, the learned hedges approach references computed by dynamic programming, and a single distributional critic trained without a preference can serve preferences chosen after training.
papers.summary: Deep hedging trains a neural-network hedging policy for a risk preference fixed before training, so every new preference requires a new policy and, in actor-critic methods, a new critic. The distributional variant proposed here learns the quantiles of the hedging profit and loss and applies the risk preference afterwards as a weight on those quantiles, covering expected shortfall, its mixtures, and the entropic utility. A lower bound with matching gradient reduces risk-sensitive hedging to a sequence of risk-neutral problems, yielding policy-search and actor-critic algorithms. In numerical experiments the learned hedges approach dynamic-programming references, and **a single distributional critic trained without a preference can serve preferences chosen after training**.

papers.title: Computing Weighted Set Covers with Heterogeneous Stochastic Oracles: Deadline-Constrained Token Complexity
papers.abstract:
We study computation in which a probabilistic Turing machine (PTM) uses AI systems, abstracted as heterogeneous stochastic oracles (HSOs), to solve Weighted Set Cover. A pilot study shows that an LLM can outperform weighted greedy. HSOs differ in capabilities, response distributions, latencies, and token costs. We study how the PTM selects HSOs to obtain, by a deadline and with a required success probability, a full cover satisfying a prescribed weight threshold, and we analyze expected token cost.
  For queries requesting full covers, assuming independent call successes and uninformative failures, we characterize by linear programming the minimum expected token cost for every feasible success probability. An optimal policy randomizes over at most two preselected sequences of oracle batches. Among policies attaining maximum success probability, the expected cost reduction of two-batch selection relative to querying all oracles in one batch is nonnegative and submodular. We construct an FPTAS for near-optimal cost reduction under heterogeneous response-time bounds. Computing an optimal two-batch selection is NP-hard but admits a pseudopolynomial algorithm for positive integral expected token costs.
  For partial-cover responses, the PTM combines returned sets across batches and turns. Once their union covers the universe, it verifies total weight directly or obtains a guarantee from LP-dual tests on retained partial covers. We give one-turn probability, token-cost, and hardness results and adaptive token-cost bounds under per-batch assumptions. A constructed instance shows that residual-guided querying can reduce expected token cost by a factor linear in the number of possible residual subproblems.
papers.summary: AI systems are modeled as heterogeneous stochastic oracles (HSOs) that differ in capability, latency, and token cost, queried by a probabilistic Turing machine (PTM) that must produce a Weighted Set Cover below a weight threshold by a deadline with a required success probability. For queries requesting full covers, linear programming characterizes the minimum expected token cost at every feasible success probability, and **an optimal policy randomizes over at most two preselected sequences of oracle batches**. Computing an optimal two-batch selection is NP-hard but admits a pseudopolynomial algorithm, and a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme is given for near-optimal cost reduction. For partial-cover responses, a constructed instance shows residual-guided querying can cut expected token cost by a factor linear in the number of residual subproblems.

papers.title: Adding One More Agent: How AI Team Size and Formation Shape Productivity and Diversity in Human-AI Brainstorming Teams
papers.abstract: Generative AI has improved individual productivity, but whether adding a plurality of AI partners helps or hurts remains open. We crossed AI partnership (one versus two) with behavioral formation (calibrated to average human behavior versus customized by the participant) in a brainstorming experiment ($N$=168) with human-human dyads as reference. Two-AI rooms posted more ideas to the shared board, but human-authored ideas dropped substantially. With one AI partner, formation mattered: humans paired with an average-calibrated AI posted more than any other condition. With two, this effect vanished. Humans continued talking but converted fewer ideas into board posts. AI social talk predicted more human posts, while AI posting volume predicted fewer. AI presence increased global diversity of human-authored ideas, but only a second AI increased within-session differentiation. The number of AI partners and their formation can reshape what the human contributes; single-agent results do not generalize to multi-agent teams.
papers.summary: A brainstorming experiment with 168 participants crossed the number of AI partners (one versus two) with whether the AI's behavior was calibrated to average human behavior or customized by the participant, using human-human pairs as a reference. **Rooms with two AIs posted more ideas to the shared board, but human-authored ideas dropped substantially**; with one AI, humans paired with an average-calibrated partner posted more than any other condition, an effect that vanished with two. AI social talk predicted more human posts while AI posting volume predicted fewer, and only a second AI increased within-session differentiation of ideas. The authors conclude that single-agent results do not generalize to multi-agent teams.

papers.title: On the loss landscape of the linear neural network: beyond critical points
papers.abstract: While the critical points of the loss landscape in linear neural networks have been extensively studied since the seminal work of Baldi \& Hornik in the late 1980s, a description of this landscape at an intermediate or global scale is still lacking. Such a characterization is crucial, particularly as a substantial body of literature indicates that gradient descent circumvents critical points. The present article introduces an intermediate structure, termed the critical thalweg, which encompasses all critical points and exhibits key geometric properties. Beyond providing a geometric proof of Baldi \& Hornik's results using simpler assumptions than the existing literature, this framework offers a global view of the loss landscape that can be easily visualized in a two-dimensional plane. Empirical observations suggest that gradient descent is attracted toward the critical thalweg, along which the loss continues to decrease to its global minimum.
papers.summary: The critical points of the loss landscape of linear neural networks are well understood, but a description at an intermediate or global scale has been missing even though gradient descent is known to circumvent critical points. An intermediate structure called the critical thalweg is introduced, which contains all critical points, yields a geometric proof of Baldi and Hornik's classical results under simpler assumptions, and gives a global view of the landscape that can be drawn in a two-dimensional plane. Empirical observations suggest that **gradient descent is attracted toward the critical thalweg, along which the loss keeps decreasing to its global minimum**.

papers.title: Model the Annotation, Not the Noise: Semantic Annotation-Channel Prompt Learning against Noisy Labels
papers.abstract: Parameter-efficient prompt learning has become a cornerstone for adapting pre-trained vision-language models (VLMs), yet it remains highly vulnerable to label noise in few-shot Web and retrieval scenarios. Existing noise robust methods typically rely on hard sample selection or deterministic label correction, which discard valuable semantic ambiguity and overlook how observed annotations are actually generated. To bridge this gap, we reformulate noisy prompt learning through the perspective of data generation, proposing SACP, a Semantic-aware Annotation Channel-based Prompt learning framework. Instead of suppressing noise heuristically, SACP decouples latent clean-label prediction from instance-dependent annotation generation. By integrating frozen VLM semantic priors with lightweight visual residuals, SACP constructs a structured annotation channel optimized via generalized expectation-maximization with soft posteriors. Furthermore, a posterior-aware memory is introduced to preserve label uncertainty during test-time inference. Extensive experiments across different synthetic benchmarks and the real-world noisy Food101N dataset demonstrate that SACP achieves state-of-the-art performance against its counterparts in different label noise patterns, especially under severe asymmetric noise.
papers.summary: Prompt learning for adapting pre-trained vision-language models (VLMs) is vulnerable to label noise in few-shot Web and retrieval settings, and existing remedies rely on hard sample selection or deterministic label correction. `SACP`, a Semantic-aware Annotation Channel-based Prompt learning framework, instead models how noisy annotations are generated, separating latent clean-label prediction from an instance-dependent annotation channel built from frozen VLM semantic priors plus lightweight visual residuals and trained by generalized expectation-maximization with soft posteriors. A posterior-aware memory preserves label uncertainty at test time. On synthetic benchmarks and the real-world noisy `Food101N` dataset it reports **state-of-the-art accuracy across label noise patterns, especially under severe asymmetric noise**.

papers.title: Parasite Features: Causal Abstraction Through Spurious Pathways
papers.abstract: Causal Abstraction defines a notion of \emph{equivalence} between a neural network and an algorithm, thus serving as a powerful framework for mechanistic interpretability. In this paper, however, we show the existence of a class of \emph{spurious features} which straightforwardly pass such equivalence tests. Suppose there are two directions in a model's representation space where: (i) one discriminates the input based on some feature, and (ii) the other steers the model towards a certain output. Interpretability methods based on Causal Abstraction (e.g., Distributed Alignment Search) can \emph{spuriously} simulate these directions' combined behavior by leveraging pathways passing through them, giving the impression that the model implements this feature. In such cases, we say the method discovered a \defn{parasite feature}. Experimentally, we show that Distributed Alignment Search finds parasite features using linear alignment maps in two tasks: syntactic agreement and two-digit addition. Our paper highlights an important consideration for Causal Abstraction and contributes to the ongoing debate about best practices for mechanistic interpretability.
papers.summary: Causal Abstraction defines when a neural network is equivalent to an algorithm and underpins interpretability methods such as `Distributed Alignment Search`. The authors show that when one direction in representation space discriminates inputs by some feature and another steers the model toward a certain output, such methods can combine pathways through both and **pass the equivalence test for a feature the model does not actually implement**, which they call a parasite feature. Experiments find `Distributed Alignment Search` recovering parasite features with linear alignment maps on two tasks, syntactic agreement and two-digit addition.

papers.title: Coherence by Construction: Synthesizing CTI Knowledge Graphs and the Formal Limits of Coherence Validation
papers.abstract: Synthesizing relational training data such as knowledge graphs with a large language model typically emits structured objects one at a time, which keeps each object valid but leaves the relationships between them ungrounded. We study an alternative paradigm, generation by simulation: rather than describing a relational artifact, we simulate a process that produces it and take the artifact to be its causal record. Language-model agents propose intent and a deterministic referee resolves outcomes against an explicit world model, so a relation is emitted only when the event it represents occurs, making coherence a property of construction. We instantiate the paradigm for cyber threat intelligence knowledge graphs in the STIX 2.1 standard with three engines, among them an evolutionary engine applying language-model genetic operators to structured graph genomes, sharing a deterministic compiler that makes malformed and dangling output unrepresentable. We prove referential closure, causal grounding, and identifier stability, an ablation localizes each to the referee and world model rather than the policy, and two independent LLM judges reproduce the rubric's engine ranking. Our central result is cautionary, and we prove it: a validator reading any graph feature set a structure-matched random graph can reproduce is uninformative about coherence for a coherence-by-construction generator. Using Erd\H{o}s-R\'enyi controls we realize the theorem four times, as structural separation, embedding transfer, inductive link prediction, and real-data augmentation each reward a triviality rather than coherence; we give the mechanism behind each and the conditions a valid benchmark must meet.
papers.summary: Synthesizing knowledge graphs with a large language model one object at a time keeps each object valid but leaves the relations between them ungrounded. The alternative studied here is generation by simulation: language-model agents propose intent, a deterministic referee resolves outcomes against an explicit world model, and a relation is emitted only when the event it represents occurs, instantiated for cyber threat intelligence (CTI) graphs in the `STIX 2.1` standard with three engines sharing a deterministic compiler. The authors prove referential closure, causal grounding, and identifier stability, and an ablation attributes each to the referee and world model, not the policy. The central, cautionary result is a proof that **a validator reading only graph features a structure-matched random graph can reproduce is uninformative about coherence**, demonstrated four times with Erdős-Rényi controls.

papers.title: TOUMAII: A 4.5M-Pair Tool-Calling Preference Dataset and Its Source-Agnostic Generator
papers.abstract:
To autonomously execute multi-step tasks, enterprise agents must reliably interact with tools, call APIs, or query databases, making tool-calling a fundamental capability of AI models. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) optimises for producing the correct call, but never contrasts it with a plausible incorrect one. In an environment where even a minor formatting error can invalidate a call and an incorrect decision can derail the interaction, direct preference optimisation (DPO) targets exactly this contrast. DPO, therefore, requires preference pairs rather than plain demonstrations. For tool-calling, such data, especially in realistic multi-turn settings, remains extremely scarce. To address this scarcity, we introduce TOUMAII, a large-scale tool-calling preference dataset containing ~4.5M validated preference pairs, derived from Agent-Ark/Toucan-1.5M (apache-2.0) conversations. The dataset consists of multi- and single-turn interactions and includes parallel and sequential function calls. Additionally, we release TOUMAII-Gen, a synthetic data generation pipeline that consumes tool-calling SFT datasets and generates a preference dataset with naturally occurring model-generated tool-calling failure modes. To validate the effectiveness of our DPO data, we fine-tune a 3-billion-parameter model, achieving performance parity with other high-quality tool-calling preference datasets. Furthermore, we release a second small preference dataset derived from ToolACE (apache-2.0), showcasing the source-agnostic nature of our pipeline.
  We release the complete code and datasets: https://github.com/tum-ai/toumaii-gen and https://huggingface.co/collections/tum-ai/toumaii-generated-datasets
papers.summary: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) teaches a model to produce the correct tool call but never contrasts it with a plausible wrong one, which is what direct preference optimisation (DPO) targets, yet preference-pair data for multi-turn tool calling is scarce. `TOUMAII` supplies **about 4.5M validated preference pairs** derived from `Toucan-1.5M` conversations, covering single- and multi-turn interactions with parallel and sequential function calls. The accompanying `TOUMAII-Gen` pipeline turns any tool-calling SFT dataset into preference data using naturally occurring model-generated failures, and is also applied to `ToolACE`. A 3-billion-parameter model fine-tuned on the data reaches parity with other high-quality tool-calling preference datasets, and code and data are released.

papers.title: SparseHPS: A Unified Model for Human Pose and Shape across Depth Cameras and LiDARs
papers.abstract: Recovering 3D human pose and shape from point clouds is central to motion capture, robotics and self-driving vehicles, because depth cameras and LiDARs sense a person directly in metric 3D and work under any lighting. However, current approaches are each tailored to one sensor type: point density differs by more than ten times between devices, public datasets are labeled with incompatible body models, and LiDAR approaches need long input sequences to offset sparse scans. In this work, we present SparseHPS, a novel sensor-agnostic network that recovers SMPL-X pose, shape and global translation from a human point cloud with one set of weights, for single frames and streams alike. Specifically, SparseHPS encodes the cloud with a LitePT backbone over sparse voxels, represents every joint by a learnable query decoded with one common head, localizes the body by voting over voxels, and draws temporal context from a causal memory of tokens from the seven preceding frames. A single model is trained on ten datasets that mix rendered clouds with real depth-camera and LiDAR captures, all converted to one body model. Experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art results on the SLOPER4D and FreeMotion LiDAR benchmarks, where SparseHPS lowers the root-relative joint error by 22% and 11%, respectively, compared with the strongest prior method, which needs 32 frames. On real Azure Kinect captures of held-out HuMMan subjects, SparseHPS attains a joint error of 34.7 mm. Moreover, the current frame alone already yields the bulk of this accuracy.
papers.summary: Methods for recovering 3D human pose and shape from point clouds are each tailored to one sensor type, because point density, body-model labels, and sequence-length needs differ between depth cameras and LiDARs. `SparseHPS` is a single sensor-agnostic network that predicts `SMPL-X` pose, shape, and global translation using a `LitePT` sparse-voxel backbone, per-joint learnable queries, voxel voting for localization, and a causal memory of the seven preceding frames, trained on ten datasets converted to one body model. It **lowers root-relative joint error by 22% on `SLOPER4D` and 11% on `FreeMotion`** against the strongest prior method, which needs 32 frames, and reaches 34.7 mm joint error on held-out `HuMMan` Azure Kinect captures. The current frame alone already yields most of this accuracy.

papers.title: Cross-Attack Robust Aggregation for Federated Learning
papers.abstract: Federated learning (FL) lets resource-constrained IoT and edge devices train a shared model without exchanging raw data, but compromised or faulty devices can poison the global model. Existing robust aggregators each fail in some regime: naive averaging (FedAvg) collapses under high-magnitude attacks, whereas distance- and statistics-based defenses (Krum, median, trimmed mean) sacrifice accuracy on non-IID data and remain vulnerable to stealthy attacks. We present FedTether, which reweights client updates by their deviation from a coordinatewise median through a robust, dead-zoned score applied as a server-side optimizer step. Across three datasets, three attack types, and Byzantine fractions up to 40%, FedTether is the only method top-tier in every regime: it matches FedAvg under stealthy attacks with no robustness tax, exceeds robust baselines by up to 42 accuracy points, and stays accurate where high-magnitude attacks reduce FedAvg to near-random. These properties persist at 50 clients under partial participation, with no shared data or validation set.
papers.summary: Federated learning (FL) lets edge devices train a shared model without exchanging raw data, but compromised clients can poison it, and existing aggregators each fail somewhere: `FedAvg` collapses under high-magnitude attacks, while `Krum`, median, and trimmed mean lose accuracy on non-IID data and remain open to stealthy attacks. `FedTether` reweights client updates by their deviation from a coordinatewise median using a robust, dead-zoned score applied as a server-side optimizer step. Across three datasets, three attack types, and Byzantine fractions up to 40%, it is reported as the only method in the top tier in every regime, matching `FedAvg` under stealthy attacks and **exceeding robust baselines by up to 42 accuracy points**. The results hold at 50 clients under partial participation with no shared data or validation set.

papers.title: INCISE: Training-Free In-Context Segmentation of Surgical Videos
papers.abstract: Surgical video analysis requires video object segmentation (VOS), yet existing methods are commonly based on pretrained model fine-tuning using a large number of expert labels. In-context segmentation (ICS) offers the promise of bypassing this high cost by segmenting a target video using a few annotated references, which are the sole source of surgical knowledge for a frozen model. However, existing ICS methods tend to draw such references at random, which concentrate on a few views that dominate a surgical video and can miss other objects of interest (e.g., transient instruments and small structures). To address these challenges, we propose INCISE, a training-free ICS framework for surgical videos. INCISE selects unlabeled frames from multiple surgical videos that jointly cover the local appearances of a target video, and then segments the target video using these references. With only 1.7% of training frames selected and annotated as references and no target video frame labeled, INCISE obtains 67.2% mean mIoU and outperforms the best SOTA fine-tuned method by 9.2 points. We hope INCISE can help establish ICS as a practical alternative to fine-tuning in surgical video analysis and other domains with a costly labeling burden.
papers.summary: Video object segmentation (VOS) for surgical video usually depends on fine-tuning with many expert labels, while in-context segmentation (ICS) with a frozen model tends to pick reference frames at random and so misses transient instruments and small structures. `INCISE` is a training-free ICS framework that selects unlabeled frames from multiple surgical videos to jointly cover the local appearances of the target video, then segments the target from those references. With only 1.7% of training frames annotated as references and no target frames labeled, it reaches **67.2% mean mIoU, 9.2 points above the best fine-tuned method**.

papers.title: MomentMem: Memorizing Key Moments for Robot Manipulation
papers.abstract: Robotic manipulation often requires remembering visual information that is no longer observable, such as the original location of an object. Existing approaches typically rely on full observation histories, which become redundant over long horizons, or text summaries, which may omit precise visual details. We study visual moment memory, the ability to retain such details from key moments for subsequent manipulation. To support this study, we introduce VMBench, a suite of long-horizon manipulation tasks requiring memory of spatial locations, visual appearances, and their associations. We further propose MomentMem, a hierarchical architecture in which a VLM-based memorizer selects keyframes and an executor predicts actions conditioned on the selected memories. This separation enables us to evaluate memory selection alongside closed-loop task success and to study memorizer generalization independently of the executor. On VMBench, MomentMem achieves 49.9% average success, outperforming the strongest evaluated baseline by 31.7 percentage points. Moreover, we find that the memorizer transfers well to unseen appearances zero-shot. It can also adapt to an unseen task with only a few memory annotations, reaching 43.7% success, close to the 44.3% obtained with full memory supervision. Further experiments show competitive performance on RMBench and improvements in real-robot manipulation. These results highlight the value of retaining sparse visual evidence for memory-dependent manipulation. Our code is available at https://github.com/PKU-VaLuE-Lab/MomentMem.
papers.summary: Robot manipulation often depends on visual details that are no longer observable, such as where an object originally was, and full observation histories or text summaries handle this poorly over long horizons. `MomentMem` is a hierarchical architecture in which a memorizer based on a vision-language model selects keyframes and an executor predicts actions conditioned on them, evaluated on `VMBench`, a new suite of long-horizon tasks requiring memory of locations, appearances, and their associations. It achieves **49.9% average success on `VMBench`, 31.7 percentage points above the strongest evaluated baseline**. The memorizer transfers zero-shot to unseen appearances and adapts to an unseen task with a few memory annotations, with competitive results on `RMBench` and gains on real robots.

papers.title: SkillPrivus: Uncovering PRIVacy of USe Harms in Agentic Skills
papers.abstract: Agent skills extend AI assistants through installable instructions and code that can access users' files, accounts, and data. Even when performing their advertised tasks, skills may infer sensitive attributes, retain unnecessary information, or disclose data to unexpected recipients. We study these potential privacy-of-use harms through SkillPrivus, a static audit framework that analyzes skills before installation without executing them. SkillPrivus extracts data operations from code and natural-language instructions, grounds them in source evidence, and adapts Contextual Integrity to assess their appropriateness. Applied to 726 real skills from public marketplaces, 563 of which handle personal data, SkillPrivus flags at least one potential violation in 307 of these skills (54.5%), and its judgments agree with three blind human annotators on 83.2% of resolvable moves. The flagged behaviors include sensitive inferences, information use beyond the stated task, and disclosures to unexpected recipients, suggesting that privacy harms can arise from ordinary skill functionality.
papers.summary: Installable agent skills can access users' files, accounts, and data, and even while doing their advertised job they may infer sensitive attributes, retain unnecessary information, or disclose data to unexpected recipients. `SkillPrivus` is a static audit framework that analyzes a skill before installation without executing it, extracting data operations from code and natural-language instructions, grounding them in source evidence, and judging appropriateness with an adaptation of Contextual Integrity. Of 726 real skills from public marketplaces, 563 handle personal data, and **307 of those (54.5%) are flagged with at least one potential violation**. Its judgments agree with three blind human annotators on 83.2% of resolvable moves.

papers.title: Depth-Linked Residual Tokens for Multimodal Retrieval and Generation
papers.abstract: Iterative architectures such as looped language models improve parameter efficiency and reasoning capacity of transformers, yet their sequential backbone iterations introduce substantial computational latency. Conversely, parallelizable learnable special tokens (such as the register tokens in Vision Transformer) enable efficient single-pass inference, but often suffer from the absence of sequential refinement and exhibit redundant representations across tokens. To address these challenges, we introduce Depth-Linked Residual Tokens (DepThink), an efficient framework designed for multimodal retrieval and generation. Operating within a single pre-filling forward pass, DepThink appends a sequence of K learnable residual tokens whose hidden states are coupled through a lightweight, learnable residual recurrence. This mechanism enables each residual token to progressively capture complementary information missed by preceding tokens. Theoretically, we prove that DepThink provides strictly expanded geometric directional reachability over standard learnable tokens and guarantees a provable one-step descent advantage. We evaluate DepThink across multimodal retrieval and generation tasks. DepThink consistently outperforms learnable-token baselines and matches or exceeds looped architectures across dense (2B, 8B) and sparse mixture-of-experts (30B-A3B) backbones under both LoRA and full-parameter fine-tuning, while accelerating training by up to 11.9 and inference by 4.3 over looped architectures.
papers.summary: Looped language models gain parameter efficiency and reasoning capacity from repeated backbone passes but pay in latency, while learnable special tokens run in one pass yet lack sequential refinement and become redundant. Depth-Linked Residual Tokens (`DepThink`) append K learnable tokens within a single forward pass and couple their hidden states through a lightweight learnable residual recurrence, so each token captures information missed by the previous ones. Across multimodal retrieval and generation with 2B, 8B, and 30B mixture-of-experts backbones, it outperforms learnable-token baselines and matches or exceeds looped architectures while **speeding up training by up to 11.9x and inference by 4.3x over looped architectures**. The authors also prove an expanded directional reachability and a one-step descent advantage over standard learnable tokens.

papers.title: Self-verifiable LLM-driven science and why it needs human researchers
papers.abstract: Language models are now used throughout all sciences - for reading literature, extracting numbers from tables and spectra, analyzing data, drafting conclusions - and their answers arrive in the same polished confident tone whether they are right or wrong, so a result has to be re-derived by a human researcher before it can be relied on. The cost of that re-checking, not the ability to generate results, is what currently limits AI-assisted research. In the field of mathematics, this problem is solved by proof assistants like Lean 4 and Coq that let any formal statement and its proof be written down and checked - a perfect match for LLMs, which are now actively used to search for proofs with every step automatically validated, rather than relying on a human to judge the result. In this paper, we propose an extension of this approach to non-mathematical sciences. We describe an AI agent harness that aims to make LLM's scientific reasoning verifiable: the starting assumptions are proposed by LLM and reviewed by a human, and everything built on top of them is checked by a machine with Lean 4. We illustrate how this mechanism works in practice on several examples and our results show that scientific arguments in these tasks can be expressed as formal proofs from explicit assumptions, including experimental results, known theoretical statements, and additional assumptions, produced by the agent. We suggest that this approach could change how scientific research is conducted across all sciences.
papers.summary: Language model answers in scientific work arrive in the same confident tone whether right or wrong, so a human must re-derive each result, and the authors argue this checking cost is what limits AI-assisted research. Borrowing from mathematics, where proof assistants validate every step, they describe an AI agent harness in which **the model proposes starting assumptions for human review and everything built on them is machine-checked in `Lean 4`**. Several worked examples show that scientific arguments can be expressed as formal proofs from explicit assumptions, including experimental results, known theoretical statements, and additional assumptions produced by the agent.

papers.title: Reinforcement Learning Unlearns Corrupted SFT Reasoning
papers.abstract: We show that reinforcement learning (RL) in reasoning tasks can succeed even when the supervised fine-tuning (SFT) data is severely corrupted. In a mathematical reasoning dataset (GSM8K), we systematically corrupt training trajectories across 361 configurations by injecting realistic error types, varying error locations, trace-answer consistency, and corruption ratios up to 100%. While aggregated SFT-only performance steadily deteriorates under corruption (dropping from 43.61% to 13.80%), Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) post-training consistently restores model accuracy back to gold-baseline levels (approximately 60%). Crucially, initializing RL with as few as N = 8 minimal, incorrect, three-line "form-only" traces boosts post-RL performance to 69.30%, outperforming standard gold SFT initialization (60.71%) and GRPO without SFT (35.00%). Further, we show that SFT accuracy is largely uncorrelated with post-RL accuracy (r approximately 0), demonstrating a fundamental asymmetry in post-training: SFT primarily establishes structural layout (form), while RL independently discovers functional reasoning (function).
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training is tested on models whose supervised fine-tuning (SFT) data has been deliberately corrupted, using 361 corruption configurations of `GSM8K` reasoning traces that vary error type, location, trace-answer consistency, and corruption ratio up to 100%. SFT-only accuracy falls from 43.61% to 13.80% under corruption, but Group Relative Policy Optimization (`GRPO`) restores accuracy to roughly the 60% gold-baseline level. **Initializing RL with just 8 minimal, incorrect, three-line form-only traces reaches 69.30%, beating gold SFT initialization (60.71%) and `GRPO` without SFT (35.00%)**. SFT accuracy is largely uncorrelated with post-RL accuracy, which the authors interpret as SFT setting output form while RL discovers the actual reasoning.
papers.highlight_summary:
Supervised fine-tuning before RL is usually done on carefully filtered, correct reasoning traces, but this study asks whether that curation matters and finds that `GRPO` recovers almost fully from heavily corrupted SFT data. The authors interpret this as a split of roles: SFT supplies output structure ("form") while RL discovers the actual reasoning ("function").

- Six error types observed in real `GRPO` rollouts (calculation, hallucination, operator, operand, added step, forgotten step) are injected into gold `GSM8K` traces with regex and propagated to the final answer, sweeping error location, trace-answer consistency, and corruption ratios of 10–100% for **361** SFT configurations on `OLMo-2-1B`.
- Aggregated SFT-only pass@2 accuracy falls from **43.61%** to **13.80%** at 100% corruption, yet `GRPO` afterwards restores every corruption ratio to about **60%**, within 0.5 points of the gold baseline in aggregate and at most 1.83 points below it for the worst single configuration.
- SFT on just **8** incorrect three-line "form-only" traces followed by `GRPO` reaches **69.30%**, beating gold `GSM8K` SFT plus `GRPO` (**60.71%**) and `GRPO` with no SFT (**35.00%**), and nearly all form-only initializations outperform all 361 `GSM8K` initializations.
- SFT-only accuracy is essentially uncorrelated with post-`GRPO` accuracy, with Pearson r between -0.0631 and 0.0002 across pass@k and none significant, though the authors' explanation that full-trace SFT constrains RL exploration remains a hypothesis.
- The evidence is limited to one 1B model and one dataset with regex-injected numerical errors from a taxonomy covering 93.51% of observed failures, so larger models, harder tasks, and natural-language reasoning mistakes are untested.

papers.title: Windchime: an Audiovisual Installation with Audio-Language Model implementations
papers.abstract: Windchime is an audiovisual installation in which spoken language retrieves music and interactive animations from an artist authored corpus. A local Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) model transcribes each prompt while an audio-language model (ALM) embeds it and retrieval over 406 audio stems returns a soundscape with live coded Strudel fragments that layer into audio output. Simultaneously each spoken input results in retrieval of interactive Three.js animation scenes each containing unique tactile control via monome grid and arc hardware. Windchime distributes agency in three distinct directions; across the artist who authored the possible outputs, the ALM that influences what areas of the corpus can be retrieved, and the visitor whose spoken inputs result in multimodal embodied interaction.
papers.summary: `Windchime` is an art installation in which a visitor's spoken prompt retrieves music and interactive animations from a corpus authored by the artist. A local automatic speech recognition (ASR) model transcribes the prompt, an audio-language model (ALM) embeds it, and retrieval over 406 audio stems returns a soundscape layered with live-coded `Strudel` fragments, alongside `Three.js` scenes controlled through monome grid and arc hardware. The authors frame the piece as **distributing agency among the artist, the audio-language model that shapes what can be retrieved, and the visitor**.

papers.title: Pharos: Learning to Control Rare Events at Scale
papers.abstract: Rare events drive transformations across physics, chemistry and biology, yet predicting their mechanisms and rates remains a fundamental challenge. Here we introduce Pharos, a framework that learns to make rare transitions accessible while predicting how frequently they occur under physical dynamics. Through stochastic optimal control, Pharos jointly learns the probability of completing a transition and how to steer simulations toward it, allowing sampling and learning to improve one another. Across biomolecular benchmarks, Pharos learns accurate transition probabilities with order-of-magnitude gains in convergence speed over previous algorithms. It transfers across ion assembly systems in explicit solvent while maintaining accurate reaction rate predictions, scales to host-guest binding systems that span millisecond timescales, and enables chemical reaction studies with a computationally demanding machine learning interatomic potential. By combining efficient sampling, quantitative kinetics, and transferability, Pharos opens a route toward foundation models of rare event mechanisms and rates across molecular systems.
papers.summary: Rare transitions in molecular systems are hard to simulate, and both their mechanisms and their rates are difficult to predict. `Pharos` uses stochastic optimal control to jointly learn the probability of completing a transition and a policy that steers simulations toward it, so that sampling and learning improve each other. On biomolecular benchmarks it learns accurate transition probabilities with **order-of-magnitude gains in convergence speed over previous algorithms**. The authors also report transfer across ion assembly systems in explicit solvent, scaling to host-guest binding at millisecond timescales, and use with a costly machine learning interatomic potential for chemical reactions.

papers.title: Who Should Verify? Reviewer Selection with Partial Information and Outcome Audits
papers.abstract: Selecting an AI reviewer requires evidence about what it does after reading a draft. On a fixed batch of items, a team can keep the original answers or adopt one reviewer's answers throughout. We ask how much it costs to certify that the chosen procedure falls at most a specified number of correct answers short of the best available procedure, for every completion of the unobserved evidence. When all reviews are available and only verified answer keys cost money, we give an exact stopping rule and an integer program for the cheapest certificate in hindsight. When reviews and keys both have prices, a polynomial-time algorithm using the completed record approximates the minimum certificate cost within a factor logarithmic in the number of procedures. This dependence is tight to leading order unless P equals NP. Finding a certificate can be much more expensive. We exhibit a two-procedure family with $n$ unresolved items where one purchase suffices in hindsight but the exact minimax expected search cost is $(n+1)/2$. For two binary procedures under a known independent and identically distributed item law, five counts suffice to compute an optimal search policy. We replay reviews on 2,000 MMLU questions, 896 numerical reports, and 48 Singapore electricity forecast reports. With reviews available, a targeted audit used 6.9% fewer keys on MMLU and 1.2% fewer on numerical reports than a fixed order selected on development data. Compared with selection by stand-alone accuracy, the chosen procedures gained 2.94 percentage points on held-out MMLU questions and zero on numerical reports. On electricity reports, five checks certified a tie across all 48, yet each procedure was correct only eight times.
papers.summary: Choosing between keeping original answers and adopting one AI reviewer's answers across a fixed batch is framed as a certification problem: how much must be spent on reviews and verified answer keys to guarantee the chosen procedure is within a set number of correct answers of the best one. The authors give an exact stopping rule and integer program when only answer keys cost money, a polynomial-time approximation within a logarithmic factor when reviews are also priced (tight unless P equals NP), and a construction showing that finding a certificate can cost far more than verifying one. In replays on 2,000 `MMLU` questions, 896 numerical reports, and 48 electricity forecast reports, a targeted audit used 6.9% fewer keys on `MMLU` than a fixed order, and **procedures chosen this way gained 2.94 percentage points on held-out `MMLU` questions over selection by stand-alone accuracy** but nothing on numerical reports.

papers.title: Know Your Context Bank: Repairing Inconsistency and Measuring Generalization in Context-Aware Text-to-SQL
papers.abstract: Text-to-SQL systems increasingly rely on context banks: curated collections of example queries, metric definitions, and domain knowledge that tell a model how an organization writes its queries. In the enterprise, a bank grows over years as many analysts add entries, checked one at a time for correctness (does the SQL answer its own question?) and rarely for consistency with one another. Yet correctness is often loosely defined: a question seldom fixes how an entity is counted or which table defines it, so two entries can each pass review yet resolve the same decision in opposite ways. We call this condition context bank rot. A second question follows: does a system that uses a bank generalize from it, or only reproduce it? Existing benchmarks cannot tell, as they do not control how far a test question sits from the context. We answer both questions by comparing queries decision by decision, with a fast scorer distilled from human-calibrated LLM judges. Turned inward, the comparison diagnoses and repairs a bank. Fine-tuning on a cleaned BIRD-train bank beats a same-size random subset at every epoch (+2.6 points on average), and 92.4% of our removals had their SQL corrected by an independent expert audit, against 45.6% of audited entries. In-context examples that follow one convention beat those following the opposite one by 13.3 points, while a mix is barely better than none. Turned outward, the comparison generates test questions at a controlled distance from a bank, a pipeline we call CAT (Context-Aware Testing). On CAT-BIRD, for retrieval and fine-tuning alike, the benefit of a bank falls step by step with distance and is largely gone once about three quarters of a question's logic is new, and on CAT-Spider the benefit of retrieval likewise shrinks with distance.
papers.summary: Text-to-SQL systems depend on context banks of example queries and definitions that accumulate over years, and entries that each pass review can still resolve the same modelling decision in opposite ways, which the authors call context bank rot. They compare queries decision by decision using a fast scorer distilled from human-calibrated LLM judges, using it both to clean a bank and to generate test questions at a controlled distance from it in a pipeline called Context-Aware Testing (`CAT`). Fine-tuning on a cleaned `BIRD`-train bank beats a same-size random subset by 2.6 points on average, and in-context examples following one consistent convention beat those following the opposite one by 13.3 points while a mix is barely better than none. On `CAT-BIRD`, **the benefit of a bank shrinks with distance and is largely gone once about three quarters of a question's logic is new**, for retrieval and fine-tuning alike.

papers.title: What Helps Language-Model Agents Review Violent Video? A Controlled Comparison with a Human Evidence Reference
papers.abstract: Systems that flag violent video for a human operator can now be built from language models without training, by combining perception models and letting a language model decide. We ask how the observations of the perception models should reach the decision, and which evidence matters. On the XD-Violence test set (799 clips) we fix one set of perception agents (video description, object detection, sound tagging, speech recognition and speech tagging) and one reasoning model, and compare three interfaces: messages between agents, a typed evidence graph explored with tools, and flat text read in one pass; and a single audio-visual model given the raw clip. Two annotators provide a human reference that records the decision, the incident segments and whether they relied on sight, sound or speech. Flat text matches the single model (F1 0.967 against 0.968), while the graph agent and message passing are less accurate; a variant of the graph agent developed on a separate set did not close the gap, and both graph summaries and multi-turn tool use lowered accuracy. These results hold with reworded prompts and with a larger reasoning model, except that the larger model weakens message passing enough for the graph agent to beat it. Sound events improve F1 by +0.012 [+0.004, +0.021], in line with the annotators, who used sound or speech on most violent clips. Citations of stored observations are faithful, changing about half of the decisions when removed, but no more so with the graph than with flat text, and the agent pipeline costs about 3 times the GPU time of the single model. We also report two artefacts of vision-language describers that mislead pipelines built on them.
papers.summary: The study asks how the outputs of perception models should be passed to a language model that decides whether a video clip is violent. On the 799-clip `XD-Violence` test set, with perception agents and reasoning model held fixed, it compares message passing between agents, a typed evidence graph explored with tools, flat text read in one pass, and a single audio-visual model given the raw clip, against a two-annotator human reference. **Flat text matches the single model (F1 0.967 versus 0.968), while the graph agent and message passing are less accurate**, and graph summaries and multi-turn tool use lowered accuracy. Sound events add 0.012 F1, and the agent pipeline costs about three times the GPU time of the single model.

papers.title: ChatAtom: A Multi-Agent LLM System for Molecular Dynamics Simulation and Visualization
papers.abstract: Molecular dynamics (MD) simulation resolves atomic-scale motion and predicts the structural, mechanical, and dynamic properties of materials, making it cen- tral to materials design and discovery. Yet an MD study requires an expert-driven workflow: designing the simulation, writing reliable input scripts, executing them, and analyzing the results with separate tools. Here we present ChatAtom, a multi-agent large language model system that translates a natural-language request into a complete MD workflow without the user writing input scripts or analysis code. Each agent has a defined responsibility within the workflow. An orchestrator plans the study; the LAMMPS and OVITO agents each use a generator-reviewer pair to prepare and review simulation and visualization scripts before execution; a high-performance computing agent dispatches jobs to remote resources; and an analysis agent interprets the completed run. The work- flow is accessible through a browser interface that streams thermodynamic data and rendered frames during local execution, allowing users to follow the simu- lation as it progresses. The architecture also supports new capabilities through loadable skills without modifying the agents, enabling autonomous hypothesis generation and testing. We evaluate ChatAtom through script-generation bench- marks, an end-to-end study of crack propagation, and a closed-loop campaign. By bringing script generation, execution, visualization, and analysis into one reviewed and observable pipeline, ChatAtom lowers the barrier to conducting MD studies and broadens access to advanced simulation workflows.
papers.summary: Molecular dynamics (MD) studies normally require an expert to design the simulation, write input scripts, run them, and analyze results with separate tools. `ChatAtom` is a multi-agent large language model system in which an orchestrator plans the study, `LAMMPS` and `OVITO` agents each use a generator-reviewer pair to write and check scripts, a high-performance computing agent dispatches jobs, and an analysis agent interprets the run, all behind a browser interface that streams data and rendered frames. The authors claim it **turns a natural-language request into a complete MD workflow without the user writing scripts or analysis code**, and that loadable skills extend it to autonomous hypothesis generation and testing. Evaluation covers script-generation benchmarks, an end-to-end crack propagation study, and a closed-loop campaign, with no headline numbers given in the abstract.

papers.title: CADENCE:Temporally Coherent Whole-Body Human Mesh Recovery that Preserves Expressive Hand Motion
papers.abstract: Whole-body SMPL-X estimators recover body, hand, and face meshes from single images, but applied frame by frame to video they produce jittery motion. Smoothing the output removes the jitter at a cost that body-only benchmarks do not measure: a temporal filter strong enough to steady the torso also flattens the fast finger strokes that carry meaning in sign language and gesture. We present CADENCE, a whole-body SMPL-X system for monocular video designed around this trade-off. A per-frame estimator built on a shared C-RADIOv4 encoder, with a high-resolution hand pathway that reuses the same encoder on hand crops, produces each frame's estimate. An offline temporal refiner then filters the SMPL-X rotation sequence: attention along the kinematic tree selects, for every joint and every frame, a mixture of learned zero-phase filters, so the torso is smoothed while fast finger strokes pass through. On 3DPW, the refiner reduces acceleration error from 17.4 to 5.4 mm/s2 while lowering PA-MPJPE from 41.9 to 40.2 mm; generic smoothers applied to the same predictions reach 6.2 to 7.7 mm/s2. On SignAvatars/How2Sign sign-language sequences, the refiner has the lowest hand jitter among the compared smoothers while keeping a hand-speed peak amplitude of 0.98, against 0.35 for a SmoothNet retrained on the full SMPL-X vector. The per-frame estimator also obtains the lowest full-body mesh error (25.7 mm) and hand joint error (8.3 mm) among the compared methods on EHF.
papers.summary: Whole-body `SMPL-X` mesh estimators applied frame by frame to video produce jitter, and smoothing strong enough to steady the torso also flattens the fast finger motion that carries meaning in sign language. `CADENCE` pairs a per-frame estimator built on a shared `C-RADIOv4` encoder and a high-resolution hand pathway with an offline refiner that uses attention along the kinematic tree to pick a mixture of learned zero-phase filters per joint and frame. On `3DPW` the refiner cuts acceleration error from 17.4 to 5.4 mm/s² while lowering PA-MPJPE from 41.9 to 40.2 mm. On `SignAvatars`/`How2Sign` sequences it has the lowest hand jitter among compared smoothers while **keeping a hand-speed peak amplitude of 0.98, against 0.35 for a retrained `SmoothNet`**.

papers.title: Beyond Final Answers: Interpretable Tumor Immune Microenvironment Reasoning from H&E and mIF
papers.abstract: Readouts of the tumor immune microenvironment (TIME), such as CD8+ T-cell density, intra-epithelial infiltration and the Ki67 index, combine tissue architecture from H&E with cell phenotypes from multiplex immunofluorescence (mIF). Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) could automate these readouts with an explanation, but two gaps remain. Pathology MLLMs read H&E alone, while these readouts need the cell phenotypes that mIF measures. And their reasoning has no step-level truth to be checked against, so R1-style reinforcement learning rewards only the final answer and leaves the reasoning unverified. Same-section H&E and mIF provide what both gaps lack: mIF measures every cell without manual annotation, which gives cell-level ground truth for each step that clinical guidelines prescribe, from delineating a tissue compartment to counting and normalizing the marker-positive cells within it. We therefore present HERMES (H&E-mIF Reasoning with Multimodal Evidence Supervision), an R1-style MLLM that reasons jointly over paired H&E and mIF in guideline steps and is trained with a process reward that checks every stated quantity against this truth. Across four field-level TIME tasks in colorectal cancer, HERMES (4B) reaches an average accuracy of 84.5%, compared with 74.7% for the strongest of twelve proprietary, general, medical and pathology MLLMs, and a higher share of its intermediate quantities is correct than for the strongest open-weight baseline. Without the process reward, reinforcement learning barely improves on supervised fine-tuning (80.0% vs. 78.8%) and fewer stated quantities are correct; editing a decisive stated quantity changes the answer as implied in all 885 test questions. Without retraining, it keeps the highest average accuracy on an external cohort imaged with CODEX (76.4% vs. 67.3%) and on head and neck cancer, a cancer type absent from training (76.7% vs. 72.5%).
papers.summary: Readouts of the tumor immune microenvironment (TIME) need both tissue architecture from H&E stains and cell phenotypes from multiplex immunofluorescence (mIF), but pathology multimodal large language models (MLLMs) read H&E alone and their intermediate reasoning cannot be checked. `HERMES` reasons jointly over paired H&E and mIF in guideline-prescribed steps and is trained with reinforcement learning using a process reward that checks every stated quantity against cell-level ground truth derived from mIF. Across four colorectal cancer tasks, **the 4B-parameter model reaches 84.5% average accuracy versus 74.7% for the strongest of twelve baseline MLLMs**. Without the process reward, reinforcement learning barely improves on supervised fine-tuning (80.0% versus 78.8%), and the model keeps the highest accuracy on an external `CODEX`-imaged cohort and on an unseen cancer type.

papers.title: Memorization and Generalization in Generative Models: A Perspective From Energy-based Modeling and Associative Memory
papers.abstract: Generative models now write working code, produce realistic images, and hold long conversations, yet the mechanisms behind their intelligence still evade our understanding. This thesis explores that puzzle through Associative Memory (AM), in which patterns are stored as energy minima and retrieved through attractor dynamics. Beyond their capacity, AMs form new minima known as spurious states, long regarded as a failure of memory. We argue that this failure is where creativity begins, and that memorization and generalization can coexist as outcomes of one retrieval process. First, we show that diffusion models behave as AMs. With little data, a diffusion model forms a distinct basin of attraction around each training sample. As the data grows, these basins shrink, and spurious states emerge as attractors that blend stored samples yet match none of them. They are the first signs of generative capability. We characterize this transition by measuring the volume, energy, and curvature of these basins across datasets and architectures, including Stable Diffusion. We then turn to language and move beyond the energy-based view of AM. We show that uniform-state discrete diffusion models are AMs capable of retrieving unseen data, with basins of attraction that arise from conditional likelihood maximization alone. As the training set grows, basins around training examples contract while basins around unseen examples expand, until corrupted test sentences are recovered as reliably as training ones. Conditional entropy exposes this coexistence within a single sequence and cheaply diagnoses where a model lies along the transition. Together, these results suggest that AM is a general principle defined by basins of attraction, and that memorization and generalization can coexist within one model. AM thus offers a framework for asking when a generative model recalls and when it creates.
papers.summary: This thesis studies when generative models memorize and when they generalize through the lens of Associative Memory (AM), where patterns are stored as attractors and spurious states arise beyond capacity. It shows that diffusion models form a basin of attraction around each training sample when data is scarce, and that as data grows these basins shrink and spurious attractors blending stored samples appear, a transition measured via basin volume, energy, and curvature across architectures including `Stable Diffusion`. For language, uniform-state discrete diffusion models are shown to act as associative memories where **basins around training examples contract and basins around unseen examples expand until corrupted test sentences are recovered as reliably as training ones**. Conditional entropy is proposed as a cheap diagnostic of where a model sits along this transition.

papers.title: Don't Discard Your Rollouts: Reusing Teacher RL Traces for Student Distillation
papers.abstract: RL post-training methods such as PPO and GRPO are computationally expensive, with substantial resources devoted to sampling rollouts, which contain multiple completions per prompt along with their respective rewards. Canonical distillation, however, discards these traces and uses more compute to regenerate data from the final teacher. We ask if and how we can reuse the saved teacher RL rollouts to distil student models. Reusing rollouts is non-trivial: naive SFT on the rollouts underperforms canonical distillation, and naive DPO, while performant, is unstable, collapsing on weaker students. We show that treating rollout reuse as a data selection problem using metadata already recorded during GRPO substantially reduces this gap. We use prompt pass rates to order the data, using the easiest prompts for an SFT warm start prior to using mixed-success prompts for DPO. For each prompt, we use saved teacher log-likelihoods as a proxy for selecting student-compatible completions. Across mathematical reasoning and Python coding tasks, with students from multiple model families, our two-stage recipe achieves comparable average performance to canonical distillation, while incurring no additional inference cost for dataset construction.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning post-training with methods such as `PPO` and `GRPO` generates many scored rollouts that standard distillation throws away before regenerating data from the final teacher. The authors reuse these saved rollouts, finding that naive supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on them underperforms and naive `DPO` is unstable on weaker students. Their two-stage recipe uses prompt pass rates to pick easy prompts for an SFT warm start and mixed-success prompts for `DPO`, with saved teacher log-likelihoods selecting student-compatible completions. Across math reasoning and Python coding tasks with students from several model families, it **matches canonical distillation on average at no additional inference cost for dataset construction**.

papers.title: LEAN: Library-Based Adaptation for Asynchronous, Federated Fine-Tuning
papers.abstract: Federated fine-tuning of foundation models with low-rank adapters (LoRA) is typically reconciled by averaging locally trained adapters. In cross-device settings, where participants hold heterogeneous data and join or leave asynchronously, averaging is poorly suited: locally trained adapters are not identifiable up to permutation, and averages of adapters trained on dissimilar data can be uninformative or unstable. We propose a simple idea called federated library-based adaptation (LEAN), which replaces averaging altogether. The server maintains a library of rank-1 basis pairs; participants check out random subsets, fine-tune them locally as a LoRA adapter, and check them back in, so that each pair is shuffled across sites and trained on many participants' data. Because no aggregation step is required, LEAN operates fully asynchronously and communicates only low-rank parameters. We prove that, in a synchronous setting, LEAN converges to a neighborhood of a stationary point, with the shuffle canceling data heterogeneity at first order. Across image and text fine-tuning benchmarks, LEAN outperforms averaging-based baselines in most settings with substantially less communication, and remains effective under heavy data heterogeneity, where averaging-based methods fail to reach nontrivial accuracy, and under heavy asynchrony, where they degrade substantially.
papers.summary: Federated fine-tuning with low-rank adapters (`LoRA`) usually averages locally trained adapters, which works poorly when devices hold heterogeneous data and join or leave asynchronously. `LEAN` has the server keep a library of rank-1 basis pairs that participants check out in random subsets, fine-tune locally as an adapter, and check back in, so each pair is trained across many participants with no aggregation step. The authors prove convergence to a neighborhood of a stationary point in the synchronous setting, with the shuffling canceling data heterogeneity at first order. On image and text benchmarks it **outperforms averaging-based baselines in most settings with substantially less communication**, including under heavy heterogeneity where averaging methods fail to reach nontrivial accuracy.

papers.title: MedicalRSI: Medical Recursive Self-Improving Agents via Clinical Model-Harness Co-Evolution
papers.abstract: Medical agents built on large language models (LLMs) have advanced rapidly, yet most stay fixed once deployed and do not keep using their experience to improve later attempts. As a result, the same kind of error can recur across patients. To address this, existing self-improvement methods update an agent's weights or its medical harness from its own experience, but their improving strategy stays fixed and never learns which changes actually help, which caps how much the agent can improve. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) instead improves both the agent and its improving strategy. However, achieving RSI for medical agents is challenging, because clinical workflows rarely come with a reference harness, and a change that fixes early errors may not fix the problems the agent meets later. We propose MedicalRSI, an RSI framework built on Clinical Model-Harness Co-Evolution, in which one model plays two roles. The Solver is the medical agent itself, and the Improver is its learnable improving strategy, which writes a medical harness from the agent's failures. Each harness is rewarded by its gain over acting without it, and both roles are trained together, so the Improver keeps adapting to the problems the Solver has not yet solved. On multiple benchmarks and LLM backbones, MedicalRSI outperforms existing context-level and weight-level self-improvement methods and transfers well to unseen workflows, new LLMs and new databases, a step toward medical agents that keep improving.
papers.summary: Medical agents built on large language models typically stay fixed after deployment, and existing self-improvement methods use a fixed improvement strategy that never learns which changes help. `MedicalRSI` applies recursive self-improvement (RSI) by having one model play two roles: a Solver that acts as the medical agent and an Improver that writes a medical harness from the Solver's failures, with each harness rewarded by its gain over acting without it and both roles trained together. The authors report that it **outperforms existing context-level and weight-level self-improvement methods across multiple benchmarks and model backbones**, and transfers to unseen workflows, new models, and new databases. The abstract gives no specific numbers.

papers.title: NitroGen: Observations on the Action Dynamics, Visual Instruction Following, and Spatial Exploration
papers.abstract: NitroGen is an open vision-action foundation model for game control. It is trained by behavior cloning on online gameplay videos. In this paper, we study the frozen controller in Hollow Knight and Trackmania as examples along three dimensions: action adaptation, visual instruction following, and spatial exploration. Our results indicate that NitroGen can adapt its actions to local context, but it lacks the planning, recovery, and exploration needed for longer-horizon game control.
papers.summary: `NitroGen` is an open vision-action foundation model for game control trained by behavior cloning on online gameplay videos. The frozen controller is evaluated in `Hollow Knight` and `Trackmania` along three dimensions: action adaptation, visual instruction following, and spatial exploration. The results indicate that it **adapts its actions to local context but lacks the planning, recovery, and exploration needed for longer-horizon game control**.

papers.title: Search From the Start: Search-Native Pretraining for Language Models
papers.abstract: Modern language models (LMs) are increasingly deployed with access to search tools at inference. Yet pretraining remains predominantly focused on predicting static text, with search capabilities typically introduced during post-training. We propose Search-Native Pretraining as a practical route to teach search capability during pretraining from ordinary text corpora. Specifically, we augment pretraining corpus at scale with web-search queries and retrieve web response using a local index. Training on this augmented corpus teaches models to generate search calls and incorporate retrieved evidence during language modeling. Across Wikipedia and DCLM-Edu corpora and 360M to 3.3B parameter scales, search-pretrained models ("QueryLM") show improved performance on knowledge-intensive tasks and higher steerability toward the retrieved evidence. Crucially, their advantage persists after supervised fine-tuning of both search-pretrained and conventionally pretrained models, indicating that the tested post-training procedures do not fully recover the capabilities developed during pretraining. Throughout our experiments, we find that a 1.4B QueryLM consistently beats or matches the performance of a FLOP-matched 3.3B baseline model across all knowledge intensive tasks.
