The proposed architecture runs a compact Tier-1 classifier in-process on the agent's host and escalates only ambiguous queries to a Tier-2 cloud LLM judge, and is evaluated on four length-matched contrastive twin benchmarks seeded from `MedSafetyBench`, `ASQ-PHI`, and a synthetic clinical policy. Frozen local encoders match cloud models on structured PHI detection but degrade on semantic safety prompts. After fine-tuning, **a 335M-parameter `BGE-Large` classifier reaches 98.90% accuracy versus 99.20% for a zero-shot cloud LLM judge in 39.0 ms, more than 14x faster**, with residual errors concentrated in reading-level checks.

papers.title: What Does the Visual Encoder Buy? Visual Information Gain in Encoder-Free Multimodal Pretraining
papers.abstract: Recent scaling studies ask whether vision-language models still need a visual encoder by comparing encoder-free and encoder-based models on the next-token loss of the text in image-text data. This loss can fall without any use of the image, and two runs with the same loss can differ in what they take from it. Visual information gain (VIG) is the loss increase when the image is replaced by a uniform one. It splits exactly into global information, carried by image statistics, and layout information, which shuffling the patches within the image destroys. We apply it to decoders with 158M to 1.04B parameters that read pixel patches through a linear embedding, evaluated every billion tokens up to 40B, and to 19 public checkpoints. In our decoders the image lowers the loss by 3% to 46%, depending on the image type. Global information is present after the first billion tokens. Layout information starts near zero, grows slowly with training and does not grow with model size on five of six image types, and a larger batch reaches the same loss with less of it. With a frozen SigLIP 2 encoder in front of the same decoder the loss is lower only when the arrangement of the image is intact. On shuffled images the losses with and without the encoder agree to within 0.04 nats on five of six image types, so the net advantage of the encoder in the loss is layout information, above all the ability to read text in images. Public encoder-free models at production scale (Gemma 4 12B, NEO, Mono-InternVL) do acquire layout information. On the same documents they have 0.53 to 0.76 nats of it, against 0.65 to 0.82 for recent encoder-based models and 0.04 to 0.07 for our decoders, and their released training stages show it rising. These results agree with the reported parity of the two families when both are trained from scratch and place the reported advantage of a pretrained encoder in layout information.
papers.summary: Comparisons of encoder-free and encoder-based vision-language models rely on next-token text loss, which can fall without the model using the image at all. Visual information gain (VIG), the loss increase when the image is replaced by a uniform one, is introduced and split exactly into global information from image statistics and layout information that patch shuffling destroys. In decoders of 158M to 1.04B parameters reading raw pixel patches, global information appears within the first billion tokens while layout information grows slowly and mostly does not scale with model size. Adding a frozen `SigLIP 2` encoder lowers loss only when the image arrangement is intact, so **the encoder's net advantage is layout information, above all reading text in images**; production-scale encoder-free models such as `Gemma 4 12B`, `NEO`, and `Mono-InternVL` do acquire layout information at levels close to recent encoder-based models.

papers.title: ERA: Embed, Route, Adapt for Cold-Start Cross-Model Latent Retrieval
papers.abstract: Production retrieval systems are tied to the embedding model that indexed their corpus. Moving queries to a different encoder normally requires re-embedding the whole corpus, and at cold start there are no query logs while every document embedded by the new encoder incurs an API or compute cost. We present ERA (Embed, Route, Adapt), a system for cold-start cross-model latent retrieval. ERA spends a small anchor budget on maximally informative documents, selected from the existing target index via Cosine Farthest Point Sampling, trains a lightweight adapter with a Manifold Alignment Loss that couples directional alignment with orthogonal regularization to prevent representation collapse, and pairs the adapter with a deterministic router that escalates the rare, hard queries that define perceived retrieval quality. Across five BEIR datasets, ERA matches or outperforms point-wise L2 and embedding-conversion baselines, with relative gains of up to 35% nDCG@10 on Arguana, and on clustered corpora its anchor selection also improves prior methods under a fixed anchor budget. With 1.2 ms of adapter and router overhead on top of a ~20 ms local encoder, ERA at a 20% nominal escalation budget reduces end-to-end query latency from roughly 160 ms to 38-86 ms while concentrating escalations on the queries where the projection fails most.
papers.summary: Switching a production retrieval system to a new embedding model normally requires re-embedding the whole corpus, and at cold start there are no query logs to learn a mapping from. `ERA` (Embed, Route, Adapt) spends a small budget embedding anchor documents chosen by Cosine Farthest Point Sampling, trains a lightweight adapter with a Manifold Alignment Loss that combines directional alignment with orthogonal regularization, and adds a deterministic router that escalates hard queries. Across five `BEIR` datasets it matches or outperforms point-wise L2 and embedding-conversion baselines, with relative gains of up to 35% nDCG@10 on `Arguana`. At a 20% nominal escalation budget, **end-to-end query latency falls from roughly 160 ms to 38-86 ms** with 1.2 ms of adapter and router overhead.

papers.title: Partially canonical axes in large language model representations
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) develop rich internal representations of language, but whether their individual coordinate axes carry meaning, or whether meaning is encoded only in directions in representation space, is still an open question. A common assumption is that individual axes in LLMs are arbitrary. We here challenge this view: across 12 LLMs from six model families, the native axes are reliably more aligned with other models' representations, with human brain responses to language, and with interpretable linguistic features than randomly rotated axes that preserve the same geometry. The native axes nonetheless fall well short of the best achievable alignment, so LLM coordinates are not fully arbitrary but also not fully canonical: they are partially canonical. A theory of how LLMs represent language must explain both the population geometry they learn and why individual units acquire patterns of response profiles that recur across systems.
papers.summary: A common assumption holds that individual coordinate axes in LLM representations are arbitrary and that meaning lives only in directions of the representation space. Across 12 LLMs from six model families, native axes are compared with randomly rotated axes that preserve the same geometry. **Native axes are reliably more aligned with other models' representations, with human brain responses to language, and with interpretable linguistic features than rotated ones**, yet they fall well short of the best achievable alignment. The authors describe the coordinates as partially canonical, neither arbitrary nor fully privileged.

papers.title: Large Reported CHB-MIT Adaptation Gains Disappear with Pretrained Encoders and Matched Probes
papers.abstract: Dani and Liebe (2026) (DL) report that adapting the final encoder block of BIOT and CBraMod with self-supervised learning (SSL) improves CHB-MIT seizure-detection ROC-AUC by 36.2 and 29.5 points over linear probing. We investigate these results with their released code and an independent pipeline. The release loads pretrained weights for adaptation only when an otherwise unset configuration key is supplied, and its CBraMod probe reads the reconstruction head with dropout active. With pretrained initialisation and a probe on the encoder output in evaluation mode, the fixed-recipe adaptation gain on DL's split is -0.6 points for BIOT (95% interval [-3.8, +2.6]) and +0.01 for CBraMod ([-0.02, +0.04]) across five seeds. Across DL's split and five subject rotations on CHB-MIT and Siena Scalp EEG, with equally tuned linear probes (30 configurations, up to 500 epochs, validation-based early stopping), mean adaptation effects range from -1.1 to +5.7 ROC-AUC points over 18 comparisons (related settings and feature variants). Twelve of 18 support equivalence within +/-3 points under dependence-adjusted inference (8 of 12 rotation and 4 of 6 fixed-split comparisons); six are unresolved. After correcting rotation intervals for dependence, no positive effect has a 95% interval excluding zero. The +/-3 margin is an analysis threshold, not a clinically validated one, and smaller margins support fewer equivalences. Two fixed-probe gains near +21 points shrink under the same tuning, with smaller benefits unresolved. We also audit a CHB-MIT protocol shared by at least 14 papers. No tested configuration reproduces DL Table 1 as a whole. These findings concern the tested configurations; the encoder-level probe and subsequent checks were chosen post hoc.
papers.summary: A prior report claimed that adapting the final encoder block of the EEG foundation models `BIOT` and `CBraMod` with self-supervised learning (SSL) improved seizure-detection ROC-AUC on `CHB-MIT` by 36.2 and 29.5 points over linear probing. Re-examining the released code shows that pretrained weights were loaded for adaptation only when an otherwise unset configuration key was supplied, and that the `CBraMod` probe read the reconstruction head with dropout active. With pretrained initialisation and an evaluation-mode probe on the encoder output, **the adaptation gain falls to -0.6 points for `BIOT` and +0.01 for `CBraMod`** across five seeds. Across 18 comparisons on `CHB-MIT` and `Siena Scalp EEG` with equally tuned probes, twelve support equivalence within 3 points and no positive effect has an interval excluding zero, though the authors note the corrected probe and follow-up checks were chosen post hoc.

papers.title: Improving the Optimisation Landscape for Particle Mixtures
papers.abstract: Several methods in statistics and machine learning represent a predictive distribution as an equally weighted mixture of models, or particles, trained via the mixture predictive likelihood. However, we prove that the mixture predictive likelihood is poorly suited to gradient-based optimisation, because it does not identify how the mixture is decomposed across particles, so that a poorly matched particle can be starved of training signal. As a remedy, we study a convex combination between the individual risk, i.e. the average log loss of the individual particles, and the mixture risk. At the particle level, this regularised risk imposes a reverse-KL barrier on the responsibilities of the particles, so that no particle can be starved of training signal. These phenomena are illustrated in two case studies: In the first, a predictively-oriented posterior is computed using mean-field Langevin dynamics, and the numerics are well-behaved only when our regularisation is employed. In the second, ensembles of low-rank adapters are jointly fine-tuned on large language models, across four backbones and eight multiple-choice reasoning benchmarks; direct minimisation of the mixture risk leads to responsibility starvation, whose severity decreases as the competence of the backbone increases, whereas our regularised estimator attains a lower held-out mixture risk on every backbone considered.
papers.summary: Methods that represent a predictive distribution as an equally weighted mixture of models, or particles, typically train on the mixture predictive likelihood. The authors prove that this objective does not identify how the mixture is decomposed across particles, so a poorly matched particle can be starved of gradient signal. Their remedy is a convex combination of the average individual log loss and the mixture risk, which **imposes a reverse-KL barrier on particle responsibilities so that no particle can be starved**. In a mean-field Langevin case study the numerics behave well only with the regularisation, and in jointly fine-tuned ensembles of low-rank adapters across four LLM backbones and eight multiple-choice benchmarks the regularised estimator attains lower held-out mixture risk on every backbone.

papers.title: Tokenize Moments, Not Frames: Tokenizer-Aware Budget Allocation for Training-Free Video LLM Acceleration
papers.abstract: Video large language models (LLMs) represent each video with thousands of visual tokens, and training-free accelerators that prune or merge these tokens lose accuracy on long videos. Analyzing frame similarity and the vision tokenizers of 16 open models, we trace this loss to a step before token selection. Under a token budget, the frames of a long video are sampled farther apart than the roughly 2 s over which frames remain similar. The two-frame 3D patches of models such as Qwen-VL then blend two unrelated scenes into each visual token, a double exposure that arises before any pruning or merging. Fixed-size tokenizers such as InternVL's avoid this blend but respond differently to the same reduction. We propose ESSENCE, a training-free method that tokenizes moments, segments within which frames remain similar, rather than frames. Before encoding, a closed-form rule uses the sampling interval and the tokenizer class to set the number of token grids and the dimension to reduce; visual tokens are then released from later LLM layers. Against five recent accelerators on Qwen3-VL, Qwen2.5-VL and InternVL3.5, ESSENCE achieves higher accuracy in 58 of 60 comparisons at matched mean time to first token (TTFT). With 80% of the tokens, it matches the average accuracy of the full Qwen models at $1.6\times$ faster TTFT; on GLM-4.1V, it exceeds the full model by up to 3.4 points. Code is available at: https://github.com/zhkandsrz/ESSENCE.
papers.summary: Training-free accelerators that prune or merge visual tokens in video LLMs lose accuracy on long videos, and an analysis of 16 open models traces this to a step before token selection. Under a token budget, frames are sampled farther apart than the roughly 2 seconds over which they stay similar, so the two-frame 3D patches of models such as `Qwen-VL` blend unrelated scenes into each token. `ESSENCE` instead tokenizes moments, segments in which frames remain similar, using a closed-form rule based on sampling interval and tokenizer class, and then releases visual tokens from later LLM layers. Against five recent accelerators on `Qwen3-VL`, `Qwen2.5-VL`, and `InternVL3.5` it **wins 58 of 60 comparisons at matched time to first token (TTFT)**, and with 80% of the tokens it matches full `Qwen` accuracy at 1.6x faster TTFT.

papers.title: Self-similar Organization of Information in Language
papers.abstract: How much information relevant to predicting the future of a passage (i.e. predictive information) is carried by the preceding text, and how is this information distributed along that history? These questions are fundamental to understanding both the statistical structure of language and what large language models (LLMs) can learn about it. Indeed, LLMs trained to predict the next token in text must exploit this predictive information, so its organization determines how the structure of language becomes available to the model to learn. We develop a theory for the organization of predictive information based on the scaling behavior of a family of information measures, and the theory predicts that if this organization has the same form at all measured length scales -- i.e., it has a self-similar structure -- then the information measures evaluated at different lengths collapse onto a common form. We observe this scaling collapse in long text documents, showing that predictive information is present at every length scale we measure and has a self-similar structure. Self-similarity is a considerably stronger property than showing the existence of long-range dependencies, and it constrains the process generating the text. More broadly, our results give quantitative support to the empirical observation that conditioning on more distant text continues to reveal new structure in language to LLMs.
papers.summary: How much information about a passage's future is carried by preceding text, and how that information is spread across the history, determines what next-token predictors can learn. A theory based on the scaling behaviour of a family of information measures predicts that if predictive information is organized the same way at all length scales, the measures at different lengths collapse onto a common form. **This scaling collapse is observed in long text documents, indicating that predictive information is present at every measured length scale with a self-similar structure**. The authors note that self-similarity is a stronger property than long-range dependence and constrains the process generating the text.

papers.title: SecretAgent: A Multi-Agent Framework for Privacy Protection against Vision Language Models
papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) can infer private information from shared images, including locations, personally identifiable information (PII), and personal attributes such as age and sex, even from medical images. Adversarial perturbations can protect such information against black-box VLMs, but existing methods overlook image quality and introduce visible artifacts into the images they protect. We present SecretAgent, the first general multi-agent framework that protects image privacy against VLMs while preserving visual fidelity. LLM agents iteratively locate the visual evidence that reveals private information and adapt an invisible perturbation to the target VLM's answers and to an appearance reviewer agent, which rejects any candidate with visible artifacts. We instantiate SecretAgent with two complementary variants: SecretAgent-Gradient optimizes the perturbation through six surrogate encoders for cross-model transferability, and the gradient-free SecretAgent-Tool composes procedural noise and achieves the best perceptual fidelity on three of the five datasets. Experiments on four privacy applications (geolocation, PII, facial, and medical) across five datasets and six VLMs show that SecretAgent preserves image quality substantially better than existing methods while achieving state-of-the-art privacy protection in every application, and that its protection transfers to other VLMs.
papers.summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) can infer locations, personally identifiable information (PII), and personal attributes from shared images, and existing adversarial-perturbation defences leave visible artifacts. `SecretAgent` is a multi-agent framework in which LLM agents iteratively locate the visual evidence revealing private information and adapt an invisible perturbation based on the target VLM's answers, while a reviewer agent rejects candidates with visible artifacts. One variant optimizes the perturbation through six surrogate encoders for transferability, and a gradient-free variant composes procedural noise. Across four privacy applications, five datasets, and six VLMs, it **reports state-of-the-art privacy protection in every application while preserving image quality substantially better than prior methods**, with protection transferring to other VLMs.

papers.title: MG-EDA: Maturity-Gated Skew-Normal Estimation of Distribution Algorithms
papers.abstract: Gaussian estimation of distribution algorithms shrink their variance on slopes and stall far from the optimum. This paper equips the corrections that act along the direction of movement -- a mean shift, an elongation of the covariance along the path and a skewness -- with the rule they lack: a calibrated gate, driven by a maturity statistic of the population, decides whether, how strongly and for how long each correction acts, and when the gate is closed the algorithm is exactly the estimation of multivariate normal algorithm (EMNA). The statistic is a cumulative path of whitened mean shifts with an inverse-Wishart correction, whose expectation is one under a null model without systematic movement and whose quantiles give thresholds with known false-alarm rate. It gates the three corrections as three rank-one terms of one matrix sampling equation, the skewness being carried by a skew-normal sampler that preserves the estimated mean and covariance; all vanish at maturity. We call the resulting algorithm the maturity-gated EDA (MG-EDA). A full factorial study on a training set of black-box optimization benchmarking (BBOB) functions separates the parameters: variance scaling is the prerequisite, the mean shift needs a feedback correction removing the injected shift from the statistic, the elongation turns the variance loss on a slope into a gain, and the skewness substitutes for the mean shift rather than complementing it. On held-out instances MG-EDA with the first- and second-order corrections is significantly better than the skewness-only predecessor and than EMNA with variance scaling, ties with EMNA with anticipated mean shift, and trails the adapted maximum-likelihood Gaussian model (AMaLGaM) in 20 dimensions.
papers.summary: Gaussian estimation of distribution algorithms, a class of black-box optimizers, shrink their variance on slopes and stall far from the optimum. `MG-EDA` adds three corrections along the direction of movement, a mean shift, a covariance elongation, and a skewness, each switched by a calibrated gate driven by a maturity statistic with a known false-alarm rate; when the gate is closed the method is exactly the estimation of multivariate normal algorithm (`EMNA`). A factorial study on black-box optimization benchmarking (`BBOB`) functions finds that variance scaling is a prerequisite and that skewness substitutes for the mean shift rather than complementing it. On held-out instances, **`MG-EDA` significantly beats its skewness-only predecessor and `EMNA` with variance scaling, ties `EMNA` with anticipated mean shift, and trails `AMaLGaM` in 20 dimensions**.

papers.title: CENTRY: A Probabilistic Latent-State Model for Continual AI Risk Estimation, Monitoring, and Regulation
papers.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems are increasingly deployed in safety-critical applications, yet existing AI safety frameworks primarily define, categorize, or govern AI risk rather than proposing implementable models and methods for continually estimating, monitoring, and regulating risk throughout an AI system's operational lifetime. This paper proposes CENTRY, a probabilistic framework that enables continual risk estimation, monitoring, and regulation of a deployed AI system from its interactions with its environment. The framework models AI risk as arising from three intrinsic sources: datasets, hardware resources, and models/algorithms. A structured latent-variable model is developed in which the latent representation is decomposed into a fast interaction subspace that captures the evolving AI--environment dynamics and three slow latent subspaces that encode the long-term risk states associated with the dataset, hardware, and model components. Rather than requiring a ground-truth risk label at every time step, the component-risk states are treated as latent variables and are learned by maximizing a variational evidence lower bound, optionally informed during training and continual refinement by evidence-supported behavior--cause records. The resulting framework unifies continual probabilistic inference, online risk estimation, and adaptive risk regulation in an implementable architecture. Under the explicit assumptions stated for the corresponding results, we establish formal guarantees spanning safety, learning, inference, and operations, including finite-horizon and asymptotic risk-budget compliance, regret and convergence bounds for adaptive regulation, consistency and identifiability of component-risk ratings, and detection-delay, false-alarm, containment, and computational-complexity characterizations.
papers.summary: Existing AI safety frameworks mostly define or categorize risk rather than offering implementable methods for estimating and regulating it throughout a deployed system's lifetime. `CENTRY` is a probabilistic latent-variable model that **attributes risk to three sources, datasets, hardware resources, and models or algorithms, each tracked as a slow latent state alongside a fast subspace for AI-environment interaction**. The risk states are learned by maximizing a variational evidence lower bound without per-step risk labels, optionally informed by behavior-cause records. The contribution is theoretical: under stated assumptions the authors establish guarantees including risk-budget compliance, regret and convergence bounds for adaptive regulation, identifiability of component-risk ratings, and detection-delay and false-alarm characterizations.

papers.title: CodeReviewBench: An Automated Benchmark for Evaluating the Software Factory
papers.abstract: As AI agents ship more code with minimal human oversight, code review becomes the critical quality-control checkpoint -- but one without a reliable, objective verifier: review quality is nuanced and ultimately a judgment call by the PR author. Existing benchmarks are structurally misaligned with this: annotators are third-party reviewers, like the bots they evaluate, not the PR authors who actually decide what to fix. They also rely on small, static issue sets that require full re-evaluation as tools update, limiting how frequently progress can be tracked. We introduce CodeReviewBench, built on a fundamentally different signal: revealed developer preferences -- if a developer acts on a bot's suggestion, we treat it as useful; if they ignore it, we do not. This signal is mined daily from the public GitHub event stream, yielding 500K+ judged PRs across 18 tools, and refreshes continuously as tools evolve. We validate the developer preference against an independent offline benchmark: the two agree on precision rankings and independently detect the same product updates within days of vendor releases. Together, these form the benchmark.
papers.summary: Evaluating AI code review tools is hard because review quality is a judgment call by the pull request (PR) author, while existing benchmarks rely on third-party annotators and small static issue sets. `CodeReviewBench` instead uses revealed developer preferences: a bot's suggestion counts as useful if the developer acts on it and not if they ignore it. The signal is mined daily from the public GitHub event stream, yielding **more than 500K judged PRs across 18 tools**, and refreshes continuously as tools change. Validation against an independent offline benchmark shows the two agree on precision rankings and detect the same product updates within days of vendor releases.

papers.title: Spectral Estimation with Deformed Decompression
papers.abstract: Sample covariance matrices are fundamental objects in machine learning and statistics, with valuable information encoded into their eigenvalues. When treating modern problems, the scale of these matrices can become prohibitive for tractable computation. This creates a critical need for "spectral decompression": a method for inferring the eigenspectrum of a very large-scale model using only information from its smaller realizations. Existing methods fall into two main categories: those relying on spectral inversion; and those that rely on Free Decompression techniques. On the one hand, spectral inversion is a fundamentally ill-posed problem that is notoriously unstable, often failing to yield reliable results in finite-size settings. On the other hand, while Free Decompression was recently proposed to address this scaling, its reliance on the Nica-Speicher framework restricts its use to unitarily invariant ensembles, a symmetry condition that subsampled covariance matrices fail to satisfy. In this work, we introduce Deformed Decompression (DD), a novel framework for the stable, forward-extrapolation of spectral densities. By leveraging properties of the companion matrix, DD recasts the spectral decompression problem as a directed evolution of the Stieltjes transform of the companion matrix. This approach bypasses the instabilities of traditional inversion and provides a robust methodology for scaling covariance matrices and even their generalized variants (including Hessian matrices) that lack unitary invariance. We demonstrate the utility of our framework through experiments on a variety of random matrix examples, showing that DD successfully captures the complex spectral signatures of large-scale systems.
papers.summary: Inferring the eigenvalue spectrum of a very large sample covariance matrix from smaller realizations is unstable when done by spectral inversion, and the recent Free Decompression approach requires unitary invariance that subsampled covariance matrices lack. Deformed Decompression (`DD`) **recasts the task as a directed evolution of the Stieltjes transform of the companion matrix, giving a stable forward extrapolation of spectral densities**. The approach extends to covariance matrices and generalized variants, including Hessians, that are not unitarily invariant. Experiments on a range of random matrix examples show it captures the spectral features of the large-scale systems.

papers.title: Tracking and Limiting Unsupported Claim Propagation in Multi-Agent LLM Systems: A Provenance-Aware Framework
papers.abstract: This research examines how unsupported claims change as they move through multi-agent pipelines. It also examines whether preserving provenance can reduce these changes. We test both homogeneous and heterogeneous pipelines. Homogeneous pipelines use the same model across agents, while heterogeneous pipelines use different models. We compare the baseline with a provenance-aware framework. The framework passes each claim with its support status, source, evidence and transmission history. No new evidence is introduced during transmission. We measure changes in claim meaning, unsupported detail accretion, semantic drift, and provenance preservation. These metrics show whether the framework limits unsupported changes as claims pass between agents.
papers.summary: Unsupported claims can change as they pass between agents in multi-agent LLM pipelines, and the study asks whether preserving provenance limits those changes. Homogeneous pipelines using one model and heterogeneous pipelines using different models are compared with and without a framework in which **each claim travels with its support status, source, evidence, and transmission history**, and no new evidence is added along the way. Measurements cover changes in claim meaning, accretion of unsupported detail, semantic drift, and provenance preservation. The abstract describes the experimental design and metrics but reports no quantitative results.

papers.title: Beyond Prompt Heuristics: Assessing Child Safety Alignment in LLMs
papers.abstract: Child-safety taxonomies typically characterize safety risks through a predefined set of harm categories, and existing evaluations largely operationalize these categories using prompts that explicitly invoke them. However, child-safety considerations can also arise in seemingly benign requests that lack recognizable harm-category cues. We therefore investigate how child-safety alignment generalizes to such settings. Across six models, we find considerably higher misalignment rates on requests without recognizable harm-category cues than on those containing such cues (80.0, 54.0, and 48.4 percentage-point gaps for Qwen3.5-27B, GPT-5.4-mini, and Claude-Haiku-4.5, respectively). Through controlled behavioral and mechanistic analyses, we find that introducing a single harm-associated word reduces misalignment across most models, with mechanistic evidence suggesting that child-safety reasoning may rely in part on lexical and semantic associations with words in the prompt. Our findings motivate evaluations that treat child safety as context-dependent, and not reducible to a fixed set of harm categories.
papers.summary: Child-safety evaluations of LLMs mostly use prompts that explicitly invoke predefined harm categories, leaving open how models behave on seemingly benign requests that carry child-safety implications without such cues. Across six models, misalignment rates are considerably higher on requests without recognizable harm-category cues, with **gaps of 80.0, 54.0, and 48.4 percentage points for `Qwen3.5-27B`, `GPT-5.4-mini`, and `Claude-Haiku-4.5`**. Adding a single harm-associated word reduces misalignment in most models, and mechanistic analysis suggests child-safety behaviour depends partly on lexical and semantic associations with words in the prompt. The authors argue for evaluations that treat child safety as context-dependent rather than reducible to fixed harm categories.

papers.title: Keep the Process, Change the Supplier: Runtime Governance for Tool-Using AI Agents
papers.abstract: Tool-using AI agents propose actions whose authorization and external effects cannot be inferred from generated text alone. We study an execution boundary that separates agent proposals from business-controlled authority, context disclosure, and supplier selection. The Open Process Control Plane (OPCP) mediates capability calls and records uncertain outcomes when a supplier may have acted without returning an acceptable reply. We evaluate this runtime with scripted requests and synthetic suppliers: 2,400 fault episodes across four policies, 60 process-termination/restart episodes, 19,000 timed calls across 19 configurations, five targeted mutations over 43 fixtures, and 160 substitution records. No language model or autonomous agent is evaluated. OPCP and a conservative composition agree on all measured fault outcomes. Both recover after definite refusal without cross-supplier duplication; retry-all duplicates effects in every tested lost-reply-after-commit case. Persistent runtime state prevents cross-supplier replay in the restart experiments, while same-supplier duplicate prevention also requires supplier idempotency. At 128 suppliers, best-score routing has a median latency of 1.411 ms versus 0.261 ms for pinned routing. All five selected mutations are detected, and record enumeration exposes acceptance of an empty regression set. These results characterize an execution mechanism relevant to agent governance, including its costs and assumption boundaries. They do not establish improved agent task success, prompt-injection resistance, or real-vendor model portability.
papers.summary: Actions proposed by tool-using AI agents carry authorization and side-effect questions that cannot be read from generated text, so the authors study an execution boundary separating agent proposals from business-controlled authority, context disclosure, and supplier selection. The Open Process Control Plane (`OPCP`) mediates capability calls and records uncertain outcomes when a supplier may have acted without returning an acceptable reply. Evaluation uses only scripted requests and synthetic suppliers, with no language model or agent involved, across 2,400 fault episodes, 60 restart episodes, and 19,000 timed calls. `OPCP` **recovers after definite refusals without cross-supplier duplication, whereas a retry-all policy duplicates effects in every tested lost-reply-after-commit case**; the authors state that the results do not establish improved agent task success, prompt-injection resistance, or real-vendor portability.

papers.title: Right Numbers, Wrong Story: When LLMs Narrate Financial Changes Beyond Their Inputs
papers.abstract: A financial report drafted by an LLM can state every number correctly but still go beyond its input, adding judgments and causes that no one supplied. We call these additions unsupported framing and find them far more often in LLM drafts than in reports written by proInput facts Revenue +3% Higher prices 10-K filings Revenue increased 3% on higher prices. 10-K writer Revenue surged 3% on higher prices, due to strong demand. LLM Fits the size? Surged: Unusual for 3% In the input? In the input? Strong demand: Not in input Higher prices: Kept fessionals, and attempts to fix them by prompting with how each word is used instead make such judgments more frequent. We therefore propose FrameCheck, a plug-in that sits beFrameCheck Revenue increased 3% on higher prices. No extra model call Judgment word Unsupported cause Supported cause tween the LLM and human review to keep each draft within its input. Specifically, FrameCheck 1) guides the draft with professional examples that report a change of similar magnitude, 2) flags judgments that professionals would not use and causes the input does not give, and 3) removes them by rule, without a model call. In experiments on 17 open LLMs and 3M drafts, FrameCheck removes almost all unsupported framing from drafts and brings the judgment rate close to that of the writers of 10-K filings, the annual reports that US firms file with regulators. Code is available at github.com/seunghan96/framecheck.
papers.summary: LLM-drafted financial reports can state every number correctly yet add judgments and causes that were never in the input, which the authors call unsupported framing. They find it far more often in LLM drafts than in professionally written reports, and prompting with word-usage guidance makes such judgments more frequent. Their plug-in `FrameCheck` guides drafts with professional examples of similar-magnitude changes, flags judgment words professionals would not use and causes absent from the input, and removes them by rule with no extra model call. Across 17 open LLMs and 3M drafts, it **removes almost all unsupported framing** and brings the judgment rate close to that of `10-K` filing writers.

papers.title: When Perception Collides with Priors: Diagnosing Modal Polarization in Video Understanding Models
papers.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have achieved strong video comprehension, largely benefiting from extensive training on realistic video data. However, when video perception severely conflicts with internal priors or common sense, we identify a critical failure pattern termed Modal Polarization, where models fail to integrate modalities and instead bifurcate into two distinct extremes: Cognitive Inertia, where models rigidly adhere to priors despite contradictory visual evidence, and Perceptual Inertia, where they blindly trust video perception while ignoring logical inconsistencies. To investigate this, we introduce TheaterBench, a benchmark designed to expose Modal Polarization using counter-intuitive scenarios that violate physical laws or common sense - situations rarely encountered in standard training distributions. Extensive experiments reveal that current state-of-the-art (SOTA) models exhibit severe Modal Polarization, and many de-hallucination methods merely rebalance the trade-off between Perceptual and Cognitive Inertia rather than fundamentally resolving the conflict. This work serves as a foundational step for evaluating and enhancing the perceptual-cognitive equilibrium of future video understanding models.
papers.summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are tested on videos whose content conflicts sharply with common sense or physical laws. The authors identify a failure pattern they call Modal Polarization, in which models either cling to their priors despite contradictory visual evidence (Cognitive Inertia) or trust the video while ignoring logical inconsistencies (Perceptual Inertia). Their benchmark `TheaterBench` uses counter-intuitive scenarios to expose this. State-of-the-art models show severe polarization, and **many de-hallucination methods merely shift the trade-off between the two extremes** instead of resolving the conflict.

papers.title: Run One, Get Two: Near-Free Streaming Safety Checks for Local LLMs
papers.abstract: Local LLM assistants decode for one user at a time, so decoding is bound by memory bandwidth and leaves compute idle. Streaming safety checks today trade accuracy against cost. A dedicated guard model is accurate but nearly doubles the latency per token, while a hidden-state probe is cheap but less accurate. We present ToRA, an adapter that runs a second model as an extra row in the generator's decode step, sharing its weights and KV cache. Dual-row kernels read each weight once for both rows. On Qwen3-0.6B, ToRA matches or beats a dedicated streaming guard, with higher F1 on 12 of 17 benchmarks. It detects 11.8 points more unsafe responses than the probe at a similar cost, under 4% added latency per token.
papers.summary: Streaming safety checks for local LLM assistants currently force a choice between an accurate dedicated guard model that nearly doubles per-token latency and a cheap but less accurate hidden-state probe. `ToRA` is an adapter that runs a second model as an extra row in the generator's decode step, sharing its weights and KV cache, with dual-row kernels that read each weight once for both rows. This exploits the fact that single-user decoding is bound by memory bandwidth and leaves compute idle. On `Qwen3-0.6B` it beats a dedicated streaming guard's F1 on 12 of 17 benchmarks and detects 11.8 points more unsafe responses than the probe, at **under 4% added latency per token**.

papers.title: MixFold: Sub-4-Bit Mixed-Precision LLM Inference via Output-Channel Grouping on Mobile NPUs
papers.abstract: Sub-4-bit quantization allows mobile devices to run larger LLMs, but its memory savings do not always translate into faster decoding on mobile NPUs. Their matrix units support only a few native integer datatypes, and converting unsupported weight formats on the vector unit can erase the gains from fewer bits. Mixed precision faces an additional constraint: each matrix-unit tile uses one datatype. MixFold executes 3-bit and perfectly symmetric 2-bit weights using native integer operations without expanding the weights to wider datatypes during decoding. MixFold then assigns datatypes to output-channel groups aligned with the matrix-unit tiles, enabling finer-than-layer assignment without disrupting matrix-unit execution. We compare MixFold with llama.cpp Hexagon backend on the Qualcomm Hexagon NPU of a Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5. Across the Qwen3 model family, MixFold achieves comparable or higher accuracy than llama.cpp's sub-4-bit formats at matched bits per weight, while decoding 1.16-1.41 times faster and generating 1.5-4.3 times more tokens per joule.
papers.summary: Sub-4-bit quantization saves memory on phones but often fails to speed up decoding on mobile neural processing units (NPUs), because their matrix units support only a few native integer datatypes and each tile must use one datatype. `MixFold` executes 3-bit and perfectly symmetric 2-bit weights with native integer operations, without expanding them to wider datatypes, and assigns datatypes to output-channel groups aligned with matrix-unit tiles for finer-than-layer mixed precision. Against the `llama.cpp` Hexagon backend on a Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5, across the `Qwen3` family, it matches or exceeds accuracy at equal bits per weight while decoding **1.16-1.41 times faster and generating 1.5-4.3 times more tokens per joule**.

papers.title: Affine-Image Propagation for Tight and Scalable Neural Network Verification
papers.abstract: While bound propagation methods are highly effective for certifying neural networks against $\ell_{\infty}$ adversaries, tight and scalable verification for $\ell_{2}$ adversaries remains a significant open challenge. Existing methods incur geometric loss by enclosing preactivation sets in elementwise intervals or axis-aligned ellipsoids, and functional loss by restricting the linear bounds constructed over those domains. Consequently, tight $\ell_{2}$ verification is currently restricted to Lipschitz-regularized networks where these approximations are accurate. In this paper, we introduce affine-image SDP-CROWN, a novel bound propagation method that better approximates preactivation domains using affine-image constraints and jointly optimizes the linear bound to adapt to the resulting domain. To bypass the prohibitive computational cost of dense semidefinite constraints required by the affine-image representation, we replace them with scaled diagonal-dominance conditions, allowing a GPU-accelerated implementation. Our method preserves the bound propagation recursion and can be integrated with branch-and-bound. On five MNIST and CIFAR-10 non-Lipschitz-regularized networks, our method improves verified accuracy over state-of-the-art methods by 17% to 57.5%. With branch-and-bound, these improvements increase to between 27% and 63.5%.
papers.summary: Certifying neural networks against L2-bounded adversarial perturbations has so far been tight only for Lipschitz-regularized networks, because existing bound propagation methods enclose preactivation sets in loose intervals or axis-aligned ellipsoids. The proposed `affine-image SDP-CROWN` approximates those sets with affine-image constraints and jointly optimizes the linear bounds, replacing costly dense semidefinite constraints with scaled diagonal-dominance conditions so it runs on GPUs. On five `MNIST` and `CIFAR-10` networks without Lipschitz regularization, it raises verified accuracy over prior state of the art by **17% to 57.5%**, and by 27% to 63.5% when combined with branch-and-bound.

papers.title: Contexture: Runtime Context Eviction for High-Throughput Agent Serving
papers.abstract:
LLM agents such as Hermes, OpenClaw, and Codex repeatedly resend growing execution histories, increasing shared GPU key-value (KV) cache demand in high-bandwidth memory (HBM). We show that shared KV capacity limits agent-serving throughput. Existing context-reduction methods lack global cache-state visibility, while runtime KV managers lack tool-execution information. Tracing tokens to their originating tool operations reveals that later operations supersede earlier outputs and associated turns, identifying 64% of recorded final-history tokens as removal candidates.
  We present Contexture, a harness- and model-agnostic architecture for runtime context eviction. Contexture separates the harness's full conversation history from the model's execution context, reducing subsequent requests' KV demand without modifying harness logic or model execution. It combines tool-execution information with global visibility into shared KV pressure and prefix residency: supersession identifies removal candidates, while runtime state determines when removal justifies sacrificing cached computation. This coordination reduces memory demand and decode KV traffic while limiting re-prefill interference with concurrent decoding, without additional model calls or training. Across two models, two harnesses, and two benchmarks, Contexture improves throughput under SLO by 20-73% over the best of no eviction, harness compaction, AgentDiet, and Continuum, and by 7-63% over observation masking in five of eight configurations, and reduces GPU energy per completed session by up to 11%. It also raises throughput under SLO by 23% over LMCache alone on H100. Live-agent experiments show a mean accuracy improvement of 1.4 percentage points over unloaded no eviction, with a worst-case loss of 3.7 points, while observation masking loses 3-28 points.
papers.summary: LLM agents repeatedly resend growing execution histories, and the authors show that shared GPU key-value (KV) cache capacity is what limits agent-serving throughput. Tracing tokens to the tool operations that produced them shows that later operations supersede earlier outputs, marking 64% of final-history tokens as removal candidates. `Contexture` separates the harness's full conversation history from the model's execution context and evicts superseded content when global cache pressure justifies losing cached computation, with no extra model calls or training. Across two models, two harnesses, and two benchmarks, it improves throughput under service-level objectives by **20-73%** over the best of no eviction, harness compaction, `AgentDiet`, and `Continuum`, with a mean accuracy gain of 1.4 points and a worst-case loss of 3.7 points.

papers.title: Privacy Protection in Self-Evolving Personal Agents: Persistent Memory and Cross-Carrier Transfer
papers.abstract: Personal agents carry private experience into later decisions through persistent memory. This thematic survey compares memory admission, maintenance, release, and withdrawal by protected change, observer, and validation setting. Direct evidence in the screened corpus comes from controlled memory workflows. Three worked scenarios follow one private fact through booking, feedback-driven learning, and withdrawal. We show when prompt revision and memory reads compose, when skills inherit a private head's bound, and why reader non-use does not establish cleanup of learned state. Diagnostic experiments measure the utility costs of wider label protection and broad memory deletion, and test how missing lineage obscures descendants.
papers.summary: Personal agents with persistent memory carry private experiences into later decisions, raising the question of how that information is admitted, maintained, released, and withdrawn. This thematic survey compares protection approaches across those four stages and follows one private fact through three worked scenarios: booking, feedback-driven learning, and withdrawal. It analyzes when prompt revision and memory reads compose, when skills inherit a privacy bound, and argues that **a reader not using a fact does not establish that learned state has been cleaned up**. Diagnostic experiments measure the utility cost of wider label protection and broad memory deletion, and show how missing lineage hides derived data.

papers.title: Distributional Algebro-Geometric Persistence (dAGP): Wasserstein-Stable Polynomial-Relation Signatures
papers.abstract: A circle and a quartic superellipse have the same homology, but their defining equations have degrees two and four, respectively. We study this algebraic distinction for point-cloud distributions. For a probability measure $\mu$ on $\Omega=[-1,1]^d$ and an orthonormal polynomial feature map $\phi_m$ of degree $m$, the moment matrix $G_m(\mu)=\mathbb{E}_{X\sim\mu}[\phi_m(X)\phi_m(X)^\top]$ satisfies $c^\top G_m(\mu)c=\mathbb{E}_\mu[f_c(X)^2]$, so coefficient directions associated with its small eigenvalues represent low-degree polynomials that nearly vanish on $\mu$. Counting these near-relation directions across degree $m$ and the tolerance $\varepsilon$ gives a two-parameter integer signature. We call this representation distributional algebro-geometric persistence (dAGP), the population counterpart of the point-cloud algebro-geometric persistence (AGP) construction. For empirical measures, dAGP is the sample-normalised counterpart of point-cloud AGP. We also show that $\mu\mapsto G_m(\mu)$ is Lipschitz in the $1$-Wasserstein distance, so its ordered eigenvalues vary Lipschitz-continuously under transport of mass, while its threshold counts remain unchanged under perturbations satisfying a spectral-margin condition. We give an explicit support-localised Lipschitz constant and identify the regime in which the resulting guarantee is informative. Experimentally, the population noise-floor prediction agrees with the finite-sample mean to $0.1\%$, within sampling error. At a selected tolerance, relation onset orders the conic, quartic, and non-algebraic closed curves, while their count profiles distinguish them from the two-dimensional control. Calibration identifies an empirical tolerance range. A $100$-repetition sensitivity study quantifies onset recovery and shows that the count grid and two continuous spectral baselines nearly saturate the four-family discrimination task.
papers.summary: Shapes with identical homology, such as a circle and a quartic superellipse, can still differ in the degree of their defining polynomial equations, and this work builds a signature that captures that difference for point-cloud distributions. Distributional algebro-geometric persistence (`dAGP`) counts the small eigenvalues of a polynomial moment matrix across polynomial degree and tolerance, since those directions correspond to low-degree polynomials that nearly vanish on the distribution. The authors prove **the moment matrix is Lipschitz in the 1-Wasserstein distance**, so the eigenvalues are stable under mass transport and the counts are unchanged under a spectral-margin condition. Experiments show the signature orders conic, quartic, and non-algebraic curves by relation onset, though two continuous spectral baselines also nearly saturate the discrimination task.

papers.title: From Letter-of-Credit Requirements to Executable Specifications: Evaluating Verification Accuracy and Completeness
papers.abstract: In letter-of-credit (LC) document examination, a correct final decision does not show that every requirement was examined. We therefore evaluate examination requirement by requirement and make each requirement executable. A language model converts the bill of lading (BL) and commercial invoice (IV) requirements of a credit into atomic conditions and logical structures, and a deterministic verifier retrieves the named evidence and computes each outcome, so every check can be compared with a gold encoding and traced to logged evidence. Because LC records are confidential, our on-premises 9B parser is fine-tuned only on synthetic pairs built from templates and human-reviewed public document values. On 345 real LC cases, final-decision accuracy proves misleading: a constant PASS rule has the highest raw accuracy while examining nothing. Although it never sees a real record during training, the fine-tuned parser detects 93% of the atomic requirements its ontology covers and reconstructs 86% of the covered requirements exactly. It verifies 82% of the evaluable requirements correctly, against 54% for a tool-using agent, and leads the agent on both satisfied requirements and discrepancies. It also completely examines 1.8 times as many cases as few-shot prompting of the same model, while direct prediction and the agent complete none. Executing the gold encodings with the same verifier shows that some of the remaining errors, missed discrepancies included, come from the operators and normalization, which a better parser alone cannot fix. Every rejection comes with a trace of the units and evidence behind it, which suits examiner-in-the-loop review.
papers.summary: In letter-of-credit (LC) document examination, a correct final decision does not show that every requirement was actually checked, so this work evaluates requirement by requirement. A fine-tuned on-premises 9B language model converts bill-of-lading and commercial-invoice requirements into atomic conditions and logical structures, and a deterministic verifier retrieves the evidence and computes each outcome with a traceable log. The parser is trained only on synthetic pairs because real records are confidential. On 345 real cases a constant PASS rule has the highest raw final-decision accuracy, while the parser verifies **82% of evaluable requirements correctly versus 54% for a tool-using agent**.

papers.title: Reward Integrity in Adversarial Reinforcement Learning for LLM Guardrail Red-Teaming
papers.abstract: We study reward fidelity in an adversarial reinforcement-learning loop for red-teaming financial-services language-model guardrails. Apparent wins can arise when an attack omits prescribed personally identifiable information (PII), or when a reward judge credits a response that did not break the targeted policy. On attacker-generated and public benchmark examples, TypeSafe Jev checks whether the prescribed PII is present. For outcome scoring, we compare the decision models TypeSafe Jev, Laya (pretrained and post-trained), and pretrained CLM-8B with logged Opus 4.8 judgements from a replay corpus. Post-training markedly improves Laya's agreement with the judge. A separate author-reviewed off-target set establishes that Opus can award false wins. The findings motivate specialised decision-model judges for checking prescribed PII in attack inputs and scoring target responses against the intended policy.
papers.summary: Adversarial reinforcement-learning loops for red-teaming financial-services LLM guardrails can register false wins, either because an attack omits the personally identifiable information (PII) it was supposed to contain or because the reward judge credits a response that did not break the targeted policy. The authors use `TypeSafe Jev` to check for prescribed PII, and compare `TypeSafe Jev`, `Laya` (pretrained and post-trained), and `CLM-8B` against logged `Opus 4.8` judgements on a replay corpus. Post-training markedly improves `Laya`'s agreement with the judge, and an author-reviewed off-target set shows that **the `Opus` judge itself can award false wins**. They argue for specialised decision-model judges for both input checking and outcome scoring.

papers.title: JevRisk: Zero-Shot Financial Risk Assessment with a Language Decision Model
papers.abstract: Banks must monitor every customer's financial risk, such as money laundering and credit default, by interpreting financial activity in the context of the customer's profile. Existing risk monitoring systems of banks are mostly based on expert-designed risk indicators, which apply predefined thresholds to every customer and cannot adapt to their personal situations. Supervised models recognise risk patterns from labelled customers, but each label often needs an expert's review or months of repayment history, which is slow and costly. Financial risk assessment therefore calls for a zero-shot decision system that minimises the need for labels and generalises across customers and risk types. To this end, we present JevRisk, a system for zero-shot financial risk assessment with a language decision model. JevRisk works in two steps. First, following regulatory guidelines in the finance domain, JevRisk computes exact risk indicators with code. Second, the language decision model (e.g., \jev{}) reads these indicators together with the customer's profile and activity, judges the case in context with broad world knowledge, and returns the score of high risk. We evaluate JevRisk on the anti-money laundering task with public synthetic data from Scotiabank and on the credit risk task with real data from Home Credit and Lending Club. On both tasks, JevRisk outperforms rule-based and unsupervised methods, and is on par with or better than supervised methods (e.g., GBDT and TabPFN) trained on about a thousand labelled customers.
papers.summary: Bank risk monitoring relies on fixed expert-designed thresholds that ignore individual context, or on supervised models that need slow and costly labels. `JevRisk` takes a zero-shot approach in two steps: code computes exact risk indicators following regulatory guidelines, then a language decision model reads those indicators with the customer's profile and activity and returns a high-risk score. It is evaluated on anti-money-laundering with public synthetic data from Scotiabank and on credit risk with real data from `Home Credit` and `Lending Club`. It outperforms rule-based and unsupervised methods and is **on par with or better than supervised methods such as GBDT and `TabPFN` trained on about a thousand labelled customers**.

papers.title: Scalable Evaluation of Medical AI using Evidence-based Practice Recommendations
papers.abstract: Rigorously evaluating medical artificial intelligence (AI) requires testing open-ended clinical management across diverse presentations and stages of care. However, existing benchmarks rely on manual expert authoring, limiting coverage across conditions, conditional care pathways, and evolving guidelines. We develop an automated pipeline that extracts and verifies structured clinical criteria and branching decision trees from practice recommendations to generate scenarios spanning the care continuum, including nuanced presentations and practice variations across regions and guideline editions. Applied to 436 BMJ Best Practice clinical monographs (354 US, 82 International), this yields 3,200 scenarios spanning differential diagnosis, investigations, treatment, and complications, plus targeted suites for regional specificity (731 US/International pairs) and temporal freshness (630 scenarios). To grade responses, we develop a clinician-calibrated autorater that scores management plans on a 4-point rubric stratifying deviations by clinical severity. Across Gemini models, scaling improves adherence, while web search (+0.8 percentage points [pp] on average) and multi-sample synthesis (+2.2 pp) combine additively (+2.8 pp). In context, full monographs consistently trail condensed excerpts. On targeted suites, web search narrows international performance gaps (+4.2 pp) and improves adherence to newly updated guidance (+4.6 pp). In a study with Primary Care Physicians (n = 9) across 200 scenarios, AI assistance raises adherence from 50.5% to 70.0%, driven largely by fewer clinical omissions. Overall, our results demonstrate a scalable evaluation setup using an evidence-based corpus originally written to guide human clinical decision-making, and demonstrate its viability to assess medical AI and its assistance on clinician decision-making.
papers.summary: Medical AI benchmarks depend on manual expert authoring, which limits coverage of conditions, branching care pathways, and changing guidelines. An automated pipeline extracts and verifies clinical criteria and decision trees from 436 `BMJ Best Practice` monographs, producing 3,200 scenarios across diagnosis, investigations, treatment, and complications, plus suites for regional differences and guideline freshness, graded by a clinician-calibrated autorater. Across `Gemini` models, larger models adhere better, and web search and multi-sample synthesis add about 2.8 percentage points combined. In a study of nine primary care physicians over 200 scenarios, AI assistance raised guideline adherence **from 50.5% to 70.0%**, mainly by reducing omissions.

papers.title: Fair Property Tax: Reducing Regressivity in Machine-Learning Valuation
papers.abstract: Advanced machine-learning models are increasingly used for property valuation in tax assessment. Although these models can achieve high predictive accuracy, they may systematically assign higher valuation-to-sale ratios to lower-priced properties, a pattern known as regressivity. In collaboration with the Cook County Assessor's Office (CCAO), we develop and evaluate two training methods that substantially reduce this regressive pattern while maintaining price-scale predictive accuracy. The Direct method has been incorporated into CCAO's public residential valuation software. Retaining the LightGBM model class used at CCAO, we propose a Direct penalty on squared covariance between log valuation errors and log sale prices, and an observation-additive Surrogate that yields a weighted squared-error loss. We evaluate both methods in our implementation of the CCAO workflow, using seven chronological validation folds, a held-out test set, and a 2025-forward test set. Measured by the magnitude of price-related bias (PRB), regressivity falls by approximately 49% on held-out sales and 39% on 2025 sales at a Surrogate setting selected by cross-validation, relative to the same LightGBM model fitted without the penalty. Price-scale $R^2$ is essentially unchanged. Its small rise, from 0.893 to 0.897 on held-out sales and from 0.904 to 0.908 on 2025 sales, reflects overall valuation level. Log-price RMSE rises by 3.1% and 1.7%, respectively. Paired sale-bootstrap 90% intervals for the PRB reductions lie within about two percentage points of these estimates. In an additional eight-county benchmark, both methods reduce regressivity in every county, with higher log-price prediction error as the expected tradeoff. These findings demonstrate a practical way to reduce measured regressivity within an existing assessor workflow while preserving price-scale predictive performance.
papers.summary: Machine-learning property valuation models used for tax assessment can systematically over-value lower-priced homes relative to their sale prices, a pattern called regressivity. Working with the Cook County Assessor's Office, the authors add two training objectives to the existing `LightGBM` model: a Direct penalty on the squared covariance between log valuation errors and log sale prices, and a Surrogate that reduces to a weighted squared-error loss. Measured by price-related bias, regressivity falls by **about 49% on held-out sales and 39% on 2025 sales**, with price-scale R-squared essentially unchanged and log-price RMSE up 3.1% and 1.7%. The Direct method has been incorporated into the county's public valuation software, and both methods reduce regressivity in all eight counties of an additional benchmark.

papers.title: FoRe: A Force-Guided Framework for Autonomous Grasp Recovery in Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have demonstrated strong performance in grasp-based manipulation, yet reliable recovery from local grasping failures remains challenging. Specifically, in pick-and-place tasks, policies may continue transport after a failed grasp instead of retrying, potentially reflecting overreliance on proprioceptive cues for stage progression and limited retry supervision. Existing recovery approaches typically rely on deployment-time guidance or demonstration augmentation. We introduce Force-guided Recovery (FoRe), a framework for autonomous recovery from local grasping failures. Using force feedback, FoRe partitions demonstrations into approach-grasp and transport-placement stages to train separate policies. To supplement limited retry supervision, FoRe then initializes a dedicated retry policy from the approach-grasp policy and refines it through local reinforcement learning (RL) from post-failure states. To avoid inappropriate stage progression, a controller combines force feedback with grasp-command status at inference to coordinate the stage policies, detect grasp failures, and invoke the retry policy. We also construct LIBERO-SUCTION, a force-augmented suction manipulation benchmark adapted from LIBERO, with complete demonstration trajectories for policy training. FoRe consistently improves task success rates for VLA-Adapter and $\pi_{0.5}$ on LIBERO-SUCTION, LIBERO, and real-world tasks. On LIBERO-SUCTION, average absolute gains are 18.4% and 6.5%, respectively. The corresponding real-world absolute gains are 25.0% and 21.7%. FoRe also remains effective with only one demonstration per task on both simulation benchmarks.
papers.summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) robot policies often carry on with transport after a failed grasp instead of retrying. Force-guided Recovery (`FoRe`) uses force feedback to split demonstrations into approach-grasp and transport-placement stages with separate policies, trains a dedicated retry policy through local reinforcement learning from post-failure states, and uses a controller that combines force feedback with grasp-command status to detect failures and invoke the retry. The authors also build `LIBERO-SUCTION`, a force-augmented suction manipulation benchmark. `FoRe` improves `VLA-Adapter` and `π0.5` by 18.4% and 6.5% absolute on `LIBERO-SUCTION`, and by **25.0% and 21.7% absolute on real-world tasks**.

papers.title: Many Plans at Once: Diverse Top-Quality Planning in Continuous Time
papers.abstract: Planners for physical systems usually return a single trajectory, which leaves no alternative when an unmodeled constraint invalidates the chosen route or downstream preferences change. A set of plans computed in advance provides ready-made alternatives and warm-starts for fast adaptation, but only if the plans are both low-cost and mutually distinct. Discrete planning addresses this with top-quality and diverse planning, but these ideas do not transfer to continuous time, where every valid trajectory has infinitely many valid near-copies, and existing trajectory planners converge to one or a few solutions. We present Many Plans at Once (MPAO), which treats every plan it finds as a reason to search elsewhere: it samples untrained neural networks whose outputs meet the boundary conditions by construction, trains corrections shared by networks from the same distribution, stores every validated plan, and adapts its sampling to what it has found, which makes it anytime. We define the goal by bringing the cost bound of top-quality planning and the distinctness threshold of diverse planning to continuous time. Under equal budgets against five baselines, MPAO is the only method that solves all 40 instances across four domains. On contact-rich manipulation, it is the only method with plans within 25% of the best known cost on one task, and returns about ten times as many such plans as the strongest baseline on the other two.
papers.summary: Trajectory planners for physical systems usually return one plan, leaving no fallback when an unmodeled constraint invalidates it. Many Plans at Once (`MPAO`) carries the cost bound of top-quality planning and the distinctness threshold of diverse planning over to continuous time, where every valid trajectory has infinitely many near-copies. It samples untrained neural networks whose outputs satisfy the boundary conditions by construction, trains shared corrections, stores every validated plan, and adapts its sampling to what it has found, making it an anytime method. Under equal budgets against five baselines, it is **the only method that solves all 40 instances across four domains**, and on two contact-rich manipulation tasks it returns about ten times as many near-best plans as the strongest baseline.

papers.title: Loop-OPF: Solver-Informed Learning for Optimal Power Flow with Inference-Time Topology Adaptivity
papers.abstract: Learning for optimal power flow (OPF) has recently been advocated to accelerate OPF solutions by using a pre-trained neural network (NN) to predict directly from given inputs such as the load demand. However, existing learning-for-OPF methods largely fall short of ensuring the optimality and feasibility of their predictions. They also struggle to adapt at inference time to unseen topology scenarios, such as those caused by line or generator outages. This work puts forth Loop-OPF, a solver-informed NN that builds its layers from the iterations of the primal-dual hybrid gradient (PDHG) method. Under standard convexity and regularity conditions on DC-OPF, the resultant fixed-point output of Loop-OPF is thus optimal and feasible. To speed up PDHG across diverse OPF scenarios, Loop-OPF learns certain PDHG parameters in a self-supervised manner, without any OPF solution labels. We adopt the deep equilibrium (DEQ) framework for training so that the memory cost does not grow with the number of layers. As the grid topology enters every layer as an input, the same trained Loop-OPF directly adapts to unseen contingencies without retraining. Numerical tests on the IEEE 300-bus and PEGASE 1354-, 2869-, and 9241-bus networks have demonstrated the accuracy and topology adaptivity of the proposed Loop-OPF over competing learning-for-OPF methods.
papers.summary: Neural networks that predict optimal power flow (OPF) solutions directly from load demand generally cannot guarantee optimality or feasibility, and struggle with unseen grid topologies such as line or generator outages. `Loop-OPF` builds its layers from iterations of the primal-dual hybrid gradient (`PDHG`) method, so that under standard convexity conditions on DC-OPF **its fixed-point output is optimal and feasible**. It learns `PDHG` parameters in a self-supervised way without solution labels and trains with the deep equilibrium framework to keep memory cost independent of depth. Because topology is an input to every layer, the trained model adapts to unseen contingencies without retraining, as shown on `IEEE 300-bus` and `PEGASE` networks of up to 9,241 buses.

papers.title: Ruby: State-of-the-Art Potency Prediction across Discovery Regimes Using Learned Structural Representations
papers.abstract: Small-molecule drug discovery proceeds through repeated design-make-test-analyze cycles. The goal is often to maximize potency while keeping other properties within the ranges required for a viable therapeutic candidate. Compound prioritization places different demands on computational methods as drug discovery progresses from hit identification through hit-to-lead and lead optimization, with changing computational budgets and increasing amounts of on-target experimental data. We introduce Ruby, a Robust Universal Binding affinitY predictor that uses intermediate representations from the structural foundation model Pearl without requiring an explicit binding pose for every compound. Ruby is trained on proprietary data plus GenesisPotency-2026, an audited public-source potency training dataset released for academic and commercial use under a CC BY-SA 4.0 license with row-level provenance and audit annotations. Ruby achieves the highest aggregate early enrichment across seven public hit-identification targets among evaluated methods, with adjustable inference effort trading off enrichment and computational cost over more than two orders of magnitude. Ruby achieves the highest average correlations across four public benchmarks: OpenFE, CASP16, FEP+ 4, and OpenBind. Ruby significantly outperforms other methods in zero-shot prediction across eight biochemical and cellular assays from five ongoing Genesis-Incyte programs, widening its performance advantage relative to the public benchmarks. Ruby continues to improve more than other methods when all are given the opportunity to recalibrate using earlier assay measurements. Together, these contributions provide an annotated training resource for the field and a state-of-the-art potency predictor for broad screening, prioritization within related chemical series, and assay-specific prediction as experimental measurements accumulate.
papers.summary: Predicting small-molecule potency places different demands on computational methods as drug discovery moves from hit identification to lead optimization. `Ruby` is a binding affinity predictor that uses intermediate representations from the structural foundation model `Pearl` without needing an explicit binding pose per compound, trained on proprietary data plus the newly released, openly licensed `GenesisPotency-2026` dataset. It achieves the highest aggregate early enrichment on seven public hit-identification targets and **the highest average correlations on `OpenFE`, `CASP16`, `FEP+ 4`, and `OpenBind`**. Its advantage widens in zero-shot prediction on eight assays from five ongoing industry programs.

papers.title: Same Facts, Different Decision: Fact-Invariant Manipulation and Provenance-Based Defense in Typed Decision Models
papers.abstract: Typed decision models such as TypeSafe's Jev answer only with a probability, an option, or a score, so software can act on them directly. Their inputs, however, often include text from outsiders. Prior attacks test this risk poorly. Injected instructions rarely work on these models, and added facts can make a changed decision correct. We show that outside comments can persuade these models to make a wrong decision without adding any fact. We propose LEVER, an attack that writes such comments with four levers from argumentation theory, uses a separate verifier to discard any comment that adds a fact, and searches for effective comments guided by the model's output probabilities. We further propose the Provenance Gate, a defense that accepts a changed decision only if the model reaches it again without the outside comments. On three benchmarks, LEVER flips about a third of Jev's correct decisions, 2.8 times as many as the strongest prior attack under the same limit on facts, and more on five other models. The gate blocks all of these attacks with at most one extra query and still accepts trusted updates.

papers.title: Integral Multipliers and Arithmetic Obstructions for Two-Hidden-Layer ReLU Maxima
papers.abstract: We study exact representations of maximum functions by ReLU networks with two hidden layers and integer parameters. The least positive output multiplier is two for the six-input maximum, and either two or six for the seven-input maximum. We obtain these bounds from integral cubical fillings and a coefficient-preserving passage from polytope identities to networks. For the coordinate-facet complex of the six-simplex, we compute a coning index of six over the integers and three after inverting two, allowing arbitrary integral directions within each facet. A class in the homology of the unrestricted kernel complex characterizes the remaining seven-input problem; its vanishing is equivalent to an integral filling of a fixed target. We also construct a finite character that separates rational from three-local representability in a dictionary containing two known constructions and all pairs of edge-disjoint three-edge forests. This obstruction permits nonsymmetric coefficients and is confined to the specified dictionary. Control of lower-dimensional remainders yields a sufficient criterion in the top-dimensional quotient. Exact certificates and verification programs accompany the finite calculations.
papers.summary: Typed decision models such as `TypeSafe`'s `Jev` answer only with a probability, option, or score so software can act on them directly, but their inputs often include text from outsiders. The `LEVER` attack writes persuasive comments using four levers from argumentation theory, uses a verifier to discard any comment that adds a fact, and searches for effective comments using the model's output probabilities. On three benchmarks it **flips about a third of `Jev`'s correct decisions**, 2.8 times as many as the strongest prior attack under the same limit on facts, and more on five other models. The proposed `Provenance Gate` defense accepts a changed decision only if the model reaches it again without the outside comments, blocking all these attacks with at most one extra query.

papers.title: Toward a digital twin of the ICU patient: Forecasting and treatment response in a generative event model
papers.abstract: A digital twin of a patient in intensive care would forecast the patient's course and what a treatment would change. Generative event models, trained to continue a patient's electronic health record (EHR), have been proposed as a path toward such twins. We trained TWICE, a 79M-parameter decoder-only transformer, on the ICU records of one academic health system (127,332 training patients and 1.57 billion tokens). We evaluated it on clinical prediction tasks, generation fidelity, individual trajectories and counterfactual validation. Reading 19 clinical outcomes off 50 simulated futures, with no task-specific training, TWICE matched the best of 144 supervised configurations on held-out patients (mean AUROC 0.836 vs. 0.834).
