It led on events that change care within a day and trailed on death. With the training data fixed, more and longer simulated futures were worth more than a 6.8-fold larger model. Its generated records matched real ones closely and were as specific to each patient as its own variability allowed. Its predicted risk rose as events approached. Pre-specified controls showed that it reproduced the side effects of drugs and was barely moved by an inert drug. On the values that treatments are given to correct, however, an opposite treatment moved its forecasts like the right one. TWICE forecasts ICU events about as well as task-specific models, and we see it as a step toward a digital twin of the ICU patient.
papers.summary: Generative models trained to continue a patient's electronic health record have been proposed as a route to digital twins that forecast a patient's course and their response to treatment. `TWICE` is a 79M-parameter decoder-only transformer trained on intensive care records of 127,332 patients (1.57 billion tokens) from one health system. Reading 19 clinical outcomes off 50 simulated futures with no task-specific training, it **matched the best of 144 supervised configurations (mean AUROC 0.836 vs. 0.834)**, and more and longer simulations helped more than a 6.8-fold larger model. It reproduced drug side effects and barely responded to an inert drug, but on the values treatments are meant to correct, an opposite treatment moved its forecasts like the correct one.

papers.title: Mind World Models: Joint Learning of Motor EEG Representations and Action-Conditioned World Dynamics
papers.abstract: Motor decoding from electroencephalography (EEG) supports non-invasive brain-computer interfaces, yet existing methods either rely on costly cue-based trials and coarse categorical labels or use pretraining objectives that do not directly capture how movement unfolds, limiting their ability to learn transferable motor representations. To this end, we propose the Mind World Model (MWM), a framework that learns motor EEG representations from scalable naturalistic EEG and egocentric video without action annotations. MWM treats EEG observed up to the current frame as the latent action of a world model: a mind model encodes the EEG, and a world model uses it to predict the representation of a future frame, yielding a movement-grounded pretraining objective. We further introduce the Lateralization-Aware Transformer (LAT), which uses frame averaging to separate shared bilateral from side-specific lateral features, encoding hemispheric correspondence to reduce the burden of learning left-right relationships from data. MWM pretraining produces two models: a mind model for downstream motor decoding and a world model that can be adapted to prediction conditioned on real actions, opening a scalable and flexible path to collect egocentric data for embodied AI. Across 9 classification and 7 regression tasks, the mind model improves task-averaged balanced accuracy by 5.9% and Pearson correlation by 16.2% relative to the strongest baseline in each task family. Compared with an inverse-dynamics latent-action baseline, the world model achieves lower prediction error and benefits 3.3 times more from matched real actions within recordings and 4.7 times more on held-out subjects.
papers.summary: Decoding movement from electroencephalography (EEG) usually depends on costly cue-based trials with coarse labels, or on pretraining objectives that do not capture how movement unfolds. The `Mind World Model` (`MWM`) pretrains on naturalistic EEG paired with egocentric video and no action annotations, treating the EEG seen so far as the latent action a world model uses to predict the representation of a future frame; a `Lateralization-Aware Transformer` (`LAT`) separates shared bilateral features from side-specific ones. Across 9 classification and 7 regression tasks, the resulting EEG encoder improves **task-averaged balanced accuracy by 5.9% and Pearson correlation by 16.2% relative to the strongest baseline in each task family**. The world model also has lower prediction error than an inverse-dynamics latent-action baseline and benefits 3.3 times more from matched real actions within recordings and 4.7 times more on held-out subjects.

papers.title: Disentangling Verbalized Evaluation Awareness and Refusal through Neuron-Level Intervention
papers.abstract: As large reasoning models (LRMs) become more capable, reliable evaluation becomes essential. LRMs can sometimes recognize that they are being evaluated, a phenomenon known as \emph{evaluation awareness}. This phenomenon raises concerns about whether safety behavior, particularly refusal behavior, generalizes from evaluation to deployment. Prior work manipulates \emph{verbalized evaluation awareness (VEA)} through activation steering and observes higher refusal rates when VEA is present, but the mechanisms underlying this connection remain poorly understood. We identify \emph{VEA neurons} by contrasting their activations in VEA and non-VEA reasoning segments. Intervening on 5,000 VEA neurons reduces the VEA rate from 12.6--51.8\% to at most 1.4\% across the model benchmark combinations in our main experiments, and lowers a probe score for unverbalized evaluation awareness (unVEA). In QwQ-32B, VEA-neuron intervention also reduces refusal even in rollouts without VEA; VEA text itself explains only 4--10\% of the decrease. We further show that their down-projection vectors contain refusal components, and preserving these components during intervention partially restores refusal while maintaining VEA suppression, accounting for about half of the refusal decrease and providing a mechanistic explanation for the connection between evaluation awareness and refusal. Finally, across the OLMo 3 SFT, DPO, and RLVR checkpoints, the VEA rate on SorryBench and StrongREJECT is similar after SFT and DPO but substantially higher after RLVR, alongside an increase in the number of VEA neurons. Together, these findings show that VEA text itself has a limited effect on refusal, and that VEA neurons integrate evaluation awarenss and refusal.
papers.summary: Reasoning models sometimes state that they are being tested, called verbalized evaluation awareness (VEA), and earlier work linked this to higher refusal rates without explaining the mechanism. The authors identify VEA neurons by contrasting activations in VEA and non-VEA reasoning segments, and intervening on 5,000 of them cuts **the VEA rate from 12.6-51.8% to at most 1.4%** across the main model and benchmark combinations. In `QwQ-32B` the intervention also lowers refusal in rollouts with no VEA, with the VEA text itself explaining only 4-10% of the drop, while refusal components in the neurons' down-projection vectors account for about half of it. Across `OLMo 3` checkpoints, the VEA rate on `SorryBench` and `StrongREJECT` is similar after supervised fine-tuning and DPO but substantially higher after the RLVR stage.

papers.title: Hypergraph Structural Entropy-Enhanced Hierarchy-Aware Semi-Supervised Graph Classification
papers.abstract: Semi-supervised graph classification aims to learn graph-level representations by leveraging a large number of unlabeled graphs alongside a small set of labeled ones, effectively mitigating the issue of label scarcity. Despite significant progress by various semi-supervised learning strategies, complex relationships among graph vertices beyond pairwise edges, especially hierarchical structures, remain underexplored by existing methods. In this work, we propose a Hypergraph Structural Entropy-Enhanced hierarchy-aware framework, namely HypSEE, for semi-supervised graph classification. Specifically, we first construct walk-induced and embedding-derived hypergraphs to capture hierarchy-aware local and long-range higher-order relationships within graphs. Then, we devise a hierarchical hypergraph pooling approach guided by hypergraph structural entropy (HSE) to facilitate hierarchical representation learning in hypergraphs. Lastly, we employ an anchor graph-based consistency strategy to mutually align the representations from these two hypergraph views, enhancing the learning efficacy on unlabeled data. Extensive experiments on 8 benchmark datasets demonstrate the state-of-the-art performance of our approach.
papers.summary: Semi-supervised graph classification learns graph-level representations from a few labeled graphs and many unlabeled ones, but existing methods largely ignore higher-order and hierarchical relationships among vertices. `HypSEE` builds two hypergraph views of each graph, one induced by walks and one derived from embeddings, pools them hierarchically under the guidance of hypergraph structural entropy, and aligns the two views with an anchor-graph consistency strategy to exploit unlabeled data. The authors report **state-of-the-art performance on 8 benchmark datasets**.

papers.title: Action-Conditioned Spatio-Temporal Forecasting
papers.abstract: We study spatio-temporal forecasting in networked systems under specified actions. The challenge is to capture the action's effects without predicting spurious changes in unaffected regions. However, direct supervision and evaluation of these effects require paired futures with and without the action, whereas observational trajectories reveal only the realized future. We introduce PairST, a benchmark comprising six datasets across traffic, power transmission and water distribution, with paired reference and intervened futures simulated from the same system state. These pairs enable separate evaluation of affected-region forecast accuracy and quiet-region response error. We further propose ActionST, which forecasts the intervened future by writing an explicit response onto an intervention-independent reference forecast. Specifically, node-time addressing constructs a query for each response position, a state-conditioned response writer computes candidate responses, and a graph-aware locality gate controls their strength. Experiments on six datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of ActionST at new action targets, with the lowest mean absolute error on five datasets and the best average rank. Our source code and the PairST benchmark are available at https://github.com/yutong-xia/ActionST.
papers.summary: Forecasting how a networked system responds to a specified action is hard to supervise or evaluate, because observational data only shows the future that actually happened. `PairST` is a benchmark of six simulated datasets across traffic, power transmission, and water distribution that pairs reference and intervened futures from the same system state, allowing separate measurement of accuracy in affected regions and spurious responses in unaffected ones. The accompanying `ActionST` model writes an explicit response onto an intervention-independent reference forecast, using node-time addressing, a state-conditioned response writer, and a graph-aware locality gate. On new action targets it achieves **the lowest mean absolute error on five of the six datasets** and the best average rank.

papers.title: Actions Speak Louder than Words: Stateful Privacy Sniffing of LLM Agents via Behavioral Covert Channels in Web Interactions
papers.abstract:
LLM agents increasingly rely on Web interaction, issuing searches, following links, and reading pages, to complete complex user tasks. Since each action is driven by the agent's private context, including the user's prompt, dialogue history, memory, and connected data, it also opens a new privacy exposure surface. Prior attacks either passively analyze network traffic, which yields only coarse correlations, or hijack the agent through indirect prompt injection, which must place sensitive content in an outgoing field and is blocked by content-level defenses. Whether an attacker can actively recover fine-grained private context without any explicit transmission thus remains insufficiently understood.
  Our insight is that an agent's benign Web decisions themselves leak private context, as what it chooses to visit encodes whether, which, and in what order it acts, forming a behavioral covert channel. Building on this, we design SNOOP, a stateful hierarchical probing framework that narrows a coarse-to-fine hypothesis tree per task and reconstructs user queries and profiles from the agent's observable paths. Across four agents and three LLM backbones on 500 StackExchange queries and 378 multi-turn iKAT dialogues, SNOOP recovers query concepts with an average F1 of 0.89 and user profiles with an F1 of 0.80, while four representative agent defenses change its recovery by less than 0.03 F1. Since no sensitive content is ever transmitted, content-level inspection cannot detect this leakage; we therefore propose Selection-Obfuscated Retrieval (SOR), which acquires resources under a fixed budget independent of private context and confines the agent's selection to a local snapshot, cutting SNOOP's F1 to 0.39 without additional LLM inference.
papers.summary: The pages a web-browsing LLM agent chooses to visit depend on its private context, so those choices can leak the user's prompt, history, and profile even when no sensitive text is ever transmitted. `SNOOP` exploits this behavioral covert channel with a stateful, hierarchical probing framework that narrows a coarse-to-fine hypothesis tree and reconstructs user queries and profiles from the agent's observable navigation paths. Across four agents and three LLM backbones on 500 StackExchange queries and 378 multi-turn `iKAT` dialogues, it recovers **query concepts with an average F1 of 0.89 and user profiles with an F1 of 0.80**, and four representative agent defenses change that by less than 0.03 F1. The proposed defense, `Selection-Obfuscated Retrieval` (`SOR`), fetches resources under a fixed budget independent of private context and confines selection to a local snapshot, cutting the attack's F1 to 0.39 with no extra LLM inference.

papers.title: Isolating the Language Shell: A Content-Controlled Study of Multilingual Reasoning
papers.abstract: Multilingual reasoning distillation requires choosing the language in which teacher reasoning is presented, yet existing recipes often entangle linguistic form with differences in generation, translation, and filtering. We construct content-controlled supervision by rendering the same verified English trajectories into English, translated target-language, and language-mixed shells, and fine-tune two pretrained students in three target languages, evaluating them on multilingual mathematical reasoning at two difficulty levels. Even with the underlying reasoning content held fixed, we find that shell choice can change downstream accuracy, with effects varying across students, languages, and difficulty levels. Pre-training compatibility does not consistently track these outcomes, and even when our tests find no clear accuracy difference between shells, their output-language behavior can still differ substantially. These results suggest that the supervision shell is a distinct design choice in multilingual reasoning distillation.
papers.summary: When distilling reasoning into multilingual models, the language in which the teacher's reasoning is written is usually entangled with differences in generation, translation, and filtering. This study holds content fixed by rendering the same verified English reasoning trajectories as English, translated target-language, and language-mixed versions, then fine-tunes two students in three target languages and tests them on multilingual mathematical reasoning at two difficulty levels. The authors find that **the choice of language shell alone can change downstream accuracy**, with effects that vary by student, language, and difficulty. Pre-training compatibility does not consistently predict the outcome, and shells with no clear accuracy difference can still produce substantially different output-language behavior.

papers.title: A Continuous Relaxation of Quantization-Aware Training
papers.abstract: Quantization is a critical piece of the deployment pipeline in the era of large generative models. Low-bit quantization, particularly 2-bits or sub-2-bits, is a notoriously difficult problem, particularly when using a channelwise quantization scheme which has been shown as a leading candidate for hardware-efficiency. The key challenges with low-bit quantization range from limited quantization levels to saddle points or flat regions in the loss surface. In this paper, we look at the problem of flat quantization loss surfaces through a lens of dynamically changing bitwidth. Unlike existing techniques which either change the bit-precision abruptly or keep it fixed, we propose to gradually alter the bitwidth as the model trains. To this end, we propose RelaxQAT, a continuous relaxation of the QAT process. We also provide simple theoretical and empirical insights behind why RelaxQAT helps the QAT performance. Our extensive experiments demonstrate up to 6.3% average accuracy gains on vision and up to 7.7% better average accuracy on natural language tasks, compared to the leading QAT methods.
papers.summary: Quantization-aware training (QAT) at 2 bits or below is difficult, especially with channelwise schemes, partly because the loss surface contains flat regions and saddle points. `RelaxQAT` treats bitwidth as a continuously relaxed quantity that is changed gradually during training, rather than fixed or switched abruptly, and the authors provide simple theoretical and empirical arguments for why this helps. They report **up to 6.3% average accuracy gains on vision tasks and up to 7.7% on natural language tasks** over leading QAT methods.

papers.title: Learning 3D MRI Representations with Generative Adversarial Networks
papers.abstract: Learning representations of visual images is a challenging task. It requires extracting abstract patterns from high-dimensional data without explicit supervision. This becomes pronounced with 3D MR imaging due to sparse features, higher dimensional inputs, and smaller datasets. Many state-of-the-art representation learning algorithms successfully rely on transformers and diffusion-based architectures. However, these methods struggle with smaller datasets. In effect, solution methods relax the problem by slicing 3D volumes and solving the problem for 2D medical imaging, resulting in a loss of spatial 3D information. We present R2RG, a representation learning method based on Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), with Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) honing the reconstruction task. Our key insights lie in exploiting architectural biases in 3D CNNs, combined with data-efficient auto-encoding GANs and a composite loss function to enhance reconstruction fidelity and stabilize training. Our experiments on three standard datasets and a locally collected dataset show that R2RG not only achieves superior performance but also generalizes to heterogeneous and smaller datasets. Furthermore, representations learned with R2RG outperform those learned with contrastive-based representation learning methods on Parkinson's and Alzheimer's disease classification. Our work demonstrates that reconstruction-based representation learning is a promising direction for 3D medical imaging under limited data availability.
papers.summary: Representation learning for 3D magnetic resonance imaging is hampered by small datasets, sparse features, and high-dimensional inputs, and transformer and diffusion methods often fall back on 2D slices, losing spatial information. `R2RG` instead uses 3D convolutional networks with a data-efficient auto-encoding generative adversarial network and a composite loss intended to improve reconstruction fidelity and stabilize training. On three standard datasets and a locally collected one, the authors report superior performance and generalization to smaller, heterogeneous datasets, and the learned representations **outperform contrastive representation learning on Parkinson's and Alzheimer's disease classification**.

papers.title: Structural Agreement Indicates Prediction Accuracy For Protein-Ligand Co-Folding
papers.abstract: Co-folding models predict the structures of proteins and their bound ligands, but their accuracy varies across targets. Their usefulness therefore depends on knowing which predictions a user can trust. Confidence scores are intended to guide that choice. However, across seven co-folding models, we show that confidence-based selection offers little improvement over choosing a prediction at random. For approximately three-quarters of structures, predictions are either exclusively correct or incorrect, leaving no opportunity for ranking to change the outcome. Moreover, high confidence does not reliably discriminate correct top-ranked predictions from incorrect ones. We find that structural agreement among predictions is a more accurate measure of likely success than current confidence scores. We capture this with the Concentration of Repeated Ensembles (CORE) Score, which combines cluster tightness with ensemble support. CORE Score discriminates top-1 success and oracle success, achieving mean ROC AUCs of 0.866 and 0.838, compared to 0.757 and 0.759 for ipTM. CORE Score also outperforms training set similarity measures, including ligand Tanimoto, protein sequence, and Runs N' Poses similarity, despite requiring no experimental ligand pose. Structural agreement is therefore a practical indicator of reliability and a baseline for evaluating future confidence estimators, without requiring an additional trained uncertainty estimator.
papers.summary: Co-folding models predict protein-ligand structures along with confidence scores meant to indicate which predictions to trust. Across seven such models, the authors show that confidence-based selection is little better than picking a prediction at random, in part because for roughly three-quarters of structures the predictions are all correct or all incorrect. They propose the `CORE Score` (Concentration of Repeated Ensembles), which combines cluster tightness with ensemble support to measure structural agreement among predictions. It discriminates top-1 and oracle success with **mean ROC AUCs of 0.866 and 0.838, versus 0.757 and 0.759 for `ipTM`**, and also outperforms training-set similarity measures without needing an experimental ligand pose.

papers.title: NightmareDiscourseBench: A Benchmark Dataset for Fictional Direct Discourse Identification Pipelines
papers.abstract: In this paper we introduce a new benchmark dataset, NightmareDiscourseBench, for testing NLP pipelines that identify forms of direct discourse in English-language fiction. We first review existing publicly available benchmarks (providing summary statistics and reviewing available metadata) for this task, identifying theoretical inconsistency and exclusive focus on speech as primary issues in this domain. We then overview our narrative theory-based framework for classifying and evaluating different forms of direct discourse, and finally describe NightmareDiscourseBench, a new benchmark test set of 12 text samples accompanied by metadata pertinent to the task of direct discourse identification.
papers.summary: Pipelines that identify direct discourse in English-language fiction are tested on benchmarks that the authors find theoretically inconsistent and focused exclusively on speech. After reviewing existing public benchmarks and their metadata, they lay out a classification and evaluation framework grounded in narrative theory. The resulting `NightmareDiscourseBench` is **a test set of 12 text samples** with metadata relevant to direct discourse identification.

papers.title: Rethinking Cross-Sensor Domain Adaptation for Bridge Point Cloud Semantic Segmentation
papers.abstract: Segmentation models for bridge point clouds lose accuracy when trained on terrestrial laser scanning (TLS) data and applied to mobile laser scanning (MLS) data. This study re-examines the SemanticBridge TLS-to-MLS protocol to determine how sampling density, surface roughness, color, and acquisition viewpoint are expressed in the 8-cm sparse-voxel representation, and how adaptation gains depend on source-model convergence. Using one sparse-convolution U-Net, we combine raw-point statistics with controlled input perturbations and compare adaptive batch normalization, entropy minimization, Mean Teacher, and confidence-filtered self-training under 100- and 300-epoch schedules. TLS and MLS have similar nearest-neighbor spacing after preprocessing (12.08 and 12.02 mm), and a 4-mm perturbation of TLS points changes voxel occupancy by only 4.4%. Color distributions differ systematically, but zeroing color on identical voxels changes target mean intersection over union (mIoU) by only +0.02, and by +0.06 after the color augmentation is scale-corrected. The sensors also observe different portions of the bridge, yielding different class proportions. A 300-epoch source-only model obtains 57.80 mIoU on the paired-bridge protocol. Confidence-filtered self-training improves the 100-epoch baseline, but from a converged model it changes target mIoU by -0.97 (source-selected checkpoints) and -2.44 (final-50-epoch means). Repeated evaluation (standard deviation 0.27-0.64) and seed variation (1.88 across three seeds) are comparable to several method differences. Adaptation results on this benchmark therefore depend on representation scale, source-model convergence, and evaluation variability.
papers.summary: Segmentation models for bridge point clouds lose accuracy when trained on terrestrial laser scanning (TLS) data and applied to mobile laser scanning (MLS) data, and this study re-examines the `SemanticBridge` TLS-to-MLS protocol to find out why. Using one sparse-convolution U-Net with controlled input perturbations, it finds that density, roughness, and color differences barely matter at the 8-cm voxel scale, while the two sensors observe different parts of the bridge and so different class proportions. Comparing adaptive batch normalization, entropy minimization, `Mean Teacher`, and confidence-filtered self-training, the authors find that self-training helps an under-trained 100-epoch baseline but **changes target mean intersection over union by -0.97 to -2.44 when starting from a converged 300-epoch model**. Seed variation of 1.88 across three seeds is comparable to several of the differences between methods.

papers.title: PACE: Policy Augmentation and Compensation With Explicit Disturbance Estimation for Robust Locomotion
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning has made quadrupedal locomotion remarkably robust. To handle unmodeled dynamics and external disturbances, domain randomization is usually employed to make a policy hedge against every condition it might meet. However, maintaining accurate tracking across varying dynamics and generalizing beyond the sampled range remain challenging. Here we show that explicitly estimating the disturbance and feeding the resulting estimation back into both the policy and the controller can relax this compromise. We introduce Policy Augmentation and Compensation with Explicit disturbance estimation (PACE). The framework lumps payload variations, center-of-mass (CoM) shifts, actuator degradation, and external forces into one joint-space disturbance. A nonlinear observer subsequently recovers this disturbance online without requiring joint acceleration measurements. The disturbance estimation provides feedforward torque compensation as the foundational control pathway and further augments the policy observation to enable disturbance-aware action generation. Considering the learning difficulty of fast-varying contact effects, we further provide an analytical contact estimation approach from joint and inertial measurements, without demanding force sensors. Across eleven simulated dynamics conditions, PACE reduces velocity-tracking error by 18.1% to 57.0% against state-of-the-art baselines, and maintains improved tracking under out-of-distribution (OOD) commands. Notably, in real-world experiments, the deployed real robot carried an 11.5 kg payload, nearly equal to its own mass. It also negotiated unseen 16 cm step-downs and crossed five outdoor terrains. The policy was trained exclusively on flat ground in simulation with at most 3 kg of added mass.
papers.summary: Quadruped locomotion policies trained with reinforcement learning usually rely on domain randomization, which trades away tracking accuracy and generalizes poorly beyond the sampled range. `PACE` lumps payload changes, center-of-mass shifts, actuator degradation, and external forces into one joint-space disturbance, estimates it online with a nonlinear observer that needs no joint acceleration measurements, and uses the estimate both for feedforward torque compensation and as an extra policy observation; contact is estimated analytically without force sensors. Across eleven simulated dynamics conditions it reduces velocity-tracking error by 18.1% to 57.0% against baselines. A policy trained only on flat ground in simulation with at most 3 kg of added mass let the real robot **carry an 11.5 kg payload, nearly equal to its own mass**, and handle unseen 16 cm step-downs and five outdoor terrains.

papers.title: Dynamic Token Merging for Efficient Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) represent each image with hundreds of visual tokens, which can make inference costly even when a prompt depends on only part of the image. Dynamic Token Merging (DTM), introduced in MrT5 for byte-level text encoders, learns which tokens to remove: a lightweight delete gate scores contextualized hidden states, acts as a differentiable attention bias during training, and physically removes tokens at inference. We argue that DTM is a general token deletion framework rather than a byte-level technique, and extend it to the vision modality and to decoder-only models. Applying DTM to T5Gemma 2 and Gemma 3 yields V-MrT5Gemma2, which deletes visual tokens inside a bidirectional multimodal encoder, and V-MrGemma3, which compacts the prompt and its key-value caches during decoder-only prefill. Across ten benchmarks, DTM's advantage over attention-based and random deletion grows with the deletion rate and is largest on document, chart, and scene-text reading. At 80% visual token deletion (approximately 60% fewer FLOPs), DTM raises accuracy over FastV from 51.8 to 63.0 on ChartQA and from 63.3 to 67.8 on TextVQA with V-MrT5Gemma2, as well as from 62.2 to 68.8 and from 71.2 to 75.1 with V-MrGemma3, retaining 90-96% of unpruned performance on both tasks with significant efficiency gains. These results support DTM as a general framework for efficient transformers.
papers.summary: Vision-language models spend hundreds of tokens on each image, which makes inference expensive even when the prompt concerns only part of it. Dynamic Token Merging (DTM), a learned delete gate originally introduced in `MrT5` for byte-level text encoders, is extended here to visual tokens and to decoder-only models, producing `V-MrT5Gemma2` from `T5Gemma 2` and `V-MrGemma3` from `Gemma 3`. Across ten benchmarks, its advantage over attention-based and random deletion grows with the deletion rate and is largest on document, chart, and scene-text reading. At 80% visual token deletion (about 60% fewer FLOPs), it **retains 90-96% of unpruned performance on `ChartQA` and `TextVQA`**, for example raising `ChartQA` accuracy over `FastV` from 51.8 to 63.0 with `V-MrT5Gemma2`.

papers.title: COMPASS: Cross-modal Observation with Multi-Path Adaptive Stopping and Selection for Early Time Series Classification
papers.abstract: Early time-series classification (ETSC) balances predictive performance against the amount of observed data. In multimodal settings, modality-associated and fused branches may differ in predictive ability at the same observed prefix, motivating joint decisions about when to stop and which branch should provide the final prediction. We propose COMPASS, a two-stage framework that preserves two modality-associated temporal branches and one fusion branch. The first stage combines cross-modal feature exchange and gated fusion with branch-wise supervision at every prefix. The second stage optimizes a shared four-action controller to continue observation or terminate through one of the frozen branches. Experiments on six physiological and wearable datasets compare COMPASS with multimodal adaptations of five ETSC baselines. COMPASS achieves the best average ranks in accuracy-earliness harmonic mean, AUROC, and earliness within this comparison set. At identical learned stopping times, branch selection improves mean accuracy over fusion readout on five of the six datasets, with gains of 2.35 and 2.16 percentage points on ISRUC-Sleep and UCDDB, respectively. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work on joint stopping and branch selection for multimodal early time series classification.
papers.summary: Early time-series classification (ETSC) trades predictive performance against how much of a sequence is observed, and with multimodal inputs the per-modality and fused branches can differ in reliability at the same prefix. `COMPASS` first trains two modality-associated branches and one fusion branch with cross-modal feature exchange and supervision at every prefix, then trains a four-action controller that either keeps observing or stops and outputs the prediction of one frozen branch. On six physiological and wearable datasets it achieves the best average ranks among multimodal adaptations of five ETSC baselines in accuracy-earliness harmonic mean, AUROC, and earliness. At identical stopping times, **selecting a branch beats the fusion readout on five of the six datasets**, with gains of 2.35 and 2.16 percentage points on `ISRUC-Sleep` and `UCDDB`.

papers.title: Online Learning for Minimizing Maximum Tardiness in Single-Machine Scheduling
papers.abstract:
We study online learning for minimizing maximum tardiness (\OMMT) in single-machine scheduling. In each round, the learner selects a permutation of \(n\) fixed jobs, representing a schedule. The environment then reveals a processing time and a due date for each job, and the learner incurs a vector-valued loss whose components correspond to the tardiness of the individual jobs. The goal of the learner is to minimize \(\alpha\)-regret, the difference between the learner's maximum cumulative tardiness and \(\alpha\) times that of the best fixed permutation in hindsight, for as small \(\alpha\) as possible. We investigate OMMT under both stochastic and adversarial environments. In the stochastic setting, we prove that the expected \(1\)-regret of the Follow-the-Leader (FTL) algorithm is \(
  O\!\left(\frac{n\log n}{\Delta^2}\right) \), together with a corresponding high-probability bound, where \(\Delta\) is a distribution-dependent gap parameter. At round \(t \in \{1,\dots,T\}\), FTL runs in \(O(tn^2)\) time and \(O(tn)\) space. In the adversarial setting, we prove that, for any \(0<c<\log_2 n/16\), the \(\alpha\)-regret is \(\Omega(T)\) whenever \(\alpha<\log_2 n/16-c\). We then reduce OMMT to a surrogate online learning problem and apply Follow-the-Perturbed-Leader (FTPL), obtaining an expected \(\alpha\)-regret bound of \(O(n^2\sqrt{T})\) for \(\alpha=O(\log n)\). Thus, the logarithmic dependence of \(\alpha\) on \(n\) is tight up to constant factors. Each FTPL update admits a mixed-integer programming formulation whose size is polynomial in \(n\) and \(t\).
papers.summary: The setting is online learning for single-machine scheduling: each round the learner picks an ordering of n fixed jobs, processing times and due dates are then revealed, and the aim is low alpha-regret on maximum cumulative tardiness against the best fixed ordering in hindsight. In the stochastic case, Follow-the-Leader achieves expected 1-regret of O(n log n / Delta^2), where Delta is a distribution-dependent gap. In the adversarial case, regret is linear in T whenever alpha is below roughly (log2 n)/16, while a reduction to a surrogate problem solved with Follow-the-Perturbed-Leader gives O(n^2 sqrt(T)) expected alpha-regret for alpha = O(log n). Together these show that **the logarithmic dependence of alpha on n is tight up to constant factors**.

papers.title: Decision Models Are General-Purpose Process Reward Models
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) from verifiable outcomes gives a language agent one reward per episode: every step is credited alike, and nothing about the task is learned when all rollouts fail. The last mile, step-level credit, usually requires step labels, a learned critic, costly LLM judges or hand-written rules. We introduce DM-PRM, which turns a general-purpose decision model -- one answering yes/no questions with probabilities -- into a general-purpose process reward model (PRM), zero-shot: no step labels, no fine-tuning, no critic. DM-PRM asks one question per step and adds the standardised answers to the advantage. It plugs into any policy-gradient method; one model, with one question text per environment, serves household tasks, web shopping and multiple RL methods. With Qwen2.5-1.5B it lifts GRPO by over twenty points on ALFWorld and over ten on WebShop, overtakes GiGPO on ALFWorld and learns in far fewer iterations; it also improves GiGPO and GraphGPO on both benchmarks and reaches the highest success of our comparison, ahead of critic-based PPO and of state-of-the-art GiGPO, HGPO and GraphGPO. Its scores locate useful steps in failed rollouts, and trained agents drop idle actions and explore instead of circling. DM-PRM shows that step credit need not be learned: it can be asked for.
papers.summary: Training language agents with reinforcement learning from verifiable outcomes yields one reward per episode, so every step is credited equally and nothing is learned when all rollouts fail. `DM-PRM` uses a general-purpose decision model, one that answers yes/no questions with probabilities, as a zero-shot process reward model (PRM): it asks one question per step and adds the standardized answers to the advantage, with no step labels, fine-tuning, or learned critic. Using `Qwen2.5-1.5B`, it **lifts `GRPO` by over twenty points on `ALFWorld` and over ten on `WebShop`**, also improves `GiGPO` and `GraphGPO`, and reaches the highest success rate in the authors' comparison. Its scores identify useful steps inside failed rollouts, and trained agents drop idle actions and explore rather than circling.

papers.title: When Do LLM-Elicited Priors Help? A Controlled Audit of Language Models as Priors for Small-Sample Bayesian Regression
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly asked where to center the coefficients of a small-sample Bayesian regression, but the evidence is unclear: benchmarks are often built to match the prior and models may remember them. We audit this practice with one frontier and one flash-tier model, using hidden feature names, post-cutoff housing data and a pre-specified test that gives features the wrong descriptions. First, the models share their errors (correlation $0.92$--$0.99$ across draws, vendors and paraphrases): averaging $20$ draws is no more accurate than one, and treating draws as independent creates overconfidence. Much of this error comes from reporting each feature's effect alone, not with the others held fixed. Second, against the best classical prior, the LLM center helps clearly on one of four benchmarks (RMSE $-5.8\%$), marginally on two, and hurts mean RMSE on the fourth. Third, the LLM's stated uncertainty is unreliable; letting the data set the prior scale cuts the harm of a wrong center four-fold against a unit-variance prior. A pre-specified external test returned the verdict \textsc{partial}: on $18$ rule-selected problems the center helps on six and hurts on four, and a hard trust gate trusts a harmful prior while an evidence-weighted mixture is safer.
papers.summary: Large language models are increasingly asked to suggest where to center coefficient priors for small-sample Bayesian regression, but existing evidence is clouded by benchmarks that match the prior or may be memorized. This audit tests one frontier and one flash-tier model using hidden feature names, post-cutoff housing data, and a pre-specified test with deliberately wrong feature descriptions. Errors are shared across draws, vendors, and paraphrases (correlation 0.92-0.99), so averaging 20 draws is no more accurate than one, and against the best classical prior the LLM-suggested center **helps clearly on only one of four benchmarks (RMSE -5.8%)**, marginally on two, and hurts on the fourth. The models' stated uncertainty is unreliable; letting the data set the prior scale cuts the harm of a wrong center four-fold, and an evidence-weighted mixture is safer than a hard trust gate.

papers.title: Accelerating Muon with Spectral Residual Correction
papers.abstract: Muon constructs matrix updates by applying a matrix-sign transformation to momentum. A common route to accelerating Muon is to modify the gradient or momentum before this transformation. We explore a complementary direction: refining the parameter step while retaining Muon's momentum recursion. Derived from the parameter subproblem of the ADMM-Inspired Momentum framework, AIMuon uses the gradient--momentum residual to correct the tentative spectral step. The residual undergoes a separate matrix-sign transformation, while spectral--nuclear duality determines the relative weighting of the momentum and residual directions. In practice, both directions are approximated with Newton--Schulz iterations and their combination is rescaled to match Muon's update magnitude. We establish a stochastic stationarity bound for the corresponding exact iteration. On GPT-2-small, GPT-2-medium, and Qwen3-0.6B, AIMuon reaches Muon's final validation loss with 8.98\%, 10.05\%, and 6.49\% fewer optimization steps, respectively, while achieving lower final validation loss than Muon, Muon-Nesterov, and MONA.
papers.summary: The `Muon` optimizer builds matrix updates by applying a matrix-sign transformation to momentum, and most attempts to speed it up modify the gradient or momentum before that step. `AIMuon`, derived from an ADMM-inspired momentum framework, instead keeps the momentum recursion and corrects the parameter step using the gradient-momentum residual, which gets its own matrix-sign transformation and is weighted via spectral-nuclear duality; both directions are approximated with Newton-Schulz iterations. The authors prove a stochastic stationarity bound for the exact iteration. On `GPT-2-small`, `GPT-2-medium`, and `Qwen3-0.6B`, it reaches Muon's final validation loss in **8.98%, 10.05%, and 6.49% fewer optimization steps**, and ends with lower loss than `Muon`, `Muon-Nesterov`, and `MONA`.

papers.title: Weight-space programming and mechanistic interpretability for model editing in particle physics
papers.abstract: We demonstrate that weight-space programming and edits guided by sparse autoencoders can remove unwanted aspects of a particle-physics foundation model through direct edits to its weights. In a foundation model trained on jets, we observe that adding a single soft neutral particle causes large changes in jet classification, violating infrared safety. We locate the responsible attention heads with mechanistic analysis and trace the flaw's origin to pretraining on datasets with different reconstruction thresholds. We then propose two targeted approaches to repair the flaw: by removing three latent directions identified with sparse autoencoders, and by letting language-model agents edit the weights directly, without gradients and with only 50 queries to the model. Both their edits individually remove almost the entire flaw and leave the rest of the model's response nearly unchanged. Compared to fine-tuning, both methods change far fewer parameters. Although built only on $W$ and QCD jets, the edits carry over to all signal classes, the pretrained generator, and a newly trained regression head.
papers.summary: A particle-physics foundation model trained on jets changes its classification sharply when a single soft neutral particle is added, violating the physical requirement of infrared safety. Mechanistic analysis locates the responsible attention heads and traces the flaw to pretraining on datasets with different reconstruction thresholds. Two repairs are tested: removing three latent directions found with sparse autoencoders, and letting language-model agents edit the weights directly without gradients using only 50 queries to the model. **Each edit on its own removes almost the entire flaw** while leaving the rest of the model's response nearly unchanged and altering far fewer parameters than fine-tuning, and the fixes carry over to all signal classes, the pretrained generator, and a newly trained regression head.

papers.title: Fooling the Mind Twice: Human Detection of Audiovisual Deepfakes Under Repeated Exposure and Corrective Feedback
papers.abstract: Human deepfake detection remains unreliable, and whether reassessment with corrective feedback improves subsequent judgments remains unclear. This study examined differences between initial and repeated deepfake assessments among 110 participants using audiovisual stimuli from the FakeAVCeleb and Deepfake Detection Challenge (DFDC) datasets. Participants evaluated 40 videos from each dataset in phase 1 (PhaseI) and reassessed the same videos in phase 2 (PhaseII) under a procedure combining repeated presentation and corrective feedback. For the FakeAVCeleb dataset, the participants' mean accuracy increased by 4.68 percentage points from 63.30 in PhaseI to 67.98 in PhaseII (t(109)=5.61, p<.001, d_z=0.54). A judgment-level logistic regression with standard errors clustered by participant and video produced a consistent result: beta=0.208, SE=0.040, z=5.23, p<.001, {OR}=1.23. For the DFDC dataset, the participants' mean accuracy increased by 8.64 percentage points from 59.52% in PhaseI to 68.16% in PhaseII (t(109)=7.37, p<.001, d_z=0.70); the logistic model yielded: beta=0.375, SE=0.065, z=5.78, p<.001, {OR}=1.46. Improvements primarily came from fewer false negatives, while false-positive rates remained unchanged. However, judgment reversals occurred in 27.55% of FakeAVCeleb and 32.91% of DFDC assessments, with some initially correct judgments becoming incorrect upon reassessment. Despite the accuracy gains, repeated assessment did not eliminate judgment instability or residual error. Participants also exhibited consistent overconfidence, with mean self-rated confidence exceeding actual accuracy by 11.99 percentage points for FakeAVCeleb and 12.82 percentage points for DFDC across both phases. These findings indicate that repetition with corrective feedback moderately improves deepfake detection but does not fully resolve the limitations of human judgment.
papers.summary: Whether people get better at spotting deepfakes when they re-evaluate videos with corrective feedback is tested with 110 participants, who judged 40 audiovisual clips each from `FakeAVCeleb` and the Deepfake Detection Challenge (`DFDC`) dataset and then reassessed the same clips under repeated presentation combined with feedback. Mean accuracy rose **from 63.30% to 67.98% on `FakeAVCeleb` and from 59.52% to 68.16% on `DFDC`**, mainly through fewer false negatives, with false-positive rates unchanged. Judgments flipped in 27.55% and 32.91% of assessments respectively, including some correct answers becoming incorrect. Self-rated confidence exceeded actual accuracy by about 12 percentage points on both datasets across both phases.

papers.title: How Far Does Lossless Re-tokenization Move an RLVR Update?
papers.abstract: Language models assign different probabilities to token sequences that decode to the same string. In reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR), a trainer that re-encodes sampled text may train on a different token sequence with the same reward. We ask how far this moves a training update, and whether the movement has a consistent direction. From one checkpoint, we compare updates on the same rollouts, canonical and with selected tokens split into two pieces, against an update on a different batch. On Qwen2.5-0.5B with three-digit addition, splitting about one token in 25 moves the update 0.556 times as far as replacing the batch. The ratio rises with the fraction split in four models and depends on which tokens are split; within a checkpoint, the displacements share a direction across batches. In a tabular model with one table per tokenization and a single sampled string, we prove that whenever two strings below an unsampled prefix differ in probability, only the zero full-gradient step agrees across tokenizations, however it is weighted. In an audit that decodes and re-encodes resampled rollouts, re-encoding touches up to 5.2% of rollouts but at most 0.08% of tokens, far below the split fractions we test. Training on fixed rollouts, the canonical arm finishes ahead in 14 of 18 pre-registered pairs; the interval for the mean accuracy difference includes zero over all pairs and excludes it only under the registered exclusion rule, which favours the canonical arm.
papers.summary: In reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR), a trainer that decodes and re-encodes sampled text may train on a different token sequence for the same string and reward, and the authors measure how far that shifts a gradient update. On `Qwen2.5-0.5B` with three-digit addition, splitting about one token in 25 moves the update **0.556 times as far as replacing the whole batch**, with the ratio growing with the split fraction across four models and the displacements sharing a direction across batches. A tabular analysis proves that when two strings below an unsampled prefix differ in probability, only the zero full-gradient step agrees across tokenizations. In practice, re-encoding touches up to 5.2% of rollouts but at most 0.08% of tokens, and the canonical arm finishes ahead in 14 of 18 pre-registered training pairs, although the mean accuracy difference excludes zero only under the registered exclusion rule.

papers.title: Auditing and Adapting kNNGuard for Long-Context Prompts
papers.abstract: Training-free activation guardrails such as kNNGuard score prompts by comparing last-token LLM hidden states (the Layer Ensemble branch, kNNGuard LE) and sentence embeddings (all-MiniLM-L6-v2, Embedding-kNN) against a small reference bank (50 examples per class), combining the two branches into a Fused Ensemble (kNNGuard FE). While effective on short inputs (up to 256 tokens), standard kNNGuard degrades substantially on long inputs (over 1000 tokens): averaged across Qwen3.5-4B and Gemma-4-E4B-it, kNNGuard LE AUROC drops from 0.742 (0.777 and 0.706) to 0.554 (0.587 and 0.521) on Content Harm Moderation (Aegis-2.0), and from 0.994 (0.995 and 0.992) to 0.556 (0.598 and 0.513) on RAG Hallucination Detection (HaluBench). We trace this degradation to three causes: (1) hidden-state drift as sequence length increases, (2) hard 256-token truncation in MiniLM, and (3) signal dilution when a long document is compressed into a single final-token vector. We then evaluate three training-free adaptations: a Length-Routed Dual Bank, a long-context embedding model (Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B), and Strided Window Pooling across intermediate token positions. On Content Harm Moderation, dual-bank routing and strided window pooling raise long-context kNNGuard LE AUROC from 0.554 to 0.828 (+0.274 AUROC) and fused kNNGuard FE AUROC from 0.721 to 0.886 (+0.164 AUROC) with no latency overhead from bank routing. On RAG Hallucination Detection, where the guardrail must verify logical consistency between a generated answer and a retrieved passage, sentence-embedding kNN remains near random chance across all lengths, while length-matched LLM hidden states (kNNGuard LE) recover medium-length detection (AUROC = 0.853) but remain limited on over-1000-token passages (AUROC = 0.607) due to final-token dilution over long contexts.
papers.summary: `kNNGuard` is a training-free guardrail that scores prompts by comparing last-token hidden states and sentence embeddings against a small reference bank, and it degrades sharply on inputs over 1000 tokens: its hidden-state branch falls from 0.742 to 0.554 AUROC on `Aegis-2.0` content moderation and from 0.994 to 0.556 on `HaluBench` hallucination detection, averaged over `Qwen3.5-4B` and `Gemma-4-E4B-it`. The authors attribute this to hidden-state drift with sequence length, the 256-token truncation in `all-MiniLM-L6-v2`, and signal dilution in a single final-token vector. Three training-free fixes are tested: a `Length-Routed Dual Bank`, the long-context `Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B` embedder, and `Strided Window Pooling`. On content moderation, dual-bank routing plus strided pooling raise long-context AUROC **from 0.554 to 0.828** for the hidden-state branch and from 0.721 to 0.886 for the fused ensemble, while hallucination detection on passages over 1000 tokens stays limited at 0.607.

papers.title: ORION: Exact Canonical-State Supervision for Systematic Generalization in Transformers
papers.abstract: Autoregressive Transformers generally fail on out-of-distribution reasoning due to two primary reasons: positional corruption over long sequences and structural state drift across deep execution steps. We introduce ORION, a framework that supervises exact canonical execution states via auxiliary heads to anchor latent trajectories to valid computational manifolds. Across Folding, GridShift, and CLRS-30, a pre-registered 2 x 2 factorial shows that RoPE and ORION address orthogonal axes. RoPE recovers length extrapolation (59.8%), while ORION recovers depth extrapolation (66.7%). Moreover, their combination complementarily achieves strict additive gain in joint length-depth extrapolation, while either method alone offers near satisfactory results. Negative controls confirm that the gain depends strictly on exact canonical alignment; hashed state statistics fail to constrain depth extrapolation.
papers.summary: Autoregressive Transformers often fail on out-of-distribution reasoning, which the authors attribute to positional corruption over long sequences and state drift across deep execution steps. `ORION` adds auxiliary heads that supervise exact canonical execution states during training, and a pre-registered 2 x 2 factorial on `Folding`, `GridShift`, and `CLRS-30` crosses it with `RoPE` positional encoding. The two address separate axes: `RoPE` recovers length extrapolation (59.8%) while **`ORION` recovers depth extrapolation (66.7%)**, and their combination gives an additive gain on joint length-depth extrapolation. Negative controls using hashed state statistics do not help depth extrapolation, indicating that the gain depends on exact canonical alignment.

papers.title: Writing Weights or Training Them? Spatial Reasoning through Weight-Space Programming and Low-Rank Adaptation
papers.abstract: Weight-space programming lets a language model inspect and edit another model's weights, offering an alternative to gradient-based adaptation. We evaluated both approaches using Qwen3.5-0.8B on a fixed reference-frame task (128 items), StepGame (200 items), and two untrained distance-comparison tasks. With thinking enabled, the public patch (p50c) raised mean accuracy from 0.0% to 22.1% on the reference-frame task and from 19.2% to 33.7% on StepGame across three sampling seeds. Randomly permuting its weight change removed the gain. Further closed-form edits did not improve on p50c, whereas a rank-1 LoRA adapter trained on worked solutions reached 100% and 98.8%, respectively, with 0.09% trainable parameters. Removing the worked solutions from supervision prevented the adapter from passing the learning gate. The trained adapters reached 82% accuracy on unseen StepGame sentence templates, 42% on held-out difficulty levels 6-10 after training on levels 1-5, and 33-50% on unseen heading-answer combinations. Their target gains coincided with a sharp decline on the distance tasks: accuracy fell from 94% and 92% under p50c to 0-2%, and their outputs applied the StepGame solution template to distance questions. With thinking disabled and reasoning requested in the visible answer, the base model also solved the distance tasks while remaining weak on the target tasks. The comparison reveals a trade-off between improving spatial task performance and preserving neighbouring skills: the public edit restored completion while preserving distance performance, whereas supervised adaptation produced much larger target gains together with interference across tasks.
papers.summary: Weight-space programming, in which a language model inspects and edits another model's weights directly, is compared against gradient-based low-rank adaptation on spatial reasoning with `Qwen3.5-0.8B`. A public closed-form patch (`p50c`) lifts accuracy from 0.0% to 22.1% on a reference-frame task and from 19.2% to 33.7% on `StepGame`, whereas a rank-1 `LoRA` adapter trained on worked solutions reaches 100% and 98.8% with 0.09% trainable parameters. The adapter's gains come with interference: **accuracy on two untrained distance-comparison tasks falls from 94% and 92% under the patch to 0-2%**, as the adapter applies the `StepGame` solution template to distance questions. The trained adapters also generalize unevenly, reaching 82% on unseen sentence templates but 42% on held-out difficulty levels.

papers.title: Exercised, Rarely Recovered: What Public Reports Say About Recovery in 50 AI Agent Harnesses and Runtimes
papers.abstract: When an AI coding agent deletes the wrong files or a long agent run crashes, users fall back on recovery mechanisms: resume from a checkpoint, undo, ask for approval, read the log. Research runtimes promise stronger guarantees, such as saga-style compensation and transactional rollback. We ask what public evidence shows about whether either kind works in real use. Under a protocol frozen before data collection, we graded 12 persistent agent runtimes, 26 coding-agent harnesses and 12 research runtimes on eight recovery mechanisms, from not found to exercised in a real run, with two blind coding passes, adjudication and re-verification against archived sources. Recovery is exercised almost everywhere in practice: 11 of 12 runtimes and 25 of 26 harnesses have at least one real-use report. Yet of 128 such reports, only 19 describe the run fully recovering; 54 are partial and 45 failed. Checkpoint/resume recovered once in 27 reports, rollback once in 15. Research runtimes show the opposite profile: guarantees evaluated on benchmarks, none reported in operation, and compensation of external effects, their central guarantee, is offered by no harness at all.
papers.summary: Public reports are used to assess whether recovery mechanisms in AI agent systems, such as checkpoint/resume, undo, approval prompts, and rollback, actually work in real use. Under a protocol frozen before data collection, 12 persistent agent runtimes, 26 coding-agent harnesses, and 12 research runtimes were graded on eight recovery mechanisms with two blind coding passes and adjudication. Recovery is exercised nearly everywhere, but **of 128 real-use reports only 19 describe a full recovery**, with 54 partial and 45 failed; checkpoint/resume recovered once in 27 reports and rollback once in 15. Research runtimes show the reverse pattern, with guarantees evaluated on benchmarks but none reported in operation, and compensation of external effects is offered by no harness.

papers.title: PLoQ: A Prompt-Specific Low-Rank Basis for 4-bit Quantization of LLM Activations
papers.abstract: Low-bit activation quantization of large language models remains challenging, as a small number of dominant directions dictate the quantization range. State-of-the-art methods isolate these directions in a high-precision subspace through transformations calibrated offline and folded into the weights, which fixes the subspace for all prompts, leaving each prompt's few unique directions unprotected, and rules it out wherever no weight can absorb the transformation. We present PLoQ, a prompt-adaptive low-rank decomposition that extracts the dominant activation components before quantization, quantizes them separately, and restores them within the layer's GEMM, without modifying the weights. The low-rank component's basis is estimated from each prompt during prefill and reused throughout decoding. At the same bit width as state-of-the-art mixed-precision quantization (4-bit weights, activations and K/V cache with an eighth of the channels at 8 bits, about 4.2 bits per activation on average), PLoQ outperforms it on all six Llama and Qwen models from 1B to 70B parameters, at up to 8k tokens (16k on two of them), recovering up to 46% of the perplexity that the state of the art still loses to 4-bit activations. On Llama-3.1-8B at 8k tokens it adds only 4% to prefill and 8% to decoding.
papers.summary: Quantizing large language model activations to 4 bits is hard because a few dominant directions dictate the quantization range, and existing methods isolate those directions with offline-calibrated transformations folded into the weights, fixing the protected subspace for all prompts. `PLoQ` instead estimates a low-rank basis from each prompt during prefill, quantizes the dominant components separately, and restores them inside the layer's matrix multiply without modifying weights. At roughly 4.2 bits per activation, it outperforms state-of-the-art mixed-precision quantization on all six `Llama` and `Qwen` models from 1B to 70B parameters, **recovering up to 46% of the perplexity that the prior method still loses to 4-bit activations**. On `Llama-3.1-8B` at 8k tokens the overhead is 4% on prefill and 8% on decoding.

papers.title: Separating Automation Gains from Agent Contributions in AI-Assisted Model Validation
papers.abstract: LLM agents are being proposed for bank model validation, yet evaluations that compare agent-assisted work with manual practice credit the agent with gains that come from digitized evidence and deterministic tests. We propose a staged architecture in which an LLM-free controlled workflow (P1) is both the fallback and the control arm for individually authorized agent tasks (P2), and an attribution protocol that credits an agent only for faults P1 does not already report. The protocol charges decoy false alarms, unnecessary actions and endorsed developer assertions, counts invalid outputs as misses, folds newly automatable findings back into P1 with discovery credit, and fixes safety bounds and a break-even cost gate in advance. On a synthetic credit-scorecard harness, five scripted reference policies show why this matters: naive case accuracy (4/6) and pooled detection (3/5) tie four flawed policies, whereas the protocol separates all five and credits only the reference policy with detection beyond P1. One fold-back round raises a P1-parroting policy's naive scores without any change to the policy. A regression matrix of sixteen mutants covers nine ways in which earlier versions of the evaluation passed misleadingly. No LLM agent has been evaluated yet; we specify a falsifiable pilot.
papers.summary: Evaluations of LLM agents for bank model validation tend to credit the agent with gains that actually come from digitized evidence and deterministic tests. The authors propose a staged architecture in which an LLM-free controlled workflow (`P1`) serves as both fallback and control arm for individually authorized agent tasks (`P2`), together with an attribution protocol that credits an agent only for faults `P1` does not already report and charges it for false alarms, unnecessary actions, and invalid outputs. On a synthetic credit-scorecard harness with five scripted reference policies, naive accuracy and pooled detection tie four flawed policies, whereas **the protocol separates all five and credits only the reference policy with detection beyond the baseline workflow**. No LLM agent has been evaluated yet; the work specifies a falsifiable pilot.

papers.title: Epistemic Guard: Out-of-Process MCP Receipt Proxying, Post-Turn Prose Supervision, and Provenance-Gated Memory for Tool-Using Autonomous Agents
papers.abstract: Language-model agents using the Model Context Protocol (MCP) face three runtime verification gaps: (i) action fabrication, where post-tool prose narrates side effects that failed, timed out, or never ran; (ii) provenance collapse, where unverified model prose or web text enters durable memory alongside executed tool outputs; and (iii) syndicated echo amplification, where mirrored web pages satisfy multi-source corroboration from one origin. Existing MCP firewalls inspect wire calls before execution, while LLM-judge guardrails require multi-gigabyte VRAM without binding prose to receipts. We present epistemic-guard (v0.5.2), an open-source Python library and out-of-process stdio MCP receipt proxy (15 modules, 0 MiB GPU VRAM). epistemic-guard isolates Ed25519 signing keys out of process, writes RFC 6962 Merkle logs with AER-1 receipt translation, checks post-turn prose on CPU with SHA-256-verified OpenVINO INT8 encoders (4 models, 279.48 MB total; 82.67 MB on the supervision path), gates SQLite writes across 7 provenance domains, and collapses verbatim and lightly edited wire-syndicated RAG mirrors. On conformance suites, epistemic-guard rejects 100.0% of tampered receipts (200 Merkle leaves), passes 58/58 official AER-1 ingestion vectors and 50/50 reference-verified AER-1 exports, verifies 100.0% of 40 fault-injected wire calls and 100 concurrent appends with 0 key leaks, and blocks 100.0% of 100 unauthorized memory writes. Across $N=250$ frozen-benchmark traces, epistemic-guard reaches 93.2% accuracy at 17.9 ms warm median CPU latency (8.62 ms single-clause; 921.8 ms cold-start load), beating 12B-14B GPU judges by 6.4-6.8 points ($p=0.0259$, $p=0.0095$) at 4.26-4.5$\times$ lower latency; on $N=60$ live mcp-proxy traces, it catches 96.15% of hazards at 76.67% accuracy (38.24% FPR; $+18.34$ points over Stage-1-only, $p=0.001$) in 9.16 ms p50.
papers.summary: Agents using the Model Context Protocol (MCP) can narrate tool side effects that never happened, write unverified prose into durable memory alongside real tool outputs, and treat mirrored web pages as independent corroboration. `epistemic-guard` is an open-source Python library and out-of-process MCP proxy that signs tool receipts with keys held outside the agent process, records them in Merkle logs, checks post-turn prose against receipts with small CPU-only encoders, gates memory writes by provenance, and collapses syndicated mirrors. It passes its conformance suites, including rejecting all tampered receipts and blocking all 100 unauthorized memory writes, and on 250 frozen-benchmark traces reaches **93.2% accuracy at 17.9 ms median CPU latency**, 6.4-6.8 points above 12B-14B GPU judge models. On 60 live proxy traces it catches 96.15% of hazards but at 76.67% accuracy and a 38.24% false-positive rate.

papers.title: Reasoning in Two Dimensions: Quantifying Chain-of-Thought Faithfulness and Efficiency
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning exposes intermediate steps, but a correct answer does not establish that an LLM relies on the dependence expressed by those steps or reasons efficiently. We operationalize CoT faithfulness and efficiency within a common framework. Specifically, we represent a CoT as a semantic reasoning graph and decompose the model's predictive dependence along two complementary axes: dependence explained by semantic support versus additional reasoning history, and dependence allocated to answer-reaching versus off-path reasoning. This decomposition yields global and step-level measures of unfaithfulness and inefficiency. Controlled interventions show that the proposed metrics respond to hidden dependence and induced off-path reasoning as intended. Across mathematical and multi-hop reasoning tasks, answer-level unfaithfulness is consistently associated with greater predictive uncertainty, whereas both unfaithfulness and inefficiency exhibit weak or inconsistent associations with answer correctness. We further derive theoretically grounded, graph-aware fine-tuning objectives that improve the targeted reasoning properties without directly optimizing the computationally expensive metrics or compromising answer accuracy. Results indicate that accuracy and brevity provide incomplete assessments of reasoning quality: reliable CoT evaluation should also consider whether the LLM's predictive dependence is faithfully represented and efficiently allocated.
papers.summary: A correct answer from chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning does not show that the model actually relied on the stated steps or reasoned efficiently. The authors represent a CoT as a semantic reasoning graph and decompose the model's predictive dependence along two axes, semantic support versus additional reasoning history and answer-reaching versus off-path reasoning, yielding global and step-level measures of unfaithfulness and inefficiency that respond as intended to controlled interventions. Across mathematical and multi-hop tasks, answer-level unfaithfulness is consistently associated with higher predictive uncertainty, while **both unfaithfulness and inefficiency show weak or inconsistent associations with answer correctness**. Graph-aware fine-tuning objectives derived from the framework improve the targeted properties without reducing accuracy.

papers.title: EgoSurgHands: An Egocentric 3D Hand Pose Dataset & Benchmark for Open Surgery Training
papers.abstract: Surgical skill assessment, AR guidance, and robot learning from demonstration all benefit from 3D tracking of the surgeon's hands, yet no surgical dataset offers real egocentric articulated 3D hand pose. We introduce EgoSurgHands, a benchmark for real-captured egocentric hand pose estimation in open surgery training on synthetic pads. Captured with multi-sensor glasses, it contains 41,909 training hand-instance rows across 55 procedure recordings and 9,476 human-validated evaluation rows across 13 held-out recordings, spanning 13 tasks, 3 glove colors, and 4 trainees from first-year medical student to third-year resident. Each frame carries a multi-sensor stack: intrinsics, hand landmarks with per-hand confidence, timestamps, and eye gaze, plus SLAM extrinsics where SLAM succeeded. Evaluation labels combine sensor-fused pseudo-ground truth, human cross-review of every frame, surgeon adjudication of flagged cases, and an independent multi-view triangulated reference. Alongside the within-corpus, procedure-disjoint split, a leave-one-wearer-out protocol tested unseen trainees. Across eight methods evaluated zero-shot, from MANO-based reconstructors to the two-hand IntagHand and the keypoint-only MediaPipe Hands, egocentric pretraining was associated with stronger transfer on every held-out wearer. WildHands and JointTransformer had 18\% and 40\% lower PA-MPJPE, respectively, than the non-egocentric HaMeR. JointTransformer was the best performing model with an error of 14.95 mm. A substantial surgical domain gap remains, and the widely deployed MediaPipe Hands detected a hand in only 24.1\% of evaluation rows. As a baseline, a 58K-parameter residual corrector (JRN) on frozen backbones reached 10.96-14.85 mm PA-MPJPE on held-out wearers for the two ego-pretrained backbones. We release the dataset and benchmark code at https://egosurghands.github.io
papers.summary: No existing surgical dataset provides real egocentric articulated 3D hand pose, which is needed for skill assessment, AR guidance, and robot learning from demonstration. `EgoSurgHands` supplies 41,909 training hand instances from 55 recordings and 9,476 human-validated evaluation instances from 13 held-out recordings of open-surgery training on synthetic pads, captured with multi-sensor glasses across 13 tasks and 4 trainees. Among eight methods evaluated zero-shot, egocentric pretraining was associated with stronger transfer, with **`JointTransformer` best at 14.95 mm error** and `MediaPipe Hands` detecting a hand in only 24.1% of evaluation rows. A 58K-parameter residual corrector on frozen backbones reaches 10.96-14.85 mm on held-out wearers, and the dataset and benchmark code are released.

papers.title: One state, many questions: Opsis gives a frontier model typed eyes for pathology
papers.abstract: A synoptic pathology report is a checklist of questions with fixed answer sets, many composed from others. Pathology foundation models answer them accurately with one classifier trained with labels for each, and frontier language models, which compose freely, cannot fit a slide of fourteen thousand tiles in their context. On 189 breast report questions, frontier models that read a written description of the slide or look at a thumbnail and tiles of it answer at 0.50 to 0.66, below the majority class at 0.67. A description is written before the question is known, and a look covers a handful of tiles. We present Opsis, which lets the model ask instead: a typed question interface on a frozen pathology encoder. A slide is encoded once, a question names an operator, arguments and candidates given at runtime, and the answer is a probability over the candidates. We build it as a 10 M parameter decoder on frozen Virchow2 tokens (Opsis-S) and inside Qwen3-VL-8B (Opsis-V). Asking Opsis-S, four frontier models answer the breast questions at 0.78 to 0.79, and on 3,797 pan cancer questions asking is 8.6 points above reading. On 995 composite questions that Opsis-S was never trained on, a frontier model composing its answers reaches 0.76, against 0.69 when it looks at the slide and 0.78 for ABMIL trained on each composite. On a pan cancer question set over 10,712 TCGA slides, one Opsis-S decoder matches linear probes trained per question on TITAN and PRISM2 embeddings (average accuracy 0.69 against 0.70 and 0.68). Opsis-S also separates CAMELYON16 metastases without training on that cohort (AUROC 0.86) and localises necrosis from report labels alone (tile AUROC 0.93).
papers.summary: Synoptic pathology reports consist of many fixed-answer questions, but frontier language models cannot fit a whole slide of thousands of tiles in context and, given a written description or a thumbnail with a few tiles, answer 189 breast report questions at 0.50 to 0.66, below the 0.67 majority-class rate. `Opsis` provides a typed question interface on a frozen pathology encoder: a slide is encoded once, and each query names an operator, arguments, and candidate answers, returning a probability over the candidates. Built as a 10M-parameter decoder on frozen `Virchow2` tokens (`Opsis-S`), it lets **four frontier models answer the breast questions at 0.78 to 0.79**, and on 995 composite questions it was never trained on a frontier model composing its answers reaches 0.76, near the 0.78 of `ABMIL` trained per composite. One decoder also matches per-question linear probes on `TITAN` and `PRISM2` embeddings across 10,712 `TCGA` slides.

papers.title: Reliable Behavior Discovery via False Discovery Rate Control
papers.abstract: Reliable methods for discovering behavior patterns in large generative models are increasingly essential as models become both more complex and capable. We formalize behavior discovery as a problem class of interest and highlight the task of controlling false discovery rate (FDR) as crucial for guaranteeing reliability in behavior discovery. Building upon the multiple hypothesis testing literature, we propose DISCO (Discovery through Iterative Search with COarsened $e$-processes), a method which provably controls FDR in behavior discovery under mild conditions. DISCO improves power over previous related eBH-based approaches by allowing for adaptivity to a data-dependent number of hypotheses to be tested. We demonstrate empirically that DISCO controls FDR with higher power than comparable approaches on both synthetic data and a novel empirical evaluation of FDR-controlling methods in settings where large generative models act as both discovery engines and targets. Code is available at https://github.com/google-deepmind/disco .
papers.summary: Discovering behavior patterns in large generative models is formalized as a problem class in which controlling the false discovery rate (FDR) is the key reliability requirement. The proposed method, `DISCO` (Discovery through Iterative Search with COarsened e-processes), builds on multiple hypothesis testing and **provably controls FDR under mild conditions** while adapting to a data-dependent number of hypotheses, which improves power over earlier `eBH`-based approaches. Experiments on synthetic data and on a new evaluation in which large generative models act as both discovery engines and targets show FDR control with higher power than comparable methods. Code is released.

papers.title: Schema-Validated LLM Workflows: A Benchmark Protocol and Comparative Evaluation Across Six Python Implementations
papers.abstract:
Large language models are increasingly used to extract records, generate SQL, summarize reports, answer policy questions, and route operational work. At these software boundaries, parseable output is necessary but does not establish task correctness. We present a reproducible benchmark protocol, a public executable artifact, and a confirmatory live API evaluation that separate structural validity from task-specific correctness across five business workflow tasks and six Python implementation conditions: PydanticAI, LangGraph, DSPy, CrewAI, Agno, and a framework-free SDK reference.
  We hypothesize that (H1) schema validity and task quality are separable, (H2) structured-output binding paths are heterogeneous under a shared model and lowest-common-denominator contract, and (H3) condition-by-task interactions concentrate failures rather than shifting all tasks equally. Confirmatory analysis uses distinct task instances (100 extraction and 50 per other task, with three nested replicates) under a frozen analysis plan, yielding a 5400-row primary matrix with equivalence margins and Holm-adjusted contrasts against the SDK reference.
  In the eligible confirmatory run, overall schema validity was 0.684 and mean automated quality was 0.638. PydanticAI, LangGraph, and DSPy retained near-ceiling schema validity with mean quality 0.91-0.94, while the plain SDK, Agno, and CrewAI conditions were substantially lower in this package and model configuration. Schema-valid rows still produced many task-score flags, especially in extraction and compliance QA, and quality residuals show strong condition-by-task interactions (including a workflow collapse for CrewAI). Labelled ablations address retry budgets and feature-using mechanisms; primary contrasts remain system-configuration findings, not causal attributions to marketed library features.
papers.summary: Parseable LLM output at software boundaries does not guarantee task correctness, so the authors build a benchmark protocol that separates schema validity from task-specific quality across five business workflow tasks and six Python implementations: `PydanticAI`, `LangGraph`, `DSPy`, `CrewAI`, `Agno`, and a framework-free SDK reference.
