A confirmatory live API run under a frozen analysis plan yields a 5400-row matrix with overall schema validity of 0.684 and mean automated quality of 0.638. **`PydanticAI`, `LangGraph`, and `DSPy` kept near-ceiling schema validity with mean quality of 0.91-0.94**, while the plain SDK, `Agno`, and `CrewAI` conditions scored substantially lower, including a workflow collapse for `CrewAI`. Schema-valid outputs still drew many task-score flags, and the authors frame the contrasts as system-configuration findings and not causal attributions to library features.

papers.title: Recurrent Amplification and Exact Nonexpansiveness Criteria for Query-Driven Erasure
papers.abstract: The Query-derived Erase Direction (QED) augments a rank-one linear attention update with a key-orthogonal query component. Under scalar decay, this correction leaves the eigenvalues of each homogeneous state transition unchanged, while the propagation of an initial perturbation depends on the ordered product of these transitions. We construct a periodic token sequence with fixed key and query projections for which every one-step spectral radius is below one but the spectral radius of the period product exceeds one. The same construction yields a sufficient condition for mean-square growth under independent uniform token sampling. For rank-one erasure with channel-wise decay, we derive a necessary and sufficient spectral-norm test for one-step nonexpansiveness that can be evaluated in $O(d)$ time. The test agrees with direct singular value decomposition on all 1,800 operators evaluated. In a counterfactual replay of a selected head of Qwen3.5-0.8B-Base, the terminal gain on a 4,096-token repeated-text sequence increased from 0.99938 to 1.3977 with the feature and checkpoint gate trajectories held fixed.
papers.summary: The Query-derived Erase Direction (`QED`) adds a key-orthogonal query component to a rank-one linear attention update, and under scalar decay this leaves each state transition's eigenvalues unchanged even though perturbation growth depends on the ordered product of transitions. The authors construct a periodic token sequence in which every one-step spectral radius is below one yet the spectral radius of the period product exceeds one, and derive a sufficient condition for mean-square growth under uniform token sampling. For rank-one erasure with channel-wise decay they give a necessary and sufficient spectral-norm test for one-step nonexpansiveness computable in O(d) time, which agrees with direct singular value decomposition on all 1,800 operators tested. In a counterfactual replay of one head of `Qwen3.5-0.8B-Base`, the terminal gain on a 4,096-token repeated-text sequence **rose from 0.99938 to 1.3977**.

papers.title: Federated and Balanced $k$-means: Communication Efficiency, Privacy, and Heterogeneity
papers.abstract: Collaborating on data across organizations in healthcare and finance demands methods that preserve privacy while enabling effective analysis. Vertical Federated Learning (VFL) facilitates clustering across data where different parties hold different features of the same entities without sharing raw data. However, existing VFL clustering methods suffer from two key limitations: vulnerability to information leakage and the creation of imbalanced clusters. To address these limitations, we propose Fabric, a balanced and privacy-preserving federated $k$-means algorithm. Our method decomposes the balanced clustering problem into independent subproblems for each client, using the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM) to efficiently handle the balance constraints. Under the semi-honest model, Fabric provides provable privacy guarantees by injecting calibrated noise into local objective evaluations. Extensive evaluations on ten real-world datasets show that Fabric achieves a superior utility-privacy trade-off compared with state-of-the-art methods and converges faster. Specifically, Fabric reduces SSE by 29.1\% on average and improves balance performance by 1.41$\times$, while being 26$\times$ faster on average.
papers.summary: Vertical Federated Learning (VFL) lets parties holding different features of the same entities cluster jointly without sharing raw data, but existing methods leak information and produce imbalanced clusters. `Fabric` is a balanced, privacy-preserving federated k-means algorithm that decomposes the balanced clustering problem into independent per-client subproblems, handles the balance constraints with the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM), and injects calibrated noise into local objective evaluations for provable privacy under the semi-honest model. On ten real-world datasets it **reduces sum of squared errors by 29.1% on average**, improves balance by 1.41×, and runs 26× faster on average than state-of-the-art methods.

papers.title: CoEvoBench: Can LLMs Drive Recursive Co-Evolution of Agentic Systems?
papers.abstract: The performance of an LLM agent depends on both its model and its harness, the code that mediates its interaction with tools and environments. Can LLM researchers drive this co-evolution as a recursive improvement process, deciding round after round which component to change when each change alters the value of the other? Existing benchmarks evaluate post-training or data research with the harness out of scope, or harness optimization with the model fixed, leaving this joint decision unmeasured. We introduce CoEvoBench, a benchmark that evaluates LLMs as researchers co-evolving the model and harness of a target agent across five agentic domains. Researchers start from a common base model and initial harness, train and revise within a 24-hour budget, and submit a model-harness pair that is scored on separate test tasks. Across five frontier researchers, the strongest closes more than four fifths of the gap to an instruction-tuned reference system, and co-evolution succeeds on interaction tasks but rarely on long-horizon coding. These results suggest that current LLMs can make a strong first improvement, but cannot yet turn feedback from an improved system into the next one. CoEvoBench provides a controlled testbed for measuring the research capabilities that recursive co-evolution requires.
papers.summary: An LLM agent's performance depends on both its model and its harness, and `CoEvoBench` tests whether LLMs acting as researchers can improve the two jointly, choosing round after round which component to change. Across five agentic domains, each LLM researcher starts from a common base model and initial harness, trains and revises within a 24-hour budget, and submits a model-harness pair scored on separate test tasks. Among five frontier researchers, **the strongest closes more than four fifths of the gap to an instruction-tuned reference system**, with co-evolution succeeding on interaction tasks but rarely on long-horizon coding. The authors conclude that current LLMs can make a strong first improvement but cannot yet turn feedback from an improved system into the next one.

papers.title: Highly Efficient Vertical Federated Clustering with Triangle-Inequality-based Pruning
papers.abstract: In many real-world scenarios, multiple parties hold complementary feature subsets for the same samples but cannot share raw data. This makes efficient clustering over distributed feature subsets an important and challenging problem. While vertical federated learning (VFL) enables such collaboration, existing VFL clustering methods often require many communication rounds or substantial local computation. To address these limitations, we first propose TriCD, an exact pruning method for CDKM that preserves the same cluster assignments under the same initialization. TriCD constructs triangle-inequality bounds on demand to skip redundant objective evaluations with negligible extra space. Building upon this, we propose FedTriCD, an efficient federated clustering algorithm. By decomposing the global objective into client-local subproblems, FedTriCD enables pruning-based local optimization using only local data. FedTriCD further reduces communication by allowing multiple local updates between server synchronizations. A proximal regularization term is introduced to control the drift caused by infrequent communication. Our theoretical analysis establishes the exactness and finite convergence of TriCD and provides a bounded-error server-side update guarantee for FedTriCD. Experiments on multiple real-world datasets demonstrate the efficiency and clustering quality of the proposed methods. TriCD achieves up to a 50.07$\times$ speedup over \Lloyd's algorithm. Moreover, FedTriCD achieves competitive clustering quality while requiring fewer local evaluations and fewer communication rounds than state-of-the-art federated clustering methods.
papers.summary: Clustering over feature subsets held by different parties under vertical federated learning (VFL) typically needs many communication rounds or heavy local computation. `TriCD` is an exact pruning method for `CDKM` that builds triangle-inequality bounds on demand to skip redundant objective evaluations while producing the same cluster assignments, and `FedTriCD` extends it to the federated setting by decomposing the objective into client-local subproblems, allowing multiple local updates between synchronizations, and adding a proximal term to control drift. Theory establishes exactness and finite convergence for `TriCD` and a bounded-error server update for `FedTriCD`. On real-world datasets `TriCD` achieves **up to a 50.07× speedup over Lloyd's algorithm**, and `FedTriCD` reaches competitive clustering quality with fewer local evaluations and communication rounds than prior federated methods.

papers.title: CTRL: Concurrent Training and Rollout for LLM Reinforcement Learning via GPU Co-Residency
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training of large language models runs two GPU workloads with different hardware demands: rollout decoding, which is dominated by memory access and whose batch shrinks as responses finish, and a dense learner. Current systems either time-share every GPU between them, paying serial phases and switches, or split GPUs into pools whose sizes change only in whole devices. We present CTRL, which makes co-residency a third RL execution layout: every GPU runs a learner rank beside a persistent rollout engine, sharing the device under CUDA MPS. A host-owned learner makes the layout fit: optimizer state stays in host memory, and policy weights stream layer by layer through a bounded GPU window. A publication gate trains each ready batch first and waits only before releasing the next policy, keeping a dropless staleness bound. A step-time bound guides compute-share selection, and a GPU-time ledger explains overlap and sharing costs. On H100, A800, and RTX 4090 GPUs with Qwen3 models, CTRL achieves 1.11-2.24$\times$ the throughput of the stronger of verl's asynchronous baselines across 24 workload settings with the staleness limit set to two, and 1.23$\times$ verl's colocate_async on eight H100 GPUs. With the same learner, co-residency is 1.10-1.26$\times$ faster than time-sharing on all three platforms and 1.10-1.30$\times$ faster than the best measured whole-GPU split on H100 DAPO-Math workloads at 256-528 trajectories per step, on four and eight GPUs.
papers.summary: A stereo visual-inertial quadrotor cannot tell at onset whether a camera blackout is timed or tied to its position, yet the two need opposite responses: hover-and-wait completes 93 of 96 timed blackouts but 0 of 96 spatial outages. The authors frame recovery as a worst-condition active-observability problem and add a portable module at the reference interface of an unchanged host controller, coordinating loss detection, jerk-limited braking, bounded backward probing, and rejoining with no retraining. On a preregistered 48-scene benchmark of 1,920 flights, the full `MPPI` configuration reaches **88.5% worst-condition completion**, 29.2 points above `DATT-L1` and ahead of all six external baselines, and attaching the module to `SimpleFlight` raises its worst-condition completion by 17.7 points to 86.5%. Trace diagnostics indicate that survival hinges on visual-inertial re-acquisition when vision returns, not on suppressing blind inertial drift.

papers.title: Portable Active Recovery under Timed and Position-Dependent Visual Outages
papers.abstract: When a camera blackout depends on physical position rather than elapsed time, stable hovering prevents visual recovery and mission completion. On stereo visual-inertial quadrotors without external localization, an exogenous timed blackout and an endogenous position-dependent dark zone appear identical at loss onset yet require opposite responses: hover-and-wait completes 93/96 timed blackouts but 0/96 spatial outages (13 hard failures), whereas blind continuation traverses many spatial zones yet fails heavily during timed blackouts. We formulate visual-outage recovery as a worst-condition active-observability problem and introduce a portable recovery module at the reference interface of an unchanged host controller with zero retraining. Using deployable telemetry alone, the module coordinates visual-loss detection, jerk-limited braking, bounded backward probing, settled rejoining, height-integral trim, and an optional gated prior-map branch. On a preregistered 48-scene benchmark (1,920 flights), our full MPPI configuration reaches 88.5% [81.2, 94.8] worst-condition completion, outperforming development-selected DATT-L1 by +29.2 pp [17.7, 40.6] and exceeding all six external baselines after Bonferroni correction. Attached without retraining to SimpleFlight, the module lifts worst-condition completion by +17.7 pp [7.3, 28.1] to 86.5% (and 90% across 1.0x/1.25x speeds, 0/80 hard failures). Trace diagnostics reveal that survival hinges on visual-inertial re-acquisition asymmetry at vision return -- not blind IMU drift suppression - and uncover a bias-drift map crossover confirmed on 72 held-out EuRoC windows.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training of large language models runs rollout decoding and a dense learner on GPUs, and current systems either time-share each GPU between the two or split GPUs into whole-device pools. `CTRL` introduces a co-residency layout in which every GPU runs a learner rank beside a persistent rollout engine under CUDA MPS, made to fit by keeping optimizer state in host memory and streaming policy weights layer by layer through a bounded GPU window, with a publication gate that bounds policy staleness without dropping batches. On H100, A800, and RTX 4090 GPUs with `Qwen3` models it achieves **1.11-2.24× the throughput of the stronger of `verl`'s asynchronous baselines** across 24 workload settings. With the same learner, co-residency is 1.10-1.26× faster than time-sharing and 1.10-1.30× faster than the best whole-GPU split on `DAPO-Math` workloads.

papers.title: A Plan or an Adversarial Example? A Round-Trip Check for Latent World Models
papers.abstract: If we optimize an image until a classifier is confident it shows a cat, we may get an adversarial example, not a cat. Planning with a latent world model is a similar search for actions whose predicted future is closest to the goal. Is the result a plan, or an adversarial example of the world model? We show that it can be either. On the released DINO-WM and LeWM, more iterations of the cross-entropy method (CEM) lower the predicted cost but lose up to half of the problems CEM had already solved. The model's own predictions do not reveal these failures. We propose a simple test that executes the plan after every iteration and counts the problems a planner solves and then loses. Unlike an image, a plan comes with its actions, which our round-trip check reads back from the predicted states with a small network, penalizing mismatches. The check reads back the sum of each block of five actions, the part that two consecutive predicted states determine. Without retraining the world model and at only 0.2% to 3.1% more planning time, it improves the widely used planners CEM and MPPI on three released world models, and gains more where planners lose more problems. Without replanning, success rises from 0.39 to 0.76 on Wall with DINO-WM and from 0.56 to 0.94 for MPPI on JEPA-WM. With replanning (MPC), it rises from 0.70 to 0.81 on Cube with LeWM.
papers.summary: Planning with a latent world model searches for actions whose predicted future matches a goal, which can yield an adversarial example of the model instead of a workable plan. On the released `DINO-WM` and `LeWM`, running more iterations of the cross-entropy method (CEM) lowers predicted cost but loses up to half of the problems it had already solved, and the model's own predictions do not reveal these failures. The proposed round-trip check uses a small network to read the summed actions of each five-action block back from consecutive predicted states and penalizes mismatches, adding only 0.2% to 3.1% planning time and requiring no world-model retraining. Without replanning, success rises **from 0.39 to 0.76 on `Wall` with `DINO-WM`** and from 0.56 to 0.94 for `MPPI` on `JEPA-WM`; with replanning it rises from 0.70 to 0.81 on `Cube` with `LeWM`.

papers.title: When Students Fail to Learn from Teachers: Learning Dynamics of On-Policy Distillation
papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) has become a core technique for post-training large language models, enabling students to learn from dense token-level supervision on their own generations. However, even with a capable teacher, OPD training can be unstable, leading to excessive response length, repetitive generation, and severe performance degradation. One example is \textit{spurious agreement}, where the student maintains high overlap with the teacher at the states visited but produces repetitive generations. Although such failures have been observed, the mechanisms behind these failures remain poorly understood. To address this gap, we investigate OPD through the lens of learning dynamics, tracing three mechanisms from local analysis to subsequent on-policy sampling. We first identify states where sampled-token OPD updates fail to correct teacher--student mismatch and characterize them using the student's mass on the teacher's top-$p$ set. We then show that learning from the teacher is difficult at mismatched states and that their gradients can also affect with learning at other tokens. Finally, using a termination-token mismatch as a case study, we study how continued training on mismatched states influences on-policy sampling, suppressing the student's current modes and leading the student toward states where the teacher is unreliable . These findings help explain the benefits of supervised fine-tuning (SFT) initialization and motivate targeted correction of states where student and teacher are mismatched.
papers.summary: On-policy distillation (OPD), where a student language model learns from a teacher's token-level supervision on the student's own generations, can become unstable and produce overly long, repetitive outputs even with a capable teacher. The authors analyze its learning dynamics and trace three mechanisms: sampled-token updates fail to correct teacher-student mismatch at certain states (characterized by the student's probability mass on the teacher's top-p set), gradients from those states interfere with learning at other tokens, and **continued training on mismatched states suppresses the student's current modes and pushes it toward states where the teacher is unreliable**. A termination-token mismatch serves as the case study, and the findings help explain why supervised fine-tuning (SFT) initialization helps and motivate targeted correction of mismatched states.

papers.title: Distillation with Errors: Sparse Unbiased Backpropagation for Knowledge Distillation
papers.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) trains a student to match a teacher's output distribution. However, full-vocabulary KD requires costly output-head backpropagation. To reduce this cost, we introduce Distillation with Errors (DWE). Our key insight is that minibatch training already approximates the training gradient, so per-position backpropagation does not need to be exact. DWE therefore exploits the zero-sum structure of logit gradients to construct sparse paired gradient estimates whose expectation matches the full-vocabulary gradient. It then uses geometry-aware pairing and stratified sampling to further reduce estimation variance. We prove that the estimator is unbiased and evaluate DWE's gradient estimation accuracy and training efficiency. At the same sampling budget, DWE reduces hidden-state and output-weight gradient MSE by 63.5% and 57.9%, respectively, compared with importance sampling. In off-policy KD, it achieves up to a $1.95\times$ output-head speedup and reduces training time by 10.4-15.7% relative to full-vocabulary KD. In on-policy distillation (OPD), it achieves up to a $2.20\times$ output-head speedup. DWE maintains competitive downstream performance in both settings. Our code is available at https://github.com/dwe-lab/DWE.
papers.summary: Full-vocabulary knowledge distillation (KD) requires expensive backpropagation through the output head at every position. `DWE` (Distillation with Errors) exploits the zero-sum structure of logit gradients to build sparse, paired gradient estimates that are provably unbiased, and uses geometry-aware pairing and stratified sampling to reduce variance. At the same sampling budget it cuts hidden-state and output-weight gradient error by 63.5% and 57.9% versus importance sampling, and it delivers **up to a 1.95x output-head speedup in off-policy KD (10.4-15.7% less training time) and up to 2.20x in on-policy distillation** while keeping downstream performance competitive.

papers.title: Spatiotemporal Landslide Runout Reconstruction from Sparse Observations with LAPIS-SHRED
papers.abstract: Reconstructing the spatiotemporal evolution of landslide runout from limited observations is a central challenge in geohazard assessment: transient flow dynamics are rarely observed directly, and available data are often confined to post-event deposits or brief monitoring windows. We apply LAPIS-SHRED (LAtent Phase Inference from Short time sequence using SHallow REcurrent Decoders) to reconstruct runout events near Mount St. Helens, USA. Trained on physics-based simulation ensembles, the framework supports both backward reconstruction from single frame and forward prediction from short initial window across different runout regimes. Using 32 sensor observations from a single timepoint, LAPIS-SHRED recovers complete runout trajectories with NRMSE below 5.8%, robust across varying observational and training conditions. Validation against observed deposits yields spatial correlation of r = 0.843 against the calibrated simulator's r = 0.853. These results suggest that latent-space temporal inference offers a viable pathway for spatiotemporal landslide reconstruction under extreme observational constraints typical of field settings.
papers.summary: Landslide runout is rarely observed while it happens, so its evolution usually has to be inferred from post-event deposits or brief monitoring windows. The authors apply `LAPIS-SHRED` (LAtent Phase Inference from Short time sequence using SHallow REcurrent Decoders), trained on physics-based simulation ensembles, to runout events near Mount St. Helens, supporting both backward reconstruction from a single frame and forward prediction from a short initial window. From 32 sensor observations at a single timepoint it **recovers complete runout trajectories with normalized error below 5.8%**, and its spatial correlation with observed deposits is r = 0.843 against 0.853 for the calibrated simulator.

papers.title: MAPES: Multi-Value Alignment Pipeline via Expert Specialization
papers.abstract: Aligning large language models (LLMs) with human preferences requires simultaneously satisfying multiple, often competing values. Existing preference optimization methods collapse these into a single implicit signal, and even multi-objective extensions optimize within a shared parameter space, leaving cross-value conflicts unresolved. We propose MAPES, a multi-value alignment paradigm in which conflict resolution is a first-class concern at every pipeline stage: it first decomposes supervision into value-specific experts trained in isolated parameter subspaces, then recomposes them via preference-aware value merging and a lightweight harmonization stage that aligns the merged model with the expert ensemble. Across five preference alignment benchmarks, MAPES outperforms strong direct preference optimization (DPO) variants and multi-objective baselines on the benchmark-level average, with no large degradation on GSM8K and GPQA; matched controls isolate the contribution of each stage.
papers.summary: Aligning large language models with human preferences involves several competing values, which existing preference optimization methods collapse into one signal or optimize in a shared parameter space. `MAPES` instead trains value-specific experts in isolated parameter subspaces, recombines them with preference-aware merging, and adds a lightweight harmonization stage that aligns the merged model with the expert ensemble. Across five preference alignment benchmarks it **outperforms strong direct preference optimization (`DPO`) variants and multi-objective baselines on the benchmark-level average**, with no large degradation on `GSM8K` and `GPQA`, and matched controls isolate each stage's contribution.

papers.title: Cross-Platform Production Signatures of State-Linked Information Operations
papers.abstract: An information operation active on several platforms presents different names, personas, and topics on each. Its working routine is harder to change. We call this routine the operation's production signature: the regularities in when and how its accounts post, reply, and repost. We measure it from timestamps and coarse action types only, using no content, profile metadata, or network ties, as timing and action profiles for accounts and learned action-gap policies for populations. We then ask which parts of a signature carry over to another platform and which belong to a single operation. We train models on Twitter archives of four state-linked operations and apply them to Internet Research Agency (IRA) accounts on Reddit, with no Reddit training labels. They rank the IRA accounts at AUC 0.90-0.94. Content detectors on the same route fall from 0.98 within a platform to 0.81. Daily phase accounts for most of the transfer. Posting volume reverses direction between platforms, and action mix follows the role accounts hold on each platform. What transfers is not unique to the IRA: a second operation shares the same working-hours window, and action-gap policies separate every operation from organic accounts (AUC 0.96-1.0) without consistently ranking their own operation first. On 938 Telegram channels, groups that forward the same sources keep ordinary hours and pace but publish original posts in the same ten-minute windows more often than chance. This pattern is invisible when accounts are examined one at a time. Our results suggest that timing and action traces learned on one platform can help flag likely operations on another.
papers.summary: State-linked information operations change names, personas, and topics across platforms, but their working routine of when and how accounts post, reply, and repost is harder to disguise. The authors measure this production signature from timestamps and coarse action types alone, train models on Twitter archives of four operations, and apply them to Internet Research Agency (IRA) accounts on Reddit with no Reddit labels. The models **rank the IRA accounts at AUC 0.90-0.94, while content detectors on the same route fall from 0.98 within a platform to 0.81**, with daily phase accounting for most of the transfer. On 938 Telegram channels, groups forwarding the same sources publish original posts in the same ten-minute windows more often than chance, a pattern invisible when accounts are examined one at a time.

papers.title: Double counting in LLM evidence fusion: exact posteriors separate rule compliance from posterior gain
papers.abstract: Language models fuse reports in retrieval, multi-agent consensus and agent memory, where treating shared-source reports as independent can double count evidence. A common remedy is an instruction to count each source once. Its value depends on the receiver's raw baseline. Pricing it needs an exact reference. We build the graded-dependence exact reference: binary worlds with single-report reliability 0.65 and four dependence levels, whose disclosed parameters give every world an exact posterior and every rule a target risk. The paired gain protocol scores raw and instructed answers of four configurations on 2,976 worlds. Agreement and gain separate in both directions. At $\delta$ = 0, claude-opus-5-5 and gpt-6.1-sol agreed with the rule within 0.001 in 744 of 744, and the instruction raised their posterior mismatch by 0.044; gpt-6-luna agreed in 165 of 744 and gained 0.0140 (95% interval 0.0064 to 0.0219); claude-haiku-5-5's gain moved from -0.0295 ($\delta$ = 0) to +0.0302 ($\delta$ = 1) (descriptive). The prespecified first-child endpoint contrast, gain at $\delta$ = 1 minus $\delta$ = 0, was 0.0342 (0.0303 to 0.0382). In the preregistered tests, the raw source-weight contrast was positive (0.259, 95% interval 0.182 to 0.337; Holm rejected zero) and the grouping endpoint difference was not detected (0.0004, -0.0023 to 0.0031). This interval excludes differences larger than 0.0031 in magnitude and lies within the registered precision bound of $\pm$0.0046. The reference prices the rule before any model call. The paired gain, estimable as a Brier difference on labelled deployment items, decides adoption per receiver and prompt condition.
papers.summary: Language models that combine reports in retrieval, multi-agent consensus, or agent memory can double count evidence when reports share a source, and the usual fix is an instruction to count each source once. The authors build a synthetic reference of 2,976 binary worlds with known report reliability and four dependence levels, so every world has an exact posterior, and score raw versus instructed answers from four model configurations. Following the rule and gaining accuracy turn out to be separate: at zero dependence, **`claude-opus-5-5` and `gpt-6.1-sol` already agreed with the rule in 744 of 744 worlds and the instruction worsened their posterior mismatch by 0.044**, while `gpt-6-luna` agreed in 165 of 744 and gained 0.0140. The authors conclude that the instruction should be adopted per receiver and prompt condition, based on a paired gain that can be estimated on labelled deployment items.

papers.title: Do Senior Agents Do Their Job? Measuring Role Integrity in How LLM Agents Use Subordinate Material
papers.abstract: Multi-agent LLM systems increasingly divide long tasks among subagents whose reports a senior agent turns into the final answer. Such a division of labor pays off only if each agent, and above all the senior agent, carries out the duties of its role. Current evaluations, however, mostly score the final answer, and a fluent, well-cited answer cannot show whether the senior agent weighed its subagents' reports or merely aggregated them. To assess whether a senior agent meets its assigned responsibilities, we define role integrity as the preservation of an agent's functional responsibilities when it acts on its subordinates' material. To measure it, we introduce RI-Bench, a behavioral benchmark grounded in the structures and public records of three institutional hierarchies: peer review, appellate adjudication, and parliamentary inquiry. We choose these hierarchies because their rules explicitly assign the senior role a duty toward subordinate material, and together they cover three basic duties: to weigh, to verify, and to relay. Rather than scoring output correctness, we measure how senior agents' outputs respond to controlled changes in subordinate material, using rule-based checks and a rubric-guided LLM judge calibrated against human annotation. Across eight LLMs and over 12,000 agentic episodes, senior agents rarely adopt a planted procedural error (2.9% of rulings) but often follow a majority of generic reviews (up to 71% of decisions) or drop witnesses' stated limitations (up to 65% of cited claims). Obligation prompts reduce these failures without removing them, and they also shift behavior in the control conditions. These findings motivate direct, obligation-specific evaluation of role integrity rather than inferring it from general capability or explicit role instructions. Code and data are available at https://github.com/jxtse/ri-bench.
papers.summary: Multi-agent LLM systems hand subtasks to subagents whose reports a senior agent turns into a final answer, but scoring only that answer cannot show whether the senior agent weighed the reports or merely aggregated them. `RI-Bench` measures this role integrity using tasks modeled on peer review, appellate adjudication, and parliamentary inquiry, checking how senior agents' outputs respond to controlled changes in subordinate material across the duties to weigh, verify, and relay. Across eight LLMs and over 12,000 episodes, senior agents **rarely adopt a planted procedural error (2.9% of rulings) but follow a majority of generic reviews in up to 71% of decisions and drop witnesses' stated limitations in up to 65% of cited claims**. Prompts spelling out the obligation reduce these failures without removing them and also shift behavior in the control conditions.

papers.title: Dynamic Memory-enhanced Pattern Relevance Prediction for Long-tailed Graph Classification
papers.abstract: Long-tailed graph classification (LTGC) is common in real-world graph datasets, where a few large head graphs provide rich structural information while many smaller tail graphs offer fewer structural cues, making it harder to learn discriminative representations for tail graphs. To address this size-based imbalance, we propose Dynamic Memory-enhanced Pattern Relevance Prediction (DMPRP), which transfers structural patterns from head graphs to tail graphs. Given a graph representation as a query, a dynamic expert memory module inspired by Knowledge-diverse Experts (KDEX) generates a residual vector that augments the original representation. We train the module using co-occurrence triplets sampled from head graphs at the node, rooted subgraph, and random-walk neighborhood levels. Experiments on five graph classification benchmarks show that DMPRP improves tail performance, and ablation studies show that both the expert module and random-walk supervision contribute to these gains. A controlled experiment on PTC further examines pattern transfer when smaller graphs are denser than larger ones. Our code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/DMPRP-73A5.
papers.summary: In long-tailed graph classification (LTGC), a few large head graphs carry rich structural information while many small tail graphs offer few cues, making tail representations hard to learn. `DMPRP` (Dynamic Memory-enhanced Pattern Relevance Prediction) transfers structural patterns from head to tail graphs using a dynamic expert memory module that generates a residual vector to augment each graph representation, trained on co-occurrence triplets at the node, rooted-subgraph, and random-walk neighborhood levels. On five graph classification benchmarks it **improves tail performance, with ablations showing both the expert module and random-walk supervision contribute**, and a controlled experiment on `PTC` examines transfer when smaller graphs are denser than larger ones.

papers.title: How Does SAM-3 Adapt? Capacity, Update Geometry, and Domain Transfer
papers.abstract: Promptable segmentation foundation models are increasingly used in specialized domains, but it remains unclear how SAM-3 should be fine-tuned when adapting it beyond its original training distribution. We study this question by comparing five adaptation families --LoRA, HiRA, KRAdapter, QuanTA, and Full Fine-Tuning-- across five segmentation datasets spanning medical imaging, remote sensing, and dense material segmentation. Across these datasets, compact parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods often match or approach Full Fine-Tuning in DSC and IoU, suggesting that strong in-domain adaptation does not always require updating the full model. However, this performance cannot be explained by nominal adapter rank or trainable parameter count alone. To investigate why different methods perform similarly, we analyze their update spectra and their behavior under LoveDA Urban/Rural transfer. Our SVD analysis shows that Full Fine-Tuning updates are spectrally compressible. However, successful PEFT methods do not simply recover the same update directions; instead, they often concentrate changes in different components and subspaces. The domain-transfer study further shows that methods with similar in-domain performance can respond differently under distribution shift. Together, these results suggest that SAM-3 adaptation is often capacity-saturated in practice, while competitive fine-tuning arises through method-specific update paths rather than a single low-rank approximation to Full Fine-Tuning.
papers.summary: How the promptable segmentation model `SAM-3` should be fine-tuned for specialized domains is unclear, so the authors compare `LoRA`, `HiRA`, `KRAdapter`, `QuanTA`, and full fine-tuning on five datasets spanning medical imaging, remote sensing, and dense material segmentation. **Compact parameter-efficient methods often match or approach full fine-tuning in Dice and IoU**, yet neither adapter rank nor trainable parameter count explains the results. Spectral analysis shows full fine-tuning updates are compressible, but the successful adapters concentrate their changes in different components and subspaces rather than recovering the same directions, and methods with similar in-domain scores diverge under `LoveDA` Urban/Rural distribution shift.

papers.title: GaLF-ST: Gaussian Latent Fields for Spatial Transcriptomics Reconstruction
papers.abstract: Spatial transcriptomics (ST) measures gene expression at known tissue locations to reveal tissue organization and cellular function. Expression prediction requires modeling both local spatial relationships and associations among genes. Existing methods typically model expression using coordinate networks without explicit spatial parameterization. To address limited spatial sampling and sparse expression observations of ST, some methods firstly fit intermediate embeddings and then train expression predictors, but a latent representation suited to expression reconstruction may be difficult to predict from spatial coordinates. The two training stages can impose different demands on the latent representation. In this paper, we propose GaLF-ST, a Gaussian latent field method in which learnable Gaussian centers and anisotropic covariances determine the weights of latent vectors at each location. A shared nonlinear decoder maps their weighted average to multigene expression. In GaLF-ST, observed expression error jointly updates the Gaussian geometry, latent vectors, and decoder parameters. We further establish a unified benchmark across seven dataset groups and three held-out fractions, comparing GaLF-ST with four representative methods using the same locations, splits, gene panels, and scoring rules. Across tissues and observation densities, GaLF-ST achieves leading overall reconstruction performance, recovering spatial gene expression patterns and preserving tissue domains from limited observations while substantially reducing runtime and GPU memory usage.
papers.summary: Spatial transcriptomics (ST) measures gene expression at known tissue locations, and reconstructing expression from sparse observations requires modeling both spatial relationships and associations among genes. `GaLF-ST` represents tissue as a Gaussian latent field, where learnable Gaussian centers and anisotropic covariances weight latent vectors at each location and a shared nonlinear decoder maps the weighted average to multi-gene expression, with everything trained jointly from expression error rather than in two stages. On a unified benchmark of seven dataset groups and three held-out fractions against four representative methods, it **achieves leading overall reconstruction performance while substantially reducing runtime and GPU memory usage**.

papers.title: Structure Over Scale: Rethinking Adaptation for Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards
papers.abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) is often framed as a choice between the expressivity of Full Fine-Tuning (FFT) and the efficiency of Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA). We find that this framing misses an important variable: the geometry of the update. Under a common cold-start GRPO protocol, LoRA exhibits rank collapse: performance remains broadly stable at low rank, then fails abruptly as rank increases. On DeepMath-Hard, for example, accuracy drops from 73.1% at r=64 to 4.7% at r=128. In contrast, Weight-Decomposed Low-Rank Adaptation (DoRA) and Quantum-Informed Tensor Adaptation (QuanTA) remain stable over a wider tested optimization region and are competitive with FFT while updating less than 0.6% of the model parameters. Spectral analysis reveals a corresponding difference in learned update structure: collapsed LoRA concentrates its update energy into relatively few effective directions, whereas structured adapters produce substantially more distributed updates. These results suggest that nominal rank and parameter count alone are insufficient to characterize adaptation in RLVR - the structure imposed on the reachable update manifold also matters. Finally, across three 8B base models, adapter behavior aligns with both frozen-weight spectral structure and reported pre-training scale, motivating the Model Maturity Hypothesis: the adaptation geometry that works best may depend on properties already encoded during pre-training. We present this as a falsifiable hypothesis rather than a causal conclusion. The code can be found here https://github.com/Shrimpstanot/structure-over-scale
papers.summary: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) is usually framed as a trade-off between Full Fine-Tuning (FFT) and Low-Rank Adaptation (`LoRA`), but the authors argue the geometry of the update matters as well. Under a common cold-start `GRPO` protocol, `LoRA` shows rank collapse, staying stable at low rank and then failing abruptly: on `DeepMath-Hard`, **accuracy drops from 73.1% at r=64 to 4.7% at r=128**. Weight-Decomposed Low-Rank Adaptation (`DoRA`) and Quantum-Informed Tensor Adaptation (`QuanTA`) stay stable over a wider region and are competitive with FFT while updating less than 0.6% of parameters, and spectral analysis shows collapsed `LoRA` concentrates update energy in few directions. Across three 8B base models, adapter behavior tracks frozen-weight spectral structure and pre-training scale, which the authors offer as a falsifiable Model Maturity Hypothesis.

papers.title: Where Structure Enters a World Model: From Predictive Fit to Physical Rollout
papers.abstract: Predictive world models learn to forecast observations, but accurate short-term predictions do not necessarily produce physically coherent behavior over longer horizons. We investigate how incorporating physical structure can strengthen world models while retaining their underlying predictive objectives. Across token-based models of planetary motion and JEPA-style visual models of mechanical systems, we study conserved-quantity supervision, symmetry-aware representations, temporal consistency, and learned structured dynamics. In planetary motion, angular-momentum supervision improves autonomous next-token forecasting, while the benefits of temporal regularization depend on the accompanying physical objective and representation. In visual models, generating rollouts through supervised energy-based dynamics heads produces more faithful trajectories and phase-space evolution. Together, these findings highlight the importance of how physical structure participates in prediction: improvements in an auxiliary physical readout or a local acceleration estimate do not automatically translate into more reliable long-horizon behavior. Evaluations across initial conditions and physical parameter shifts further reveal where these benefits persist and where generalization remains limited. Our study supports physical structure as a practical means of improving predictive world models and provides a unified framework for understanding its effects on representations, learned transitions, and autonomous rollouts. The central lesson is that effective physical inductive biases should help models both represent physical regularities and use them to generate future states.
papers.summary: Predictive world models can forecast the next observation accurately yet drift into physically incoherent behavior over long horizons. The authors test several ways of injecting physical structure, including conserved-quantity supervision, symmetry-aware representations, temporal consistency, and learned structured dynamics, in token-based models of planetary motion and JEPA-style visual models of mechanical systems. Angular-momentum supervision improves autonomous next-token forecasting, and generating rollouts through supervised energy-based dynamics heads yields more faithful trajectories, but **gains in an auxiliary physical readout or local acceleration estimate do not automatically translate into more reliable long-horizon rollouts**. Tests across initial conditions and physical parameter shifts show where the benefits persist and where generalization remains limited.

papers.title: Git History Is a Pangenome: Repetition in Code Training Corpora and What Deduplication Removes, Keeps and Misses
papers.abstract: Code models are increasingly trained on the full history of software repositories, every version of every file, rather than on a single snapshot. The tools that deduplicate training data were built for snapshots, and what they do to a history has not been measured. We measured it on a pre-registered random sample of 306 public repositories, 25 mature projects, and the 12 repositories behind the SWE-bench benchmark. A history is mostly repetition: in the vocabulary of text indexing, a pangenome, one text in many near-identical variants. The history of a typical repository holds the equivalent of 19 copies of its current code, and a mature repository holds 89. The reason is that each edit changes a few lines and leaves the rest of the file in place: nine tokens in ten of a changed file already existed before the change. Exact-match deduplication removes none of these copies, since no two versions are identical. Large training pipelines already deduplicate their snapshots by grouping near-identical files and keeping one. Applied across versions, the same step brings the repetition down to about two copies. But two problems remain. The deduplicator keeps one version of each file, and in widely used implementations, including the one we measured, the rule for choosing that version ignores dates, so for half of all files the version kept for training is an old one. Sorting versions newest first before deduplicating fixes the problem at almost no cost. The second problem is benchmark answers. Benchmarks such as SWE-bench test a model on real bug fixes, and a merged fix survives in a median of 18 later versions of the files it changed. Therefore, removing benchmark fixes needs a separate step that checks every version. We turn the measurements into a short set of rules for teams that train on code history, and release the instruments and frozen outputs.
papers.summary: Code models are increasingly trained on full repository histories, but deduplication tools were built for single snapshots and their effect on histories had not been measured. On a pre-registered sample of 306 public repositories, 25 mature projects, and the 12 repositories behind `SWE-bench`, the authors find **a typical history holds the equivalent of 19 copies of its current code and a mature one 89**, because nine in ten tokens of a changed file already existed before the change. Exact-match deduplication removes none of this, while near-duplicate grouping cuts it to about two copies but, in widely used implementations, keeps an old version for half of all files, which sorting newest-first fixes at almost no cost. Benchmark fixes also survive in a median of 18 later versions of the files they changed, so removing them requires a separate step that checks every version.

papers.title: The Vulnerability Window: Decision Instability in Quantized Reward Models
papers.abstract: Reward models and LLM judges are routinely quantized to 4 bits so that scoring many candidates stays affordable, and the usual check is that benchmark accuracy barely moves. That check is close to blind. Across eight reward models from two families (0.6B-8B), three generative judges and four 4-bit quantizers, quantization rewrites 1.1-12.3% of pairwise preference decisions on RewardBench while aggregate accuracy moves by as little as 0.03 points (p = 1.00), because the errors it fixes and introduces cancel. Flips concentrate where the full-precision margin is small relative to the quantization noise scale sigma: a Gaussian approximation Phi(-|m|/sigma) describes the aggregate rate, over-predicting it in all 30 scalar settings and failing for generative judges, and occupancy of the resulting vulnerability window falls from 25% to 7% with model size, which is what makes small judges fragile. The churn stays within noise under benign best-of-16 and becomes clear under adversarial pressure for some quantizers (146:54 harmful:helpful flips on one family, reversing sign on another). Downstream it changes what ships: across six (model, quantizer) pairs from two families, 14.6-65.7% of problems get a different best-of-64 selection while only 2.6-9.6% get a different final answer, with selections changing 5-8x more often than answers in every pair, and the pair the benchmark calls identical (0.03 points, p = 1.00) still changes 34.5% of them. Benchmark churn ranks that downstream change (rho = 0.89); benchmark accuracy does not order it reliably. Held-out audits then locate the useful diagnostic in the margin rather than the Gaussian: every margin-based predictor orders flips identically (AUC 0.927), and on the level a directly measured churn rate wins in-distribution. As a routing signal it is matched by plain top-k. The contribution is the characterization, not the model.
papers.summary: Reward models and LLM judges are commonly quantized to 4 bits and validated by checking that benchmark accuracy barely moves. Across eight reward models (0.6B-8B), three generative judges, and four 4-bit quantizers, **quantization rewrites 1.1-12.3% of pairwise preference decisions on `RewardBench` while aggregate accuracy moves by as little as 0.03 points**, because the errors it fixes and introduces cancel. Flips concentrate where the full-precision margin is small relative to quantization noise, and smaller models have far more decisions in that window (25% versus 7%), which makes small judges fragile. Downstream, 14.6-65.7% of problems get a different best-of-64 selection though only 2.6-9.6% get a different final answer, and the benchmark flip rate predicts that downstream change (rho = 0.89) where accuracy does not.

papers.title: Co-Evolving Behavioral Agents and Detectors for Adaptive Information Operations
papers.abstract: Detectors of state-sponsored information operations (IOs) are trained on campaigns that platforms have already taken down. They lose much of their accuracy on an actor they have not seen, even though no operator in the archived data is trying to avoid them. A real operator wants two things, to reach an audience and to avoid being caught. We present IO-AI, a framework that gives simulated agents these two capabilities, engagement and evasion, and tests what each one does to detection. The agents are built from the posting behavior of real campaigns and choose the emotion, type, and timing of each post. An agent and a detector then train against each other in turn. We rank the trained agents by how hard they are to detect and train one detector on them from easiest to hardest. On 20 Twitter IO campaigns, this detector reduces missed detections of adaptive agents by 65% relative to a detector trained only on the archived campaigns, at a similar false-alarm rate. On actors it has never seen it reaches an F1 of 0.81, against 0.62. We find that an agent trained to seek engagement becomes easier to catch, because it learns the fast, emotional retweeting that archived campaigns were caught producing. An agent that was trained for engagement before the game keeps its engagement lead after it learns to evade. We also introduce a behavioral distance metric that compares two groups of accounts using only their unlabeled posting histories. The larger the distance between two groups, the worse a detector trained on one does on the other (Spearman rho = -0.58), so the metric can be used to choose which new groups to test first.
papers.summary: Detectors of state-sponsored information operations are trained on campaigns already taken down and lose accuracy on unseen actors, even though no operator in the archives was trying to evade them. `IO-AI` builds simulated agents from real campaign posting behavior that choose the emotion, type, and timing of each post, trains agents and detectors against each other in turn, and then trains one detector on the agents ordered from easiest to hardest to detect. On 20 Twitter campaigns this detector **reduces missed detections of adaptive agents by 65% at a similar false-alarm rate and reaches F1 0.81 versus 0.62 on unseen actors**. Agents trained for engagement become easier to catch because they learn fast, emotional retweeting, and a behavioral distance metric computed from unlabeled posting histories predicts how poorly a detector transfers between groups (Spearman rho = -0.58).

papers.title: FM4SAR-Bench 1.0: Towards A Fair Benchmark for Evaluating Foundation Models for SAR Image Interpretation
papers.abstract: Foundation models have advanced SAR image interpretation but created a heterogeneous, fragmented model ecosystem. Existing models differ substantially in their input, training data, objectives, architectures, and release policy, yet the field lacks a unified taxonomy and comparative framework. Current evaluations rely primarily on task-specific benchmarks, which are ill-suited to fair comparison among models with fundamentally different input-output formats and task paradigms, and often overlook data transparency, reproducibility, interpretability, and deployment readiness. Limited SAR data accessibility also means high reported performance does not guarantee access to training data, code, or weights, limiting reproduction, benchmarking, and deployment. To address these issues, we propose a systematic taxonomy and hierarchical evaluation framework for SAR-related foundation models: five rating levels, six dimensions, and fine-grained criteria, with separate protocols for VFMs and VLMs. Beyond overall ratings, it yields interpretable multidimensional capability profiles and supports user-defined weighting, so rankings follow user priorities. Utilizing a fixed auxiliary multimodal large language model in combination with human review, we conduct a systematic meta-analysis and multidimensional assessment of 76 VFMs and 40 VLMs. In terms of SAR benchmark task performance under our framework, SAR-native VLMs do not significantly outperform remote sensing VLMs pretrained on mixed multimodal corpora in which SAR is one of several modalities. This lack of clear advantage is largely due to data availability: large-scale, high-quality, public annotated SAR data remain scarce, restricting both model and training-data scale for SAR-native models. The framework provides a structured basis for requirement-aware model selection and remains extensible as new models emerge.
papers.summary: Foundation models for SAR image interpretation differ widely in inputs, training data, objectives, architectures, and release policies, and task-specific benchmarks cannot compare them fairly or account for transparency, reproducibility, and deployment readiness. `FM4SAR-Bench 1.0` proposes a taxonomy and hierarchical evaluation framework with five rating levels, six dimensions, and separate protocols for vision foundation models and vision-language models, supporting user-defined weighting of the dimensions. Applying it to 76 vision and 40 vision-language models, using a fixed auxiliary multimodal LLM plus human review, the authors find **SAR-native vision-language models do not significantly outperform remote sensing models pretrained on mixed multimodal corpora**. They attribute this to the scarcity of large, high-quality public annotated SAR data.

papers.title: From Acting to Learning: Experience Selection toward Continually Learning Agents
papers.abstract: Successful agent interactions provide training data, but success alone does not determine which records a student should learn from. We examine experience selection for a 4B language agent as a component of continual agent learning. Nine selectors are compared across two fixed experience pools, eight initialization seeds, and two sampling seeds, yielding 288 trained students. Each student is evaluated on 128 development task groups with a common executor. With equal global selection freedom, 256 distinct contents, and 768 training presentations, optimizer-aware gradient selection reaches 81.45\% and 73.19\% success in the two pools. Its gains over global random selection are 8.25 and 5.96 percentage points; gains over global high-NLL selection are 4.10 and 4.05 points. All eight initialization-level contrasts are positive against both baselines in each pool. Relaxing coverage constraints improves gradient selection but reduces random-selection performance, showing that the ranking rule and selection space must be considered together. A separately frozen replication on 128 reserved task groups is complete; its equal-source gradient-minus-random and gradient-minus-high-NLL differences are +7.03 and +5.03 points, respectively.
papers.summary: Successful agent interactions can be reused as training data, but success alone does not say which records a student model should learn from. The authors compare nine experience selectors for a 4B language agent across two fixed experience pools and multiple seeds, training 288 students and evaluating each on 128 development task groups. With matched selection budgets, **optimizer-aware gradient selection reaches 81.45% and 73.19% success in the two pools, 8.25 and 5.96 points above global random selection** and about 4 points above selecting high-loss examples. Relaxing coverage constraints helps gradient selection but hurts random selection, and a frozen replication on 128 reserved task groups gives gains of +7.03 and +5.03 points over the two baselines.

papers.title: Hierarchical Hybrid-Coordinate Flow Matching for Accurate and Physically Plausible Apo-to-Holo Protein Generation
papers.abstract: Predicting holo-like protein conformations from apo structures is essential in structure-based drug design. Most existing apo-to-holo models operate in Cartesian space and achieve strong global accuracy. However, high global accuracy does not ensure physically valid local backbone geometry. Internal-coordinate models offer local control and validity, but regressive generation can amplify angular errors, known as the lever-arm effect. We introduce CrypticFlow, a hierarchical flow-matching model that combines these two complementary representations. An ESM-3-conditioned E(3)-equivariant graph network first generates sparse C$\alpha$ anchors in Cartesian space. A conditional midpoint Transformer then recursively fills the gaps in local internal coordinates. During recursive generation, the decoder constrains the distance between each midpoint and any sequence-adjacent parent anchor to the corresponding apo C$\alpha$-C$\alpha$ distance. On the D3PM test split, CrypticFlow achieves the lowest median and mean C$\alpha$ RMSD at published baseline capacities. Across five independent training models, the median and mean direct RMSD are 1.333 $\pm$ 0.056 angstroms and 2.766 $\pm$ 0.041 angstroms, respectively. The quality of local geometry also improves substantially. Our model achieves 99.58 $\pm$ 0.02% adjacent-distance fidelity and 95.87 $\pm$ 0.25% pseudo-angle fidelity, measured within 0.2 angstroms and 20{\deg} of the holo reference. Then, we reconstruct the predicted C$\alpha$-only traces into all-atom structures using the cg2all coarse-to-all-atom backmapping method and evaluate their physical and geometric quality with MolProbity. Our model achieves a MolProbity score of 3.034 $\pm$ 0.054, outperforming the evaluated baselines. These results show that a hierarchical flow-matching model with hybrid coordinates can recover global accuracy while retaining local fidelity.
papers.summary: Predicting ligand-bound (holo) protein conformations from unbound (apo) structures matters for structure-based drug design, but Cartesian-space models can produce invalid local backbone geometry while internal-coordinate models amplify angular errors along the chain. `CrypticFlow` is a hierarchical flow-matching model that first generates sparse C-alpha anchors in Cartesian space with an `ESM-3`-conditioned equivariant graph network, then recursively fills the gaps in internal coordinates with a midpoint Transformer constrained by apo distances. On the `D3PM` test split it achieves the lowest C-alpha error among baselines, with **median RMSD of 1.333 angstroms alongside 99.58% adjacent-distance fidelity and 95.87% pseudo-angle fidelity**. After all-atom reconstruction with `cg2all`, it also obtains the best `MolProbity` score among evaluated baselines at 3.034.

papers.title: BusemannFormer: Horospherical Self-Attention for Hyperbolic Graph Transformers
papers.abstract: Hyperbolic neural networks excel on hierarchical graph data, yet existing hyperbolic Transformers largely adapt conventional attention without explicitly exploiting the ideal boundary, a geometric structure closely tied to tree hierarchy. We propose Horospherical Self-Attention (HSA): each query selects an ideal-boundary direction and scores keys by their Busemann depth along that direction, yielding a token-to-token hyperbolic attention kernel. We establish a flat-limit connection to dot-product attention, characterize score level sets as horospheres, and bound key-side gradients. HSA is integrated into BusemannFormer, a fully hyperbolic graph Transformer, with a log-depth variant that uses query depth to modulate attention concentration. We further introduce a finite-boundary-dictionary extension supporting linear-complexity global attention. Experiments on hierarchical and citation graphs show that BusemannFormer-LD outperforms the evaluated baselines on several node-classification benchmarks and achieves competitive performance across diverse graph structures.
papers.summary: Existing hyperbolic Transformers mostly adapt conventional attention without using the ideal boundary, a geometric structure closely tied to tree hierarchy. Horospherical Self-Attention (HSA) has each query pick a boundary direction and score keys by their Busemann depth along it, and the authors show a flat-limit connection to dot-product attention, characterize score level sets as horospheres, and bound key-side gradients. The mechanism is built into `BusemannFormer`, a fully hyperbolic graph Transformer with a log-depth variant and a finite-boundary-dictionary extension for linear-complexity global attention. On hierarchical and citation graphs, **`BusemannFormer-LD` outperforms the evaluated baselines on several node-classification benchmarks** and is competitive across diverse graph structures.

papers.title: FedQCal: Quadratic Programming with Dual-Space Calibration for One-Shot Federated Learning
papers.abstract: One-shot federated learning must combine heterogeneous client models after a single upload. Different local class distributions make it difficult to decide which client updates to retain. We propose FedQCal, which uses a reference model trained on a small labeled server set to define alignment requirements for aggregation. The key idea is to retain sufficient reference alignment while avoiding unnecessarily large aggregation coefficients. A minimum-norm quadratic program (QP) enforces these requirements. Classification loss on the same server examples selects a merge through two dual variables, so the alignment thresholds need not be prescribed in advance. We prove that the selected coefficients remain exact QP solutions at their induced thresholds. A perturbation bound explains how coefficient norm limits the amplification of projection errors. Experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and SVHN show gains over one-round FedAvg in most settings. Ablations support reference-guided weighting and coefficient calibration, even with one labeled server image per class.
papers.summary: One-shot federated learning must merge heterogeneous client models after a single upload, and differing local class distributions make it hard to decide which client updates to keep. `FedQCal` trains a reference model on a small labeled server set and solves a minimum-norm quadratic program (QP) that retains sufficient alignment with that reference while avoiding unnecessarily large aggregation coefficients, with the alignment thresholds chosen through two dual variables using classification loss on the same server examples. The authors prove the selected coefficients are exact QP solutions at their induced thresholds and give a perturbation bound linking coefficient norm to error amplification. Experiments on `CIFAR-10`, `CIFAR-100`, and `SVHN` show **gains over one-round `FedAvg` in most settings, even with one labeled server image per class**.

papers.title: Felid: A Flexible and Efficient Design for Transformer Fine-Tuning over Encrypted Data
papers.abstract: Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) enables non-interactive, privacy-preserving transformer fine-tuning, protecting highly sensitive data as inputs to large language models. Prior work has predominantly pursued efficiency gains through architectural refinements, yet overall performance remains bounded by the substantial cost inherent in encrypted computation. To address these issues, we target the bottleneck at the ciphertext operation level. Concretely, we propose a novel packing strategy that supports batching over a flexible number of inputs, making it well-suited for fine-tuning workloads. In addition, we design operation-specific matrix evaluation algorithms that significantly reduce (i) the number of ciphertext rotations and relinearizations, and (ii) the number of bootstrapping invocations. Additionally, we exploit functional bootstrapping to fold the evaluation of element-wise activation functions directly into the bootstrapping step, thereby reducing overall computational complexity. As a result, our framework achieves a $30\times$ reduction in ciphertext rotations and relinearizations across all matrix operations, as well as a $2.5\times$ reduction in FHE bootstrapping invocations over the entire computation flow, compared to the latest state-of-the-art work. It is worth noting that our system completes fine-tuning of a 2-layer BERT-style model with a batch size of 16 in 650 seconds, achieving a $8\times$ speedup over the state-of-the-art work.
papers.summary: Fine-tuning transformers under Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) keeps sensitive training data private but remains bounded by the cost of encrypted computation. `Felid` targets the ciphertext-operation level with a packing strategy that batches a flexible number of inputs, operation-specific matrix evaluation algorithms, and functional bootstrapping that folds element-wise activation functions into the bootstrapping step. The authors report a 30x reduction in ciphertext rotations and relinearizations across matrix operations and 2.5x fewer bootstrapping invocations than the prior state of the art. Fine-tuning a 2-layer `BERT`-style model with batch size 16 completes in 650 seconds, **an 8x speedup over the previous best system**.

papers.title: Learning Adaptive Defense Strategies: Fine-Tuned LLMs for Network Security Games under Network Mobility
papers.abstract: Large language models(LLM) show promise for strategic reasoning, yet their ability to compute game-theoretic equilibria under dynamic conditions remains largely unexplored. This work investigates whether fine-tuned LLMs can serve as solver-free surrogates for online equilibrium computation in honeypot allocation, a setting in which network mobility continuously reshapes the underlying attack graph and forces repeated re-solving of a two-player zero-sum game. We construct a dataset of 270 security games on networks of 8--25 nodes with solver-grounded equilibrium labels, and evaluate four classes of predictor over 1{,}524 held-out mobility events: non-learned baselines, six open-weight architectures evaluated zero-shot, the same six after LoRA fine-tuning, and four proprietary models as an external reference point. Predictions are scored without post-hoc repair against exact game-theoretic criteria: exploitability against an optimal attacker best-response, equilibrium support accuracy, and distributional distance. Fine-tuning reduces exploitability across every architecture, and fine-tuned open-weight models of modest size outperform every zero-shot predictor, including proprietary ones; no zero-shot model at any tier reaches the floor set by uniform allocation. Stratifying by mobility type exposes a qualitative shift that aggregate metrics conceal: zero-shot models do not condition on whether a departing node lies on an attack path, while fine-tuned models recover this distinction. We further find that validation loss is negatively rank-correlated with task performance, and that output validity, rather than predictive accuracy, is the binding constraint on further progress.
papers.summary: Honeypot allocation on a network whose nodes move requires repeatedly re-solving a two-player zero-sum security game, and the authors test whether fine-tuned large language models can act as solver-free surrogates for that equilibrium computation. They build 270 games on networks of 8 to 25 nodes with solver-derived equilibrium labels and compare non-learned baselines, six open-weight models zero-shot, the same six after `LoRA` fine-tuning, and four proprietary models over 1,524 held-out mobility events, scoring exploitability, equilibrium support accuracy, and distributional distance. Fine-tuning lowers exploitability for every architecture, and **modestly sized fine-tuned open-weight models beat every zero-shot predictor, including proprietary ones, while no zero-shot model reaches the floor set by uniform allocation**. Validation loss turns out to be negatively rank-correlated with task performance, and output validity rather than predictive accuracy is identified as the binding constraint.

papers.title: GEG-SAM: Gaze Exploration-Guided Segment Anything Model for Weakly Supervised Polyp Segmentation
papers.abstract: Endoscopist gaze offers an unobtrusively acquired record of lesion-oriented visual exploration during routine clinical inspection, providing relevant supervision for tasks. However, existing methods treat fixations as isolated spatial prompts directly associated with the target, overlooking the fact that natural gaze records a continuous visual search process in which fixations are temporally connected, spatially organized, and coupled with the visual content. Interpreting each fixation independently based only on its local visual content overlooks the temporal evolution and spatial organization of the gaze trajectory, whereas modeling relations among fixations alone cannot reveal the visual semantics of the regions they attend to. To this end, we propose the Gaze Exploration-Guided Segment Anything Model (GEG-SAM), a principled weakly supervised framework designed to explicitly exploit structured gaze relations and their corresponding visual cues to modulate SAM for polyp segmentation. Specifically, GEG-SAM captures structured gaze relations by modeling the temporal dynamics and spatial topology of gaze exploration. It then associates these relational representations with fixation-aligned visual context to derive gaze-conditioned tokens, which are further injected into the frozen SAM encoder to modulate its pretrained image features. In this way, GEG-SAM effectively exploits the rich information embedded in gaze exploration to guide SAM toward lesion-oriented segmentation. Extensive experiments on five public polyp segmentation datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, improving the mean Dice by 9.30 percentage points over the strongest weakly supervised baseline.
papers.summary: Endoscopist gaze is a cheap source of supervision for polyp segmentation, but existing methods treat each fixation as an isolated point prompt and ignore that gaze is a continuous, spatially organized search process. `GEG-SAM` models the temporal dynamics and spatial topology of the gaze trajectory, ties those relational representations to the visual content at each fixation to form gaze-conditioned tokens, and injects them into the frozen `SAM` (Segment Anything Model) encoder to modulate its image features. On five public polyp segmentation datasets it improves mean Dice by **9.30 percentage points over the strongest weakly supervised baseline**.

papers.title: What Does Matching a Human Intervention Effect Establish? Benchmark Checks for LLM Simulations
papers.abstract: LLM simulations are validated by equivalence with human effects, yet a zero reference passes whenever the human 90 percent interval lies inside the margin, as the human benchmark shows before simulation. When the zero reference fails, planned precision gives independent simulations the margin up to which passing is a 5 percent test of response. In an exploratory 70-experiment reanalysis, 72 percent of GPT-4's $\pm$0.20 SD passes were zero-reference passes; GPT-4 passed 16 contrasts the zero reference failed (1.58 expected without response). In a preregistered audit, Claude Sonnet 5.5 passed three intention targets, all zero-reference passes, and the registered belief-gradient control; norm beliefs changed 0.065 SD against humans' 0.351 (zero-reference check added after unblinding; norm beliefs emphasized after inspection). Registered tests detected no overestimation; average-effect intervals excluded overestimation above 0.08 SD. A group audit's precision floor is 1.33 facts against a 2.9-fact effect. Report the zero-reference threshold beside every equivalence decision.
papers.summary: LLM simulations of human participants are commonly validated by showing their intervention effects are statistically equivalent to human effects, but a simulation that shows no response at all also passes whenever the human 90 percent interval already lies inside the equivalence margin. The authors formalize this zero-reference check, along with a precision-based margin up to which a pass still counts as a test of response, and apply both to existing and new data. In an exploratory reanalysis of 70 experiments, **72 percent of `GPT-4`'s passes at a ±0.20 SD margin were zero-reference passes**, although it also passed 16 contrasts that the zero reference failed, against 1.58 expected without any response. In a preregistered audit, `Claude Sonnet 5.5` passed three intention targets that were all zero-reference passes, and shifted norm beliefs by 0.065 SD against 0.351 SD in humans; the authors recommend reporting the zero-reference threshold beside every equivalence decision.

papers.title: A Frugal AI Framework for India: Responsible and Right-sized AI
papers.abstract: India's AI debate often swings between two insufficient options: replicating the compute-intensive, capital-heavy foundation-model programmes of the United States or China, or remaining a downstream adopter of foreign AI with localised interfaces and safeguards. Neither serves a country that must deliver AI to a very large, diverse population across uneven infrastructure and within constrained budgets. This white paper from the Centre for Responsible AI (CeRAI), IIT Madras, proposes a third path: Responsible Frugal AI, which applies principle-based frugal engineering alongside Responsible AI. Responsible Frugal AI is right-sized AI: it fixes the functional requirement first, asks whether AI is needed at all, and then chooses the smallest sufficient model, meeting the requirement with minimal resources while keeping a verified margin, robustness and responsible governance. The framework applies frugality across four dimensions (data, compute, model and operations) through seven levers spanning the AI lifecycle, each with practices and measures. It calls for public AI rails, vernacular-first design, measured resource use, human oversight for high-stakes decisions, and a cap on total resource consumption so that efficiency gains are not cancelled out by rising usage. We argue that India is resource-imbalanced rather than resource-poor, and that frugal principles offer the most viable route to population-scale deployment, fit naturally with India's digital public infrastructure, and make sovereignty operational by preserving India's capacity to specify, deploy, govern, inspect and adapt its AI systems. A seven-point adoption checklist and eleven policy statements translate the framework into practice, positioning AI in India as a responsible, frugal public-value system that maximises social value per rupee and per joule.
papers.summary: A white paper from the Centre for Responsible AI at IIT Madras argues that India should neither replicate the compute-heavy foundation-model programmes of the United States and China nor remain a downstream adopter of foreign AI. It proposes Responsible Frugal AI, which fixes the functional requirement first, asks whether AI is needed at all, and then chooses the smallest sufficient model with a verified margin, robustness, and responsible governance. The framework applies frugality across **four dimensions (data, compute, model, and operations) through seven lifecycle levers**, and calls for public AI infrastructure, vernacular-first design, human oversight of high-stakes decisions, and a cap on total resource consumption. A seven-point adoption checklist and eleven policy statements translate it into practice.

papers.title: Lift Out, Kick In: Decoupling Event Effects for Time Series Forecasting
papers.abstract: Real-world time series are often shaped by exogenous events whose effects are superimposed on the system's underlying temporal dynamics. Historical observations therefore entangle persistent dynamics with event-induced deviations, making it difficult to determine which patterns should be extrapolated and which should be attributed to specific event contexts.
