Existing event-aware forecasting methods can incorporate event information or model event-related variation, but typically treat historical event attribution and future event generation separately. We propose Loki (Lift Out, Kick In), a general event-aware forecasting framework built on a shared Event Response Function (ERF). The ERF models event effects according to event type and relative temporal position and is shared across the historical and forecast windows. Loki lifts out estimated event-induced deviations from historical observations before forecasting, then uses the same ERF to kick in responses to known future events. This formulation separates event-response modeling from temporal forecasting while coupling historical attribution and future generation through a shared mechanism. Across five forecasting benchmarks, Loki achieves the best standardized MAE on all five datasets, reducing error by approximately 2.2%-11.7% over the strongest non-Loki baseline. Ablations and controlled analyses further support the roles of Lift Out, Kick In, shared response modeling, and compatibility across forecasting backbones.
papers.summary: Time series shaped by exogenous events mix persistent dynamics with event-driven deviations, which makes it unclear which historical patterns a forecaster should extrapolate. `Loki` uses a single Event Response Function (ERF), which models an event's effect by its type and relative temporal position, to subtract estimated event effects from the history before forecasting and then add back responses to known future events. Across five forecasting benchmarks it achieves the best standardized mean absolute error on every dataset, **reducing error by roughly 2.2% to 11.7% over the strongest competing baseline**. Ablations support the contribution of each stage, of sharing the response function, and of compatibility with different forecasting backbones.

papers.title: How Much of a Calculation-Error Rate Is Not Arithmetic: Auditing the FinReason Cup 2026 Task 3 Metric with a Deterministic Rule System
papers.abstract:
Task 3 of the FinReason Cup 2026 scores a system on two values per case, the one an XBRL filing reports and the one its own calculation relationships imply, and labels each failure as structural, extraction or calculation. This report shows that the calculation-error rate so defined does not count arithmetic failures, and bounds how far it is from one using the published board alone. One of the three rules behind the benchmark, DQC_US_0015, has an answer that is the negation of the reported value (in all 110 published practice cases, against 1 of 120 and 6 of 102 for the other two), so a calculation label on such a case records a wrong fact or a wrong route, not a wrong sum. Subtracting the available structural and extraction labels from each entry's error count on that rule gives a floor: the bound is positive for 22 of the 23 ranked entries, and at the top it is sharpest, with at least 11 of 12 and 12 of 13 calculation errors of the two joint-first entries falling on cases where no arithmetic remained. The calculation-error rate of the best systems on this task is almost entirely not arithmetic.
  The vehicle for that result is an entry that reconstructs the three data-quality rules the benchmark is drawn from, DQC_US_0015, DQC_US_0117 and DQC_US_0126, as a deterministic system with no learned parameters, no training step and no external service, running all 680 cases in 1.4 seconds. It scores 96.62% under the offline judge on development and 95.29% on the published test set, and its residual error concentrates in cases where a concept carries several equally flagged facts and the question names no dimensional member. Reading those error classes against the per-rule accuracies is what exposed the metric, which is why both are reported here.

papers.title: cmHC: Balancing Stream Mixing in Hyper-Connections via Geometric Contraction
papers.abstract: Manifold-constrained Hyper-Connections (mHC) extends residual connections to multiple streams and stabilizes residual propagation by constraining stream-mixing residual matrices to the Birkhoff polytope, the set of doubly stochastic matrices. In this work, we investigate how to effectively mix residual streams within the Birkhoff polytope. We reveal a mixing trade-off: when under-mixed residual matrices stay close to the vertices of the Birkhoff polytope, hyper-connections will degenerate into a set of nearly independent streams; when over-mixed residual matrices are concentrated around the uniform barycenter of the polytope, streams will become less distinguishable from each other. We theoretically validate our findings by bounding the cumulative residual mixing, stream difference and gradient difference of mixing coefficients across layers. Motivated by these findings, we propose Contraction for Manifold-Constrained Hyper-Connections (cmHC), an exact doubly stochastic method which geometrically contracts the Birkhoff polytope toward its interior. This contraction mitigates under-mixing by forcing the residual matrices to explore deeper into the polytope, with a provable stream mixing bound and no new parameterization. Moreover, we apply a moderate contraction at the shallow layers to prevent over-mixing, enabling stable gradient propagation on extremely large-scale model pretraining. Extensive experiments across dense and mixture-of-experts models at various parameter scales demonstrate the effectiveness and scalability of cmHC. We also develop fused operators for cmHC on Ascend NPUs, reducing hyper-connection execution latency by up to 44.8%.
papers.summary: Manifold-constrained Hyper-Connections (mHC) extend residual connections to multiple streams by constraining the stream-mixing matrices to be doubly stochastic, that is, to lie in the Birkhoff polytope. The authors identify a trade-off: matrices near the polytope's vertices leave the streams nearly independent, while matrices near its uniform centre make the streams indistinguishable, and they bound cumulative mixing, stream difference, and gradient difference across layers. Their method, `cmHC`, geometrically contracts the polytope toward its interior to prevent under-mixing without new parameters, and applies a milder contraction in shallow layers to avoid over-mixing. Experiments on dense and mixture-of-experts models at several scales are reported as showing effectiveness and scalability, and fused operators for Ascend NPUs cut hyper-connection latency by **up to 44.8%**.
papers.highlight_summary:
Multi-stream hyper-connections constrained to the Birkhoff polytope tend to stay stuck near a permutation vertex, so streams are merely permuted rather than mixed, while pushing too far toward the uniform barycenter makes streams indistinguishable. `cmHC` addresses this trade-off by geometrically contracting the polytope toward its interior, and applies that contraction only mildly and only in the shallowest layers.

- Each permutation basis matrix in `mHC-lite` is replaced by a smoothed version controlled by a coefficient λ, which is equivalent to interpolating the residual matrix toward the uniform barycenter, keeps it exactly doubly stochastic, guarantees every entry is strictly positive, and adds **no new parameters**.
- A Dobrushin-coefficient bound shows cumulative mixing compounds exponentially with the number of contracted layers, and further bounds (relying on a local linear approximation of the Transformer branch) show even a small contraction shrinks stream differences and flattens the mixing-coefficient gradients, which motivates contracting only the first K layers.
- On `nanoGPT-S/M/L` with 4 streams, λ=0.97 with K=2 gets the best average loss rank on both `OpenWebText` (**1.3**) and `FineWeb-Edu` (**2.8**), cutting `OpenWebText` validation loss versus `mHC-lite` by **0.0073**, **0.0024** and **0.0045** at 12, 24 and 48 layers, whereas strong all-layer contraction (λ=0.70) is worse than `mHC-lite` at 48 layers (3.2169 vs 3.1949).
- On DeepSeek-style MoE models trained on `FineWeb-Edu`, `cmHC` ends the 6B run **0.002** below `mHC` and **0.005** below `mHC-lite` in training loss at step 71.5k, leads `mHC` by **0.0157** at step 2k of the 300B run with smoother gradient norms, and its fused Ascend NPU operators cut hyper-connection forward-plus-backward latency by **44.8%** at hidden size 2,048, falling to 24.1% at 7,168.
- The gains sit in the third or fourth decimal of loss and are often comparable to the reported standard deviations, `FineWeb-Edu` wins are not uniform (`mHC-lite` is best on `nanoGPT-S` and `KromHC` has the best `nanoGPT-L` validation loss), evaluation is loss-only with no downstream tasks, the 300B comparison is an early snapshot against `mHC` alone, and the latency figure excludes the Transformer sublayer.

papers.title: EDAGoat: An EDA-Aware Agent for Project-Level GPU Optimization
papers.abstract: GPU acceleration has transformed electronic design automation (EDA), yet further improving expert-engineered GPU tools still demands substantial manual effort. Automating this work calls for coding agents that can trace bottlenecks across host and device code while preserving correctness and design quality. We introduce EDAGoat, to our knowledge the first EDA-aware GPU optimization agent for this task. Its optimization enhancement (OE) mode guides edits with four cross-project GPU optimization patterns. Its mandatory validation (MV) mode requires the agent to test the edited program against the EDA constraints its changes could affect. Our benchmark covers five GPU EDA projects across four task families and 55 circuit inputs, measuring complete-solve runtime and verifying the resulting designs. Each configuration runs three independent searches per project. A search qualifies only if its solver passes correctness and design-quality checks on all public and hidden inputs. With DeepSeek, generic prompting qualifies in 7 of 15 searches and OE in 6 of 15, despite a higher best speedup on four projects. Adding MV raises this to 13 of 15 and, on every project, exceeds both generic baselines in mean and best speedup and OE in mean speedup; the geometric mean of per-project mean speedups rises from 1.11x (1.36x with OE) to 1.53x. With GPT-6 Astra, EDAGoat qualifies in all 15 searches and improves both speedup metrics over generic prompting on every project, lifting the same geometric mean from 1.26x to 1.57x. These results show that agents can use EDA knowledge to find further speedups in expert-tuned tools while preserving design correctness and quality, establishing EDA-aware GPU optimization as a new direction for agent research.
papers.summary: Squeezing further speed out of expert-engineered GPU tools for electronic design automation (EDA) takes substantial manual effort, since bottlenecks span host and device code and edits must preserve correctness and design quality. `EDAGoat` is a coding agent with an optimization enhancement (OE) mode that guides edits using four cross-project GPU optimization patterns and a mandatory validation (MV) mode that forces it to test edits against the EDA constraints they could affect. On a benchmark of five GPU EDA projects and 55 circuit inputs with `DeepSeek`, generic prompting produces a qualifying solver in 7 of 15 searches, while **adding mandatory validation raises this to 13 of 15 and lifts the geometric-mean speedup from 1.11x to 1.53x**. With `GPT-6 Astra`, all 15 searches qualify and the same geometric mean rises from 1.26x to 1.57x.

papers.title: DepthMSA: Combinatorial Training and Budget-Aware Depth Allocation for Multimodal Sentiment Analysis
papers.abstract: State-of-the-art multimodal sentiment analysis (MSA) models rely on large pretrained encoders, yet typically process every modality to its full depth, regardless of its computational cost or predictive contribution. This raises a fundamental question: how should limited computation be allocated across modalities to preserve predictive performance? We reveal a substantial mismatch between the computational cost of modality encoders and the predictive benefit of processing them more deeply, suggesting that different modalities require different encoding depths. However, enabling heterogeneous depths introduces a key challenge: representations extracted at different depths must still be effectively fused. To address this, we propose $\textbf{DepthMSA}$, a budget-aware framework that supports flexible modality depths within a single MSA model. Specifically, we introduce combinatorial anytime training, which supervises the fusion head across all cross-modal depth combinations using a single full-depth encoder pass. At inference, a training-free, cost-aware allocator selects the configuration with the lowest validation-calibrated error under a sample-specific FLOPs budget. On CMU-MOSEI, DepthMSA maintains accuracy within one percentage point of the full-depth model while reducing measured FLOPs by 45\%, or by 82\% with a separately trained skip-enabled variant. When a CLIP visual encoder dominates computation, the allocation shifts toward reducing visual depth, achieving 56\% fewer FLOPs at unchanged accuracy. Compared with ADMN, an adaptive layer-allocation method that trains a controller for each budget, the skip-enabled variant reaches its accuracy with 3.2$\times$ fewer FLOPs and lower latency, without any per-budget training. Our project is available at https://pwang322.github.io/DepthMSA/.
papers.summary: Multimodal sentiment analysis (MSA) models usually run every modality's pretrained encoder to full depth, even though encoder cost and predictive benefit are poorly matched across modalities. `DepthMSA` trains the fusion head on all cross-modal depth combinations from a single full-depth encoder pass, then uses a training-free allocator at inference to pick the configuration with the lowest validation-calibrated error under a per-sample FLOPs budget. On `CMU-MOSEI` it stays **within one percentage point of full-depth accuracy while cutting measured FLOPs by 45%**, or by 82% with a separately trained skip-enabled variant. Against `ADMN`, which trains a controller for each budget, the skip-enabled variant matches accuracy with 3.2x fewer FLOPs and no per-budget training.

papers.title: Backbone-Specific LoRA Geometry: Orthogonality, Superposition, and Provenance
papers.abstract: Sharing one low-rank adaptation (LoRA) update across pretrained models simplifies deployment. Composition methods typically combine updates from a common backbone, while cross-model transfer transforms updates for a target backbone. The conditions for sharing updates across backbones while preserving accuracy and distinguishing individual contributions remain unclear. Our idea is to use backbone-specific update directions as signatures of their training backbones. We derive a cross-backbone correlation bound from attention symmetries and equivariant LoRA learning under independent, uniform pretrained feature orientations. A local gradient-flow model explains positive mean correlation between independent runs on the same backbone and task. These patterns motivate cosine-based backbone identification and inner-product tests for registered-adapter reuse without coordinate alignment. Experiments on CLIP backbones show that shared sums achieve nearly the same mean accuracy as separate adapters. Cosine scores reliably identify source backbones across the evaluated tasks. Registered adapters remain detectable in sums of adapters from different backbones.
papers.summary: The authors ask when one low-rank adaptation (LoRA) update can be shared across different pretrained backbones while keeping accuracy and still distinguishing each adapter's contribution. They treat backbone-specific update directions as signatures of the training backbone, deriving a bound on cross-backbone correlation from attention symmetries and using a local gradient-flow model to explain positive correlation between independent runs on the same backbone and task. This motivates cosine-based backbone identification and inner-product tests for detecting registered adapters without coordinate alignment. In experiments on `CLIP` backbones, **summed adapters reach nearly the same mean accuracy as separate ones**, cosine scores reliably identify the source backbone, and registered adapters remain detectable inside sums of adapters from different backbones.

papers.title: Improved Accuracy Scaling with Problem Complexity in LLM Arithmetic Reasoning Using Executable Symbolic Representations
papers.abstract: High accuracy on mathematical benchmarks does not establish whether reasoning remains reliable as problem complexity increases. We examine how executable symbolic representations change accuracy scaling in large language models compared with natural-language reasoning. To address this limitation, we introduce the GSM Arithmetic Benchmark (GSM-AB), a controlled benchmark that independently varies operand digit length and operation count to probe numerical scale and compositional complexity. We find that executable representations can improve accuracy and slow its decline as complexity increases. Lean reduces average sensitivity to operand digit length at every tested model size. By contrast, slower degradation with increasing operation count emerges at the larger model sizes. A Python program-of-thought (Python-PoT) control shows a similar operation-axis pattern, suggesting that this finding is not specific to Lean. These findings show that reasoning representation shapes arithmetic accuracy scaling and support executable symbolic representations for more reliable reasoning on complex arithmetic tasks.
papers.summary: High scores on math benchmarks do not show whether a language model's reasoning holds up as problems get harder, so the authors build the GSM Arithmetic Benchmark (`GSM-AB`), which independently varies operand digit length and number of operations. They compare natural-language reasoning with executable symbolic representations, namely `Lean` and a Python program-of-thought control (`Python-PoT`). **`Lean` reduces sensitivity to operand digit length at every tested model size**, while slower degradation with increasing operation count appears only at the larger model sizes. The Python control shows a similar operation-count pattern, suggesting the effect is not specific to `Lean`.

papers.title: LingSante-Pulse: Unified Physiological Pretraining through Random-Feature Prediction and Cross-Modal Alignment
papers.abstract: Clinical monitoring and wearable devices capture complementary physiological signals, but their partially overlapping modality coverage makes within-signal information and cross-modal relationships difficult to exploit jointly. We introduce LingSante-Pulse, a unified, general-purpose and flexible physiological representation framework that learns from these heterogeneous recordings. A shared, signal-conditioned encoder processes each physical channel independently and supports different numbers and combinations of signals for multimodal assessment and single-sensor inference. Pairwise cross-modal alignment, structured random-feature prediction (RFP) and masked waveform reconstruction jointly learn physiological relationships and preserve informative within-signal structure. Across 38 general physiological task configurations spanning PPG, ECG, EEG and EMG, the frozen encoder achieves the best dataset-balanced mean rank in each domain. In sleep assessment, multimodal staging on the HMC dataset and EEG-only staging on the Sleep-EDF dataset reach Macro-F1 scores of 0.7784 and 0.7941, respectively, while single-lead ECG apnea screening achieves an AUROC of 0.9183. Controlled experiments show that function prediction and waveform reconstruction provide complementary supervision for retaining temporal and rhythmic information. Representations learned under continually refreshed random supervision generalize to unseen teacher realizations, and correct auxiliary modality correspondence improves respiration-only representations. These results demonstrate that a single encoder can learn reusable physiological features across signal types, prediction targets and sensor configurations from partially overlapping recordings.
papers.summary: Clinical monitors and wearables record complementary physiological signals with only partially overlapping modality coverage, which makes it hard to learn within-signal structure and cross-modal relationships together. `LingSante-Pulse` uses a shared, signal-conditioned encoder that processes each channel independently and is trained with pairwise cross-modal alignment, structured random-feature prediction (RFP), and masked waveform reconstruction. Across 38 task configurations spanning PPG, ECG, EEG, and EMG signals, **the frozen encoder achieves the best dataset-balanced mean rank in every domain**. It reaches Macro-F1 of 0.7784 for multimodal sleep staging on `HMC` and 0.7941 for EEG-only staging on `Sleep-EDF`, and an AUROC of 0.9183 for single-lead ECG apnea screening.

papers.title: Parameter-Efficient Adaptation of Qwen3-VL for Handwritten Mathematical Expression Recognition
papers.abstract: Handwritten mathematical expression recognition (HMER) requires joint recovery of symbol identity and two-dimensional syntax, so a locally plausible transcription may still be structurally wrong. We study whether a compact vision-language model can be adapted to generate linearized Symbol Label Graphs (SLGs) under limited computing resources. Starting from a 4-bit Qwen3-VL-4B checkpoint, we apply rank-16 Low-Rank Adaptation to the vision, language, attention, and MLP modules and train with instruction-formatted CROHME 2019 examples. We compare this model with an internally implemented ViT-Transformer baseline, a zero-shot Qwen3-VL configuration, and additional internally evaluated alternatives. On the 1,198 valid CROHME test examples, the CROHME-only model obtains 524 exact matches (43.74%) and a corpus BLEU-4 score of 77.67, compared with 4.92% and 43.26 for the task-specific ViT baseline. An ablation that adds 2,000 manually written, formula-guided samples decreases exact match to 42.32%, exposing a domain-alignment issue rather than an automatic benefit from more data. The principal contribution is therefore an evidence-backed, resource-efficient formulation of HMER as multimodal structural generation, together with a controlled data-composition ablation and an analysis of the remaining gap between local token overlap and globally correct structure.
papers.summary: Handwritten mathematical expression recognition (HMER) requires recovering both symbols and two-dimensional layout, and the authors test whether a compact vision-language model can generate linearized Symbol Label Graphs (SLGs) under limited compute. They apply rank-16 Low-Rank Adaptation to a 4-bit `Qwen3-VL-4B` checkpoint and train on instruction-formatted `CROHME 2019` examples. On 1,198 valid test examples the adapted model reaches **43.74% exact match and 77.67 corpus BLEU-4, against 4.92% and 43.26 for an in-house ViT-Transformer baseline**. Adding 2,000 manually written, formula-guided samples lowers exact match to 42.32%, which the authors attribute to a domain-alignment issue.

papers.title: Explicit Style Extraction for Personalized Long-Form Text Generation
papers.abstract: Personalized long-form generation asks a language model to write new text the way a specific user would. The standard recipe, retrieval-augmented generation, places a few of the user's past texts in the prompt but leaves the model to decide what to take from them. We introduce StylePrism, a taxonomy of 28 stylistic aspects in seven categories, and SP-Refine, an inference-time method that makes style extraction an explicit step: the model first fills StylePrism with the user's patterns, quoted evidence, and habits to avoid, then drafts from the user's samples and revises the draft twice against this profile, guided by its own style scores. On the three long-form tasks of LongLaMP with three LLMs, SP-Refine outperforms LongLaMP's retrieval-augmented baseline in 25 of 27 ROUGE and METEOR comparisons, by 10.2% on average and by up to 35.8%. Annotating users' own texts with the extracted profiles shows that StylePrism captures concrete, checkable habits, from the order of rhetorical moves to a reviewer's sign-off. Ablations show that the profile helps as revision guidance, not as a replacement for the samples: writing from the profile alone is worse in all 27 comparisons, while a single implicit-inference call is a cheaper alternative that comes close. Oracle variants that let the reviser see the reference, together with reference-free controls, show that larger refinement gains require information unavailable at inference time.
papers.summary: Personalized long-form generation usually relies on retrieval-augmented prompting with a few of the user's past texts, leaving the model to decide what stylistic cues to take from them. The authors define `StylePrism`, a taxonomy of 28 stylistic aspects in seven categories, and `SP-Refine`, an inference-time method that first fills the taxonomy with the user's patterns, quoted evidence, and habits to avoid, then drafts from the samples and revises twice against that profile. On the three long-form tasks of `LongLaMP` with three language models, it **beats the retrieval-augmented baseline in 25 of 27 ROUGE and METEOR comparisons, by 10.2% on average**. Ablations show the profile works as revision guidance and not as a substitute for the samples, and that a single implicit-inference call is a cheaper alternative that comes close.
papers.highlight_summary:
Retrieval-augmented personalization puts a user's past texts in the prompt but leaves the model to decide what to imitate. `StylePrism`, a taxonomy of **28 stylistic aspects** in seven categories, and `SP-Refine`, an inference-time method, turn style extraction into an explicit, inspectable step that guides revision of a draft.

- `SP-Refine` makes four calls to the generator: it fills the `StylePrism` schema from the `k=4` retrieved samples with patterns, quoted evidence and habits to avoid, drafts from the samples alone, revises against the profile while self-scoring five style criteria, and then revises again targeting the weakest criteria.
- On the three long-form `LongLaMP` tasks with `DeepSeek-V4-Flash`, `Grok-4.1-Fast` and `GPT-5.4-nano`, it beats the `LongLaMP` retrieval baseline in **25 of 27** ROUGE and METEOR comparisons, by **10.2%** on average and by up to **35.8%** (METEOR on review writing with GPT), with both losses on METEOR with Grok.
- An LLM judge rates style fidelity higher than the baseline in **8 of 9** generator–task settings, by 0.21 points on average on a 1–5 scale, while task quality is higher in 7, equal in 1 and lower in 1.
- Ablations show that most of the gain comes from the drafting prompt rather than the explicit profile: the single-call `SP-Infer` draft comes close to `SP-Refine` and beats it on overlap metrics with DeepSeek in 8 of 9 comparisons, while writing from the profile without the samples (`SP-Profile`) is worse in **all 27**.
- Oracle variants show that larger refinement gains require seeing the reference, and the evaluation has no human judges, relies on a reference-anchored LLM judge that is also one of the generators, and covers only English data in the `LongLaMP` user setting with a fixed retriever.

papers.title: EAF-TTS: Rethinking Codec-Latent Coordinates for Flow TTS
papers.abstract: Latent text-to-speech (TTS) systems generate codec latents decoded by a frozen decoder, but good reconstruction does not ensure geometry suitable for Flow generation from isotropic Gaussian noise. We present Embedded Acoustic Flow TTS (EAF-TTS), an acoustic-latent adaptation of ELF with phone- and duration-conditioned generation, shared-network terminal correction, and frozen WaveVAE decoding. EAF-TTS supports a fixed ZCA interface estimated from training data and adding no learned parameters. The codec, conditioning modules, Flow backbone, and 20-call inference are shared. The intervention is the full ZCA coordinate protocol---training and sampling coordinates, induced loss metric, and terminal perturbation---not an inference-only transform. In single-speaker LJSpeech, the 64-D training-latent covariance has condition number 1355.44. On text-disjoint Val399 strict-GT with fixed E100 raw checkpoints across three matched seeds, ZCA improves UTMOS22 Strong---an automatic naturalness proxy, not human MOS---by $+0.405\pm0.027$ over Scalar normalization (mean $\pm$ seed SD of per-seed paired differences). Absolute scores remain below codec-reference levels. Without retraining, ZCA-5 retains $+0.375\pm0.027$ UTMOS over Scalar-20 while reducing generation-path RTF by $3.34\times$. This three-seed analysis shows no statistically detectable WER or exact-match degradation, but does not establish equivalence. ZCA-3 gives $5.03\times$ with a $+0.165$ UTMOS advantage. At matched reduced call counts, ZCA's advantage shrinks, indicating full-step headroom rather than better low-step integration. A secondary text-only selected-checkpoint result is directionally consistent but confounded by checkpoint type. We claim only proxy-naturalness and measured quality--latency effects within this protocol; human listening, blind text, and broader validation remain necessary.
papers.summary: Latent text-to-speech (TTS) systems generate codec latents for a frozen decoder, but latents that reconstruct well are not necessarily shaped well for flow-based generation from isotropic Gaussian noise. `EAF-TTS` adapts `ELF` to acoustic latents and applies a fixed ZCA whitening transform, estimated from training data with no learned parameters, to the training and sampling coordinates, the induced loss metric, and the terminal perturbation. On single-speaker `LJSpeech`, across three matched seeds, whitening improves `UTMOS22`, an automatic naturalness proxy and not a human rating, by **+0.405 ± 0.027 over scalar normalization**, and a 5-call variant keeps +0.375 while reducing the generation-path real-time factor by 3.34x. The authors limit their claims to proxy naturalness and measured quality-latency effects, noting that human listening tests and broader validation are still needed.

papers.title: Neural Defend Ranks #1 in Global Audio Deepfake Detection Benchmark - ARCAS on the Podonos Independent Leaderboard
papers.abstract: Commercial detectors of AI-generated audio are usually promoted with results on internal test sets that buyers cannot inspect. Independent benchmarks with private labels give a more reliable comparison. We report the results of Neural Defend's ARCAS foundation models on the Podonos audio deepfake detection benchmark, an independent leaderboard that scores commercial detection APIs and open-source detectors on one held-out set of real speech and speech from current text-to-speech and voice-cloning systems, delivered in six file formats, against labels that only Podonos holds. In the release of 29 October 2026, which covers 28 systems from 16 commercial vendors and the leading open models, ARCAS 290M and the smaller ARCAS 90M share first place, ahead of every other commercial system, including Resemble AI, Hiya, Pindrop, Hive, and Reality Defender. Both models make fewer errors than any other system by a statistically clear margin, keep false positives and false negatives in balance at their default threshold, process every submitted file without rejection, and sit on the accuracy--latency frontier of the leaderboard. As for every commercial system added since Podonos retired its API runner, the ARCAS predictions were submitted by Neural Defend and scored by Podonos against its private labels. We describe the benchmark's construction and protocol in full, reproduce the complete leaderboard and its history across five releases, and analyse error balance, statistical separation, speed, and the gap between commercial and open-source detectors. The results agree with the companion evaluation of ARCAS 290M on the complete test sets of ten public benchmarks and establish ARCAS as the most accurate AI-generated audio detector evaluated on this independent benchmark.
papers.summary: Neural Defend reports how its `ARCAS` audio deepfake detectors performed on the `Podonos` benchmark, an independent leaderboard that scores commercial APIs and open-source detectors on a held-out set of real and synthetic speech in six file formats against privately held labels. In the 29 October 2026 release covering 28 systems from 16 commercial vendors plus leading open models, **`ARCAS 290M` and the smaller `ARCAS 90M` share first place**, with the vendor stating that both make fewer errors than any other system by a statistically clear margin and keep false positives and false negatives balanced. The predictions were submitted by Neural Defend and scored by Podonos. The report also describes the benchmark's construction, reproduces the leaderboard across five releases, and analyses the gap between commercial and open-source detectors.

papers.title: Correct Precedents Induce Policy Violations in On-Device LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Local-cloud agent systems pair a cloud model with a small on-device agent that acts on private data, often as the last check before an irreversible action. We identify, for the first time, a failure in which such an agent is led into a violation by its own correct decisions within a session. After it correctly releases an item whose restriction was lifted, it becomes more likely to release the next item that is still restricted. Because the trigger is a correct decision, a history with no faulty step can still end in a violation. We call this failure correct-precedent generalization and find it in 13 open-weight models from nine developers. A single correct precedent can cut the safe rate of the most affected agent roughly in half, and the risk compounds when a refused request is simply sent again in a new session. Interventions on the agent's history indicate that it carries its decision on the released item over to the restricted one instead of checking that item's status. Building on this finding, we propose Paired Decision Distillation (PDD), which distills the decisions of a weakly affected teacher into a LoRA adapter. PDD restores the safe rate to nearly 100% in every distilled model, without extra prompt text or model calls.
papers.summary: Small on-device agents in local-cloud systems are often the last check before an irreversible action on private data, and the authors identify a failure in which the agent's own correct decisions lead it to a violation. After correctly releasing an item whose restriction was lifted, the agent becomes more likely to release the next item that is still restricted, a pattern the authors call correct-precedent generalization and observe in 13 open-weight models from nine developers. **A single correct precedent can roughly halve the safe rate of the most affected agent**, and the risk compounds when a refused request is resent in a new session. Their fix, Paired Decision Distillation (`PDD`), distills a weakly affected teacher's decisions into a `LoRA` adapter and restores the safe rate to nearly 100% in every distilled model without extra prompt text or model calls.

papers.title: CoPyro: Feeding Copy Proposals to Parallel Drafters
papers.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates language generation by letting a target model verify several draft tokens in one forward pass. Earlier neural drafters such as EAGLE extend each candidate sequence one token at a time. Recent work has turned to parallel drafters such as DFlash, which predict a whole block at once. Another approach uses n-gram retrieval to find an earlier occurrence of the current context suffix and copy the tokens that followed it directly into the draft. We introduce CoPyro, which feeds these copied tokens into a parallel drafter in place of masks. The drafter learns from context which tokens to keep and which to revise as it predicts the block in its usual forward pass. Across eight benchmarks on Qwen3-4B, CoPyro improves overall acceptance length for all four parallel drafters tested, with gains of 2.19-5.08% when trained on 100K samples. With DFlash trained on 710K samples, overall gains range from 1.08% to 2.00% across the tested model sizes and temperatures. Code generation benefits most in both settings. On Qwen3-8B, processing the proposals adds an average of 0.24 ms per decoding round in Transformers.
papers.summary: Speculative decoding speeds up generation by having a target model verify several drafted tokens in one forward pass; parallel drafters such as `DFlash` predict a whole block at once, while n-gram retrieval instead copies the tokens that followed an earlier occurrence of the current context. `CoPyro` combines the two by feeding the copied tokens into a parallel drafter in place of mask tokens, so the drafter learns which to keep and which to revise. On eight benchmarks with `Qwen3-4B`, it improves acceptance length for all four parallel drafters tested, with **gains of 2.19% to 5.08% when trained on 100K samples** and 1.08% to 2.00% for `DFlash` trained on 710K samples. Code generation benefits most, and on `Qwen3-8B` processing the proposals adds an average of 0.24 ms per decoding round.

papers.title: A Stationarity-Based Regret Framework for Time-Varying Nonconvex Composite Optimization
papers.abstract: This paper studies time-varying nonconvex composite optimization, where decisions are made sequentially and classical value-based regret notions are generally ill-posed. We introduce a stationarity-based performance framework defined through local regret measures built from first-order optimality conditions, and identify minimal structural requirements under which such measures constitute sound performance criteria. This abstraction encompasses canonical optimality measures, including the proximal-gradient residual, and collapses to classical dynamic regret in convex settings. We then focus on the proximal-gradient residual as a concrete and algorithmically meaningful instantiation for general composite problems. In convex problems, we show that the resulting local regret is equivalent to standard dynamic regret. In nonconvex settings, we establish that sublinear stationarity-based regret is unattainable without temporal regularity, and introduce a gradient-variation budget that captures this necessity. Under this model, we analyze online proximal-gradient methods and prove sublinear regret guarantees in both nested multi-call and fully incremental single-call oracle regimes, highlighting the tradeoff between per-round computational effort and achievable performance. Finally, we demonstrate how the proposed framework extends to nonconvex multiplayer games by interpreting equilibrium-seeking dynamics through stationarity-based regret, and corroborate the theoretical findings with numerical experiments.
papers.summary: In time-varying nonconvex composite optimization, decisions are made sequentially and the usual value-based notions of regret are generally ill-posed. The authors define local regret measures built from first-order optimality conditions, focusing on the proximal-gradient residual, and show that this measure is equivalent to standard dynamic regret in the convex case. For nonconvex problems they prove that **sublinear stationarity-based regret is unattainable without temporal regularity**, introduce a gradient-variation budget to capture that requirement, and establish sublinear regret guarantees for online proximal-gradient methods in both multi-call and single-call oracle regimes. The framework is also extended to nonconvex multiplayer games and supported by numerical experiments.

papers.title: NavTTT: Adaptive Parametric Memory via Hierarchical Test-Time Training for Vision-and-Language Navigation
papers.abstract: Vision-and-language navigation (VLN) demands that agents accumulate and reason over streaming visual observations throughout long navigation episodes. Existing approaches struggle to maintain long-term history, constrained by the finite context capacity of transformer architectures. To solve the problem, fast-weight test-time training (TTT) provides a mechanism for encoding streaming observations into an evolving parameter state. However, existing TTT does not distinguish informative observations from repetitive visual content, allowing redundant tokens to interfere with the retention of information needed for subsequent decisions. We propose Navigation-Conditioned Test-Time Training (NavTTT), which introduces adaptive memory formation and hierarchical memory integration for vision-and-language navigation. NavTTT leverages global navigation context to prioritize informative visual evidence and integrates language instructions with spatial information to construct spatially grounded memory representations. Episode-local nonlinear fast weights store these representations as Adaptive Parametric Memory (APM), preserving history beyond the visual context for later decisions. To reduce cross-layer coupling in memory formation, NavTTT maintains independent fast-weight memories across multiple decoder depths. This decoupled design prevents errors or biases from spreading across different memory levels. Meanwhile, it enables shared historical information to be independently represented at various levels of abstraction. Experiments demonstrate strong navigation performance on VLN-CE benchmarks and effective instruction following on a real robot.
papers.summary: Vision-and-language navigation (VLN) agents must retain long histories of streaming observations, but transformer context limits make this hard, and existing fast-weight test-time training (TTT) stores redundant visual tokens alongside useful ones. `NavTTT` uses global navigation context to prioritize informative observations, combines language instructions with spatial information, and writes the result into episode-local nonlinear fast weights called `Adaptive Parametric Memory`. It keeps **independent fast-weight memories at multiple decoder depths** so errors do not spread between memory levels. The authors report strong results on `VLN-CE` benchmarks and effective instruction following on a real robot.

papers.title: Bel: Step-Level Policy Improvement of Visual Agents Without Training
papers.abstract: A visual agent acts on what it sees: it taps and types on a screen, or points on a camera image to show a robot where to act. One wrong step can fail its task, yet the right action is often among its own samples, passed over by its greedy decode. Choosing it is a visual judgment, since an action is best judged where it acts, not by its text or coordinates alone: as text, a tap is two numbers; drawn on the screen, it is the Post button of an empty draft. We find that this is decisive: given the screenshot and a tap's coordinates, a decision model chooses among GUI-R1-3B's samples significantly worse on average than when the tap is drawn where it lands. Bel turns this finding into a method that trains nothing and needs only a frozen policy's samples and an image on which each action can be drawn. It marks each candidate on its own copy of the image it acts on, asks a decision model for the probability that executing it is the right decision, so that every kind of action shares one scale, and acts on another candidate only when greedy scores below a threshold and trails it by a margin. On recorded GUI steps, for each of three policies, Bel significantly beats greedy decoding on mobile, web and desktop screens alike and, on the same candidates, gives each a significantly higher mean step success than voting, CATTS, the trained GUI-Critic-R1 and two prompted Qwen3-VL judges shown the same marks; it also significantly improves the much larger Qwen3-VL-235B-A22B on every step-level test set. With GUI-R1-3B's thresholds unchanged, Bel significantly raises live AndroidWorld and MiniWoB++ task success for two other policies and robot-pointing success for three policies on each of two groups of benchmarks. Judging each action where it acts thus gives step-level policy improvement of visual agents without training, with significant gains for GUI agents and robot pointing.
papers.summary: Visual agents that tap on screens or point in camera images often have the correct action among their sampled candidates but miss it under greedy decoding. `Bel` requires no training: it draws each candidate action on its own copy of the image, asks a decision model for the probability that executing it is right, and overrides the greedy choice only when greedy scores below a threshold and trails by a margin. The underlying finding is that **a decision model picks among `GUI-R1-3B`'s samples significantly worse from raw coordinates than when the tap is drawn where it lands**. On recorded GUI steps it beats greedy decoding, voting, `CATTS`, the trained `GUI-Critic-R1` and prompted `Qwen3-VL` judges for three policies, and it raises live task success on `AndroidWorld` and `MiniWoB++` as well as robot-pointing success.

papers.title: LiDAR Signals for Robot Locomotion: Spherical Range Images Enable Robust Sim-to-Real Transfer
papers.abstract: Existing legged-locomotion systems commonly rely on depth images or online elevation maps. However, depth-based policies suffer from perceptual sim-to-real discrepancies due to imperfect depth sensor modeling, while map-based approaches are vulnerable to drift and misalignment. LiDAR offers direct measurements of the surrounding geometry, but raw LiDAR scans lack a compact, structured representation for high-frequency control. We propose a LiDAR perception pipeline that maintains perceptual consistency across simulation and reality through sensing- and representation-level alignment. At the sensor level, we recover frame-wise angular sampling patterns from the physical LiDAR and replay them in simulation with GPU ray casting. At the representation level, simulated and real returns undergo the same spherical range image encoding, yielding a fixed-size policy observation for end-to-end training and direct deployment without teacher--student distillation, online elevation mapping, or adaptation. Experiments show that our range-image policies achieve stronger sim-to-real transfer than depth- and elevation-map-based baselines, while ablations confirm the importance of the proposed sensing components. More visualizations and real-world videos are available at the \href{https://lidar-img.github.io/}
papers.summary: Legged-robot locomotion policies that rely on depth images suffer from sim-to-real gaps in sensor modeling, while elevation-map approaches are prone to drift and misalignment. The proposed LiDAR pipeline recovers the physical sensor's frame-wise angular sampling patterns and replays them in simulation with GPU ray casting, then encodes both simulated and real returns as the same fixed-size spherical range image. Policies are trained end to end and deployed directly, **without teacher-student distillation, online elevation mapping, or adaptation**. Experiments show stronger sim-to-real transfer than depth- and elevation-map-based baselines, and ablations support the sensing components.

papers.title: CreditFilter: Calibrated Token Weights over the Within-Response Entropy Rank for RLVR
papers.abstract: Critic-free reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) typically assigns a uniform advantage to every token. Token-reweighting heuristics like the 80/20 mask favor high-entropy tokens, but fail to measure a token's actual impact on the outcome. We formalize this impact as the forking value: the variance of the success probability over the policy's next-token choices. The expected forking values along a response sum exactly to the reward variance. Token credit is thus, in expectation over a prompt's responses, a fixed budget spent at the forks. This motivates weights that redistribute credit within a response. The forking value factorizes into a fork consequence, which requires costly continuations to estimate, and a fork probability, which the softmax provides. On Qwen3-8B-Base, this fork probability decays exponentially with a token's within-response entropy rank at class-specific rates, revealing that most tokens carry negligible forking value. CreditFilter weights each token by an exponential window over the same rank. The window is calibrated to this fork-probability envelope, under an approximately flat fork consequence. CreditFilter needs no extra forward passes and is stabilized by difficulty damping and an entropy-gated fallback. Averaged over three seeds, it outperforms DAPO by 7.7 points on MATH500 and by 10.5 and 9.1 points on AIME24 and AIME25. Its dynamically adaptive variant matches it. The ablations show that both parts matter: ranking tokens within each response rather than across the batch, and matching the window's decay rate to the envelope. Code is available at https://github.com/yoctta/CreditFilter.
papers.summary: Critic-free reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) usually gives every token in a response the same advantage, and entropy-based reweighting heuristics do not measure a token's actual effect on the outcome. The authors define a token's forking value as the variance of success probability over the policy's next-token choices, show that expected forking values along a response sum exactly to the reward variance, and observe on `Qwen3-8B-Base` that fork probability decays exponentially with a token's within-response entropy rank. `CreditFilter` weights tokens with an exponential window over that rank, needing no extra forward passes. Averaged over three seeds it **outperforms `DAPO` by 7.7 points on `MATH500` and by 10.5 and 9.1 points on `AIME24` and `AIME25`**.

papers.title: LongCat Recall Sparse Attention: Co-Designing Key Organization and Retrieval for Long-Context Inference
papers.abstract: Retrieval-based sparse attention, exemplified by DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA), reduces attention computation by selecting a small subset of key-value entries. However, selecting these entries can still require searching the entire visible history. For long sequences, retrieval becomes a major bottleneck, limiting the efficiency gains from sparse attention. To address this problem, we propose LongCat Recall Sparse Attention (LRSA), which combines fine-grained representatives with paged retrieval in an incrementally maintained index. LRSA partitions the sequence into time buckets that can be indexed independently as new keys arrive, without regrouping existing history. Within each bucket, it organizes indexing keys into capacity-balanced directional groups and packs a fixed number of complete groups into each page, retaining a separate center for every group. These centers provide fine-grained representatives for page selection, after which refinement scores members of the selected pages together with sink, sliding-window, and visible unindexed candidates to select the final Top-$K$ logical positions. To execute this retrieval process efficiently, we store members in reordered pages, fuse construction stages according to group size, and share storage for overlapping fixed candidates across queries during chunked prefill. These choices support regular member access while reducing kernel launches during construction and repeated candidate transfers. Moreover, we integrate LRSA into SGLang to maintain the index during inference, overlapping asynchronous index construction for new buckets with subsequent computation and reusing compatible bucket indices and member pages after a prefix match in the original key-value pool. With a 1024K-token context, LRSA accelerates key selection by 4.70$\times$ over DSA and combined selection and attention by 35.60$\times$ over full attention.
papers.summary: Retrieval-based sparse attention such as `DeepSeek Sparse Attention` (DSA) cuts attention cost by selecting a few key-value entries, but selecting them can still mean searching the entire visible history, which becomes the bottleneck for long sequences. `LongCat Recall Sparse Attention` (LRSA) partitions the sequence into time buckets that are indexed incrementally, organizes keys within each bucket into capacity-balanced directional groups packed into pages, and selects pages via per-group centers before refining to the final Top-K positions. It is integrated into `SGLang` with asynchronous index construction and index reuse after prefix matches. At a 1024K-token context, LRSA **speeds up key selection by 4.70x over DSA and combined selection and attention by 35.60x over full attention**.

papers.title: More Bits Won't Fix It: Diagnosing and Treating an Ill-Conditioned Backward Pass (A Case Study on Gemma-4)
papers.abstract: During LoRA fine-tuning of Gemma-4 (12B and 31B) on long prompts, whether they contain CT images, natural photos, or about 2,000 tokens of text, bf16 and fp32 gradients agree in the upper third of the language model (cosine similarity 0.96 or above) but are nearly orthogonal in the lower third. On image prompts, we trace the effect to an ill-conditioned backward path. The fp32 gradient is unchanged by element-wise relative noise of $10^{-6}$ on hidden states, confirming that fp32 is a valid reference. At $10^{-4}$, however, its cosine similarity with the noise-free gradient falls below 0.9 in 7 of 10 measurements, whereas bf16 forward states differ from fp32 states by about 1% per token. State swaps and backward-only interventions localize this sensitivity in Gemma-4-12B to the MLPs of layers 19-21 at image-token positions, where the gradient can be dominated by a single low-information patch. Detaching that path in the backward pass (while leaving the forward pass unchanged) keeps the gradient stable at $10^{-4}$ (cosine similarity 0.97 or above across all five measurements), lowers the median pre-clipping gradient norm from 8.5 to 0.63, and improves validation loss on a CT lesion-grounding task from 0.336 $\pm$ 0.019 to 0.296 $\pm$ 0.003 (four seeds; every modified run beats every baseline run). The gain disappears when the lower layers are frozen, and an fp32 run still exhibits gradient spikes (maximum norm 39,862) and fails to match this improvement. These training results cover one task and one model.
papers.summary: During `LoRA` fine-tuning of `Gemma-4` (12B and 31B) on long prompts, bf16 and fp32 gradients agree in the upper third of the language model but are nearly orthogonal in the lower third. On image prompts the cause is traced to an ill-conditioned backward path rather than insufficient precision: in `Gemma-4-12B` the sensitivity localizes to the MLPs of layers 19-21 at image-token positions, where a single low-information patch can dominate the gradient. Detaching that path in the backward pass only stabilizes the gradient, lowers the median pre-clipping gradient norm from 8.5 to 0.63, and **improves validation loss on a CT lesion-grounding task from 0.336 ± 0.019 to 0.296 ± 0.003**, while an fp32 run still shows gradient spikes and does not match the gain. The training results cover one task and one model.

papers.title: Proactive Defense Benchmark against Deepfake Generation
papers.abstract: Despite the proliferation of proactive defenses against deepfakes, the lack of a unified evaluation protocol precludes fair comparison and masks critical vulnerabilities. To bridge this gap, we present the first comprehensive benchmark that systematically assesses disruption, robustness, and transferability encompassing pixel, perceptual, and identity metrics. Our extensive analysis reveals that fidelity and identity metrics capture orthogonal performance axes, often leading to conflicting interpretations when relied upon individually. Furthermore, we identify a fundamental trade-off where peak white-box performance signals overfitting, and we introduce a calibrated evaluation to correct generator-induced identity bias. By exposing these blind spots, we establish a rigorous standard to guide the development of genuinely generalizable protections. Project page is available at: https://proactivedefensebenchmark.github.io/
papers.summary: Proactive defenses that perturb images to disrupt deepfake generation lack a unified evaluation protocol, which makes methods hard to compare. The authors present a benchmark assessing disruption, robustness, and transferability with pixel, perceptual, and identity metrics. Their analysis finds that **fidelity and identity metrics capture orthogonal performance axes and can give conflicting conclusions when used alone**, and that peak white-box performance signals overfitting. They also introduce a calibrated evaluation to correct identity bias induced by the generator.

papers.title: A preference for local interaction between layers emerges during training
papers.abstract: A deep neural network is a stack of layers, and all layers are trained to lower one shared error. A change in one layer can therefore reach every other layer. Because the error is shared by all layers, one would expect the other layers to respond alike, whether they are next to the changed layer or far from it. We find that early in training the response is weak and its order by distance is not stable. As training proceeds, the response grows, and neighboring layers come to respond to changes in each other more strongly than layers further apart, in almost every network. This locality forms during training, although training links every layer to every other. We show this by pushing one layer of a copy of the network at many stages of training and measuring how much of the push reaches each of the other layers. The experiments use 512 five-layer networks trained on modular addition with each of two optimizers, AdamW and stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics.
papers.summary: Because all layers of a deep network are trained against one shared error, a change in one layer might be expected to affect all others equally regardless of distance. By perturbing one layer of a copy of the network at many training stages and measuring how much of the push reaches each other layer, the authors find the response is weak and unordered early in training. As training proceeds, **neighboring layers come to respond to each other more strongly than distant layers in almost every network**. The experiments use 512 five-layer networks trained on modular addition with `AdamW` and stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics.

papers.title: No Perfect Guardrail & No Perfect Guard: On the Decidability of Output Policies for Large Language Models
papers.abstract:
Expecting guardrails to provide a general guarantee of safety fails to recognize the limits of computational enforcement and policy specification. We argue that promising such perfection is an ethical failure of precision, and that invoking it to abdicate responsibility is a moral failure. Guardrails can support responsible action, but cannot relieve researchers, developers, policymakers, or users of their obligations to examine what they claim, permit, and prevent.
  We establish a precise computational boundary. If every finite string is a possible output of a language model, a computable guard that blocks every forbidden output and passes every permitted one exists if and only if the policy is decidable. For an undecidable policy, every guard misclassifies infinitely many strings, and every guard that blocks all forbidden outputs excludes infinitely many permitted ones. We apply this characterization to arithmetic truth, program behavior, and harmful instructions to an idealized recipient. We distinguish guards from execution monitors, identify bounded and interceptable cases admitting exact enforcement, and explain why the results establish no positive lower bound on average error.
  Exact enforcement does not establish that a policy adequately captures safety. Conservative exclusion may withhold warnings, remedies, or challenges needed to recognize the policy's own defects. Human oversight cannot substitute for judgment: an apparent controller can become an instrument of purposes they have ceased to examine. Responsible governance requires continued critical challenge and the intellectual and moral humility to recognize possible flaws in our machines, rules, policies, and ourselves. The impossibility of a general assurance of perfection is a condition responsible practice must confront, not a responsibility that another guardrail - or another guard - can remove.
papers.summary: Guardrails on language model outputs are examined from a computability standpoint, alongside an ethical argument that they cannot relieve developers, policymakers, or users of responsibility. Assuming every finite string is a possible model output, the authors prove that **a computable guard that blocks every forbidden output and passes every permitted one exists if and only if the policy is decidable**; for undecidable policies every guard misclassifies infinitely many strings, and any guard blocking all forbidden outputs also excludes infinitely many permitted ones. The characterization is applied to arithmetic truth, program behavior, and harmful instructions, and the authors identify bounded and interceptable cases where exact enforcement is possible. They note the results give no positive lower bound on average error.

papers.title: Semiparametric Efficiency for Entropic Optimal Transport under Structured Distribution Shift
papers.abstract: Can structural information improve estimation of entropic optimal transport (EOT), and when is the gain zero? We study a fixed-dimensional exponential density ratio model (DRM) with a nonparametric baseline, compact support, and fixed positive regularization. At positive limiting sampling fractions, an exact projection identity quantifies the variance gain from the restriction. The pooled empirical-likelihood estimator attains the restricted bound and supports asymptotically valid confidence intervals when the bound is positive. Even under correct specification, the gain can be zero and can shrink as the tilt space expands. The same projection residual determines direction-specific first-order bias under local misspecification. When both samples grow and the target fraction vanishes, a zero first-order tilt derivative can leave source fluctuations and quadratic tilt error as the leading terms. Their balance gives a phase transition in the limiting distribution. A continuous example gives different convergence rates for two correctly specified bases at the same distribution pair. Controlled experiments assess the fixed-proportion theory. Natural-data comparisons distinguish variance reductions from improvements in reference RMSE driven by smaller reference bias.
papers.summary: The question studied is whether structural knowledge about distribution shift can improve statistical estimation of entropic optimal transport (EOT). Under a fixed-dimensional exponential density ratio model (DRM) with a nonparametric baseline, an exact projection identity quantifies the variance gain, and a pooled empirical-likelihood estimator attains the restricted efficiency bound with asymptotically valid confidence intervals. The analysis shows that **the gain can be zero even under correct specification and can shrink as the tilt space expands**. When the target sample fraction vanishes, the limiting distribution exhibits a phase transition between source fluctuations and quadratic tilt error.

papers.title: EAGLE: Entity-Aware Grounding with Layered Evidence for High-Resolution Image Understanding
papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) still struggle with fine-grained understanding of high-resolution images: attention heads vary in their reliability for grounding target entities and their attributes, while localized details are often disconnected from the broader scene context. We propose EAGLE (Entity-Aware Grounding with Layered Evidence for High-Resolution Image Understanding), a plug-in framework that jointly selects grounding signals and organizes hierarchical visual evidence. EAGLE employs a fine-grained dataset to screen visually-grounded attention heads, followed by entity-aware grounding to extract target-specific regions. It then integrates hierarchical evidence construction and question-guided routing to select optimal view combinations, feeding them into the frozen MLLM to enhance fine-grained visual understanding. Experiments with Qwen2.5-VL-7B and InternVL3-8B demonstrate that EAGLE consistently improves performance across both backbones and achieves SOTA results on V*, HRBench-4K, and HRBench-8K compared with existing methods using the same backbone.
papers.summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) struggle with fine-grained understanding of high-resolution images because attention heads vary in grounding reliability and local details get disconnected from scene context. `EAGLE` is a plug-in framework that screens visually grounded attention heads using a fine-grained dataset, extracts entity-specific regions, builds hierarchical visual evidence, and routes question-appropriate view combinations into the frozen model. With `Qwen2.5-VL-7B` and `InternVL3-8B` backbones, the authors report **consistent gains on both backbones and the best results among same-backbone methods on `V*`, `HRBench-4K`, and `HRBench-8K`**.

papers.title: Error-Corrected Physics-Informed Neural Operator for Optimal Control of Unmanned Aerial Vehicles under Uncertainty
papers.abstract: We solve open-loop optimal control problems under parametric uncertainty using a physics-informed DeepONet that returns trajectories for all sampled scenarios in one evaluation. Trained only on the residual at generic controls, the operator is reused across targets and horizons. Because a gradient-based optimizer exploits surrogate errors, we correct the prediction by one Newton step on the dynamics, computed for all scenarios and times by one parallel scan. The corrected state has a second-order error bounded by the residual alone, and the corrected cost is honest for every control up to the sampling error. On a fixed-wing UAV benchmark, the corrected operator matches the accuracy of a batched Adam solver and an Ipopt solver at equal sample size and is 8 times faster than the Adam solver on the same GPU at a few hundred scenarios and 15 times faster than Ipopt on a CPU.
papers.summary: Open-loop optimal control under parametric uncertainty is solved with a physics-informed `DeepONet` that returns trajectories for all sampled scenarios in a single evaluation and is reused across targets and horizons. Because gradient-based optimizers exploit surrogate errors, the prediction is corrected by one Newton step on the dynamics, computed for all scenarios and times in one parallel scan, giving a second-order error bounded by the residual. On a fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicle benchmark, the corrected operator matches the accuracy of batched `Adam` and `Ipopt` solvers at equal sample size and is **8 times faster than the Adam solver on the same GPU and 15 times faster than Ipopt on a CPU**.

papers.title: Do Companies Deliver on Their IPO Claims?
papers.abstract: Initial public offering (IPO) filings describe what a company does and what it intends to become. Yet whether individual forward-looking claims are subsequently realized is difficult to assess. We introduce Vision Follow-Through (VFT), a benchmark and agentic pipeline that separates claim extraction, category assignment, verifiability, and evidence-grounded follow-through assessment. \vftclaims{} contains 5,066 human-annotated claim spans from 50 IPO filings, while \vftverify{} adds verifiability tiers, follow-through outcomes, and cited later evidence for 1,000 claims. Across language models, classifying human-annotated claims is substantially easier than extracting claims from full filings. Extraction coverage also varies sharply by category, with Organizational/Culture claims recovered far less often than Market Opportunity claims. Follow-through assessment poses a separate challenge: model judgments diverge from human assessments in different ways rather than exhibiting a single consistent bias. These results show that reliable assessment of corporate follow-through requires both finding the relevant claims and grounding subsequent judgments in later evidence.
papers.summary: Whether forward-looking claims in initial public offering (IPO) filings are later realized is hard to assess at scale. `Vision Follow-Through` (`VFT`) is a benchmark and agentic pipeline separating claim extraction, category assignment, verifiability, and evidence-grounded follow-through assessment, with 5,066 human-annotated claim spans from 50 filings and a 1,000-claim subset carrying verifiability tiers, outcomes, and cited later evidence. Across language models, **classifying human-annotated claims is substantially easier than extracting claims from full filings**, and extraction coverage varies sharply by category. Model follow-through judgments diverge from human assessments in different ways rather than showing one consistent bias.

papers.title: DermKG: A Concept-Centric Knowledge Graph for Interpretable Skin Disease Diagnosis from Dermatological Morphology
papers.abstract: Dermatologists describe lesions with a standardized morphological lexicon, which makes concept-based models attractive for interpretable skin disease diagnosis. How much diagnostic information these concepts actually carry, however, is rarely quantified. We present DermKG, a concept-centric knowledge graph built on the expert-annotated SkinCon subset of Fitzpatrick17k (3,230 images, 48 concepts, 113 diseases). DermKG has 3,452 nodes of 8 types and 19,365 edges of 11 relation types, and encodes disease concept profiles, concept co-occurrence, a three-level diagnostic hierarchy, and 20 clinical morphology rules, all of which are supported by the training data (15 strong, 5 moderate). An information-ceiling analysis shows that the 3,230 lesions collapse onto only 813 distinct concept vectors, bounding concept-only top-1 accuracy at 38.9\% for diseases and 77.6\% for the nine categories. Within this bound, DermKG-Net, a graph neural network that scores lesions against disease prototypes and aggregates them along the hierarchy, raises category-level balanced accuracy from 0.257 to 0.411 over the strongest of 11 baselines (paired bootstrap difference $+0.150$, 95\% CI $[0.073, 0.231]$) and more than doubles minority-category recall. Ablations show that most of this gain comes from the hierarchical prototype objective, with a smaller contribution from graph structure. DermKG further yields rule-based reasoning chains and concept-level explanations for individual predictions.
papers.summary: Concept-based models for skin disease diagnosis rely on dermatologists' morphological vocabulary, but how much diagnostic information those concepts carry is rarely measured. `DermKG` is a knowledge graph built on the expert-annotated `SkinCon` subset of `Fitzpatrick17k` (3,230 images, 48 concepts, 113 diseases), encoding disease concept profiles, co-occurrence, a three-level diagnostic hierarchy, and 20 clinical morphology rules. An information-ceiling analysis shows the lesions collapse onto 813 distinct concept vectors, **bounding concept-only top-1 accuracy at 38.9% for diseases and 77.6% for the nine categories**. Within that bound, the graph neural network `DermKG-Net` raises category-level balanced accuracy from 0.257 to 0.411 over the strongest of 11 baselines.

papers.title: Belief-State Management Meets Rubric Rewards for Agentic Forecasting
papers.abstract: Current large language model (LLM) agents still struggle to forecast real-world events. This stems from two primary limitations: i) standard ReAct harness accumulates reasoning and evidence within one growing context, and ii) outcome-based rewards in forecasting lead to a slow and noisy signal that cannot distinguish sound reasoning from lucky guesses. To address these, we introduce a forecasting training framework including harness design and post-training. For the harness side, we propose Proactive Belief-State Management (PBM), equipping agents with a fold tool to compress lengthy context into compact belief states and reset the context for subsequent exploration. For the training side, we develop SEIPH, a five-dimensional, outcome-blind rubric, providing process-quality rewards. Using the rubric-based reward, we post-train a 35B model with PPO and GRPO, yielding DeepForecaster-PPO and DeepForecaster-GRPO. Theoretically, we prove that idealized fold-based stopping converges and calibrated local rewards reduce segment-level gradient variance. Empirically, DeepForecaster-PPO (35B) achieves the best Brier score on both ForecastBench and Polymarket-Sim, outperforming frontier agents based on DeepSeek-V4-Pro (1.6T), Kimi-K2.6 (1T), and GPT-5.5. DeepForecaster-GRPO ranks second on both FutureX metrics. Ablations reveal that PBM also improves the untrained base model without any training. Calibration analysis shows that DeepForecaster-PPO makes more accurate high-confidence predictions than Qwen3.6 and GPT-5.5. Trajectory analysis further shows that forecasts generally improve from the first to the final belief state as agents gather evidence and revise their judgments.
papers.summary: Large language model agents forecast real-world events poorly, which the authors attribute to `ReAct` harnesses accumulating everything in one growing context and to outcome-based rewards being slow and noisy. They propose `Proactive Belief-State Management` (PBM), which gives agents a fold tool to compress context into compact belief states and reset, and `SEIPH`, a five-dimensional outcome-blind rubric that rewards process quality, used to post-train a 35B model with `PPO` and `GRPO`. **`DeepForecaster-PPO` (35B) achieves the best Brier score on both `ForecastBench` and `Polymarket-Sim`**, ahead of agents built on `DeepSeek-V4-Pro`, `Kimi-K2.6`, and `GPT-5.5`. Ablations show PBM also improves the untrained base model.

papers.title: Preserving Pretrained CFG Structure in RL for Diffusion Models with Conditional Contrast Regularization
papers.abstract: Reinforcement Learning (RL) has become an important component in the post-training of diffusion models. In practice, however, standard RL often improves the target reward without reliably preserving holistic generation quality, leading to unstable reward-quality trade-offs that we view as a form of reward hacking. Since Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) is known to improve visual clarity, prompt alignment, and perceptual quality in generation, we investigate whether its underlying structure can serve as a useful prior during RL. We present a unified geometric view that interprets both CFG and RL as correction vectors in a common prediction space, and identify the projection of the RL-induced correction onto the pretrained CFG correction as a useful diagnostic of quality-related structural preservation. Geometric analysis and rotation intervention further show that the pretrained CFG direction carries information useful for generation quality that reward-driven RL updates do not necessarily preserve. Based on this insight, we propose Conditional Contrast Regularization (CCR), which uses the frozen reference model's conditional contrast as a local structural prior during RL. Experiments across multiple reward settings and backbones show that CCR more consistently preserves generation quality while maintaining competitive reward, yielding a better reward-quality trade-off than standard RL and generic regularization methods.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning used to post-train diffusion models often raises the target reward while degrading overall generation quality, which the authors treat as a form of reward hacking. They interpret both Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) and reinforcement learning updates as correction vectors in a shared prediction space and use the projection of the learned correction onto the pretrained CFG correction as a diagnostic of quality preservation. `Conditional Contrast Regularization` (`CCR`) uses the frozen reference model's conditional contrast as a local structural prior during training. Across multiple reward settings and backbones, **`CCR` preserves generation quality more consistently while keeping reward competitive** compared with standard RL and generic regularizers.

papers.title: EgoLAM: Learning Latent Actions from Hand and Head Motion
papers.abstract: Latent action models let a robot policy learn from video by turning the change between two frames into a training target. In egocentric video, a cup can move across the image because a hand pushes it or because the wearer turns. Both changes help predict the next frame, but only the first describes manipulation. During training, EgoLAM supervises the action code with measured wrist motion and supplies camera motion separately to the forward model. Even when the wearer turns while pushing a cup, the training target still describes how the hand pushed it. The action encoder pools object slots around each hand, and wrist translation and rotation can be decoded from the code in a common reference frame. Extracting a code then requires only two RGB frames. Alongside LARYBench classification and regression, we measure how much wrist motion a frozen code retains and how strongly it responds to a synthetic view or lighting change. EgoLAM has the highest hand-motion decoding score among eight evaluated models. Across three LIBERO suites, policies pretrained on its codes and fine-tuned on expert demonstrations achieve 79.38% mean success, 28.73 points above expert behavior cloning and 9.76 points above the strongest other latent action model in each suite on average.
papers.summary: Latent action models let robot policies learn from video by encoding frame-to-frame change, but in egocentric video that change mixes hand manipulation with the wearer's own camera motion. `EgoLAM` supervises the action code with measured wrist motion during training and supplies camera motion separately to the forward model, so the code describes only the hand; at inference it needs just two RGB frames. It achieves the highest hand-motion decoding score among eight evaluated models. Across three `LIBERO` suites, policies pretrained on its codes reach **79.38% mean success, 28.73 points above expert behavior cloning** and 9.76 points above the strongest other latent action model on average.

papers.title: HookEvo: A Framework for Coordinated Plugin Evolution on Hook-Enabled Agent Runtimes
papers.abstract: Repairing failures in tool-using agents can require coordinated changes to how the harness interprets tool receipts, assembles context, and checks actions. We introduce HookEvo, a framework that uses an existing agent runtime's lifecycle hooks to evolve task-specific harnesses. We instantiate HookEvo on DeepSeek Harness. In each round, a separate improver diagnoses failures from execution traces and proposes a candidate. HookEvo evaluates the candidate against the current harness on matched tasks and carries the retained version into the next round. A single candidate can jointly edit executable plugin handlers and the state they share within a task, allowing a tool receipt to inform context and control a later action. Using a frozen Qwen3-4B executor, the selected harnesses lead the reported Qwen3-4B comparisons, achieving 95.41% on ALFWorld, 70.56% on DBBench, 48.17% on WebShop, and 41.67% on OSBench.
