Across three improvers and three edit scopes, from skill text to single-component and coordinated executable edits, GPT-6.1 Sol shows the largest average gain from the broadest scope. Our code is available at https://huangshengzebluesky.github.io/hookevo/.
papers.summary: Fixing failures in tool-using agents can require coordinated changes to how the harness interprets tool receipts, assembles context, and checks actions. `HookEvo` uses an existing agent runtime's lifecycle hooks to evolve task-specific harnesses: each round, a separate improver model diagnoses failures from execution traces and proposes a candidate that can jointly edit executable plugin handlers and their shared state, which is kept only if it beats the current harness on matched tasks. Instantiated on `DeepSeek Harness` with a frozen `Qwen3-4B` executor, the selected harnesses reach **95.41% on `ALFWorld`, 70.56% on `DBBench`, 48.17% on `WebShop`, and 41.67% on `OSBench`**. Among three improvers and three edit scopes, `GPT-6.1 Sol` gains most on average from the broadest scope of coordinated executable edits.

papers.title: Observed, Curated, Reused: Observation Bias in Clinical AI Evaluation
papers.abstract:
Clinical AI evaluations are vulnerable to observation bias embedded in routine medical documentation, which captures only what clinicians notice, test, and record rather than a complete clinical picture. As this evidence travels into publications and reference knowledge graphs, crucial distinctions disappear: unexamined symptoms blur with confirmed negatives, and chronological disease progression is lost. Surviving evidence can also enter both the benchmark query and the reference knowledge base, creating a self-referential loop where a patient is evaluated against clues derived from their own published case report.
  To quantify this bias, we tracked 6,503 clinical cases across six historical Human Phenotype Ontology (HPO) releases (October 2021-June 2026) to identify when HPO first cited the publications describing them. This yielded a confirmatory cohort with an observable "source ingestion" event, where HPO cited a case's source publication as target-disease evidence. Diagnostic rankers depended heavily on these source publications: for our primary semantic ranker (Resnik), publication-weighted mean reciprocal rank rose from 0.26 before paper ingestion to 0.84 upon inclusion in HPO, but collapsed to 0.05 when source-linked assertions were counterfactually removed. Two additional rankers (IC-cosine and LIRICAL) reproduced this trajectory, and control experiments confirmed the diagnostic jump was driven by the patient's publication rather than background HPO growth.
  Clinical AI systems may therefore score well because their knowledge base contains evidence linked to the test case's source publication, rather than through generalization. Modern knowledge is not the problem; evaluation evidence must match the claim. Trustworthy benchmarks must separate patients, source-linked evidence, and time: historical tests should use only knowledge available at the intended decision time.
papers.summary: Clinical AI benchmarks can be inflated when a patient's published case report feeds both the test query and the reference knowledge base. Tracking 6,503 clinical cases across six releases of the Human Phenotype Ontology (HPO) from October 2021 to June 2026, the authors identify when each case's source publication was first cited as disease evidence. For the primary `Resnik` semantic ranker, **publication-weighted mean reciprocal rank rose from 0.26 before the paper's ingestion to 0.84 after, and collapsed to 0.05 when source-linked assertions were removed**; `IC-cosine` and `LIRICAL` showed the same pattern. They conclude that benchmarks should separate patients, source-linked evidence, and time, using only knowledge available at the intended decision time.

papers.title: Can Reasoning and Image Description Enhance Yes/No Visual Mathematical Understanding?
papers.abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have achieved strong performance on general visual tasks, yet their ability to understand mathematical images remains limited. This paper investigates whether explicit reasoning and textual image descriptions can enhance VLMs' performance on binary yes/no visual mathematical questions. To achieve this, we curated a paired evaluation set to benchmark prominent open-source VLMs under varying prompt and input conditions. In particular, we leverage Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting and use textual descriptions, either replacing or augmenting visual inputs, to isolate and evaluate mathematical comprehension. Our results show that explicit reasoning improves performance, especially in paired consistency accuracy, while textual image descriptions do not consistently help and may degrade performance. These findings suggest that reasoning is important for stable visual mathematical judgement, whereas description-based intermediates require more careful design.
papers.summary: Vision-language models remain weak at understanding mathematical images, and this study tests whether explicit reasoning or textual image descriptions help on binary yes/no visual math questions. Using a curated paired evaluation set, the authors benchmark open-source models with Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting and with descriptions that either replace or augment the image. **Explicit reasoning improves performance, especially paired consistency accuracy, while textual descriptions do not consistently help and can degrade results**.

papers.title: $\gamma$-Scape: An Agent-Centric World for Mobile Embodied Intelligence
papers.abstract: Recent embodied agents construct and adapt robot behavior through executable programs, tool use, and interaction feedback. Studying these systems in mobile manipulation calls for physical worlds that connect agent-directed execution with its physical consequences and reusable interaction experience. We introduce $\gamma$-Scape, an agent-centric simulation and benchmark platform for mobile embodied intelligence. Agents compose motion tools and learned skills to carry out complete tasks that combine navigation and manipulation in a persistent physical world. BenchForge grounds structured objectives in physical task instances with instructions, reference programs, and goal evaluators, defining task goals while preserving agents' choice of valid solutions. An agentic collection harness further enables agents to produce demonstrations by carrying out contact-rich interactions through sustained control and physical feedback. Assisted reference execution and human guidance provide complementary experience. The resulting tool traces and aligned observation-action records support program refinement and policy learning, with common task-goal criteria for subsequent evaluation. We benchmark representative agent systems on complete tasks and demonstrate contact collection and trace-informed program revision. Together, these workflows provide infrastructure for research on embodied recursive self-improvement.
papers.summary: Embodied agents that write programs and call tools to control robots need simulated worlds where those programs have physical consequences and leave reusable experience. `γ-Scape` is a simulation and benchmark platform for mobile manipulation in which agents compose motion tools and learned skills to complete combined navigation-and-manipulation tasks in a persistent world, with `BenchForge` generating task instances that come with instructions, reference programs, and goal evaluators. **An agentic collection harness lets agents produce contact-rich demonstrations themselves**, and the resulting tool traces and aligned observation-action records are used for program revision and policy learning. The authors benchmark representative agent systems on complete tasks and demonstrate contact collection and trace-informed program revision.

papers.title: A Framework for AI-Ready Data in Earth and Environmental Science
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI), specifically machine learning (ML), is increasingly integral to Earth and environmental research, yet the suitability of current research data infrastructures for supporting AI workflows remains poorly defined. While the FAIR principles provide a foundation for scientific data management, they do not explicitly address several requirements arising when datasets are used for training, evaluating, and deploying AI models. This article presents a practically motivated framework for assessing and improving AI-readiness of research data within distributed Earth and environmental data infrastructures. The framework was developed through a structured, community-driven process, beginning with a review of existing literature and readiness frameworks combined with feedback from a limited survey of scientists applying ML methods. Its main aspects were shaped by a multidisciplinary expert group representing data providers, infrastructure developers, data managers, and AI practitioners. It identifies 25 criteria covering data preparation, data quality, documentation, access, and supervised learning targets. The criteria emphasize aspects particularly relevant to AI applications, including provenance, treatment of missing data, bias documentation, uncertainty characterization, machine-actionable metadata, efficient access formats, and the quality and reproducibility of target generation. Application to a broad range of representative environmental use cases highlights how the relevance of individual criteria varies by application. We argue that AI-readiness should be understood primarily as a property of transparency and fitness for purpose rather than as a fixed level of data quality. The framework lays a foundation for communication and community-driven action to advance AI-ready data and support next-generation AI-enabled scientific workflows.
papers.summary: The FAIR data-management principles do not cover several requirements that arise when Earth and environmental datasets are used to train, evaluate, and deploy machine learning models. Through a literature review, a small survey of practitioners, and a multidisciplinary expert group, the authors develop an assessment framework of **25 criteria spanning data preparation, data quality, documentation, access, and supervised learning targets**, with emphasis on provenance, missing-data handling, bias documentation, uncertainty, and machine-actionable metadata. Applying it to a range of environmental use cases shows that the relevance of individual criteria varies by application, and the authors argue AI-readiness is a matter of transparency and fitness for purpose instead of a fixed quality level.

papers.title: Do Language Models Know Which Words Steer Their Reasoning?
papers.abstract: While chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting elicits intermediate reasoning steps from language models, it is unclear which words in the context actually steer the CoT. We identify Phantom Context Influence (PCI): language models are disproportionately steered by semantically irrelevant context words, even as the same models deny those words' relevance when asked. To localize PCI, we introduce Leave-One-Out Word JSD analysis, which removes one context word at a time from the otherwise intact context to isolate its marginal effect on the next-token distribution; words whose removal flips the prediction (pivot words) are passed to the same LLM to self-judge whether it recognizes this predictive dependence. Across four models and three benchmarks, language models largely do not know which words steer their reasoning, a mismatch we call the Generation-Judgment Contradiction. Inspired by this phenomenon, we propose Online KV Suppression: it scores every prompt word's influence over the whole chain of thought in a single pass, then zeroes the KV-cache entries of the highest-influence word the model itself judges inert and redecodes. This single-word intervention improves CoT accuracy across four models and five reasoning benchmarks, by up to 8.9 percentage points on math reasoning benchmark.
papers.summary: Which context words actually steer a model's chain-of-thought (CoT) is examined with `Leave-One-Out Word JSD` analysis, which removes one word at a time and measures the change in the next-token distribution. The authors identify Phantom Context Influence (PCI): models are disproportionately steered by semantically irrelevant words yet deny those words matter when asked, a mismatch observed across four models and three benchmarks. Building on this, `Online KV Suppression` scores each prompt word's influence in a single pass, zeroes the KV-cache entries of the most influential word the model judges inert, and redecodes. This single-word intervention improves CoT accuracy across four models and five reasoning benchmarks, by **up to 8.9 percentage points on a math reasoning benchmark**.

papers.title: SAVIOR: Sample-efficient Adaptation of Vision-Language Models for OCR Representation
papers.abstract: Optical Character Recognition (OCR) pipelines and vision-language models exhibit high accuracy on standard OCR and document-understanding benchmarks, yet they systematically underperform on document patterns that are operationally critical in financial workflows. These patterns include vertical or rotated text, logo-embedded vendor names, fine-print regulatory clauses, degraded scans, and complex multi-column layouts. While underrepresented in public datasets, they constitute a substantial portion of real-world failure cases. We introduce SAVIOR, a sample-efficient data curation methodology that targets such high-impact failure scenarios to adapt vision-language models for robust financial OCR. We further propose PaIRS, a structure-aware evaluation metric that measures layout fidelity by comparing pairwise spatial relationships between tokens. Fine-tuning Qwen2.5-VL-Instruct with SAVIOR-Train achieves a word recall of 0.93. When the resulting layout-aware OCR output is used as context for document question answering, it attains an F1 score of 0.89, outperforming both open- and closed-source models such as GPT-4o, Mistral-OCR, PaddleOCR-VL, and DeepSeek-OCR.
papers.summary: Optical Character Recognition (OCR) systems and vision-language models score well on standard benchmarks but fail on patterns common in financial documents, such as rotated text, logo-embedded vendor names, fine print, degraded scans, and multi-column layouts. `SAVIOR` is a sample-efficient data curation methodology that targets these failure cases, accompanied by `PaIRS`, a metric that measures layout fidelity by comparing pairwise spatial relationships between tokens. Fine-tuning `Qwen2.5-VL-Instruct` on `SAVIOR-Train` reaches a word recall of 0.93, and using its layout-aware output as context for document question answering yields **an F1 of 0.89, ahead of `GPT-4o`, `Mistral-OCR`, `PaddleOCR-VL`, and `DeepSeek-OCR`**.

papers.title: Spiking Neural Networks Incrementally Track Firing-Rate Networks
papers.abstract: Understanding how spiking neural networks (SNNs) efficiently process data streams is key to (i) studying how biological brains conserve energy for lifelong predictions and (ii) enabling efficient continuous AI inference. In this work, we propose a theory on how an SNN incrementally tracks its corresponding firing-rate network, a continuous-valued neural network (ANN). We prove that the output of a discrete SNN continuously tracks the instantaneous ANN output implicitly determined by the SNN input. Based on this principle, we develop LIF-Stream, a conversion framework for efficient SNN inference over unbounded data streams. It enables the converted SNN to reuse its prior activation state and compute only the activation updates between frames, thereby reducing the average number of time steps needed per frame. Specifically, LIF-Stream controls the SNN to continuously track the reference ANN output, which gives a high-accuracy prediction for every frame. Evaluation on three large-scale streaming inference benchmarks with distinct modalities shows that LIF-Stream achieves the best efficiency-accuracy trade-off compared to high-accuracy SNN techniques.
papers.summary: A theory is proposed for how a spiking neural network (SNN) relates to its corresponding firing-rate network, a continuous-valued artificial neural network (ANN), when processing data streams. The authors prove that **the output of a discrete SNN continuously tracks the instantaneous ANN output determined by the SNN's input**. They use this to build `LIF-Stream`, an ANN-to-SNN conversion framework that reuses the prior activation state and computes only the activation updates between frames, reducing the average number of time steps per frame. On three large-scale streaming inference benchmarks across different modalities, it reports the best efficiency-accuracy trade-off among high-accuracy SNN techniques.

papers.title: Reasoning in Fewer Tokens: Concept-Normalized Multilingual Scratchpads and Reversible Model-Adaptive Reasoning Codes
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought prompting significantly improves the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs) but incurs high inference costs due to lengthy autoregressive decoding. While previous efficiency approaches reduce costs by discarding tokens or utilizing continuous latent representations, these lossy methods fundamentally sacrifice interpretability and auditability. In this work, we introduce a novel compression framework for intermediate reasoning. We apply Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) to reasoning corpora to learn a compressed vocabulary of Private Use Area (PUA) tokens, each representing frequent semantic spans. After expanding the LLM's vocabulary, we fine-tune the model via strictly 1:1, our method is lossless. We evaluate our approach on Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-14B, and Qwen2.5-32B across four diverse benchmarks. Our method reduces total generated tokens by 14.7% on average with reasoning trace lengths dropping by up to 27.1%, while incurring a negligible average accuracy cost of 1.6 percentage points. Crucially, this approach is orthogonal to existing lossy methods, allowing practitioners to stack lossless and irreversible compression techniques. We demonstrate that a compressed intermediate language provides a highly efficient computational resource that accelerates inference while fully preserving the transparency of LLM reasoning.
papers.summary: Chain-of-thought reasoning is expensive because of long autoregressive decoding, and existing fixes that drop tokens or reason in continuous latents sacrifice the ability to audit the reasoning. The approach here applies Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) to reasoning corpora to learn a vocabulary of Private Use Area (PUA) tokens that each stand for a frequent semantic span, expands the model's vocabulary, and fine-tunes it to reason in this compressed code, which the authors describe as lossless and reversible. Evaluated on `Llama-3.1-8B`, `Qwen2.5-14B`, and `Qwen2.5-32B` across four benchmarks, it **cuts total generated tokens by 14.7% on average** and reasoning traces by up to 27.1%, at an average accuracy cost of 1.6 percentage points. The authors note it can be stacked with lossy compression methods.

papers.title: H-MSAE: Hierarchical Sparse Concept Coverage for Efficient and Diverse Instruction Data Selection
papers.abstract: Large instruction-tuning corpora contain substantial semantic redundancy, motivating the selection of compact subsets that preserve useful supervision while reducing training cost. Existing diversity-aware selectors often rely on generated semantic tags and explicit graph structures, introducing considerable annotation and preprocessing overhead. We introduce H-MSAE, a hierarchical sparse instruction selection framework that organizes multi-resolution concepts learned by a Matryoshka sparse autoencoder into a coarse-to-fine hierarchy. Quality-weighted, diminishing-return coverage with ancestor propagation promotes high-quality and non-redundant semantic coverage, while pool-relative length constraints regulate subset composition. We motivate this design through a local quality-diversity analysis of subset SFT utility and examine it using example-quality and representation-space diversity diagnostics. On Tulu 3 data pool, H-MSAE achieves the highest Final Avg among the evaluated 50K selectors across scales and initialization. The selected subset also exhibits the highest mean quality and effective rank among the evaluated methods. By avoiding full-pool generative tagging and supporting efficient sparse selection, H-MSAE reduces measured end-to-end runtime by approximately $5\times$ relative to MIG.
papers.summary: Instruction-tuning corpora are highly redundant, and existing diversity-aware subset selectors depend on generated semantic tags and explicit graphs that are costly to build. `H-MSAE` instead organizes multi-resolution concepts learned by a Matryoshka sparse autoencoder into a coarse-to-fine hierarchy, then selects examples using quality-weighted, diminishing-return coverage with ancestor propagation and pool-relative length constraints. On the `Tulu 3` data pool it achieves the highest final average score among the evaluated 50K-example selectors, with the highest mean quality and effective rank. By avoiding full-pool generative tagging, it **reduces end-to-end runtime by roughly 5x relative to `MIG`**.

papers.title: GGDriver: Glance at What Is Shared, Gaze at What Differs for Perception-Free Planning
papers.abstract: A planner deciding whether to turn left or continue straight needs to inspect different parts of the scene for each maneuver. Yet many end-to-end driving planners evaluate every candidate trajectory against the same compressed scene representation. We let each candidate select the visual evidence used to refine and score it. A global glance first produces trajectory hypotheses from shared scene features. We then project a corridor around each trajectory into the camera views and use the resulting mask to attend to patch features at the backbone's native resolution. After refinement, the scorer projects each final proposal again and ranks it using evidence along its own path. This geometric selection requires only the predicted trajectory and camera calibration. On three planners with different scene representations (learned registers, a perception-supervised bird's-eye-view grid, and a coarse image-token grid), adding this gaze improves planning scores. In ablations, path-aligned patches outperform both a matched number of randomly selected patches and attention over all patches. Using the gaze for ranking yields larger gains than using it for refinement alone. With a ViT-S backbone and no perception labels, GGDriver achieves a rater feedback score of 8.110 on the WOD-E2E test set, 94.2 PDMS on NAVSIM-v1, 48.6 EPDMS on NAVSIM-v2, and a closed-loop Driving Score of 72.18 on Bench2Drive.
papers.summary: End-to-end driving planners usually score every candidate trajectory against the same compressed scene representation, even though different maneuvers depend on different parts of the scene. `GGDriver` first generates trajectory hypotheses from shared scene features, then projects a corridor around each trajectory into the camera views and attends to native-resolution patch features inside it, both to refine the proposal and to rank it, requiring only the predicted trajectory and camera calibration. Added to three planners with different scene representations, this improves planning scores, and path-aligned patches beat both random patches and attention over all patches. With a `ViT-S` backbone and no perception labels, it reports **94.2 PDMS on `NAVSIM-v1`**, 48.6 EPDMS on `NAVSIM-v2`, a rater feedback score of 8.110 on `WOD-E2E`, and a closed-loop Driving Score of 72.18 on `Bench2Drive`.

papers.title: Latent Jacobian Steer: Eliciting Contact-Rich Out-of-Distribution Behaviors from Pretrained Humanoid Controllers
papers.abstract: Given a pretrained general latent-conditioned whole-body humanoid controller, say a behavioral foundation model (BFM), how can we elicit complex and contact-rich out-of-distribution behaviors? Raw joint-action exploration enables direct, task-specific adjustments but can disrupt coordination learned by the pretrained controller, whereas latent exploration retains that coordination but is difficult to steer toward desired physical effects. To combine the complementary strengths of these exploration spaces, we propose Latent Jacobian Steer (LJS), which couples sampling in direct joint-action space with the semantics of the learned frozen controller's input latent space. For a task specified through desired physical effects, we sample task-relevant joint-action perturbations and map them through a damped local inverse of the policy Jacobian to obtain candidate latent ($z$) commands. These commands are executed through the frozen pretrained policy, while exploration is directed toward the physical outcomes required by the new task. Candidate outcomes are evaluated in simulation and composed into latent-command sequences that accomplish the task. Ablations show that neither action-space nor latent-space exploration alone provides the same capability as their coupling. Across diverse out-of-distribution tasks, simulation-based searching using this method produces contact-rich behaviors, including hurdling, manipulating articulated objects, and opening doors through non-prehensile contact. Over ten seeds, LJS completes more of each humanoid task than when searching in either space alone. Beyond humanoids, it also steers a goal-conditioned dexterous hand policy through four assembly tasks better than searching in goal space directly.
papers.summary: Eliciting complex, contact-rich behaviors outside the training distribution from a frozen, latent-conditioned whole-body humanoid controller, or behavioral foundation model (BFM), is hard because joint-action exploration disrupts learned coordination while latent exploration is difficult to steer. `Latent Jacobian Steer` (LJS) samples task-relevant joint-action perturbations and maps them through a damped local inverse of the policy Jacobian into candidate latent commands, which are executed by the frozen policy, evaluated in simulation, and composed into command sequences. The search produces behaviors such as hurdling, manipulating articulated objects, and opening doors through non-prehensile contact. Over ten seeds, **LJS completes more of each humanoid task than searching in either space alone**, and it also steers a goal-conditioned dexterous hand policy through four assembly tasks better than goal-space search.

papers.title: Unimodal Shortcuts and Joint Scene-Intent Dependence in Vision-Language Safety Representations
papers.abstract: The safety of a request to a vision-language model often depends on the image: asking how to serve a dish is harmless for fresh food and harmful for spoiled food. High accuracy on situational safety benchmarks does not tell us whether a model's safety representation encodes both the scene and the user's intent, because a benchmark can often be solved from one modality alone. Studying frozen vision-language safety representations, we audit five public situational benchmarks and find that each admits a unimodal shortcut: images alone predict the labels, and on same-image prompt pairs a probe that never sees the photograph reaches 0.9645 AUROC. We therefore build a controlled evaluation that crosses safe and hazardous scenes with observation and action requests, so that no single-modality rule can exceed 0.500 group-ranking accuracy. On this control, linear probes on intermediate states of Qwen3-VL-8B and SmolVLM2-2.2B reach 0.958 and 0.930, showing that the scene-intent conjunction is linearly decodable; concatenating separately encoded image and text states already recovers most of this signal, so decodability is not evidence of a fusion mechanism. The same probes screen cheaply but generalize poorly to unseen images and other benchmarks. Reliable multimodal safety evaluation therefore needs controls that rule out unimodal shortcuts before accuracy is read as evidence of joint understanding.
papers.summary: Whether a request to a vision-language model is safe can depend on the image, but high scores on situational safety benchmarks do not show that a model's representation encodes both scene and intent. Auditing five public benchmarks, the authors find each admits a unimodal shortcut: images alone predict the labels, and **a probe that never sees the image reaches 0.9645 AUROC** on same-image prompt pairs. They build a controlled evaluation crossing safe and hazardous scenes with observation and action requests so no single-modality rule exceeds 0.500, on which linear probes on `Qwen3-VL-8B` and `SmolVLM2-2.2B` reach 0.958 and 0.930. Concatenating separately encoded image and text states recovers most of that signal, so decodability is not evidence of fusion, and the probes generalize poorly to unseen images and other benchmarks.

papers.title: Learning Interaction Dynamics via Motion-Region Guidance for Robotic Video World Models
papers.abstract: Action-conditioned video world models imagine future observations under candidate robot actions, providing a promising visual tool for robot policy evaluation and interaction simulation. However, existing video world models often optimize global reconstruction errors instead of emphasizing interaction-relevant regions. As a result, they may preserve overall scene appearance but overlook local interaction details, leading to physically implausible outcomes such as hallucinated contact effects and inconsistent robot-object interactions. We introduce MoReWorld, a unified motion-region-guided framework that uses a shared motion region, the part of the environment that moves in response to the robot's actions, to focus dynamics learning and video generation on interaction-relevant regions. The same motion region guides local motion prediction, region-aware supervision, and motion-gated future-feature conditioning. At inference time, the motion region is predicted as a motion probability map from visual history and robot actions, without requiring future observations or ground-truth motion labels. On WorldSimProbe, MoReWorld achieves the highest overall simulator-faithfulness score, with the strongest performance on local consistency, global consistency, and interaction dynamics. These results indicate that motion-region guidance helps the model preserve scene-level consistency while more faithfully predicting action-conditioned interaction dynamics.
papers.summary: Action-conditioned video world models for robotics typically optimize global reconstruction error, so they preserve scene appearance while hallucinating contact effects and producing inconsistent robot-object interactions. `MoReWorld` uses a shared motion region, the part of the environment that moves in response to the robot's actions, to guide local motion prediction, region-aware supervision, and motion-gated future-feature conditioning. At inference the region is predicted as a motion probability map from visual history and actions, without future observations or ground-truth motion labels. On `WorldSimProbe`, it achieves **the highest overall simulator-faithfulness score**, leading on local consistency, global consistency, and interaction dynamics.

papers.title: Breaking the Long Horizon: Short-Horizon Process Supervision for Long-Form Generation in LLMs
papers.abstract: Long-form generation is increasingly important for agentic LLM systems, yet current reinforcement learning methods typically optimize an entire document with a single outcome-level reward. This delayed and coarse-grained supervision makes it difficult to localize errors and assign credit across semantically distinct parts of the output. To address this, we propose a short-horizon framework that reformulates long-form generation through semantic decomposition into segment-level decisions. Each segment is generated with prefix-conditioned context, allowing cross-segment coherence to be preserved while keeping supervision local. The generated segments are then scored with rubric-based rewards for adherence, coherence, and relevance, enabling explicit local supervision at the segment level. These local rewards are used to compute step-wise advantages, yielding localized policy updates. To isolate the effect of supervision granularity, we instantiate both outcome-level supervision and our short-horizon process reward method (SH-PRM) under the same GRPO framework. Across multiple LLMs and two long-form generation benchmarks, SH-PRM consistently outperforms outcome-level supervision and strong inference-time baselines under the same optimizer and comparable budgets. Further analyses suggest that these gains primarily arise from improved credit assignment. Overall, our results suggest that aligning supervision granularity with the semantic structure of long-form generation is an effective design principle for long-form LLM training.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning for long-form generation usually assigns a single outcome-level reward to a whole document, which makes it hard to localize errors and assign credit. The proposed short-horizon process reward method, `SH-PRM`, decomposes generation into semantic segments, generates each with prefix-conditioned context, scores segments with rubric-based rewards for adherence, coherence, and relevance, and computes step-wise advantages for localized policy updates. With both variants instantiated under the same `GRPO` framework, **`SH-PRM` consistently outperforms outcome-level supervision and strong inference-time baselines** across multiple models and two long-form generation benchmarks at comparable budgets. Analyses attribute the gains mainly to improved credit assignment.

papers.title: EcomWriteBench: A Real-World Benchmark for E-commerce Writing Tasks
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used throughout e-commerce workflows to generate content that informs purchasing decisions and supports customer interactions. Evaluating these systems requires accounting for user needs, product evidence, structural constraints, and business requirements that are not fully captured by general-purpose writing benchmarks. We introduce EcomWriteBench, a real-world benchmark containing 3,861 queries from 69 e-commerce writing tasks across 13 categories and five languages. Through task-level extraction, cross-task consolidation, and refinement guided by human feedback, EcomWriteBench constructs a shared pool of 37 abilities and identifies the subset applicable to each task. Ability-wise scoring enables us to compare state-of-the-art LLMs on EcomWriteBench and characterize their relative strengths and weaknesses across fine-grained e-commerce writing abilities. We further propose a preference-calibrated weight-learning framework that converts human pairwise preferences into interpretable scoring rubrics through global, category-level, and task-level aggregation weights. This framework provides a reusable approach for translating human preferences into automated evaluation by combining ability discovery, ability-wise scoring, and preference-calibrated aggregation, and can potentially be applied to a broad range of benchmarks beyond EcomWriteBench. On held-out queries, our scoring framework achieves 88.96% agreement with human preferences, compared with 78.54% for conventional LLM-as-a-judge scoring.
papers.summary: General-purpose writing benchmarks do not capture the user needs, product evidence, structural constraints, and business requirements of e-commerce content generation. `EcomWriteBench` contains 3,861 queries from 69 e-commerce writing tasks across 13 categories and five languages, with a shared pool of 37 abilities and per-task subsets used for ability-wise scoring of large language models. The authors also propose a preference-calibrated weight-learning framework that turns human pairwise preferences into interpretable rubrics through global, category-level, and task-level aggregation weights. On held-out queries this scoring reaches **88.96% agreement with human preferences, versus 78.54% for conventional LLM-as-a-judge scoring**.

papers.title: GRACE: Controlled Evidence Interventions for Diagnosing and Improving Knowledge Integration in GraphRAG
papers.abstract: GraphRAG combines a language model's parametric knowledge with retrieved graph evidence, yet aggregate accuracy cannot show whether failures stem from missing paths, distractors, or conflicts with model knowledge. We introduce GRACE, a benchmark built by executing LC-QuAD 2.0 queries over Wikidata and applying four controlled interventions to each evidence subgraph: severing a support path, adding type-compatible distractors, attaching high-degree hubs, and replacing the supported answer with a counterfactual entity. Questions and option positions remain fixed across the five states. The validated benchmark contains 4,028 questions and 20,140 question-graph pairs. These comparisons reveal that question-only routing cannot distinguish evidence states, while relevance guidance can improve answerable states yet hurt when the support path is severed: relevant facts may not jointly suffice to answer. We propose QCFSE-SA, which combines typed local attention, global graph attention, and question-conditioned evidence guidance with a calibrated graph-support gate. With the factual context and generator held fixed, it improves controlled-state accuracy from 57.17% to 62.78% (+5.61 points; question-clustered 95% CI [+5.04, +6.17]) and broken-state accuracy from 55.41% to 67.85%. Over-abstention on semantic distractors remains an open challenge.
papers.summary: Aggregate accuracy in GraphRAG, which combines a language model's parametric knowledge with retrieved graph evidence, cannot reveal whether failures come from missing paths, distractors, or conflicts with model knowledge. `GRACE` is a benchmark built from `LC-QuAD 2.0` queries over Wikidata that applies four controlled interventions to each evidence subgraph (severing a support path, adding type-compatible distractors, attaching high-degree hubs, and swapping in a counterfactual answer), giving 4,028 questions and 20,140 question-graph pairs. The comparisons show that question-only routing cannot distinguish evidence states and that relevance guidance helps answerable states but hurts when the support path is severed. The proposed `QCFSE-SA`, which adds graph attention and a calibrated graph-support gate, **raises controlled-state accuracy from 57.17% to 62.78%** and broken-state accuracy from 55.41% to 67.85%, though over-abstention on semantic distractors remains unsolved.

papers.title: PAVE: A Harness for Geometrically Consistent Road Network Modeling with Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: Transportation models, whether they simulate traffic or support planning, are only as reliable as the road networks they run on, down to the lanes and turns at each intersection. Practitioners still take such a network from GIS files and supply its junction and movement data by hand, a task that recurs with each new base year and design alternative, or they generate it from open map data. OpenStreetMap's lane tags give the correct layout for only 13 of the 44 approaches we test; open map data are often incomplete or inaccurate. Satellite and street-level imagery, in contrast, cover all 44 and show their lanes as painted. Vision-language models (VLMs) can read such imagery, but asked directly they lose geometric consistency when the same lane must be matched across a satellite crop, street-level photos taken from different poses and an ID-labelled network. We therefore present PAVE (Perceive, Anchor, Verify, Edit), a harness in which code measures what can be measured, traffic engineering knowledge enters as general rules and checks, and the model makes only the open judgements, each anchored to network IDs so that checks catch answers that contradict a measurement, a second reading or a traffic rule. Scored against human labels at signalised intersections, PAVE raises the share of exactly correct lane layouts from 49-64% with a single request to 86-91% for two VLMs, with most of the gain coming from reading one approach at a time on traced lanes. The same division of work edits a real network to a planning brief: the model names the links and nodes of each part of a facility, and code builds the edit from a design template. Of 18 edits, 16 pass every network check, against none when the model writes its own code, and 2 contain a design or coding error, against 7. An analysis shows where VLMs lose geometric consistency and which check catches each failure.
papers.summary: Building lane-level road networks for traffic models is still done by hand or from open map data, and OpenStreetMap lane tags give the correct layout for only 13 of 44 tested intersection approaches. Vision-language models (VLMs) can read satellite and street-level imagery but lose geometric consistency when matching the same lane across views, so `PAVE` (Perceive, Anchor, Verify, Edit) is a harness in which code measures what is measurable, traffic engineering rules act as checks, and the model makes only open judgements anchored to network IDs. Against human labels at signalised intersections, it **raises exactly correct lane layouts from 49-64% with a single request to 86-91%** for two VLMs, mostly from reading one approach at a time on traced lanes. For editing a real network to a planning brief, 16 of 18 edits pass every network check, compared with none when the model writes its own code.

papers.title: WaXup: Weight Averaging of Experts as Data Augmentation for Robust Introspection
papers.abstract: As the capabilities of large language models keep improving, traditional mechanistic interpretability methods struggle to keep pace. In contrast, trainable introspection methods emerge as a promising alternative; they repurpose the model itself as a self-diagnostic tool, trained to verbalize what it has learned during finetuning in natural language. While training on datasets of finetuned experts achieves encouraging results, it currently lacks robustness and generalization. Building on the data augmentation framework of MiXup, we introduce WaXup, a method that augments the introspection training set through linear interpolation in the weight space. This is motivated by the linear mode connectivity property: weight averaged experts interpolate the behaviors of the initial experts. We evaluate WaXup on three benchmarks: hidden-behavior models, a meta-dataset of real-world NLP tasks and AuditBench, a challenging alignment auditing suite of models adversarially trained to conceal their behaviors. WaXup improves the accuracy of generated descriptions as well as robustness to various distribution shifts. We hope to improve the reliability of trainable introspection methods towards better and safer models.
papers.summary: Trainable introspection methods train a language model to describe in natural language what it learned during finetuning, but training on datasets of finetuned expert models currently lacks robustness and generalization. `WaXup` extends the `MiXup` data augmentation idea to weight space, enlarging the introspection training set by linearly interpolating expert weights, motivated by linear mode connectivity, under which weight-averaged experts interpolate the original experts' behaviors. Evaluated on hidden-behavior models, a meta-dataset of real-world NLP tasks, and `AuditBench`, a suite of models adversarially trained to conceal their behaviors, it **improves both the accuracy of generated descriptions and robustness to distribution shifts**.

papers.title: WePM: Hierarchical Conflict Reconciliation for Unified MLLMs
papers.abstract: Bringing multimodal intelligence from the cloud to users' devices keeps sensitive data local and reduces inference cost, but deploying a specialized model per capability duplicates vision-language capacity under tight memory and compute budgets. We formalize heterogeneous capability density (HCD), measuring how broadly and effectively a model serves heterogeneous task families per unit of resident inference memory. High HCD across representation, generation, and decision raises two challenges: these capabilities need visual evidence at different spatial granularities under a fixed token budget, and separately collected task corpora yield conflicting updates to shared parameters, while cross-task paired supervision is costly and ambiguous for open-ended inputs. We present WePM, a family of pocket models unifying representation, generation, and decision within one vision-language backbone. Multi-Granularity Visual Budgeting (MGVB) allocates a fixed visual-token budget across global, regional, and fine-grained banks; Unified Listwise Knowledge Distillation (ULKD) enriches separately collected data with soft teacher guidance, avoiding cross-task paired annotation; Stable and Efficient Multitask Optimization (SEMO) regulates each task's contribution through explicit loss weights and exposure schedules, with sequential gradient accumulation under memory constraints. In the joint representation-generation setting, WePM outperforms all baselines across five evaluation groups, raising the Joint score from 38.15 to 52.74. In single-task evaluation, WePM-4B attains the best average score over 30 embedding, 39 generation, and seven typed-decision benchmarks (72.86, 62.41, 61.11). Against the separate-model stack with the highest HCD, WePM achieves slightly higher balanced performance with 61.9% less resident weight memory, a 2.64-fold higher HCD.
papers.summary: Running a separate specialized multimodal model per capability on a device duplicates capacity under tight memory budgets, which the authors quantify with heterogeneous capability density (HCD), a measure of how broadly and effectively a model serves different task families per unit of resident inference memory. `WePM` is a family of small models unifying representation, generation, and decision in one vision-language backbone, using Multi-Granularity Visual Budgeting (MGVB) to split a fixed visual-token budget, Unified Listwise Knowledge Distillation (ULKD) to avoid cross-task paired annotation, and Stable and Efficient Multitask Optimization (SEMO) to balance task contributions. In joint representation-generation evaluation it raises the Joint score from 38.15 to 52.74, and `WePM-4B` has the best average over 30 embedding, 39 generation, and seven typed-decision benchmarks. Compared with the best separate-model stack, it reaches slightly higher balanced performance with **61.9% less resident weight memory**, a 2.64-fold higher HCD.

papers.title: Testing for Coordination Failures in Cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Deep parallel cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (CMARL)} trains multiple agents that all act at every time step to optimize a common objective. Like single-agent RL, CMARL can produce unsafe behaviors that violate implicit safety requirements not captured by the reward, and these behaviors are hard to explain. However, testing CMARL policies for safety has received less attention than the safety testing of single-agent RL policies. In this paper, we propose DisQ, a test case selection method that identifies failure-revealing states in value-based CMARL by exploiting a signal specific to trained Q-learning agents. The signal is the Q-value gap, an explainable metric that flags a state when the agents' estimates of the achievable return diverge by more than a calibrated threshold. DisQ selects such states for execution and skips those without a gap. Our experiments in four CMARL benchmark environments show that, in most of the evaluated configurations, DisQ improves failure detection over single-agent RL testing methods applied to CMARL, namely random testing and search-based testing with genetic algorithms. Our main contributions are the Q-value gap, an indicator of potential miscoordination computable from a single state without executing the system, and DisQ, a test case selection method that adapts existing single-agent testing methods to CMARL.
papers.summary: Policies from cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (CMARL), where several agents act at every step toward a shared objective, can violate safety requirements not captured by the reward, yet testing them has received less attention than single-agent testing. `DisQ` is a test case selection method for value-based CMARL built on the Q-value gap, which flags a state when the agents' estimates of achievable return diverge by more than a calibrated threshold, **a miscoordination indicator computable from a single state without executing the system**. States with a gap are selected for execution and the rest are skipped. In four CMARL benchmark environments, it improves failure detection over random testing and genetic-algorithm search-based testing in most evaluated configurations.

papers.title: AMARIS: Merging Generalist and Specialist LLMs via Adaptive Subspace Inheritance
papers.abstract: Domain specialization of large language models (LLMs) often improves target-domain performance but degrades broad capabilities. Model merging is an attractive training-free alternative, yet common parameter-space strategies (for example, interpolation and sparsified averaging) provide limited control over task-specific interference. We introduce Adaptive Model Alignment via Ranked Inherited Subspaces (AMARIS), a covariance-driven framework that transfers specialist updates only along selected activation directions. AMARIS formulates merging as budgeted subspace inheritance: it seeks high specialist activation capture under a regularized base-output perturbation budget, then builds a low-rank projection gate from ranked generalized eigendirections. This yields a single static merged checkpoint that concentrates transfer in high-utility, low-interference directions. We evaluate AMARIS on Qwen3-based merges (8B and 32B) across finance, instruction-following, and multilingual SEA specialization. In our evaluated settings, AMARIS reaches Pareto operating points that are competitive with strong training-free baselines, including 98.37% specialist retention with 95.16% core retention for the 8B finance setting, 103.55% core retention with 90.28% specialist retention for the 8B instruction-following setting, and 99.20% core retention with 94.80% specialist retention for the 32B SEA setting. These results support subspace-constrained merging as a practical route to compositional capability integration without additional training.
papers.summary: Specializing a large language model for a domain often degrades its general capabilities, and common training-free merging strategies such as interpolation and sparsified averaging offer little control over interference. Adaptive Model Alignment via Ranked Inherited Subspaces (`AMARIS`) treats merging as budgeted subspace inheritance: it uses activation covariances to find directions that capture specialist activations under a base-output perturbation budget, then builds a low-rank projection gate from ranked generalized eigendirections to produce a single static merged checkpoint. On `Qwen3`-based merges at 8B and 32B across finance, instruction-following, and Southeast Asian multilingual specialization, it reaches operating points competitive with strong training-free baselines, including **98.37% specialist retention with 95.16% core retention** in the 8B finance setting.

papers.title: ReActWAM: Action-Consistent Caching for Efficient World-Action Models
papers.abstract: World-action models (WAMs) often generate future visual states alongside robot actions, introducing substantial computational overhead during inference. During closed-loop execution, consecutive inference cycles often predict similar action sequences, leading to redundant computation. However, reducing this redundancy requires distinguishing consistent actions from changes that demand fresh computation. To address these challenges, we propose ReActWAM, a training-free framework that combines action-intent-guided prefix skipping with inner-chunk prediction reuse. A coarse-to-fine assessment evaluates motion changes, visual consistency, and action prediction conflicts. For eligible chunks, we draw on first-step differences to adapt the cached latent and network features to the current condition, providing an estimate at a later denoising step that bypasses the redundant prefix. Subsequent inference refines this estimate while reusing stable denoising predictions within the chunk. Experiments across LingBot-VA, FastWAM and the Cosmos family on LIBERO-Long and RoboTwin 2.0 demonstrate $1.41\times$--$5.44\times$ GPU inference speedup, with minimal degradation in task success rates. Real-world experiments on a Franka Research 3 (FR3) robot further achieve $1.46\times$ end-to-end speedup while maintaining success rate.
papers.summary: World-action models (WAMs) generate future visual states alongside robot actions, which makes inference expensive, and consecutive closed-loop inference cycles often predict similar action sequences. `ReActWAM` is a training-free caching framework that assesses motion changes, visual consistency, and action prediction conflicts, then for eligible chunks adapts cached latents and network features to skip the early denoising steps and reuses stable predictions within the chunk. Across `LingBot-VA`, `FastWAM`, and the `Cosmos` family on `LIBERO-Long` and `RoboTwin 2.0`, it delivers **1.41x to 5.44x GPU inference speedup** with minimal loss in task success. On a real Franka Research 3 robot it achieves a 1.46x end-to-end speedup while maintaining success rate.

papers.title: Gumbel Substitution: Removing Sampler Drift from RL Without Trusting the Sampler
papers.abstract: When RL rollouts come from untrusted samplers on arbitrary hardware, precision and checkpoint lag, the sampling distribution $q$ differs from the trainer's policy $p$, and training on the sampler's tokens adds a drift term equal to supervised fine-tuning toward $q$. Published corrections (TIS, MIS, IcePop, score centering, GSPO, CISPO) all need $q(y)$, which a permissionless sampler reports and can misreport. We introduce Gumbel substitution. The coordinator fixes public Gumbel noise for every token position, bit-identical across GPUs, and the sampler draws $y=\arg\max(\ell^q+G)$. The trainer recomputes $v^*=\arg\max(\ell^p+G)$, the token its own policy would have drawn with the same noise, and scores $v^*$ in the sampler's context. For a sampler that follows the protocol, $v^*$ is an exact sample from $p$ given the prefix, so the drift vanishes in expectation for any $q$, without sampler-reported probabilities. We measure the residual left by the deployed heads, bound the one added by admission gates, and state what an adaptive sampler can still do. The same comparison gives a per-token match rate that admits and pays samplers. In the lab, on a 9B model with the same head on both sides, the expected drift of uncorrected training is at least 170 to 4,800 times that of substitution. On a 2B model under strong mismatch, uncorrected training collapses while substitution stays stable, comparable to MIS with score centering given the true $q$. On a permissionless network, a 9B model was trained for 158 optimizer steps on 15.75B tokens from heterogeneous samplers, with no skipped step and 1.21% of tokens substituted; it improved on all eight held-out benchmarks.
papers.summary: When reinforcement-learning rollouts come from untrusted samplers on arbitrary hardware, the sampling distribution differs from the trainer's policy and adds a drift term, and existing corrections rely on probabilities the sampler reports and can misreport. `Gumbel substitution` has the coordinator fix public Gumbel noise per token position; the trainer recomputes the token its own policy would have drawn under that noise and scores it in the sampler's context, so drift vanishes in expectation for a protocol-following sampler without any reported probabilities. In lab tests on a 9B model, the expected drift of uncorrected training is **at least 170 to 4,800 times that of substitution**, and on a 2B model under strong mismatch uncorrected training collapses while substitution stays stable. On a permissionless network, a 9B model trained for 158 optimizer steps on 15.75B tokens with 1.21% of tokens substituted and improved on all eight held-out benchmarks.

papers.title: Composable Soft-Prompt Distillation of RL Experts: Toward Continual Post-Training
papers.abstract: RL post-training typically produces domain experts that must then be consolidated into one model, and as new experts keep arriving, this consolidation becomes a continual process. Weight merging and multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) must re-consolidate the whole model whenever an expert is added, and can erode capabilities outside the target domains. We propose Composable Soft-Prompt Distillation (CSPD), which keeps the pre-RL model frozen, distills each RL expert independently into a soft prompt, and composes experts by concatenating their prompts without joint training. A single soft prompt suffices to distill an RL expert, recovering at least 90% of the teacher's gain in 22 of 23 math, code, and agent settings. Independently trained prompts compose well. In a multi-expert setting, the average rises with every expert added, and the full composition matches MOPD (67.83 vs. 67.79). The composition generalizes best across six held-out benchmarks. Input-space adaptation adds little serving overhead, keeping throughput within 1.5% of the unadapted backbone and reaching 2.40x that of rank-4 LoRA. These results point toward continual post-training on a fixed backbone.
papers.summary: Consolidating reinforcement-learning-trained domain experts into one model by weight merging or multi-teacher on-policy distillation (`MOPD`) requires redoing the whole consolidation whenever an expert is added and can erode other capabilities. Composable Soft-Prompt Distillation (`CSPD`) keeps the pre-RL model frozen, distills each expert independently into a soft prompt, and composes experts by concatenating prompts with no joint training. A single soft prompt recovers **at least 90% of the teacher's gain in 22 of 23 math, code, and agent settings**, and the full multi-expert composition matches `MOPD` (67.83 vs. 67.79) while generalizing best across six held-out benchmarks. Serving throughput stays within 1.5% of the unadapted backbone and reaches 2.40x that of rank-4 `LoRA`.

papers.title: HR-Merge: Model Merging with Headroom-Weighted Residual Refinement
papers.abstract: Model merging combines experts fine-tuned from a shared backbone, such as LoRA adapters of a large language model, into one multi-task model without further training. Existing methods apply one rule to every task, yet the accuracy they lose is uneven across tasks. We show that the lost accuracy remains recoverable from each task's residual, its task vector minus the merged update, and that a task's validation headroom, the share of its expert validation accuracy the merge loses, indicates where recovery pays off. Residuals from different tasks interfere, so they must be merged rather than summed. We propose HR-Merge, a training-free wrapper around any merging method. It weights each residual by its task's headroom, re-merges the weighted residuals with the base operator, and adds the result back at a strength selected on validation, falling back to the base merge when no strength helps. On six NLI adapters of LLaMA-3 8B, HR-Merge lifts TIES from 93.29 to 94.29 normalized accuracy, above all tested bases, mainly by recovering its weakest task. In vision, on three CLIP backbones, up to 20 tasks, and LoRA merging, it generally improves or preserves base accuracy and yields the best model in every setting.
papers.summary: Model merging methods apply one rule to every task even though the accuracy they lose is uneven across tasks. `HR-Merge` is a training-free wrapper around any merging method: it weights each task's residual (its task vector minus the merged update) by that task's validation headroom, re-merges the weighted residuals with the base operator, and adds the result back at a validation-selected strength, falling back to the base merge when nothing helps. On six natural language inference adapters of `LLaMA-3 8B`, it lifts `TIES` from **93.29 to 94.29 normalized accuracy**, mainly by recovering the weakest task. On three `CLIP` backbones with up to 20 tasks and `LoRA` merging, it generally improves or preserves base accuracy.

papers.title: VMSA: Video Memory Skill Agent for Long Video Understanding
papers.abstract: Long-video question answering requires retrieving and integrating relevant evidence from videos spanning hours or even days. Recent agentic approaches organize video information into external memories and iteratively retrieve evidence to answer questions. However, effective retrieval and reasoning remain challenging, as agents must determine what information to search for, which memory sources to access, and how to connect evidence across distant temporal intervals. To address these challenges, we propose Video Memory Skill Agent (VMSA), a framework that jointly designs structured video memories and memory skills for long-video understanding. VMSA constructs three complementary memory components. Segment Caption Memory and Entity Event Memory serve as searchable evidence sources, while Entity-Aware Episode Memory provides broad yet detailed video context to guide evidence retrieval and reasoning. To further support effective memory utilization, VMSA induces memory skills from successful agent trajectories, incrementally refining or extending a compact skill library to guide iterative evidence retrieval, reasoning, and verification. Across seven long-video question-answering benchmarks, VMSA achieves the highest accuracy on all three week-long egocentric benchmarks, outperforming the strongest baseline by up to 9.4% on Ego-R1 Bench, and the best or competitive performance on four additional benchmarks. Ablation studies further demonstrate the contributions of all three memory components and memory skills, with memory skills also improving temporal evidence localization.
papers.summary: Answering questions about videos spanning hours or days requires an agent to decide what to search for, which memory to consult, and how to link evidence across distant time intervals. Video Memory Skill Agent (`VMSA`) builds three memories, with `Segment Caption Memory` and `Entity Event Memory` as searchable evidence sources and `Entity-Aware Episode Memory` as broad context, and induces a compact library of memory skills from successful agent trajectories to guide retrieval, reasoning, and verification. Across seven long-video question-answering benchmarks it achieves the highest accuracy on all three week-long egocentric benchmarks, beating the strongest baseline by **up to 9.4% on `Ego-R1 Bench`**, and is best or competitive on the other four. Ablations attribute gains to all three memories and to the skills, which also improve temporal evidence localization.

papers.title: PanoUAV-Track: Full-Spherical UAV Visual Tracking in the Wild
papers.abstract: Existing UAV tracking benchmarks predominantly rely on perspective cameras with limited fields of view. Omnidirectional cameras enable full-spherical observation, yet tracking from moving UAV platforms remains largely unexplored. Unlike ground-level panoramic tracking, UAV-mounted omnidirectional cameras observe targets across both azimuth and elevation, introducing geometric challenges under equirectangular projection (ERP). To investigate this setting, we capture approximately \textbf{40 hours of real-world 8K panoramic UAV video} and construct \textbf{PanoUAV-Track} through temporal clip extraction, target annotation, and the integration of simulated sequences. The resulting benchmark comprises 1,895 sequences, 507,961 frames, and 2,872 annotated objects, covering real-world daytime and nighttime scenes alongside simulation, and supporting both visual and language-based target specification. Through extensive evaluations, we reveal a clear \textbf{perspective-to-spherical} generalization gap and identify tracking degradation associated with latitude-dependent distortion and ERP seam discontinuity. To address these challenges, we propose \textbf{PanoUAV-Tracker (PUTrack)}, a geometry-aware tracking framework combining latitude-adaptive search and seam-aware periodic sampling. PUTrack improves zero-shot and in-domain tracking, particularly for seam-crossing targets. Code and benchmark resources will be available\footnote{\textcolor{tabpink}{https://libingyu01.github.io/PanoUAV-Track/}}.
papers.summary: Drone tracking benchmarks mostly use perspective cameras with narrow fields of view, leaving tracking from drone-mounted omnidirectional cameras under equirectangular projection (ERP) largely unexplored. `PanoUAV-Track` is built from about 40 hours of real 8K panoramic drone video plus simulated sequences, totaling **1,895 sequences, 507,961 frames, and 2,872 annotated objects** across day, night, and simulated scenes with both visual and language target specification. Evaluations show a clear perspective-to-spherical generalization gap, with degradation tied to latitude-dependent distortion and the ERP seam discontinuity. The accompanying `PUTrack` tracker combines latitude-adaptive search with seam-aware periodic sampling and improves zero-shot and in-domain tracking, particularly for targets crossing the seam.

papers.title: Evidence sufficiency assessment enables cost-effective review allocation in on-premise clinical AI agents
papers.abstract: On-premise clinical AI agents must auto-accept high-confidence diagnoses, deferring others to clinician review, yet token probabilities and self-reported confidence miss errors, while more reliable five-run consistency incurs fivefold compute. We propose training-free decision-point evidence sufficiency assessment and a three-tier sequential triage protocol. Masking reasoning and diagnosis, the same 4B model scores sufficiency from objective evidence via prior-debiased probabilities over five ordered levels. Calibration freezes a nominal top-50% threshold, selecting single-run, five-run consistency, or full-deferral tiers by whether the one-sided 95% Wilson lower confidence bound of pass rate among accepted cases meets the 95% clinical target line. Across 1,605 MIRA-v2, CDM, VivaBench, and in-hospital liver malignancy primary cohort cases, MIRA-v2 single-run top-50% pass rate reached 98.91%, matching five-run consistency, saving ~80% compute; CDM achieved 96.00% test attainment by escalating to the five-run consistency tier; cross-specialty, missing-imaging, and combined enriched cohorts entered the full-deferral tier, capping calibration false-certification rate at 0.00%-3.50%.
papers.summary: On-premise clinical AI agents need to auto-accept confident diagnoses and defer the rest to clinicians, but token probabilities and self-reported confidence miss errors, and five-run consistency costs five times the compute. The proposed training-free method masks the reasoning and diagnosis and has the same 4B model score how sufficient the objective evidence is, then a calibrated three-tier protocol picks single-run acceptance, five-run consistency, or full deferral based on a Wilson lower confidence bound against a 95% target. Across 1,605 cases from `MIRA-v2`, `CDM`, `VivaBench`, and an in-hospital liver malignancy cohort, the single-run top-50% pass rate on `MIRA-v2` reached **98.91%, matching five-run consistency while saving about 80% of compute**. `CDM` reached 96.00% by escalating to the five-run tier, and cross-specialty and missing-imaging cohorts were routed to full deferral.

papers.title: Taking Apart and Putting Together: Tracking Objects Through Physical Transformations
papers.abstract: We introduce Transformation Tracking and Understanding (TTU), extending video object tracking to environments where objects undergo physical assemblies and disassemblies. TTU requires continuously tracking objects through transformations, identifying new entities, maintaining a state graph of their relationships, and assigning semantic labels to transformations. While foundation models (e.g., SAM 2/3) maintain tracklets through appearance changes, they cannot update semantic identities as objects physically evolve. Prior work addresses only disassemblies, relying on expensive searches triggered only when tracking fails. We propose Tracking Instances via Proposals and Overlaps (TIPO), a training-free framework that continuously infers transformations via a generate-evaluate-judge pipeline. TIPO generates split and merge proposals from disjoint mask components, scores them against mask-decoder priors using inner and external overlap, and queries an MLLM on the top proposal for visual verification and semantic labeling. To benchmark TTU, we curate Video Instances, States, and Transformation Annotations (VISTA), a dataset including state graphs with 124 assembly and 132 disassembly events across 50 sequences and over 26,000 frames. TIPO achieves state-of-the-art tracking and state-graph accuracy on VISTA, while operating $6\times$ to $15\times$ faster than prior methods. Project page: https://davidegardenal.github.io/tipo-tracking
papers.summary: Transformation Tracking and Understanding (`TTU`) extends video object tracking to scenes where objects are assembled and disassembled, requiring trackers to identify new entities, maintain a state graph of their relationships, and label each transformation. Tracking Instances via Proposals and Overlaps (`TIPO`) is a training-free pipeline that generates split and merge proposals from disjoint mask components, scores them against mask-decoder priors using overlap measures, and asks a multimodal LLM to verify and label the top proposal. The accompanying Video Instances, States, and Transformation Annotations (`VISTA`) dataset contains 124 assembly and 132 disassembly events across 50 sequences and over 26,000 frames. `TIPO` achieves state-of-the-art tracking and state-graph accuracy on `VISTA` while running **6x to 15x faster than prior methods**.

papers.title: Beyond Linear Decodability: Understanding and Improving Instruction Following in World Action Models
papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) exhibit strong manipulation capabilities yet often fail to follow test-time language instructions. Prior work shows that non-following (NF) WAMs encode information about the instructed target, but this information does not control their behavior. By comparing NF WAM with its instruction-following (IF) counterpart, we find that target information is substantially more linearly decodable in IF WAMs, despite being encoded in both. Motivated by this observation, we introduce linear decodability supervision (LDS), a simple yet effective auxiliary training objective that promotes the linear decodability of the instructed target information. On LIBERO-CF, InternW0-$\Delta$ with LDS achieves a success rate of 74.6% and a grounding rate of 89.2%, surpassing the strongest baseline by 26.8 and 42.9 percentage points, respectively. The effectiveness of LDS challenges the prevailing interpretation that encoded target information does not contribute to WAMs' behavior. To reconcile this apparent contradiction, we propose a prior-instruction competition mechanism, which explains NF and IF behavior as arising from the dominance of prior and instruction signals, respectively. We provide causal evidence for this mechanism by evaluating two training-free interventions derived from it. We reinterpret LDS through this mechanism, showing that it acts as a form of instruction signal enhancement. Finally, more comprehensive evaluations across diverse manipulation tasks and visual domains demonstrate the consistent effectiveness of LDS.
papers.summary: World action models (WAMs) for robot manipulation often ignore test-time language instructions even though they internally encode the instructed target. Comparing non-following and instruction-following models shows the target information is far more linearly decodable in the latter, motivating linear decodability supervision (`LDS`), an auxiliary training objective that promotes that decodability. On `LIBERO-CF`, `InternW0-Δ` with `LDS` reaches **74.6% success and 89.2% grounding, beating the strongest baseline by 26.8 and 42.9 percentage points**. The authors explain the behavior through a competition between prior and instruction signals, supported by two training-free interventions, and interpret `LDS` as strengthening the instruction signal.

papers.title: Degradation of Language Models under Controlled Load: Synchronization, Rule Execution and Misfires on the Background
papers.abstract: As the load grows, a language model makes more and more errors, but different processes stand behind this decline in quality. The model may lose the correspondence with the source text, it may keep its place in the text but execute a rule wrongly, or it may change a word that no rule concerns. In this work the degradation of a model under controlled load is separated into these three components: synchronization, rule execution and misfires. The load is set by rules that replace one word with another in a meaningless text, and each kind of load (the text length, the position of a word in the answer, the replacement density, the number of rules and the place of a rule in the list) is set separately. The alignment of the answer with the reference makes it possible to follow the outcome of every word, and a statistical model that takes into account that the spread of difficulty between requests itself depends on the load restores, for each component, the laws of its dependence on every kind of load. These laws make up the passport of a model. The paper presents the method of the separation, the principles of constructing the laws and the passports of seven models built by this method; the separation opens the way to studying the fine structure of the behavior of a neural network.
papers.summary: Language model errors under growing load can stem from different processes: losing correspondence with the source text, executing a rule incorrectly, or altering a word no rule concerns. The study uses a word-replacement task on meaningless text in which text length, word position, replacement density, number of rules, and rule position in the list are each varied separately, then aligns each answer with the reference to track every word's outcome. A statistical model that accounts for load-dependent variation in request difficulty **separates degradation into synchronization, rule execution, and misfire components**, each with its own fitted laws of dependence on load. These laws form a per-model profile the authors call a passport, reported for seven models.

papers.title: Detecting Word-Substitution Poisoning of a RAG Knowledge Base with Relative Entropy and Runtime Verification
papers.abstract: A retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system answers questions using passages it retrieves from a knowledge base, so users must trust that knowledge base. We study an attacker who quietly edits existing passages by swapping words for synonyms (PWWS, TextFooler) in a cybersecurity RAG system built from MITRE ATT&CK and CAPEC. Using a reviewed 44-question benchmark, repeated paired runs and a control corpus in which only the layout changes, we find that poisoning lowers judged answer correctness from 0.714 to 0.555. The damage comes mostly from lost evidence and refusals, not from false statements. To find the edited passages, we use relative entropy. Comparing a whole passage with normal text is a weak signal. Still, one term of the relative entropy, the log-ratio between a word and its most probable synonym, works well: with a small language model as the reference, it reaches an AUROC of 0.95 and stays near chance on the control. Used as a retrieval filter, it halves how often edited text reaches the generator, and an attacker who must keep each passage as probable under the language model fails on all 57 sections it tries. Filtering does not restore correctness, because the edited passage is usually the one that held the answer. We therefore add a runtime monitor that checks each answer against trusted MITRE STIX data and remembers the passages it rejects. On its own, it reduces exposure to edited text from 0.41 to 0.26; when it may add the trusted MITRE entry as a source, correctness rises to 0.786. We report the costs and failure cases of every defence alongside its gains.
papers.summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems depend on a trustworthy knowledge base, and this study examines an attacker who swaps words for synonyms (`PWWS`, `TextFooler`) in a cybersecurity RAG system built from `MITRE ATT&CK` and `CAPEC`. On a 44-question benchmark, poisoning lowers judged answer correctness from 0.714 to 0.555, mostly through lost evidence and refusals instead of false statements. A detector based on one term of relative entropy, the log-ratio between a word and its most probable synonym under a small language model, reaches an **AUROC of 0.95** and, as a retrieval filter, halves how often edited text reaches the generator, though it does not restore correctness. A runtime monitor that checks answers against trusted MITRE STIX data cuts exposure to edited text from 0.41 to 0.26, and raises correctness to 0.786 when allowed to add the trusted entry as a source.

papers.title: Neural variational Skyrmions as a topological benchmark: emergent symmetry, precision energies and KAN--MLP comparison
papers.abstract: We propose the three-dimensional Skyrme model as a topological benchmark for neural variational methods and construct fully three-dimensional Skyrmions with baryon number $B=1,\ldots,4$ without imposing a symmetry ansatz, with high precision. For $B=2,3,4$, the relaxation of these Skyrmions starts from $B$ unit-charge lumps with random positions and orientations, which carry no symmetry information. The known toroidal, tetrahedral, and cubic Skyrmions nevertheless emerge spontaneously. The resulting variational energies for $B=1,\ldots,4$ lie slightly below the published reference values. The neural method highlights the high accuracy for retaining the topological charge, differing from $B$ by at most $10^{-6}$ in the highest-precision solutions. Our numerical method goes through physical constraint tests such as the Derrick virial relation and the Faddeev--Bogomolny bound, together with evaluation / verification through independent quadratures and resolution sweeps. We then compare Kolmogorov--Arnold networks (KANs) with multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) in more than a thousand training runs, both with and without a rational-map ansatz. With default settings, KANs appear markedly superior, but most of the gap disappears once the MLP activation function and learning rate are tuned. KANs remain more parameter-efficient and more robust at fixed epoch budget, while MLPs with the tuned activation function perform at least as well at fixed wall-clock time.
