We also argue that continuous gradient descent cannot smoothly change the topological sector of our neural field, clarifying the origin of topological freezing observed in our neural variational solvers. Our results on the neural methods applied to Skyrmions pave a research ground for AI-agentic benchmarks for classical topological solitons, toward AI-assisted soliton physics.
papers.summary: The three-dimensional Skyrme model is proposed as a topological benchmark for neural variational methods, with Skyrmions of baryon number 1 to 4 constructed without imposing a symmetry ansatz. Starting from randomly placed and oriented unit-charge lumps, the known toroidal, tetrahedral, and cubic solutions emerge spontaneously, with energies slightly below published reference values and topological charge accurate to within 10^-6 in the highest-precision solutions. In more than a thousand training runs comparing Kolmogorov-Arnold networks (`KAN`s) with multilayer perceptrons (`MLP`s), **most of the apparent `KAN` advantage disappears once the `MLP` activation function and learning rate are tuned**. `KAN`s remain more parameter-efficient and robust at a fixed epoch budget, while tuned `MLP`s do at least as well at fixed wall-clock time.

papers.title: ORBIT: Offset-based Activation Steering for Cross-lingual Multimodal Fact Verification
papers.abstract: Multimodal fact verification faces a fundamental accessibility bottleneck: while large proprietary models exhibit cross-lingual robustness, small vision-language models suffer a severe, disproportionate accuracy collapse on low-resource languages. Closing this gap traditionally requires prohibitive scale or extensive language-specific fine-tuning. In this work, we propose Offset Recovery via Bilingual Inference-time Technique (ORBIT), an algorithmic intervention that mitigates this collapse at inference time. ORBIT estimates span-specific offset vectors from parallel claim-evidence instances and applies them to claim and evidence representations, targeting the cross-lingual degradation induced by low-resource evidence. Experiments across 81 configurations reveal that ORBIT substantially recovers both accuracy and F1-score in low-resource settings, exposes calibration offset norms as a diagnostic proxy, and outperforms translation-based and steering baselines.
papers.summary: Small vision-language models lose accuracy sharply on multimodal fact verification when the evidence is in a low-resource language, a gap usually closed only with scale or language-specific fine-tuning. Offset Recovery via Bilingual Inference-time Technique (`ORBIT`) estimates span-specific offset vectors from parallel claim-evidence instances and applies them to the claim and evidence representations at inference time. Across 81 configurations, it **substantially recovers accuracy and F1-score in low-resource settings and outperforms translation-based and steering baselines**. The norms of the calibration offsets also serve as a diagnostic proxy.

papers.title: ADEPT: Adaptive Monocular Depth Estimation via Model-In-The-Loop Photometric Tuning with Capture Risk Prediction
papers.abstract: Exposure and gain determine the visual evidence available to monocular depth estimation (MDE), particularly when robot motion creates a tradeoff between light collection and motion blur. We present ADEPT, a framework that adapts these settings using learned feedback from a frozen depth model. During training, ground-truth depth identifies the lowest-error reference within a group of physically evaluated camera settings. A compact predictor learns reference-relative disagreement (RRD) between each candidate's depth prediction and the reference prediction using regression and ranking losses. At deployment, it scores observed captures using frozen-model features and camera, motion, and illumination context, without ground truth or reference images. A contextual Gaussian-process controller uses recent scores to select subsequent exposure and gain settings under motion and photometric constraints. We evaluate offline camera selection with relative and metric Depth Anything v2 and demonstrate online control with the affine-invariant variant on a mobile robot. Across nine equally weighted scene-illumination conditions, ADEPT reduces mean scale-and-shift-aligned $\mathrm{Abs}_{\mathrm{rel}}$ by 14.6% relative to built-in auto-exposure and by 10.0% relative to the best-performing evaluated prior controller.
papers.summary: Camera exposure and gain determine the visual evidence available for monocular depth estimation (MDE), especially when robot motion forces a tradeoff between light collection and motion blur. `ADEPT` trains a compact predictor of reference-relative disagreement (RRD), the gap between a candidate capture's depth prediction and that of the lowest-error camera setting, using features from a frozen depth model plus camera, motion, and illumination context. At deployment, a contextual Gaussian-process controller uses these scores to choose subsequent exposure and gain settings without ground truth or reference images. Evaluated with `Depth Anything v2` across nine scene-illumination conditions, it reduces mean scale-and-shift-aligned absolute relative error by **14.6% relative to built-in auto-exposure** and by 10.0% relative to the best prior controller tested.

papers.title: Jagged Robustness: Uneven Safety Transfer and Emerging Vulnerabilities under LLM Quantization
papers.abstract: Quantization enables efficient inference in language models through model parameter compression. This work audits the impact of quantization on capability and safety domains including model safeguards, instruction-following, ethics and bias. Through benchmarks, we find that model safeguards and bias can degrade under quantization, while other capabilities such as truthfulness remain more stable in Qwen3-4B. We define this uneven transfer of LLM capabilities under quantization as Jagged Robustness. We find multiple factors driving Jagged Robustness: task complexity, evaluation method and generation coherence. Moreover, we verify the degradation of model safeguards by observing increased compliance with unsafe requests under quantization, and demonstrate universal adversarial suffix attacks that are benign for the full model but jailbreak quantized models. The findings indicate that it is risky to assume that the performance and robustness can transfer evenly across different capability domains from full models to quantized models.
papers.summary: An audit of how quantization affects language model capabilities and safety covers safeguards, instruction-following, ethics, and bias. Benchmarks on `Qwen3-4B` show that **safeguards and bias can degrade under quantization while capabilities such as truthfulness remain more stable**, an uneven transfer the authors call Jagged Robustness and attribute to task complexity, evaluation method, and generation coherence. Quantized models comply more often with unsafe requests, and the authors demonstrate universal adversarial suffixes that are benign for the full-precision model but jailbreak its quantized versions.

papers.title: TrojanMaxxing: One-shotting VLM Backdoors with Weight-Space Programming
papers.abstract: Recent work shows that large language models (LLMs) can reason directly about the weights of other neural networks. Given only a natural-language objective, an LLM can inspect a model's weights, understand what they compute, and edit them directly without gradient-based optimization. This capability, termed weight-space programming (WSP), has been used to improve model performance on math reasoning, medical QA and other benchmarks. We propose TrojanMaxxing, a novel strategy to backdoor vision-language models (VLMs), by reframing it as a WSP task. We use Claude Opus 5.5 and Mythos 5.2 agents to backdoor VLMs without any optimization or training methods. The agents inspect the model weights, apply targeted edits, and co-design an imperceptible visual trigger that activates the backdoor. We then study the agents' strategies and present a thorough evaluation of the trojaned models on various benchmark datasets. TrojanMaxxing achieves attack success rates of 93%-100% on content moderation and 78%-100% on OCR while maintaining clean accuracy. Perhaps most consequentially, we show that injecting backdoors in a training-free manner is possible by simply, "asking an agent to do it".
papers.summary: Weight-space programming (WSP), in which an LLM inspects and directly edits another network's weights from a natural-language objective without gradient-based optimization, is applied here to planting backdoors in vision-language models (VLMs). In `TrojanMaxxing`, `Claude Opus 5.5` and `Mythos 5.2` agents inspect the weights, apply targeted edits, and co-design an imperceptible visual trigger, with no training or optimization involved. The trojaned models reach attack success rates of **93%-100% on content moderation and 78%-100% on OCR while maintaining clean accuracy**. The authors also analyze the strategies the agents used.

papers.title: Cleave: Severing Guardrails and Auditing Spectral Coupling in Open-Weight LLMs
papers.abstract: Open-weight Large Language Models (LLMs) are widely downloaded for their strong coding and reasoning capabilities and deployed locally beyond the provider's control. To prevent misuse, developers embed safety guardrails into these models before release. However, we find that these guardrails rely on the residual writing weights to trigger refusals. Based on this insight, we propose Cleave, a training-free attack that directly edits these weights to remove safety restrictions while preserving general capabilities. With Cleave, malicious users can either remove all guardrails or selectively lift only cybersecurity restrictions. Because this selective removal retains up to a 99% refusal rate on other harmful requests and avoids weight rank collapse, it evades both behavioral spot-checks and static weight audits. Across five open-weight LLMs from 7B to 320B parameters, Cleave achieves up to a 67.97% attack success rate on seven safety benchmarks, substantially outperforming existing white-box baselines. On 356 cybersecurity tasks and 15 live vulnerable services, it further boosts executable exploit generation by up to 24.0 times and compromises up to 66.7% of the targets. To counter this threat, we propose a dual-stage defense that combines pre-release subspace diagnostics with post-release weight-coupling audits, achieving 100% detection recall at a 1% false-positive rate.
papers.summary: Safety guardrails in open-weight LLMs are found to rely on the residual writing weights to trigger refusals. `Cleave` is a training-free attack that edits those weights to remove all guardrails or selectively lift only cybersecurity restrictions; the selective variant keeps up to a 99% refusal rate on other harmful requests and avoids weight rank collapse, evading behavioral spot-checks and static weight audits. Across five models from 7B to 320B parameters it achieves up to a 67.97% attack success rate on seven safety benchmarks, and on 356 cybersecurity tasks and 15 live vulnerable services it boosts executable exploit generation by **up to 24.0 times and compromises up to 66.7% of the targets**. A proposed two-stage defense combining pre-release subspace diagnostics with post-release weight-coupling audits reaches 100% detection recall at a 1% false-positive rate.

papers.title: Neurodegenerative Differential Diagnosis with Knowledge-enhanced Structural Reasoning
papers.abstract: Accurate differential diagnosis of neurodegenerative disorders remains challenging due to overlapping clinical manifestations and heterogeneous, often incomplete multimodal observations. Existing multimodal models can integrate imaging and clinical measurements but often overlook disease-specific evidence patterns and pairwise relations among competing diagnoses. We therefore propose Knowledge-enhanced Structural Reasoning (KnowSR), which aligns multimodal patient representations with a literature-grounded knowledge bank of disease prototypes, signed evidence directions, and pairwise diagnostic relations. Specifically, in KnowSR, patient-specific knowledge alignment and target-aware pooling inject structured disease evidence, while anchored relational reasoning reconciles pairwise diagnostic margins over a sparse differential graph, thereby collectively enhancing differential diagnostic capability. Across extensive experiments, KnowSR consistently outperforms 19 baselines on patient-level six-class diagnosis under patient-disjoint five-fold evaluation. This shows that grounding patient evidence in structured medical knowledge enables more effective differential diagnosis than naive multimodal fusion alone.
papers.summary: Differential diagnosis of neurodegenerative disorders is hard because clinical presentations overlap and multimodal patient data are heterogeneous and often incomplete. Knowledge-enhanced Structural Reasoning (`KnowSR`) aligns multimodal patient representations with a literature-grounded knowledge bank of disease prototypes, signed evidence directions, and pairwise diagnostic relations, then reconciles pairwise diagnostic margins over a sparse differential graph. On patient-level six-class diagnosis under patient-disjoint five-fold evaluation, it **consistently outperforms 19 baselines**.

papers.title: No Audio, No Transcripts, No Problem: LLM-based ASR Adaptation Using Only Domain Documents
papers.abstract: Can a speech recognizer be adapted to a new domain with no target audio and no transcripts, using only written documentation? This is the realistic onboarding setting: a new customer hands over raw documentation, not the transcripts that text-only adaptation normally assumes. We turn a domain's documents into adaptation text in two ways, directly as written sentences or rendered by a large language model (LLM) into synthetic spoken dialogs, and feed them to a recently proposed denoising-based text-only adaptation method. We show that, across in-domain, out-of-domain, and cross-domain settings on two corpora, document-only adaptation can match or closely approach real transcriptions; whether written or conversational rendering is best depends on speaking style and the amount of text generated. To our knowledge, this is the first study of document-only adaptation of LLM-based ASR. As no existing corpus pairs audio, transcripts, and documents, we also built and released a document-grounded benchmark.
papers.summary: The setting studied is adapting an LLM-based speech recognizer to a new domain with no target audio and no transcripts, only written documentation. Domain documents are converted into adaptation text either directly as written sentences or by having a large language model render them as synthetic spoken dialogs, and the result is fed to a denoising-based text-only adaptation method. Across in-domain, out-of-domain, and cross-domain settings on two corpora, **document-only adaptation matches or closely approaches adaptation on real transcriptions**, with the better rendering depending on speaking style and the amount of text generated. A document-grounded benchmark pairing audio, transcripts, and documents is released.

papers.title: Learned Network Dynamics for Model Predictive Traffic Signal Control under Incidents
papers.abstract: Model predictive control (MPC) of urban traffic signals relies on a model of how queues respond to signal decisions, which is hard to specify and calibrate in heterogeneous networks, particularly when incidents change capacities and turning shares. Measurements add a second limitation: the controlled lanes at the stop line are often short, so queues extending upstream of them fall outside lane-level measurements. We propose GNN-MPC, a receding-horizon controller that plans with action-conditioned network dynamics learned by graph neural networks. Phase sequences are coordinated across intersections by approximate best responses, with an acceptance test that keeps the predicted cost no higher than that of the initial plan. In microscopic simulation under non-recurrent incidents, GNN-MPC reduces travel time and increases completed trips relative to all tested controllers, on a homogeneous grid and a heterogeneous 21-intersection network. Controlled comparisons on the heterogeneous network distinguish the roles of observation and prediction. With nearly as many vehicles entering the network, GNN-MPC reduces travel time by 13% relative to MaxPressure with the same upstream measurement, and GNN-MPC without the upstream representation does not reproduce its performance. Under the same traffic measurements, planner and objective, replacing the learned dynamics with calibrated store-and-forward predictors increases travel time by 31-34%. Observing hidden demand and predicting its response to control are thus complementary requirements of network-level predictive control.
papers.summary: Model predictive control (MPC) of urban traffic signals needs a model of how queues respond to signal decisions, which is hard to calibrate when incidents change capacities and when queues extend beyond the short lanes sensors measure. `GNN-MPC` is a receding-horizon controller that plans with action-conditioned network dynamics learned by graph neural networks and coordinates phase sequences across intersections through approximate best responses with an acceptance test. In microscopic simulation under non-recurrent incidents on a homogeneous grid and a heterogeneous 21-intersection network, it reduces travel time and increases completed trips relative to all tested controllers, including a **13% travel-time reduction versus `MaxPressure`** given the same upstream measurement. Swapping the learned dynamics for calibrated store-and-forward predictors raises travel time by 31-34%, and removing the upstream representation also loses the gains.

papers.title: THRIFTY: Cost-Constrained Reasoning-Data Synthesis for Small Language Models
papers.abstract: Small language models (SLMs) are increasingly attractive for efficient, specialized deployment, and are typically trained on reasoning trajectories distilled from a larger teacher LLM. Generating this synthetic data is a major cost of the pipeline, especially when the teacher is a frontier model. Existing collection methods, however, are largely cost-unaware, or at best spread a fixed sampling budget uniformly across queries. Such allocation ignores the wide variation in problem difficulty and the strategic over- or under-sampling it invites. Thus, we propose THRIFTY, a Thompson-sampling bandit controller that spends a fixed generation-token budget to collect diverse correct reasoning trajectories, casting the task as a bandits-with-knapsacks problem with a novel diversity-aware objective. It tracks each problem's success probability with an online Beta posterior and spends each token where it expects the most new distinct correct solutions. Because repeated solutions add progressively less value, THRIFTY adaptively stops resampling saturated problems, concentrates budget on under-covered ones, and retires the unsolvable at the budget's opportunity cost. On math (AIME, MATH-500) and code (LiveCodeBench) benchmarks, THRIFTY gathers up to 22% more diverse correct trajectories per generation token than both the standard uniform-sampling recipe and the strongest adaptive baseline, with the largest gains in the scarce-budget and hard-problem regimes.
papers.summary: Small language models (SLMs) are usually trained on reasoning trajectories distilled from a larger teacher, and generating that data is a major cost that existing collection methods ignore or spread uniformly across queries. `THRIFTY` is a Thompson-sampling bandit controller that treats collection as a bandits-with-knapsacks problem with a diversity-aware objective, tracking each problem's success probability with an online Beta posterior and spending tokens where it expects the most new distinct correct solutions. It stops resampling saturated problems, concentrates on under-covered ones, and retires unsolvable ones. On `AIME`, `MATH-500`, and `LiveCodeBench`, it gathers **up to 22% more diverse correct trajectories per generation token** than uniform sampling and the strongest adaptive baseline, with the largest gains under scarce budgets and on hard problems.

papers.title: Learning When to Ask: Advisor-Aware Post-Training for SLM Agents
papers.abstract: Small language models (SLMs) are increasingly attractive for cheap, high-throughput agentic deployment, but they remain weak at multi-step reasoning and tool use that long-horizon tasks demand. We study how to post-train an SLM to seek advice from a stronger model and act on that advice itself, following an advisor-executor pattern. Out of the box, this pattern fails across open- and closed-source small-model families: wiring an SLM to an advisor is a harness-design matter that is not enough on its own. A post-training recipe is needed to teach the model when to ask, in a cost-aware fashion, and how to follow advice across steps. Our method, ADAPT (ADvisor-Aware Post-Training), is a multi-stage recipe that instills this behavior, learning entirely from the policy's own rollouts supervised by the environment's outcome, with no learned reward model or human annotation. Across three domains, compared to an untrained harness baseline, ADAPT improves success rate in embodied text reasoning (TextWorld) from 24.5% to 77.3%, code generation (LiveCodeBench) from 21.8% to 56.0%, and deep web search (GAIA) from 17.5% to 49.3%, while querying the advisor sparingly (~1.0-2.1 calls per task). On the two long-horizon domains it closes 70-85% of the gap to an oracle that perfectly times when to ask for advice, and on code generation it exceeds that oracle. The gains persist when the advisor is replaced by one unseen in training, showing that the learned help-seeking policy is robust to a changing advisor rather than tied to the one it was trained with.
papers.summary: Small language models (SLMs) are cheap to deploy as agents but weak at multi-step reasoning and tool use, and simply wiring one to a stronger advisor model does not help out of the box. `ADAPT` (ADvisor-Aware Post-Training) is a multi-stage recipe that teaches the small model when to ask for advice in a cost-aware way and how to follow it across steps, learning only from its own rollouts and environment outcomes with no reward model or human annotation. Against an untrained harness baseline, **success rates rise from 24.5% to 77.3% on `TextWorld`, 21.8% to 56.0% on `LiveCodeBench`, and 17.5% to 49.3% on `GAIA`, with only about 1.0-2.1 advisor calls per task**. The gains persist when the advisor is swapped for one unseen in training.

papers.title: Silent Arbitration: How Large Language Models Resolve Co-Authoritative Conflicting Instructions
papers.abstract: Large language models increasingly receive high-level instructions about roles, values, interests, and communication style. Such instructions can conflict even when a prompt assigns them equal authority and provides no priority rule. We study co-authoritative persona conflict, in which a single prompt jointly assigns two opposing personas. Across eight conflict types grounded in published source material and five LLMs, we measure conflict acknowledgment, resolution strategy, and directional stance. Models acknowledge incompatibility in 72% of direct checks but explicitly surface it in only 22% of task responses, revealing silent arbitration. Dominance accounts for 45% of dual-persona responses, and 35% of compromise-labeled responses retain directional lean. Prompt framing further changes the visible form of arbitration substantially more than ordinary paraphrase variation. These findings show that evaluating instruction following should assess whether models disclose conflicts, how they resolve them, and which persona their responses favor.
papers.summary: When a single prompt assigns a large language model (LLM) two opposing personas with equal authority and no priority rule, the model has to resolve the conflict somehow. Across eight conflict types and five LLMs, the authors measure whether models acknowledge the conflict, which resolution strategy they use, and which persona the response favors. **Models recognize the incompatibility in 72% of direct checks but explicitly surface it in only 22% of task responses**, a pattern the authors call silent arbitration. One persona simply dominates in 45% of dual-persona responses, 35% of responses labeled as compromise still lean one way, and prompt framing shifts the visible form of arbitration more than ordinary paraphrasing does.

papers.title: Structurally Different, Functionally Persistent: Capability Regions Under Model Optimization
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) capabilities have been associated with localized parameter regions, enabling targeted model editing and intervention. However, it remains unclear whether a region identified before model optimization remains an effective intervention target afterward. We evaluate the functional persistence and parameter overlap of coding capability regions across three instruction-tuned models under quantization, pruning, and LoRA-based adaptation. Although re-extracted regions exhibit substantial parameter reorganization, ablating the original region after optimization eliminates or nearly eliminates coding performance in almost all conditions, while magnitude-matched controls preserve performance. Partition analysis further shows that the shared subset of the original and re-extracted regions accounts for most of the observed ablation effect in the majority of conditions. These results demonstrate that parameter overlap and functional persistence are distinct: capability regions can remain causally effective intervention targets even when their parameter realization changes substantially.
papers.summary: Large language model (LLM) capabilities have been linked to localized parameter regions that can be targeted for editing, but it is unclear whether a region found before model optimization is still a valid target afterward. The authors track coding capability regions in three instruction-tuned models through quantization, pruning, and `LoRA`-based adaptation, comparing the original region against one re-extracted after optimization. Although the re-extracted regions show substantial parameter reorganization, **ablating the original region after optimization eliminates or nearly eliminates coding performance in almost all conditions**, while magnitude-matched control ablations preserve it. The subset shared by the original and re-extracted regions accounts for most of the ablation effect in the majority of conditions, so parameter overlap and functional persistence are distinct properties.

papers.title: Mechanism Parity for Simulation-Based Validation of Autonomous-Driving Perception
papers.abstract: Simulation is central to intelligent-vehicle validation, but visual realism or output agreement between a real scene and its synthetic counterpart does not prove that a perception system used the same evidence in both domains. This paper addresses that mechanism-parity gap for paired real-synthetic autonomous-driving perception. It unifies Decisive-Feature Fidelity, which compares decisive evidence maps in a frozen system under test (SUT), with Concept-Decisive Feature Fidelity, which projects decisive evidence into semantic scene concepts for diagnosis. The framework is a validation diagnostic rather than a standalone safety certificate: it asks whether output-consistent simulation also preserves the mechanism by which the perception model reaches that output. The empirical evidence comprises ten retrained diffusion ControlNet generators evaluated on a deterministic exact-geometry KITTI-Virtual KITTI 2 subset. Generated counterparts use a 1248-by-376-pixel padded inference canvas and are cropped back to the exact KITTI dimensions before evaluation. The final benchmark reports target-image, output-consistency, and mechanism metrics recomputed from a single audited output set, then adds metric-disagreement cases, bootstrap uncertainty, threshold sensitivity, and concept/cache integrity audits. Across the benchmark, output and appearance fidelity are at most weakly and inconsistently rank-correlated with decisive-mechanism distance for all three frozen SUTs, and a constructed positive control shows the estimator detects a known planted mechanism that output agreement misses, supporting decisive-evidence diagnostics for intelligent-vehicle simulation validation. All numerical claims are restricted to the declared exact-geometry benchmark, ten generators, and three frozen SUTs.
papers.summary: A synthetic driving scene can look realistic and produce the same perception output as its real counterpart without the perception model having relied on the same evidence in both. The framework combines Decisive-Feature Fidelity, which compares decisive evidence maps inside a frozen system under test (SUT), with Concept-Decisive Feature Fidelity, which projects that evidence onto semantic scene concepts for diagnosis. On a paired `KITTI`-`Virtual KITTI 2` subset with ten retrained diffusion `ControlNet` generators, **output and appearance fidelity are at most weakly and inconsistently rank-correlated with decisive-mechanism distance for all three frozen SUTs**, and a planted-mechanism control shows the estimator catches a difference that output agreement misses. The authors present it as a validation diagnostic, not a safety certificate, and restrict all numerical claims to this benchmark.

papers.title: On the Challenges of Using LLMs in High-Risk AI Recruitment: Guiding Questions for Legal Conformity with the AI Act
papers.abstract: The EU Artificial Intelligence Act (AI Act) imposes detailed obligations on providers of high-risk AI systems but offers limited operational guidance, particularly when these systems integrate third-party General-Purpose AI (GPAI) models. This paper introduces a toolkit that fosters the development of legal-by-design AI-assisted recruitment systems by translating the core legal obligations of the AI Act's conformity assessment---specifically Articles 9--15 and Annex IV---into techno-normative requirements and corresponding guiding questions. While recruitment pipelines may involve components with varying technical complexity and differing levels of algorithmic transparency, this paper focuses on the most challenging case: the integration of third-party GPAI models into critical stages of the selection process, including resume and job description parsing, applicant scoring, and shortlist generation. This scenario presents significant challenges for downstream providers of high-risk AI systems, as it underscores the difficulties in obtaining the technical information needed to demonstrate compliance with the AI Act's techno-normative requirements, both prior to and during market deployment. After introducing the toolkit and illustrating its application through a simplified example, the paper explores informational dependencies between upstream and downstream GPAI model providers. These dependencies may produce informational gaps across the AI supply chain, potentially hindering the collection of evidence necessary for the AI system provider to ensure legal compliance. The resulting lack of technical transparency negatively affects the deployer, who may struggle to maintain meaningful oversight of the system, and ultimately impacts the persons subject to the AI output.
papers.summary: The EU Artificial Intelligence Act places detailed obligations on providers of high-risk AI systems but gives little operational guidance, especially when those systems embed third-party General-Purpose AI (GPAI) models. The authors build a toolkit that translates the conformity-assessment obligations of Articles 9-15 and Annex IV into techno-normative requirements and guiding questions, applied to recruitment systems that use GPAI models for resume and job description parsing, applicant scoring, and shortlist generation. Their analysis argues that **informational dependencies between upstream model providers and downstream system providers create gaps that can prevent the downstream provider from collecting the evidence needed to demonstrate compliance**. That lack of technical transparency in turn weakens the deployer's ability to oversee the system and affects the people subject to its outputs.

papers.title: Supervaluationism about vagueness and indeterminacy: A judgment-aggregation perspective
papers.abstract: Supervaluationism about vagueness and indeterminacy is based on the idea that some sentences, or predicates within them, have multiple competing interpretations or specifications. A sentence is deemed determinately true if and only if it is true according to all specifications; and determinately false if and only if it is false according to all specifications. In all other cases, the sentence is assigned no determinate truth-value. Supervaluationism, however, is only one way of taking into account the verdicts of different specifications -- in technical terms, "aggregating" those verdicts. In this paper, we introduce insights from the theory of judgment aggregation to study a broad class of different aggregation functions. This allows us to offer an axiomatic characterization of supervaluationism, which, in turn, locates it precisely within a larger logical space of possible approaches to vagueness and indeterminacy. Among other results, we axiomatically compare supervaluationism with subvaluationism, the epistemic theory of vagueness, and Strong Kleene and LP logics.
papers.summary: Supervaluationism treats a vague sentence as determinately true only if it is true under every admissible specification of its terms, determinately false if false under all of them, and without a determinate truth-value otherwise. The authors recast this as one way of aggregating the verdicts of different specifications and apply the theory of judgment aggregation to study a broad class of alternative aggregation functions. The result is **an axiomatic characterization of supervaluationism that locates it within a larger space of approaches to vagueness and indeterminacy**. The same framework is used to compare it axiomatically with subvaluationism, the epistemic theory of vagueness, and the Strong Kleene and LP logics.

papers.title: Cecilia: Towards Layout-Inclusive Optical Music Recognition
papers.abstract: Reconstructing an editable music score requires musical events, sung text and the instructions that organise them on the page. Existing recognition targets often omit part of this information, while direct MusicXML prediction repeats substantial structural markup. We introduce Cecilia, a compact representation of canonicalised MusicXML that retains musical content, lyric attachments and layout instructions. Cecilia-OMR predicts this representation through metadata and measure-bounded music segments from shared visual memory. A learned count head determines the number of output segments. Across paired complete scores under a common tokeniser, the ratio of mean MusicXML to Cecilia sequence lengths is 27.73. Cecilia-OMR outperforms Legato 2 on Camera String Quartets and both Lieder conditions, with a four-condition OpenScore macro normalised edit distance of 0.2232 against 0.2998. Separate evaluations of lyrics, notation trees and rendered layout reveal complementary aspects of reconstruction and quantify the contribution of layout instructions. Training-stage, reward and candidate-selection studies further examine how recognition changes across model adaptation and decoding.
papers.summary: Recovering an editable score from a page image requires musical events, sung text, and layout instructions, but existing recognition targets drop some of this, and predicting `MusicXML` directly repeats a lot of structural markup. `Cecilia` is a compact representation of canonicalised `MusicXML` that keeps musical content, lyric attachments, and layout instructions, with sequences on average 27.73 times shorter than the `MusicXML` equivalent under a common tokeniser. The `Cecilia-OMR` model predicts it as metadata plus measure-bounded segments from a shared visual memory, with a learned head that decides how many segments to emit. It outperforms `Legato 2` on `Camera String Quartets` and both `Lieder` conditions, with **a four-condition `OpenScore` macro normalised edit distance of 0.2232 against 0.2998**.

papers.title: ROSWORLD: When Digital Task Competence Meets Physical Execution
papers.abstract: Computer-use agents now solve most desktop tasks through direct software input, but a robot using the same computer must turn GUI knowledge into physical contact with a keyboard and mouse. We introduce ROSWorld, a benchmark that couples a physically simulated robot workstation to a live OSWorld desktop, so that a robot and a desktop agent pursue the same goals under the same official evaluators. The evaluated model receives observations only from the workstation camera views and operates the peripherals through either a single-arm rigid probe or dual-arm dexterous hands. Across five frontier models and 40 tasks in ten applications, models that complete 31-39 tasks on the desktop complete at most 23 with the probe and 28 with the hands. Paired trajectory analysis shows that models adapt their interaction strategies toward keyboard input, yet physical execution frequently fails through missed presses, incorrect targets, and unintended contacts. ROSWorld makes the gap between knowing what to do on a computer and physically doing it measurable.
papers.summary: Computer-use agents normally act through direct software input, whereas a robot at the same computer has to turn its knowledge of the interface into physical contact with a keyboard and mouse. `ROSWorld` couples a physically simulated robot workstation to a live `OSWorld` desktop, so a robot and a desktop agent pursue the same goals under the same evaluators; the model sees only workstation camera views and operates the peripherals with either a single-arm rigid probe or dual-arm dexterous hands. Across five frontier models and 40 tasks in ten applications, **models that complete 31-39 tasks on the desktop complete at most 23 with the probe and 28 with the hands**. Trajectory analysis shows models shift toward keyboard input, but execution often fails through missed presses, incorrect targets, and unintended contacts.

papers.title: Cannot Wait to Verify: Parallel Drafting to Eliminate Verifier Idle Time in Speculative Decoding
papers.abstract: Autoregressive inference in large transformer models is limited by token-level sequential execution, resulting in high latency and low GPU utilization. Speculative decoding (SD) mitigates this bottleneck by introducing a draft-and-verifier model. However, the drafting stage remains sequential, leaving the verifier idle and underutilizing compute. To address this, we propose a plug-and-play drafting adaptive drafting method that parallelizes inference across transformer layers during draft generation. Starting from a shared hidden state, our approach evaluates multiple layers in parallel and verifies consistency by measuring divergence in hidden-state space. Layer-wise draft states are accepted when deviations are small; otherwise, a correction step is applied. By exploiting redundancy across transformer layers, our method accelerates draft generation and improves hardware utilization without modifying architectures or requiring retraining. Experimental results on NLP tasks show that our method speeds up the drafting stage by up to $1.65\times$ with minimal degradation in accuracy, while maintaining the same performance as SD.
papers.summary: Speculative decoding (SD) speeds up autoregressive inference by having a small draft model propose tokens that a larger model verifies, but drafting itself stays sequential and leaves the verifier idle. The proposed plug-and-play method parallelizes draft generation across transformer layers: starting from a shared hidden state, it evaluates multiple layers at once, accepts the layer-wise states when their divergence in hidden-state space is small, and applies a correction step otherwise. It needs no architecture changes or retraining, relying on redundancy across layers. On natural language processing tasks it **speeds up the drafting stage by up to 1.65x** with minimal accuracy degradation while maintaining the same performance as standard speculative decoding.

papers.title: From Manufacturing Event Logs to Simulation: Enabling SMEs with Agentic AI for SimPy Simulation Generation
papers.abstract: High expertise and cost barriers exclude small and medium-sized enterprises from discrete-event simulation (DES). We introduce GenAI4SimPy, a multi-agent framework powered by Qwen 3.6 (27B), an open-weight large language model, that automates end-to-end DES generation from manufacturing event logs to executable SimPy models through tool-augmented reasoning and human-in-the-loop validation. Evaluated on three execution blocks from a public smart factory dataset, the framework achieved a mean absolute percentage error of 7.9\% and coverage of failure rate for all three blocks and of throughput for two of three. A fidelity paradox was observed: accurate process-level parameters did not ensure system-level behavioral fidelity, with flow-time and throughput errors driven by misinterpreted observation-window truncation and absent system-level calibration. These results demonstrate that local open-weight models can perform DES generation at accuracy comparable to cloud-based alternatives, while identifying parameter extraction as necessary but insufficient for behavioral validity. Source code and results are available at https://github.com/RaikoPipe/genai4simpy
papers.summary: Discrete-event simulation (DES) requires expertise and budget that small and medium-sized manufacturers often lack. `GenAI4SimPy` is a multi-agent framework running on the open-weight `Qwen 3.6 (27B)` model that turns manufacturing event logs into executable `SimPy` models through tool-augmented reasoning and human-in-the-loop validation. On three execution blocks from a public smart factory dataset it reaches **a mean absolute percentage error of 7.9%**, covering failure rate for all three blocks and throughput for two of three, which the authors describe as comparable to cloud-based alternatives. They also report a fidelity paradox: accurate process-level parameters did not guarantee system-level behavioral fidelity, with flow-time and throughput errors traced to misread observation-window truncation and missing system-level calibration.

papers.title: Practical insights into controlling exponential concentration in quantum machine learning
papers.abstract: Quantum Machine Learning (QML) models are often limited by exponential concentration, where quantum observables become insensitive to input variations as system size increases. In this work, we provide a comparative empirical study of this phenomenon across Fidelity Quantum Kernels (FQK), Projected Quantum Kernels (PQK), and Quantum Extreme Learning (QEL), within a unified observable-based framework based on expectation-value variance. We investigate how measurement locality, entanglement, and circuit expressivity shape concentration across different architectures. Global fidelity-based kernels exhibit strong concentration driven by Hilbert space dimensionality, whereas local-observable approaches reduce but do not eliminate this effect. In PQK and QEL, concentration is primarily governed by entanglement and quantum dynamical expressivity, with reservoir depth emerging as a key factor in QEL architectures. We further study bandwidth scaling as a general mechanism for controlling encoding expressivity across all models. Our results indicate that bandwidth scaling effectively reduces concentration in moderate regimes by restricting the effective expressivity of the encoding, though this protective effect diminishes in highly expressive structural settings.
papers.summary: Quantum Machine Learning (QML) models suffer from exponential concentration, where measured observables become insensitive to the input as the system grows. Using a common framework based on expectation-value variance, the authors compare the effect empirically across Fidelity Quantum Kernels (FQK), Projected Quantum Kernels (PQK), and Quantum Extreme Learning (QEL), varying measurement locality, entanglement, and circuit expressivity. Global fidelity-based kernels concentrate strongly because of Hilbert space dimensionality, while local-observable approaches reduce the effect without removing it, and reservoir depth is a key factor for QEL. **Bandwidth scaling reduces concentration in moderate regimes by restricting the expressivity of the encoding, but the protection diminishes in highly expressive settings**.

papers.title: Verifying and Strengthening Neural Tangent Kernel Theory
papers.abstract:
Writing
  Neural tangent kernel (NTK) theory explains why very wide neural networks trained by gradient methods converge in the lazy-training regime. Its standard proof combines matrix concentration, random Gram matrices, continuous-time dynamics, spectral perturbation, and a bootstrap argument, but has lacked machine-checked verification. We present a Lean\~4 formalisation for two-layer networks, proving an end-to-end theorem: for a smooth bounded activation (instantiated with $\sigma=\tanh$), frozen biases, paired $\pm 1$ initialisation, and explicit width conditions, gradient flow exists uniquely with probability at least $1-\delta$, and
  $$ \|r(t)\|^2 \leq \|y\|^2 e^{-\lambda_0 t/2}. $$
  The sole data assumption is population NTK non-degeneracy, $\lambda_0>0$. Initial coercivity, kernel drift, the movement bootstrap, the residual ODE, and flow existence and uniqueness are formally proved.
  The formalisation also sharpens the standard analysis in two ways. First, replacing the conventional matrix-Bernstein variance proxy with the classical row-covariance proxy yields estimated concentration-width certificates for $\tanh$ that are $36$--$53\times$ smaller at $(m,d)=(16,8)$ and $94$--$121\times$ smaller at $(32,16)$. Lean certifies the inequality; the ratios are numerical. Second, the network Hessian has operator norm $\Theta(\sqrt{p})$ on the sup-norm parameter ball (a paper calculation), preventing the expected $O(1/\sqrt{p})$ linearisation bound via sup-norm Taylor estimates. An $L^2$ parameter geometry resolves this issue. Required widths remain polynomial but far beyond practical scales, limiting applicability.
papers.summary: Neural tangent kernel (NTK) theory explains why very wide networks trained by gradient methods converge in the lazy-training regime, but its standard proof had not been machine-checked. The authors formalise it in `Lean 4` for two-layer networks with a smooth bounded activation (instantiated with tanh), proving end to end that under explicit width conditions gradient flow exists uniquely with high probability and the squared residual decays exponentially, assuming only that the population NTK is non-degenerate. Replacing the conventional matrix-Bernstein variance proxy with a row-covariance proxy yields **estimated concentration-width certificates that are 36-53x smaller at width 16 and input dimension 8, and 94-121x smaller at width 32 and dimension 16**; Lean certifies the inequality, while the ratios are numerical. They also show that sup-norm Taylor estimates cannot give the expected linearisation bound and use an L2 parameter geometry instead, and note that the required widths remain far beyond practical scales.

papers.title: Efficient Natural Language to Temporal Logic Translation for Real-Time Physical AI
papers.abstract: Robots can be controlled to perform tasks with guaranteed correctness when the task instructions are stated in a formal language. Large language models (LLMs) have been widely used to allow users to provide such instructions in natural language (NL), by translating NL into formal language. When deploying such translators on a robot, however, we face limited computing and energy resources, while offloading computation or data to the cloud may be infeasible or undesirable. Yet an LLM is a general-purpose text generator, whereas a formula in a fixed formal language fragment follows a well-defined syntax. We therefore ask whether text generation is needed at all. For the formal language of linear temporal logic (LTL), we show that this translation can instead be broken down into answering a set of questions with pre-defined answers. We then construct a System-One model, a recent class of NL-based classifier, to provide such answers and enable us to translate a natural language instruction into an LTL instruction. On three benchmarks, our translator matches or exceeds the accuracy of the best local LLMs available, at up to one order of magnitude lower runtime and energy consumption. We show that it generalizes to unseen atomic propositions and temporal patterns.
papers.summary: Translating natural-language task instructions into a formal language lets robots execute them with correctness guarantees, but running a large language model (LLM) for that translation is costly on a robot's limited compute and energy budget. For linear temporal logic (LTL), the authors show the translation can be decomposed into a set of questions with pre-defined answers, so no free-form text generation is needed. A `System-One` model, a recent class of natural-language classifier, answers those questions and the formula is assembled from the answers. On three benchmarks the translator **matches or exceeds the accuracy of the best local LLMs at up to one order of magnitude lower runtime and energy consumption**, and it generalizes to unseen atomic propositions and temporal patterns.

papers.title: Alignment without Transfer: Tokenization Impacts Cross-lingual Representations during Multilingual Language Model Pretraining
papers.abstract: Tokenization represents one of the most crucial steps in mulilingual NLP pipelines. Yet, tokenizers routinely under-allocate vocabulary to low-resource languages. While improved allocation leads to better performance, it remains poorly understood how tokenization shapes cross-lingual representations and transfer during pretraining. To address this, we pretrain 39 mono- and bilingual 1B decoder-only models on FineWeb2-HQ across English, German, French, Arabic and Chinese, varying only the tokenizer. Our results demonstrate that improved vocabulary allocation (i) substantially raises cross-lingual representation alignment in early-to-mid layers, an effect that prior work measuring only the output layer could not observe, (ii) increases cross-lingual parametric knowledge sharing in feed-forward neurons, supported by correlational and causal evidence, and (iii) an alignment-transfer dissociation, where cross-lingual transfer remains essentially unchanged despite higher alignment. Moreover, transfer is significantly lower for cross-script bilinguals even under fair vocabulary allocation, indicating that the script barrier is not merely a tokenizer artifact. All of our checkpoints and code are publicly available.
papers.summary: Tokenizers routinely give low-resource languages too little vocabulary, yet how that choice shapes cross-lingual representations during pretraining is poorly understood. The authors pretrain 39 monolingual and bilingual 1B decoder-only models on `FineWeb2-HQ` across English, German, French, Arabic, and Chinese, varying only the tokenizer. Better vocabulary allocation substantially raises cross-lingual representation alignment in early-to-mid layers and increases knowledge sharing in feed-forward neurons, yet **cross-lingual transfer remains essentially unchanged despite the higher alignment**. Transfer is also significantly lower for bilingual pairs that cross scripts even under fair allocation, so the script barrier is not just a tokenizer artifact.

papers.title: Learning Unknown Oscillators From Bandit Feedback
papers.abstract: We study semi-bandits driven by unknown oscillators. Each round, a learner selects two of four reward channels and observes their individual rewards. Frequency errors change future reward rankings and the resulting measurements. We show when committing to one fitted oscillator lets its greedy choices expose prediction errors. Our controller bounds reward loss (regret) over a continuous confidence set and holds the longest block within budget. An online regression policy gathers observations when the check fails. Regret grows at a square-root rate, up to logarithmic factors, across all frequencies and extends to two competing oscillators. On 96 fresh synthetic instances, checked commitment uses 49 fits instead of 1,023, with 1.5% higher mean regret than fitting every round. Matched isolated timings give a 4.69-fold speedup. The confidence sets also certify trajectory regret.
papers.summary: The setting is a semi-bandit whose rewards are driven by oscillators of unknown frequency: each round the learner picks two of four reward channels and observes their rewards, and frequency errors change both future rankings and what gets measured. The proposed controller commits to one fitted oscillator for as long as a check over a continuous confidence set keeps regret (reward loss) within budget, and falls back to an online regression policy that gathers observations when the check fails. Regret grows at a square-root rate up to logarithmic factors across all frequencies, and the analysis extends to two competing oscillators. On 96 synthetic instances, **checked commitment needs 49 model fits instead of 1,023 at the cost of 1.5% higher mean regret**, with a 4.69-fold speedup in matched isolated timings.

papers.title: Typhoon OCR 2: From Thai Document Transcription to Multilingual, Multi-Task OCR
papers.abstract: Typhoon OCR 1.5 focused on reading Thai documents. However, in real-world workflows, users often need to extract specific information or preserve the structure of an entire page for further processing. Typhoon OCR 2 handles both tasks in a single model, with prompt-driven extraction and structured full-page parsing. Full-page parsing covers Thai, English, and Chinese. We release compact 2B and 0.8B models adapted from open document parsers through supervised fine-tuning on curated Thai and public multilingual data, followed by Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with task rewards and a rule penalizing unfinished responses. Among evaluated open models, Typhoon OCR 2 2B scores highest on Thai MDPBench (80.7 versus 68.9 for Typhoon OCR 1.5) and on ThaiOCRBench (59.91 versus 40.45), which covers recognition, extraction, and document understanding. The 2B model remains close to its base on English olmOCR-bench (84.7 versus 84.4) and on OmniDocBench, which evaluates English and Chinese together (90.97 versus 91.03). On MDPBench, GRPO reduces the mean share of pages with repetition loops for the 2B model from 3.2% to 0.7%, with a smaller and statistically uncertain score gain for the 0.8B model. We release the model weights, Python package, and evaluation suite.
papers.summary: `Typhoon OCR 2` extends a Thai document transcription model into a single model that handles both prompt-driven information extraction and structured full-page parsing, with parsing covering Thai, English, and Chinese. Compact 2B and 0.8B models are adapted from open document parsers by supervised fine-tuning on curated Thai and public multilingual data, followed by Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with task rewards and a penalty for unfinished responses. Among the open models evaluated, the 2B model scores highest on Thai `MDPBench` (**80.7 versus 68.9 for `Typhoon OCR 1.5`**) and on `ThaiOCRBench` (59.91 versus 40.45), while staying close to its base model on `olmOCR-bench` and `OmniDocBench`. GRPO cuts the share of pages with repetition loops for the 2B model from 3.2% to 0.7%, with a smaller and statistically uncertain score gain for the 0.8B model.

papers.title: Trained on Harm, Still Refusing: A Training-Time Defense for Code Generation
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning enables safety-aligned code language models to adapt to diverse downstream tasks. However, training on untrusted data can severely undermine their ability to refuse harmful requests. Notably, we find that models comply with harmful requests even though harmfulness information remains highly decodable from their internal representations. Moreover, an initial preference for refusal does not necessarily translate into sustained refusal behavior throughout generation. Together, these findings reveal a critical gap between recognizing harmful requests and consistently refusing to fulfill them. To address this gap, we introduce SAFEHOLD, a novel provider-enforced defense framework that preserves safety alignment during harmful fine-tuning by treating refusal as a sustained generation process rather than a single response decision. Specifically, SAFEHOLD preserves the aligned model's full-vocabulary response distribution at the initial generation position through decision-boundary anchoring, while supervising the complete refusal sequence through refusal-path reinforcement. We conduct extensive experiments evaluating safety, utility, and internal mechanisms. SAFEHOLD reduces average ASR by 72.03 percentage points relative to undefended fine-tuning, outperforming five SOTA defenses by 24.32 to 70.87 percentage points. Meanwhile, it improves average HumanEval pass@1 by 10.24 percentage points over undefended fine-tuning, while maintaining an average XSTest over-refusal rate of only 2.73 percent. Overall, these results demonstrate that SAFEHOLD effectively mitigates safety degradation during harmful fine-tuning while preserving benign-task utility.
papers.summary: Fine-tuning a safety-aligned code model on untrusted data can strip its ability to refuse harmful requests, and the authors find such models comply even though harmfulness remains highly decodable from their internal representations and an initial lean toward refusal does not hold through generation. `SAFEHOLD` is a provider-enforced, training-time defense that treats refusal as a sustained generation process: it anchors the aligned model's full-vocabulary response distribution at the first generation position and supervises the complete refusal sequence. It **reduces the average attack success rate by 72.03 percentage points relative to undefended fine-tuning**, beating five existing defenses by 24.32 to 70.87 points. Average `HumanEval` pass@1 improves by 10.24 points over undefended fine-tuning, and the over-refusal rate on `XSTest` averages 2.73 percent.

papers.title: Constraint-Aware Anticlustering Decomposition for Certifying Pairwise-Constrained Clustering
papers.abstract: Certifying the quality of feasible solutions to large-scale minimum sum-of-squares clustering with pairwise must-link and cannot-link constraints remains challenging, as it requires strong lower bounds on the optimal objective value. We propose a decomposition framework that partitions the data points into smaller subsets, called anticlusters, and solves the induced clustering subproblems to obtain a certified optimality gap for the original problem. To preserve pairwise information, we introduce the Constrained Anticlustering Problem (CAP), which assigns each connected component of the constraint graph to a single anticluster while seeking geometrically representative subsets. We formulate CAP as a mixed-integer second-order cone program and develop a variable neighborhood search heuristic to construct high-quality decompositions. The resulting lower bound remains valid even when the induced subproblems are not solved to global optimality. Extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets with up to approximately 4,000 observations show that our approach can achieve mean optimality gaps below 1% at a modest computational cost.
papers.summary: Certifying how close a feasible solution is to optimal for large minimum sum-of-squares clustering with must-link and cannot-link constraints requires strong lower bounds, which are hard to obtain at scale. The proposed decomposition partitions the data into smaller subsets called anticlusters and solves the induced clustering subproblems to obtain a certified optimality gap for the original problem. A Constrained Anticlustering Problem (CAP), formulated as a mixed-integer second-order cone program and solved with a variable neighborhood search heuristic, keeps each connected component of the constraint graph inside a single anticluster while seeking geometrically representative subsets. The lower bound stays valid even when subproblems are not solved to global optimality, and on datasets of up to roughly 4,000 observations the approach achieves **mean optimality gaps below 1%** at modest computational cost.

papers.title: Turnout: Adaptive Attention Switching for Efficient Reasoning
papers.abstract: Post-hoc transformer linearization replaces the key-value cache of full attention, which grows linearly with generation length, with a fixed size state. This change reduces memory consumption but often hurts accuracy. In reasoning tasks, which require long generations, this effect is especially pronounced. In this work we introduce Turnout, a method that mitigates accuracy loss as a result of linearization, while maintaining its memory-reduction benefits. We apply post-hoc linearization to a pretrained full-attention model, training a linear path through distillation while leaving the original full-attention path unchanged. During response generation, the resulting hybrid model retains both paths and uses a learned policy to control when each layer switches from full to linear attention. We train the policy with reinforcement learning using a reward that balances answer correctness and memory use. Empirical evaluation of our method shows that the learned adaptive policy achieves a better accuracy-efficiency Pareto frontier on reasoning tasks compared to fixed switching and static hybrid baselines.
papers.summary: Converting a pretrained transformer to linear attention after the fact replaces the key-value cache, which grows with generation length, with a fixed-size state, saving memory but hurting accuracy, particularly on reasoning tasks with long generations. `Turnout` distills a linear-attention path alongside the unchanged full-attention path and keeps both in a hybrid model. A policy trained with reinforcement learning, rewarded for both answer correctness and low memory use, decides during generation when each layer switches from full to linear attention. The learned adaptive policy **achieves a better accuracy-efficiency Pareto frontier on reasoning tasks than fixed switching and static hybrid baselines**.

papers.title: The Assistant Persona Differs Across Languages in Activation Space
papers.abstract: Large language models behave differently across languages, and are noticeably less safe in lower-resource languages. This gap is well established behaviorally, but not mechanistically. Directions in activation space, including the assistant persona direction, are almost always extracted from English and assumed to generalize across languages. We extract the assistant persona direction in 31 languages in Qwen3-32B, and find that the resulting axes differ substantially: their cosine similarity to the English axis ranges from 0.378 to 0.911. Moreover, each language's assistant persona direction and its magnitude are correlated with the language's resource level. We also find that the model's default assistant state is farther from the helpful assistant pole in lower-resource languages. Finally, steering against a language's own axis amplifies persona-based jailbreak more than steering against the English axis. These results indicate that the model does not carry a single assistant representation across languages. More broadly, the assistant persona may need to be an explicit target of multilingual alignment.
papers.summary: Large language models are known to be less safe in lower-resource languages, but activation-space directions such as the assistant persona direction are almost always extracted in English and assumed to generalize. Extracting that direction separately in 31 languages in `Qwen3-32B` shows the axes differ substantially, with **cosine similarity to the English axis ranging from 0.378 to 0.911**, and both direction and magnitude correlate with a language's resource level. The model's default assistant state also sits farther from the helpful-assistant pole in lower-resource languages. Steering against a language's own axis amplifies persona-based jailbreaks more than steering against the English axis, indicating the model does not carry a single assistant representation across languages.

papers.title: How Many Bytes Has a BPE Model Seen? Estimating Byte-Token Exposure in Pretraining from Corpus Statistics and Embedding Norms
papers.abstract: Byte-level BPE vocabularies retain 256 single-byte fallback tokens. When converting such a model into a pure byte-level model, these tokens provide the starting embeddings. How much training have they received? We estimate byte-token exposure in Qwen3.8 using two independent routes. First, we tokenize 540 MB of public corpora covering 40 domains and 33 languages, then combine per-domain token shares with assumed pretraining mixtures. Single-byte tokens account for 13 to 36% of tokens, mostly ASCII; genuine UTF-8 fallback bytes (0x80-0xFF) account for 0.15 to 0.27% under mainstream mixtures, or about 2 billion occurrences per trillion pretraining tokens. Fallback rates vary by four orders of magnitude across languages, reflecting how well each script is covered by the vocabulary. Second, we analyze embedding and output-matrix row norms for four open models, using untrained padding rows as a zero-exposure baseline and ordinary tokens with known frequencies for calibration. In all four models, the 13 bytes that cannot occur in valid UTF-8 remain at initialization, while every legal high byte lies in a high-frequency band. For Qwen3.8, the norm-based estimate agrees with the corpus estimate within a factor of four. The norm-frequency relation eventually folds, so inversion is useful only as a model-specific, order-of-magnitude estimate. No private data were used.

papers.title: Self-Supervised Continuous-Time Depth Learning and Ego-Motion Estimation from Asynchronous Events
papers.abstract: Event cameras register brightness changes pixel by pixel with microsecond precision, whereas the dense depth that could supervise them is costly to acquire and exists only at isolated instants. Condensing the stream into frames eases learning, but at the expense of the very timing that sets event sensing apart. We propose a self-supervised approach in which each event is assigned its own depth in continuous time, and the camera motion is recovered from the same observations. Supervision arises from geometry: lifted into 3D by its predicted depth and displaced by the camera motion at the instant it fired, an event should coincide with others produced by the same edge, so any misalignment exposes an error in depth or motion. Differentiable rendering then turns these per-event estimates into dense depth maps at target times within each window, faithful to the events behind them. On MVSEC, the approach outperforms prior event-only self-supervised methods in most sequences and depth ranges, with the widest margins at night, and recovers camera rotation more accurately than an earlier unsupervised event-based method. Ablations isolate the roles of local spatiotemporal context, the temporal backbone, and the alignment objective. These results position motion-compensated event alignment as a principled source of supervision for continuous-time depth and ego-motion estimation.

papers.title: Breaking the Barrier of Hard Samples: A Data-Centric Approach to Synthetic Data for Medical Tasks
papers.abstract: Data scarcity and quality issues remain significant barriers to developing robust predictive models in medical research. Traditional reliance on real-world data often leads to biased models with poor generalizability across diverse patient populations. Synthetic data generation has emerged as a promising solution, yet challenges related to these samples' representativeness and effective utilization persist. This paper introduces Profile2Gen, a novel data-centric framework designed to guide the generation and refinement of synthetic data, focusing on addressing hard-to-learn samples in regression tasks. We conducted approximately 18,000 experiments to validate its effectiveness across six medical datasets, utilizing seven state-of-the-art generative models. Results demonstrate that refined synthetic samples can reduce predictive errors and enhance model reliability. Additionally, we generalize the DataIQ framework to support regression tasks, enabling its application in broader contexts. Statistical analyses confirm that our approach achieves equal or superior performance compared to models trained exclusively on real data.

papers.title: Deep Cross-Division Network for Product-and-Ratio Feature Interactions in Industrial Ranking
papers.abstract: Learning effective feature interactions is essential for industrial recommender systems. DCN and DCNv2 efficiently automate polynomial feature crossing. However, their cross layers construct interactions using only non-negative integer powers of the input features, with the maximum degree controlled by network depth. Consequently, they cannot directly represent the reciprocal terms required for ratios, rates, and normalized counts unless such features are explicitly provided as inputs. We introduce DCDN, a Deep Cross-Division Network that augments a DCNv2-style cross layer with a division branch. DCDN jointly learns product, ratio, and mixed product-ratio interactions. We characterize the representable interactions as multivariate Laurent polynomials and show that a $K$-layer DCDN generates Laurent monomials of $\ell_1$-order up to $K+1$, with signed degree between $-K$ and $K+1$. We evaluate DCDN against a production-optimized neural-ranking baseline built around DCNv2 and supplied with manually engineered ratio features. Replacing the DCNv2 block with DCDN allowed us to eliminate the entire class of manually engineered ratio features from the model input, reducing the number of input features by $40.1\%$. DCDN is deployed in the production ranking stack of a major short-video service. In a live A/B test on this service, DCDN increased likes by $3.25\%$, shares by $16.26\%$, total view time (TVT) by $0.33\%$, and clicks to open fullscreen by $0.38\%$; all changes were statistically significant. The number of shown videos decreased slightly ($-0.24\%$). These results demonstrate that DCDN can improve user engagement while eliminating reliance on manually engineered ratio features. Our code is publicly released at https://github.com/rw404/DCDN.

papers.title: PhiJEPA: Denoising Latent Predictions for Visual Representation Learning
papers.abstract: Can a predictor trained to infer hidden image regions still help a world model plan when part of an object disappears from view and the visible context is blurred? We introduce PhiJEPA, a joint-embedding predictive architecture that adapts PhiNet's two-stage prediction to masked Transformers. From sparse, photometrically corrupted context, a Transformer block predicts hidden tokens of an independently corrupted teacher view. A token-wise MLP then maps these predictions to clean teacher tokens. Controlled ablations show that the combined objective improves dense features over the tested one-stage alternatives. Pre-trained on ImageNet-1K with $5.6\times10^{19}$ training FLOPs, PhiJEPA achieves 69.3 mIoU on linear PASCAL VOC segmentation, exceeding the evaluated I-JEPA and DSeq-JEPA checkpoints in segmentation accuracy, with 25\% fewer training FLOPs than I-JEPA. It also improves hidden-region segmentation over Simple I-JEPA (49.1 vs.\ 44.3 mIoU). As an application, we use the frozen encoder in DINO-WM on PushT, and reuse the pre-training predictor, which JEPAs usually discard, to complete occluded tokens without fine-tuning. In open-loop planning with simultaneous object occlusion and Gaussian blur ($\sigma=2$ pixels), predictor completion raises success from 33\% to 65\%, compared with 25\% for Simple I-JEPA with its predictor and 40\% for iBOT with pixel inpainting. Together, these results support two-stage latent prediction as an efficient approach to learning visual representations that remain useful under photometric degradation and support completion under partial observation.

papers.title: PaMuk-Bench: A Parallel Multilingual Multitask Benchmark for Vision-Language Tasks
papers.abstract: While vision-language models (VLMs) currently obtain notable results for highly-studied languages, e.g. English, they exhibit significant performance drops in certain low-resource languages, especially due to the lack of annotated datasets. To this end, we propose PaMuk-Bench, a novel parallel multilingual multitask benchmark for vision-language tasks. Our benchmark includes a set of over 10K curated English prompts that are translated into six languages: Arabic, Danish, French, Hindi, Italian, Romanian. Parallel translations, which are obtained via a semi-automatic process, along with accompanying generated and retrieved images enable the comparative development and evaluation of VLMs across a wide range of tasks: text-to-image generation, image captioning, content-based image retrieval, image generation difficulty estimation, image retrieval difficulty estimation. We empirically show that zero-shot English and multilingual pre-trained VLMs compare consistently worse than their fine-tuned counterparts, confirming that PaMuk-Bench is a valuable resource that can drastically reduce the language gap across a variety of VLM architectures and tasks. PaMuk-Bench is available at https://github.com/ghesil/pamuk_bench.

papers.title: Fix Where It Fails: Root-Cause-Guided Agentic Harness Optimization for Scene Graph Generation
papers.abstract: Scene graph generation (SGG) aims to detect objects in an image and predict the relationships between them. The standard PredCls, SGCls, and SGDet settings show how much performance drops without ground-truth boxes and labels, but not where or why a model fails. Knowing this would allow fixing a model where it fails, without retraining. We propose RoHa-SGG (Root-cause-guided Harness optimization for SGG), which extends agentic harness optimization to SGG. It optimizes the harness, the inference code around a frozen SGG model. RoHa-SGG has two main LLM agents. A root-cause analysis (RCA) agent finds the components where the model fails and diagnoses why, and a proposer agent searches for a harness that fixes these causes. We evaluate RoHa-SGG on Visual Genome and PSG with representative two-stage, one-stage, and multimodal-LLM SGG models. The analysis shows that the components where ground-truth triplets are lost differ across models and datasets. RoHa-SGG improves every metric on all five model-dataset combinations. Graph-constrained R@100 and mR@100 rise by up to 15.8 and 26.4 points for the multimodal LLM and by up to 3.6 and 10.1 points for the two-stage and one-stage models. With root-cause guidance, the harness search reaches the final score of an unguided search up to three times faster.

papers.title: Open CDLM: A Benchmark and Library for Continuous Diffusion Language Models
papers.abstract: Reliable comparisons of continuous diffusion language models (CDLMs) require evaluating both model fit and the distribution of generated text. Two common practices leave this goal only partially addressed. Likelihood-based evaluation often reports a variational upper bound on discrete negative log-likelihood, whose slack can confound comparisons. Generated-sample-based evaluation commonly combines generative perplexity with within-sequence unigram entropy; both scores can remain favorable even when a sampler produces the same text on every draw. We introduce \textbf{Open CDLM}, a benchmark for evaluating CDLMs and their samplers, and describe the design of an accompanying open-source library to support reproducible comparisons. For likelihood-based evaluation, we clarify which comparisons of model fit are supported by reported perplexity bounds and how those conclusions depend on the evaluation procedure. For sample-based evaluation, we use \textit{Kernel Text Discrepancy} (\textbf{KTD}) to compare collections of generated and real texts, alongside diagnostics for diversity, validity, and coverage. In controlled OpenWebText experiments, replacing a collection of texts with copies of a single selected passage improves both conventional generation scores. MAUVE detects the resulting collapse, and its response to other perturbations depends on the text representation and the type of perturbation. This work marks the beginning of Open CDLM as an open-source project for CDLM research. We will maintain and extend the library over time and welcome contributions from the community.

papers.title: On the Limits of Observability for Evaluating Coverage in Machine Unlearning
papers.abstract: Machine unlearning aims to remove the influence of any requested subset of training data while preserving utility on the remaining data. Empirical evaluations measure predictive accuracy and infer training-set membership (MIAs) from model outputs or intermediate activations. However, by focusing on selected forget sets, these evaluations can overlook Coverage, the range of requests a method can fulfill. To assess this coverage, we first conduct a stress test of observability with 502 retrained models, finding that hidden embeddings reveal known deletions missed in predictions. To characterize capacity limits on coverage, we show that distinguishing all $n$ singleton deletions with linear scores can require a shared representation of rank $\Omega(\log n)$. We further extend the bound to arbitrary subsets and show when partial deletion can appear complete. Building on this analysis, we propose CEO, a framework for evaluating unlearning coverage under limited observability. Its compositional color-shape benchmark makes forgetting and retained utility measurable from the full output distribution and provides a leave-one-out retraining oracle for each target. From a fixed number of oracle observables, we estimate empirical target coverage, the fraction of targets reliably flagged when deleted and rarely flagged under any other deletions. To recover missed deletions, CEO further expands each observable representation into high-dimensional activation space with the frozen encoder of a SAE trained on the original model. Extensive experiments of 20 baselines shows that even on this simple synthetic task, only retraining from scratch covers all deletion targets.

papers.title: Alliance Rupture and Repair in Simulating Cognitive Behavioral Therapy Dialogues
papers.abstract: In cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), routine work can strain the client-counselor working alliance, and the counselor must then notice the rupture, repair it, and adapt the work that follows.
