papers.summary: Automating meta-analysis with large language models (LLMs) requires keeping each extracted result tied to its study, comparison, population, outcome, and time point across every stage, not just extracting numbers correctly. `MetaRigor` organizes results as Study x Target units and uses Task Contracts, programmatic rules, and source binding so that the model handles context-dependent interpretation while code handles formal rules, computation, validation, and source checks. It scores 86.29% F1 for complete result delivery and 80.20% agreement on certainty-of-evidence judgments, and in a seven-case end-to-end evaluation reaches **77.01% aggregate F1, 9.78 percentage points above the strongest baseline**. Tracing outputs from three systems shows that local identity mismatches or omissions propagate into statistical inputs and the final report.

papers.title: Recoverable Symbols, Unstable Execution: Auditing Internal Pathways and Decision Identity in Visual State Tracking
papers.abstract: Visual features can retain every symbol a task needs while a model built on them still changes its answer when irrelevant parts of the image change. We study this gap in visual state tracking, where a recurrent executor reads a sequence of symbol tiles through a frozen ViT encoder and decides whether a displayed candidate equals the final state. Our diagnostic pairs each input with a donor view that preserves every queried tile, checks with a symbol-supervised decoder that the full symbol chain is recoverable from both feature sequences, and swaps individual internal channels of the same fitted executor in both directions. On 3,526 pairs in which every symbol is recovered in both views, changing the surrounding context lowers the balanced accuracy of a rotary recurrent head by 17.13 points. The loss runs mainly through the input-dependent rotation phase: restoring the original phase repairs 351 of 391 new errors and brings accuracy back to 88.54%, yet 142 individual predictions still differ from the original ones. A locked test on 192 unseen program families reproduces the pathway (28 of 29 new errors repaired; 382 of 384 predictions unchanged), and the effect partly carries over to single-image canvases. Consistency objectives derived from this analysis reduce the internal discrepancy they target but do not outperform ordinary data augmentation.
papers.summary: A model can change its answer when irrelevant parts of an image change even though its visual features still contain every symbol the task needs. The authors study this in visual state tracking, where a recurrent executor reads symbol tiles through a frozen ViT encoder, by pairing each input with a donor view that preserves the queried tiles and swapping individual internal channels between the two runs. On 3,526 pairs where all symbols are recoverable in both views, changing the surrounding context lowers balanced accuracy by 17.13 points, and **restoring the input-dependent rotation phase repairs 351 of 391 new errors**, although 142 individual predictions still differ from the originals. Consistency objectives derived from the analysis shrink the targeted internal discrepancy but do not beat ordinary data augmentation.

papers.title: Solving the pre-image problem in kernel PCA: The reproducing property is all you need
papers.abstract: Kernel PCA extends PCA to nonlinear dimensionality reduction by implicitly mapping data into a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) via the kernel trick, with applications ranging from image denoising to out-of-distribution detection. While its projection map is well understood, appropriately defining the associated reconstruction map is a longstanding challenge since projecting back from the RKHS to the input space is non-trivial. This is known as the pre-image problem. Existing approaches have tackled this problem by either relying on nonlinear optimization, which is prone to numerical instabilities and sensitive to initialization, or by solving a separate supervised learning problem, incurring additional computational overhead. Furthermore, although the projection map of kernel PCA reduces to that of standard PCA when a linear kernel is used, most of these approaches are not guaranteed to recover PCA's reconstruction map in this case, a consistency property that one would naturally expect to hold. In this paper, we leverage the reproducing property of the RKHS to derive a reconstruction map for kernel PCA that is provably consistent. Our derivations rely on the mild assumption that the RKHS either contains linear functions or the kernel is universal, which holds for standard kernels. We further extend the method to the random Fourier features (RFFs) approximation of kernel PCA by introducing a corresponding notion of RFF reproducing property. Numerical experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that the proposed method performs comparably with state-of-the-art methods across kernel choices, while remaining more computationally efficient and maintaining consistent performance in settings where these baseline methods drastically fail.
papers.summary: Kernel PCA projects data into a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS), but mapping projections back to input space, the pre-image problem, has relied on unstable nonlinear optimization or a separate supervised learning step. The authors derive a reconstruction map directly from the reproducing property of the RKHS, assuming only that the space contains linear functions or the kernel is universal, and **prove it reduces to standard PCA reconstruction when the kernel is linear**. They extend the method to the random Fourier features (RFF) approximation of kernel PCA. In experiments on synthetic and real data it performs comparably to state-of-the-art methods at lower computational cost and stays stable in settings where those baselines fail badly.

papers.title: Decision Models for Multilingual Emotion Classification: A Comparative Study Against LLMs and Encoders
papers.abstract: Decision models receive a question with a closed list of answers and return a probability for each answer instead of free text. They promise low latency and robustness to prompt wording, but no study has compared several of them with fine-tuned encoders across languages. We ask whether systems used without training on labelled data (zero-shot) can replace fine-tuning, and what the decision format adds over a general-purpose large language model (LLM). We compare three decision models (Jev, OpenAI Decisions, Strands Decider 2B) and two LLMs (GPT-6 Luna, Qwen3.5-2B), given Italian instructions, with two fine-tuned multilingual encoders (tabularisai, XLM-EMO) on four emotions (joy, sadness, anger, fear) in 10 social-media datasets in five languages, with paired difference and equivalence tests. The three best zero-shot systems (two decision models and one LLM) score on average about one macro-F1 point below an encoder fine-tuned on the target dataset; our test sets cannot exclude a gap of 4-5 points, and on single datasets either approach wins by up to 22 points. They beat encoders fine-tuned on another dataset by 8-15 points, though against XLM-EMO this may not extend to new datasets, and instructions in each text's language change their results by under 1 point. Exploratorily, they beat the strongest public emotion model used as is by about 6 points. OpenAI's decision endpoint matches GPT-6 Luna, the LLM it runs on, at a fifth of its median latency, and a 2-billion-parameter decision model beats a same-size general LLM by 10 points, owing to its training, not the decision format. The best zero-shot systems, the LLM included, have an SD of about 1 point across prompts. Without labelled data they are a strong default, and decision models add lower latency and, unlike generative LLM use, per-option probabilities. Fine-tuning won by a wide margin only on the largest dataset, GoEmotions.
papers.summary: Decision models take a question with a closed list of answers and return a probability per answer instead of free text, and the question here is whether such zero-shot systems can replace fine-tuned encoders for emotion classification. Three decision models (`Jev`, `OpenAI Decisions`, `Strands Decider 2B`) and two large language models (`GPT-6 Luna`, `Qwen3.5-2B`) are compared with two fine-tuned multilingual encoders (`tabularisai`, `XLM-EMO`) on four emotions across 10 social-media datasets in five languages. The best three zero-shot systems average **about one macro-F1 point below an encoder fine-tuned on the target dataset**, though the tests cannot rule out a gap of 4-5 points, and they beat encoders fine-tuned on a different dataset by 8-15 points. OpenAI's decision endpoint matches `GPT-6 Luna` at a fifth of its median latency, and fine-tuning won by a wide margin only on `GoEmotions`, the largest dataset.

papers.title: Beyond Math, Code, and Logic: Do Reasoning Models Transfer to Scientific Argumentation?
papers.abstract: Scientific discourse depends on argumentative reasoning: identifying claims, evaluating evidence, and constructing coherent responses. While recent advances in reasoning-capable language models have demonstrated strong performance on mathematical, coding, and logical benchmarks, their ability to engage in scientific argumentation remains unclear. We present the first systematic evaluation of language models across seven tasks spanning argument mining, rebuttal generation, and discourse-level reasoning using research papers, peer reviews, and grant proposals. Our study reveals that even frontier models with strong general reasoning skills struggle with domain-specific argumentative tasks, highlighting a fundamental capability gap. To address this, we introduce a training framework that explicitly scaffolds the argumentative reasoning process in language models, substantially improving their competence in scientific discourse. The resulting compact models approach or exceed the performance of much larger proprietary systems and generalize to unseen conversational settings, demonstrating reasoning transfer beyond task-specific supervision. These findings underscore that effective scientific argumentation is not an emergent property of scale, but requires explicit reasoning-aware training, and they point toward practical pathways for building AI systems that can contribute meaningfully to scientific discourse.
papers.summary: Reasoning-capable language models score well on mathematics, coding, and logic benchmarks, but whether that carries over to scientific argumentation has been unclear. The authors evaluate models on seven tasks covering argument mining, rebuttal generation, and discourse-level reasoning over research papers, peer reviews, and grant proposals, and find that even frontier models struggle. They then introduce a training framework that explicitly scaffolds the argumentative reasoning process. The resulting **compact models approach or exceed much larger proprietary systems** and generalize to unseen conversational settings.

papers.title: A Switching Mechanism for Selecting Environment-Adaptive Personalized Gains in Hearing Aids
papers.abstract: Personalized amplification gains for hearing aids have been shown to be preferred over prescriptive gains. Since the preferred settings can vary depending on the background audio environment, this paper presents a switching mechanism or system that automatically selects personalized gains for a current background audio environment. To prevent foreground speech from interfering with background environment analysis, a one-class voice activity detector is designed to identify speech activity from speech mixed with noise. A consistency check is conducted to enable distinguishing foreground speech from background speech, preserving babble as a background environment of interest because hearing aid users often struggle to understand speech in background babble. Sound segments without foreground speech are then analyzed by an online discovery method combining Bayesian change-point detection with a memory of previously encountered environments. This discovery method detects changes, recognizes returning environments, and discovers new ones without a predefined number of environments. Experimental results show that three-seed mean macro-averaged F1 scores of 85.53%-91.98% across eight speech/background-corpus pairs covering 36 background noise types were achieved. Furthermore, the discovery method achieved adjusted Rand indices of 0.91 and 0.96 on two families of test streams. In the same-recording-return condition of audio streams combining speech with four background audio environments often encountered by hearing aid users, the switching mechanism selected the correct personalized gain profile after 105 environment changes, recalled the stored gain profile at every return, and made no switches to an incorrect gain profile.
papers.summary: Hearing aid users prefer personalized amplification gains, but the preferred setting depends on the background sound environment, so the device needs to pick the right profile automatically. The proposed switching system uses a one-class voice activity detector plus a consistency check to exclude foreground speech while keeping babble as a background, then applies Bayesian change-point detection with a memory of past environments to detect changes, recognize returning environments, and discover new ones without a preset count. The voice activity detector reaches macro-averaged F1 of 85.53% to 91.98% across eight speech and background corpus pairs, and environment discovery reaches adjusted Rand indices of 0.91 and 0.96. In streams mixing speech with four common backgrounds, it **selected the correct gain profile after all 105 environment changes with no incorrect switches**.

papers.title: Quantitative Measurement of Pavement Distress based on Vehicle Camera and Perspective Correction
papers.abstract: Using image data is becoming an important method for highway agencies to automatically evaluate pavement conditions. However, most studies focus on improving detection accuracy rather than obtaining quantitative measurements, such as the length or area of pavement distress. Although field camera calibration can provide such measurements, it is impractical for large volumes of onboard images collected from different vehicles. This study develops a method to quantitatively measure pavement distress directly from in-vehicle camera images without on-site camera calibration. A quadrilateral region of interest is first identified based on lane detection and used to construct a perspective transformation matrix for image correction. Size correction is then performed using the proportions of road markings in the image and a specified scale, which also enables estimation of the actual width of the selected region. The corrected images are subsequently processed using object detection algorithms to obtain quantitative distress measurements. The proposed method can efficiently perform perspective correction for images collected by the same vehicle camera with minimal manual effort. The measured pavement patch lengths show a trend consistent with pavement friction data. By calibrating vehicle cameras using only image information, this study enables quantitative pavement distress detection without additional field experiments. The approach provides a practical solution for processing large volumes of vehicle-camera data, particularly as connected vehicles generate increasing amounts of uncalibrated roadway imagery.
papers.summary: Image-based pavement assessment mostly reports whether distress is present, not its length or area, and getting real measurements normally requires calibrating each camera in the field. This method avoids field calibration by using lane detection to define a quadrilateral region, building a perspective transformation from it, and correcting scale from the known proportions of road markings before running object detection on the rectified image. The result is **quantitative distress measurement from uncalibrated in-vehicle camera images** with little manual effort per camera. Measured pavement patch lengths follow a trend consistent with pavement friction data.

papers.title: AutoOntologyBench: A Task-Grounded Benchmark for Agentic Knowledge Engineering
papers.abstract: Foundation-model agents are increasingly extending beyond software engineering (SWE) into autonomous scientific research, where acquiring and integrating domain knowledge remains a critical challenge. Recent industrial advances have increasingly adopted knowledge graphs and ontology-based semantic layers to organize heterogeneous knowledge into reusable representations. We ask: Can autonomous agents construct ontologies that help them solve real tasks, and do they offer measurable benefits over alternative knowledge representations? Existing benchmarks evaluate ontology correctness or agent task success in isolation, leaving the value of autonomously acquired knowledge unresolved. We therefore introduce AutoOntologyBench, a task-grounded benchmark comprising 19,947 audited tasks grounded in 18 real-world knowledge sources across 7 domains, with source-native verification. Spanning Application, Repair, Organization, and Construction, AutoOntologyBench compares nine frontier-model agents under matched knowledge representations. Layered on retrieval, agent-built ontologies add 6.1 points of task success, yet trail an expert-derived reference by 13.0, identifying autonomous knowledge acquisition as the bottleneck to scalable scientific research. Code and resources are available at https://github.com/VinyehShaw/AutoOntologyBench.
papers.summary: Whether autonomous agents can build ontologies that actually help them solve tasks, and whether those beat other knowledge representations, has not been measured because existing benchmarks score ontology correctness and task success separately. `AutoOntologyBench` provides 19,947 audited tasks grounded in 18 real-world knowledge sources across 7 domains, spanning Application, Repair, Organization, and Construction, and compares nine frontier-model agents under matched knowledge representations. Layered on retrieval, **agent-built ontologies add 6.1 points of task success but trail an expert-derived reference by 13.0 points**. The authors identify autonomous knowledge acquisition as the bottleneck.

papers.title: Average-Depth Variable Execution via Request-Local Token Routing
papers.abstract: Layer skipping can reduce large language model inference costs, but a request budget does not specify how to allocate layer execution across generated tokens. We introduce \method{}, which allows tokens to execute different numbers of layers while matching each request's mean executed depth to a continuous budget. At each routed layer, a router reads the current token state and its request's budget and decides whether to execute the Transformer block. Tokens that skip the block pass through a lightweight residual adapter and write no key/value (K/V) entry at that layer. A single checkpoint serves requests with different budgets in the same batch. Across three LLaMA backbones, six quality metrics, and 13 budgets, AVERT is best or tied for best in 206 of 234 comparisons. Across single- and mixed-budget batches, the mean absolute per-request budget error is at most 1.15 percentage points. When grouping requests by budget leaves batches underfilled, mixing budgets reduces decode time per output token (TPOT) by 4.3--21.2%.
papers.summary: Layer skipping cuts large language model inference cost, but a per-request compute budget does not say how to distribute layer execution across the generated tokens. `AVERT` places a router at each routed layer that reads the token state and the request's budget and decides whether to run the Transformer block; skipped tokens pass through a lightweight residual adapter and write no key/value cache entry, and one checkpoint serves different budgets in the same batch. Across three `LLaMA` backbones, six quality metrics, and 13 budgets it is **best or tied for best in 206 of 234 comparisons**, with mean per-request budget error of at most 1.15 percentage points. When grouping requests by budget would leave batches underfilled, mixing budgets reduces decode time per output token (TPOT) by 4.3% to 21.2%.

papers.title: Can Vision-Language Models Synthesize Executable Game-Playing Programs?
papers.abstract: Recent advances in vision-language models (VLMs) have endowed multimodal agents with increasingly strong visual perception and long-horizon reasoning capabilities, making VLM-based autonomous game playing feasible. Existing game benchmarks primarily evaluate whether an agent can select appropriate actions from the current visual state across different scenarios and games. However, most of them adopt a step-by-step interaction paradigm where the current visual observation is sent to the agent before each action. In practical deployment, this paradigm introduces two fundamental limitations: the game loop must wait for model inference, making real-time interaction impractical, and repeated VLM calls incur substantial cost. Therefore, we propose PlayScriptBench, a script-based game benchmark that evaluates whether VLMs can synthesize an executable game-playing program from game states. This setting jointly evaluates visual grounding, understanding of game dynamics, long-horizon strategic reasoning, and executable program synthesis, providing a more comprehensive assessment of game-playing agents. To support more tractable evaluation for current general-purpose VLMs, we further introduce a four-stage pipeline --- Explore, Perception, API Construction, and Strategy Composition --- that decomposes controller synthesis into game exploration, state perception, interface construction, and strategic control, enabling agents to progressively construct an executable program. Experiments on 16 games spanning 4 genres show that even strong VLMs struggle on our benchmark, revealing a substantial gap between passive visual game understanding and executable closed-loop game control. These results establish script-based controller synthesis as a complementary direction for benchmarking VLM-based game-playing agents.
papers.summary: Game benchmarks for vision-language models (VLMs) usually send an observation to the model before every action, which makes real-time play impractical and repeated model calls expensive. `PlayScriptBench` instead asks a VLM to synthesize an executable game-playing program from game states, testing visual grounding, understanding of game dynamics, long-horizon strategy, and program synthesis together. A four-stage pipeline of Explore, Perception, API Construction, and Strategy Composition helps agents build the controller step by step. On 16 games across 4 genres, **even strong VLMs struggle**, showing a substantial gap between passive visual game understanding and executable closed-loop control.

papers.title: Shared Understanding in Human-AI Teams: Coordination Continuity in Evolving Work
papers.abstract: People are increasingly working with AI agents as part of extended, asynchronous workflows. In these settings, shared access to information does not guarantee a shared basis for action: goals, plans, and roles may persist while their current significance changes. We introduce coordination continuity, the extent to which collaborators sustain a workable basis for interdependent action as work progresses. Drawing on research on collaborative work, along with two qualitative team studies and a reflexive case from our own repository-based environment, we present a framework of three elements: durable representations of collaborative work; relative coordination properties that support interpretation of representations in the moment; and interaction mechanisms through which the status of representations can be understood and altered. We use a build-act-drift-rebuild heuristic and the notion of consequential moments to characterise when rebuilding may be needed. We draw eight design implications for collaborative AI infrastructure.
papers.summary: In long, asynchronous work with AI agents, sharing access to the same information does not ensure a shared basis for action, because goals, plans, and roles can persist while their current meaning shifts. The authors define coordination continuity as how well collaborators sustain a workable basis for interdependent action as work progresses, drawing on collaborative-work research, two qualitative team studies, and a case from their own repository-based environment. Their **framework has three elements: durable representations of the work, coordination properties for interpreting them in the moment, and interaction mechanisms for understanding and changing their status**. A build-act-drift-rebuild heuristic characterizes when shared understanding needs rebuilding, and eight design implications for collaborative AI infrastructure follow.

papers.title: RoSci: Exploring Robustness in Science VLMs
papers.abstract: Recent advancements in Vision-Language Models (VLMs) enable significant progress in scientific tasks. However, these models are generally assumed to be presented with complete and accurate information, overlooking the challenges of erroneous/missing information in wild scenarios. To address this gap, we introduce the concept of Scientific Model Robustness, which defines a model's ability to detect anomalies, assess solvability, and perform self-calibration when faced with Information Error (inconsistencies) or Information Loss (insufficiency). Specifically, we present RoSci-Bench, a diagnostic benchmark of 1,220 samples using a seed-variant strategy across six degradation types. To address VLM fragility, we further propose RoSci-Agent, a framework that employs a Parse-Verify-Decide pipeline to vet premises before reasoning. The evaluated VLMs sometimes answer questions whose premises are invalid or incomplete. RoSci-Agent achieves a higher Overall Robustness Score than the evaluated standalone VLMs. RoSci-Bench gives the multimodal reasoning community a common test of when models answer, request clarification, or reject a scientific question.
papers.summary: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) for science are generally evaluated on complete, correct inputs, leaving open how they behave when a question contains inconsistent or missing information. `RoSci-Bench` is a diagnostic benchmark of 1,220 samples built with a seed-variant strategy over six degradation types, testing whether a model detects anomalies, judges solvability, and calibrates itself. The evaluated VLMs sometimes answer questions whose premises are invalid or incomplete. `RoSci-Agent`, a Parse-Verify-Decide pipeline that vets premises before reasoning, **achieves a higher Overall Robustness Score than the standalone VLMs tested**.

papers.title: Budgeted Subset Selection with a Transferable Learned Value Model
papers.abstract: Subset selection is a fundamental task in machine learning, statistics and combinatorial optimisation, with applications in active learning, band selection, input selection and experimental design. The utility of a subset depends on information revealed only after the selection, such as labels or responses, and on interactions among selected candidates. Existing approaches combine value estimation and redundancy control in application-specific ways, which limits their use in other domains. This paper introduces Subset Acquisition with Learned Value Estimates and Search (SALVES), a framework that decomposes subset selection into two components. First, a value model is trained by supervised learning on tasks where the hidden information is known. On a new task, it predicts the utility each candidate would add to the current selection. Second, a selection step chooses the subset from these predictions, typically by simulated annealing with a diversity term penalising redundancy. The value model transfers to new classes, pretrained networks, datasets and sensors, and from synthetic to real data. On the four applications, SALVES matches or outperforms application-specific baselines on average. It requires substantially fewer bands for equal accuracy and remains reliable in input selection where individual baselines fail.
papers.summary: Choosing a good subset under a budget is hard when its utility depends on information revealed only after selection and on interactions among the chosen items, and existing methods handle this in application-specific ways. `SALVES` (Subset Acquisition with Learned Value Estimates and Search) trains a value model by supervised learning on tasks where the hidden information is known, then uses it on new tasks to predict each candidate's marginal utility, with simulated annealing and a diversity penalty making the selection. The value model transfers to new classes, pretrained networks, datasets, and sensors, and from synthetic to real data. Across four applications it **matches or outperforms application-specific baselines on average**, needing substantially fewer bands for equal accuracy in band selection.

papers.title: DPMA: Learning to Compress Mixture-of-Experts Models
papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures offer high computational efficiency, but storing all experts requires substantial memory and limits deployment on resource-constrained hardware. Most retraining-free MoE compression methods commit to either pruning or merging experts, often with a uniform compression ratio across layers. We introduce DPMA (Differentiable Prune Merge Absorb), which jointly learns compression operations and layer-wise expert allocation through gradient descent under a global expert budget. Separate learnable coefficients allow DPMA to prune experts, merge their parameters, and absorb their routing contributions by forwarding routing weights to retained experts. These coefficients and expert assignments are optimised to match the original model's outputs on calibration data while its weights remain frozen. Across four MoE models, eight multiple-choice benchmarks, and five compression ratios, DPMA achieves the highest accuracy averaged over benchmarks and compression ratios on each model among the evaluated methods. At $75\%$ expert reduction, it outperforms the strongest baseline on every model, with gains of up to $6.7$ percentage points.
papers.summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models are computationally efficient but must store every expert, which limits deployment on memory-constrained hardware, and retraining-free compression methods typically commit to either pruning or merging at a uniform ratio per layer. `DPMA` (Differentiable Prune Merge Absorb) learns by gradient descent, under a global expert budget, which experts to prune, merge, or absorb by forwarding their routing weights to retained experts, and how many experts each layer keeps, with the model weights frozen and outputs matched on calibration data. Across four MoE models, eight multiple-choice benchmarks, and five compression ratios, it has the highest average accuracy on every model among the methods compared. At 75% expert reduction it **beats the strongest baseline on every model, by up to 6.7 percentage points**.

papers.title: From Novel Combinations to Informative Absence: Structural permission, communicative opportunity, and form choice in language learning
papers.abstract: Language learners must infer which novel expressions are grammatically licensed and when continued absence is evidence against them. Our generative theory unites these capacities via counterfactual expression opportunities, decomposing utterance generation into structural permission, communicative opportunity, and form choice. First, shared predictive continuations recover structural permission for unseen word-construction pairings across 30 artificial grammars (mean AUC 0.945 after 120 sentences). Second, under hierarchical uncertainty, we derive a joint evidence law linking omissions to context diversity and within-context repetition, and an exact finite-sample context-refinement inequality. Thus, observing related expressions calibrates expected use to sharpen negative evidence, and higher expected use can drive steeper posterior declines for stronger-permission candidates (reversing initial order after six omissions in a fixed-rate example). Third, we prove that while raw counts confound semantic availability and form selection, scene-level opportunity observations identify both. Empirically, reanalyzing adult and child artificial-language experiments shows meaning-conditioned restriction; judgments of restricted combinations improve held-out production predictions across 399 participants (+0.036 nats/production). Naturalistic child-directed and child speech (11 families, six corpora) shows pervasive source-level usage clustering beyond lexical, number, and dependency-role controls, grounding hierarchical rate uncertainty. Finally, modeling causative judgments across five languages shows that structural compatibility and calibrated usage probabilities draw on distinct distributional, semantic, and discriminative cues. Together, these findings show how the organization and calibration of communicative opportunities govern the evidential value of linguistic absence.
papers.summary: Language learners have to work out which unseen expressions are grammatical and when the continued absence of an expression counts as evidence against it. The proposed generative theory splits utterance production into structural permission, communicative opportunity, and form choice, and derives how omissions, context diversity, and repetition combine into negative evidence. Shared predictive continuations **recover structural permission for unseen word-construction pairings across 30 artificial grammars with a mean AUC of 0.945 after 120 sentences**, and the authors prove that scene-level opportunity observations identify what raw counts confound. Reanalyses of artificial-language experiments with 399 participants, child-directed speech from six corpora, and causative judgments in five languages are consistent with the account.

papers.title: Enhancing Attention with Higher-Order Attention
papers.abstract: Current decoder large language models rely on a combination of attention, feed forward and residual layers. The attention used is autoregressive (AR) though this is not strictly correct, as we note. That motivates the introduction of other attention methods that, while also not strictly AR, do enhance the AR character. One is based on a decomposition of mutual information (MI) into a set of Conditional MIs (CMIs) that correlate key tokens with pairs of query tokens. A second, higher-order attention, introduces correlations between contiguous key and query tokens. A third introduces correlations between a set of key and query tokens and uses a Generalized Maximum Entropy Principle to obtain an attention expression spanning a sequence of tokens. All these methods may enhance the information content of the autoregressive probabilities that are used in inference/generation. Applications to contrastive decoding and a systematic analysis of autoregressive probabilities are presented.
papers.summary: Standard decoder attention in large language models is argued to be not strictly autoregressive, which motivates three alternative attention formulations meant to strengthen that autoregressive character. One decomposes mutual information into Conditional Mutual Informations (CMIs) that correlate key tokens with pairs of query tokens, a second `higher-order attention` correlates contiguous key and query tokens, and a third uses a `Generalized Maximum Entropy Principle` to derive an attention expression spanning a sequence of tokens. The authors claim these methods **may increase the information content of the autoregressive probabilities used in generation**, and present applications to contrastive decoding along with an analysis of autoregressive probabilities.

papers.title: QuASAR: Toward an LLM-Assisted Framework for Screening, Prototyping, and Assessing Quantum-Advantage Opportunities in Scientific Computing
papers.abstract: Identifying scientific computations that could benefit from quantum algorithms requires both domain knowledge and fluency in quantum algorithm design, expertise that rarely resides in one person. We report results from QuASAR, an experimental, two-agent, LLM-driven pipeline intended to bridge this gap. One agent screens scientific literature for computational kernels with a plausible quantum-algorithmic analogue and proposes candidates, each backed by citations. A second agent independently verifies those citations. For candidates that survive verification, it reconstructs the source's computational structure, formulates a quantum mapping, builds and executes a prototype, and benchmarks it against classical baselines. We applied this pipeline to ten candidate computations drawn from the astrophysics literature. Nine candidates were carried through to a small-scale, benchmarked prototype. We report three in detail, chosen as the clearest examples with the least redundancy across the set. They span combinatorial optimization, stochastic simulation, and Bayesian inference. The pipeline attempted to supply quantum-design expertise a domain scientist might lack, reconstructing source algorithms where one existed and building original, disclosed mappings where none did. None of the three case studies achieved quantum advantage at the tested scales, and their astrophysical framing has not yet undergone expert validation. What the experiment does show is that the pipeline can turn a published idea into a runnable prototype, which a scientist can then inspect, test against classical methods, and decide whether to pursue. QuASAR is an exploratory framework, offered to the community for evaluation, critique, and further development, with an approach that could broaden the use of quantum computing in scientific research and extend to computational improvements more generally.
papers.summary: Finding scientific computations that could benefit from quantum algorithms needs both domain knowledge and quantum-algorithm fluency, which rarely sit in one person. `QuASAR` is an experimental two-agent LLM pipeline in which one agent screens literature for candidate computational kernels with citations, and a second independently verifies the citations, formulates a quantum mapping, builds and runs a prototype, and benchmarks it against classical baselines. Applied to ten candidates from the astrophysics literature, **nine were carried through to a small-scale benchmarked prototype, but none of the three case studies reported in detail achieved quantum advantage** at the tested scales. The astrophysical framing has not yet been validated by experts, and the authors present the framework as exploratory.

papers.title: Search-RSI: Expanding Search Worlds Along Multimodal Agents' Capability Frontier
papers.abstract: Multimodal search agents answer knowledge intensive visual questions by grounding them in retrieved evidence, and recent recipes train them on multi hop tasks that are synthesized from knowledge graphs and grown online to keep pace with the agent. These recipes, however, treat the searchable world as fixed: a new question can be well formed and verifiable while its evidence is absent from the retrieval backend, so the agent issues the right query, retrieves nothing, and is penalized as if its policy were at fault. Such unreachable negatives accumulate with every round of growth. We propose Search-RSI, a recursive self improvement framework that expands the search world along the agent's capability frontier. In each round, the current policy diagnoses its partially mastered regions of a task space spanned by hop depth, relation rarity, and distractor density; new tasks there are grown together with their evidence; and the same policy decides how they are used: candidates on which its probes disagree feed reinforcement learning, while those beyond its reach become hint guided demonstrations of its own. Keeping the policy inside this loop matters: an improver frozen at the start of training loses 3.2 points. On nine multimodal search benchmarks, Search-RSI keeps improving where static task growth saturates, raising the average accuracy of the recipe it builds on by 9.8 and 9.5 points at 9B and 27B, of which 7.0 points are out of reach for a world that is merely made consistent. The loop uses no external model and only privileged task structure that is removed before training, at 1.27x the compute of static growth.
papers.summary: Multimodal search agents are trained on synthesized multi-hop tasks that grow over time, but when the retrieval backend lacks the evidence for a new question the agent is penalized for a correct query that returns nothing. `Search-RSI` is a recursive self-improvement loop in which the current policy diagnoses its partially mastered regions of a task space defined by hop depth, relation rarity, and distractor density, grows new tasks together with their evidence, and routes them either to reinforcement learning or to hint-guided demonstrations. On nine multimodal search benchmarks it **raises average accuracy over the recipe it builds on by 9.8 and 9.5 points at 9B and 27B parameters**, continuing to improve where static task growth saturates. An improver frozen at the start of training loses 3.2 points, and the loop uses no external model at 1.27x the compute of static growth.

papers.title: A Benchmark Protocol and Fairness Analysis Towards Open-Set EEG Seizure Type Classification
papers.abstract: Automated EEG seizure type classification systems are typically trained and evaluated under the closed-set assumption, where all seizure types encountered at deployment are seen during training. In clinical practice, this assumption fails: patients present with rare or atypical seizure types that fall outside the training label space, and a system that forces a wrong label is worse than one that abstains. We introduce the first open-set recognition protocol for EEG seizure type classification on the Temple University Hospital Seizure Corpus (TUSZ v2.0.3), defining known and unknown classes using the clinical taxonomy itself: seizure types with sufficient subject representation (at least 12 subjects) form the known set, and rare types form the unknown set. We evaluate seven post-hoc open-set scorers (MSP, MaxLogit, energy, Mahalanobis, kNN, GHOST, and COSTARR) applied to a partially fine-tuned EEG Foundation Model (EFM), using a subject-disjoint leave-one-class-out (LOCO) protocol over three seeds that tests whether methods can detect seizure types excluded from fine-tuning. On true unknown classes, the best scorer (Mahalanobis) reaches a mean AUROC of 0.66, and differences among the top scorers are within seed-to-seed variation. Held-out known seizure types from unseen subjects are detected only slightly above chance (AUROC 0.54-0.58 for all scorers). Per-subject rejection rates are highly uneven for all scorers, and GHOST does not significantly improve per-subject fairness over energy scoring (two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank, p >= 0.25). We release the protocol, subject splits, and code as an initial baseline; our results indicate that open-set seizure type recognition remains a hard, open problem.
papers.summary: Electroencephalography (EEG) seizure type classifiers are usually evaluated assuming every seizure type seen at deployment was present in training, which fails for rare or atypical types where abstaining is safer than a forced label. The authors define an open-set recognition protocol on the `Temple University Hospital Seizure Corpus` (`TUSZ v2.0.3`), treating seizure types with at least 12 subjects as known and rarer ones as unknown, and test seven post-hoc scorers on a partially fine-tuned EEG foundation model under a subject-disjoint leave-one-class-out (LOCO) setup. The best scorer, `Mahalanobis`, reaches **a mean AUROC of only 0.66 on true unknown classes**, and held-out known types from unseen subjects are detected barely above chance (AUROC 0.54-0.58). Per-subject rejection rates are highly uneven, and `GHOST` does not significantly improve per-subject fairness over energy scoring.

papers.title: Neural Defend ARCAS 290M: A Robust Foundation Model for AI-Generated Audio Detection
papers.abstract: Voice cloning now needs only seconds of audio, and detectors tuned to one dataset often fail when the generator, channel, or language changes. We introduce ARCAS 290M, Neural Defend's foundation model for detecting AI-generated audio. A single frozen production model, with no benchmark-specific fine-tuning, generalizes across text-to-speech, voice-conversion, and codec-language-model generators, telephone and Bluetooth channels, recording conditions, and languages. We evaluate it on the complete official test sets of ten public benchmarks, scoring every recording exactly as released, and against commercial systems on independent leaderboards. ARCAS 290M ranks first among all systems on the Podonos leaderboard and has the lowest equal error rate among commercial detectors on ASVspoof5. It separates real from AI-generated speech almost perfectly on ASVspoof5, SpeechFake, and ShiftySpeech, and detects nearly all AI-generated speech in Hindi, Tamil, Bengali, and Telugu. On every benchmark with a published zero-shot comparison, including in-the-wild audio, partial fakes, and the conditions hardest for the field, it surpasses the strongest reported detector by a wide margin. These results establish ARCAS 290M as a general-purpose foundation for AI-generated audio detection in fraud prevention, platform safety, and media verification.
papers.summary: Detectors for AI-generated audio often fail when the generator, channel, or language differs from their training data. `ARCAS 290M` is Neural Defend's detection foundation model, evaluated as a single frozen production model with no benchmark-specific fine-tuning on the full official test sets of ten public benchmarks covering text-to-speech, voice conversion, codec language models, telephone and Bluetooth channels, and several languages. The authors report that it **ranks first on the `Podonos` leaderboard and has the lowest equal error rate among commercial detectors on `ASVspoof5`**, and claim it surpasses the strongest reported zero-shot detector on every benchmark with a published comparison. The abstract gives no specific error rates.

papers.title: $\varepsilon$-SegFormer: Multi-Resolution Vision Transformers for Sparsely Supervised Segmentation in Electron Microscopy
papers.abstract: Segmenting organelles in electron microscopy (EM) volumes requires dense annotations that take experts months to produce, and every gain in imaging resolution adds to this cost. Sparsely supervised methods reduce this cost to a small fraction of labeled pixels, but the convolutional networks they build on see a limited neighborhood around each pixel, while the identity of an organelle often depends on context far beyond it. We introduce $\varepsilon$-SegFormer, a multi-resolution Vision Transformer for sparsely supervised semantic segmentation, which builds on the architecture of MuViT and extends the training method of $\varepsilon$-Seg. For each labeled pixel, $\varepsilon$-SegFormer samples views at three physical resolutions centered on it, embeds their patches into a single token sequence, and encodes every token's position in image coordinates, so that attention relates all views in one shared frame. A segmentation head classifies the pixel from the tokens around it; during training, the pixel's own token is hidden, so the label must be predicted from context rather than local appearance. The model is trained in a single stage, without pretraining, with an auxiliary reconstruction loss. On the BetaSeg FIB-SEM dataset, $\varepsilon$-SegFormer learns from about 10,000 labeled pixels among the 670 million voxels inside three cells, and, given the cell mask, segments nuclei, mitochondria and insulin granules in a slice of a fourth, unseen cell with an average Dice of 0.89 (0.91 after post-processing). Ablations show that coarser views improve accuracy and that a compact head on local tokens works best, with the wider context entering through attention in the encoder.
papers.summary: Dense annotation of organelles in electron microscopy volumes takes experts months, and sparsely supervised convolutional methods see too little context around each pixel to identify organelles reliably. `ε-SegFormer` is a multi-resolution Vision Transformer, building on `MuViT` and the `ε-Seg` training method, that samples views at three physical resolutions around each labeled pixel, embeds them into one token sequence with positions in shared image coordinates, and hides the pixel's own token during training so the label must come from context. Trained in a single stage without pretraining on about 10,000 labeled pixels out of 670 million voxels in the `BetaSeg` dataset, it segments nuclei, mitochondria, and insulin granules in an unseen cell with **an average Dice of 0.89** (0.91 after post-processing), given the cell mask. Ablations indicate that coarser views improve accuracy and that a compact head on local tokens works best.

papers.title: ChildAI-Gov: An Evidence-Linked AI System for Assessing EdTech Policies Against Children's Digital Rights
papers.abstract: We present ChildAI-Gov, an explainable AI system for assessing whether education-technology (EdTech) policies respect children's digital rights. Generative AI is reaching children's education faster than its governance can keep pace, yet checking a tool against children's rights remains manual, expert-dependent, and slow. We propose the Child Rights Impact Score (CRIS), an evidence-linked measure across five dimensions: safety, privacy, transparency, autonomy, and non-discrimination. ChildAI-Gov reads an EdTech tool's privacy or AI policy and scores each dimension by combining a large-language-model judgement (gpt-4o-mini) with a deterministic rule check. A retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) component grounds every score in the governing provisions, retrieved from a curated knowledge base of children's rights frameworks (the EU AI Act, UNICEF guidance, and others), so each score is tied to the evidence behind it and an auditor can trace which provision it rests on. We also construct AIPolicy-EdTech, a dataset of 57 real EdTech policies. On it, the five dimensions cohered as a single measure (Cronbach's alpha = 0.79), and grounding made scoring stricter while preserving rankings; an ungrounded baseline was far more lenient, passing nearly half the policies where ChildAI-Gov passed none. It offers evidence-linked decision support on documented commitments, not observation of real-world behaviour or determinations of legal compliance.
papers.summary: Checking education-technology (EdTech) tools against children's digital rights is currently manual, slow, and dependent on experts. `ChildAI-Gov` reads a tool's privacy or AI policy and computes a Child Rights Impact Score (CRIS) across safety, privacy, transparency, autonomy, and non-discrimination by combining a `gpt-4o-mini` judgement with a deterministic rule check, with retrieval-augmented generation tying each score to provisions from frameworks such as the EU AI Act and UNICEF guidance. On `AIPolicy-EdTech`, a new dataset of 57 real policies, the five dimensions cohered as one measure (Cronbach's alpha 0.79), and **an ungrounded baseline passed nearly half the policies where the grounded system passed none** while rankings were preserved. The authors note it assesses documented commitments, not real-world behaviour or legal compliance.

papers.title: Evaluating Prompting Strategies for Zero-Shot Multilingual Aspect-Based Sentiment Analysis with Large Language Models
papers.abstract: While large language models (LLMs) have advanced natural language understanding, their ability to perform complex target-aspect-sentiment detection (TASD) -- a key task within aspect-based sentiment analysis (ABSA) -- in zero-shot multilingual settings remains underexplored. Existing ABSA research predominantly focuses on English or relies on fine-tuned task-specific models, leaving a gap in understanding how open-weight LLMs handle compound sentiment triplet extraction across diverse language families and domains. We present a systematic evaluation of zero-shot multilingual TASD across 12 languages and three domains using seven instruction-tuned open-weight models -- ranging from 8B to 35B parameters across dense and mixture-of-experts (MoE) architectures -- under four prompting paradigms: monolithic, chain-of-thought, sequential, and sequential refine. Our results show that direct monolithic prompting achieves strong zero-shot performance, outperforming multi-step pipelines, while dense models consistently outperform sparse MoE architectures. Through fine-grained error taxonomy profiling and step-level pipeline tracking, we demonstrate that initial aspect term recall forms a hard bottleneck, whereas multi-step decomposition degrades extraction quality; iterative refinement only partially recovers this loss on larger models while inducing net-negative over-refinement on smaller architectures. Finally, generation volume analysis shows that multi-step strategies incur up to 2.38x token overhead without F1 gains, establishing monolithic prompting as the most effective and efficient paradigm for multilingual ABSA.
papers.summary: How well open-weight LLMs handle zero-shot target-aspect-sentiment detection (TASD), a compound triplet-extraction task within aspect-based sentiment analysis (ABSA), across many languages has been little studied. The authors evaluate seven instruction-tuned models from 8B to 35B parameters, both dense and mixture-of-experts (MoE), on 12 languages and three domains under four prompting paradigms: monolithic, chain-of-thought, sequential, and sequential refine. Direct monolithic prompting outperforms the multi-step pipelines, which incur **up to 2.38x token overhead without any F1 gain**, and dense models consistently beat MoE ones. Error analysis shows initial aspect-term recall is a hard bottleneck, and iterative refinement only partly recovers the loss on larger models while hurting smaller ones.

papers.title: $\mathtt{DistP}$: Scaling Local-Update Training with Zero-Shot Hyperparameter Transfer
papers.abstract: Local-update methods offer a communication-efficient alternative to Distributed Data Parallelism ($\mathtt{DDP}$), but introduce additional hyperparameters that require costly tuning. For $\mathtt{DDP}$, zero-shot hyperparameter transfer reduces this cost by reusing settings tuned on smaller models, but its applicability to local-update training remains unclear. We propose $\mathtt{DistP}$, a theoretical framework extending existing transfer rules from $\mathtt{DDP}$ to local-update training with varying worker counts, local steps, and outer optimizers. With averaging as the outer optimizer, $\mathtt{DistP}$ supports learning-rate transfer across width and depth while improving model quality. The tuned inner learning rate also directly transfers across synchronization intervals, but follows two regimes when increasing the global batch size: square-root learning-rate scaling for larger local batches and a fixed reference rate for additional workers. We then generalize width and depth transfer to other outer optimizers, enabling stable scaling with $\mathtt{Adam}$. However, with momentum in the outer optimizer, changing batch size or local steps can require inner--outer learning-rate tuning, consistent with prior work. In language-modeling experiments at $823$M parameters, $\mathtt{DistP}$ reduces validation loss by $8.1\%$ and improves mean downstream accuracy by $10\%$ relative to baselines without retuning at the larger scale. Fitted scaling laws suggest that this advantage grows with the compute budget, reinforcing the benefits of $\mathtt{DistP}$ for communication-efficient training.
papers.summary: Local-update training methods cut communication compared with Distributed Data Parallelism (`DDP`) but add hyperparameters that are expensive to tune, and it was unclear whether settings tuned on small models transfer to larger ones. `DistP` is a theoretical framework extending zero-shot hyperparameter transfer rules to local-update training across worker counts, local steps, and outer optimizers; with averaging it supports learning-rate transfer across width and depth, with square-root scaling for larger local batches and a fixed reference rate when adding workers. In language-modeling experiments at 823M parameters it **reduces validation loss by 8.1% and improves mean downstream accuracy by 10%** relative to baselines without retuning at the larger scale. Outer optimizers with momentum can still require joint inner-outer learning-rate tuning when batch size or local steps change.

papers.title: DOiT: Better Money-Flow Ranking Can Coexist with Worse Account Selection in Anti-Money Laundering Review
papers.abstract: Anti-money laundering (AML) review selects suspicious accounts and reconstructs transfers. Downstream graph neural networks (GNNs) rank money-flow evidence but may also reorder the account queue. DOiT separates these decisions at equal review capacity: account selection determines where graph investigation starts. Across AMLWorld and AMLNet, GNN reordering harms higher-yield upstream orders but helps lower-yield ones. On AMLWorld, this harm coexists with higher transaction average precision (AP) in dimension-matched, per-run decoders, demonstrating separable ranking abilities. At small capacities, positive neighbors can displace a denser upstream prefix and lower yield; replacement costs fall as that prefix is exhausted, allowing the preferred order to reverse. A restricted-access synthetic benchmark informed by real transaction patterns reproduces this separation and validation-based upstream preservation. Capacity-matched combination protects upstream ordering while retaining GNN money-flow analysis, admitting GNN queue influence only where held-out evidence supports it.
papers.summary: Anti-money laundering (AML) review involves both choosing which suspicious accounts to investigate and reconstructing the transfers around them, and graph neural networks (GNNs) used for the second step can also reorder the account queue. `DOiT` evaluates these two decisions separately at equal review capacity on `AMLWorld` and `AMLNet`, finding that **GNN reordering harms higher-yield upstream account orders while helping lower-yield ones**, even when the same GNN achieves higher transaction average precision. The effect depends on capacity, since at small capacities positive neighbors displace a denser upstream prefix. The authors propose a capacity-matched combination that preserves the upstream ordering and admits GNN queue influence only where held-out evidence supports it.

papers.title: SLP-Bench: Evaluating and Improving Acoustic Claims of Reasoning Audio Language Models on Clinical Speech
papers.abstract: Audio language models (ALMs) can answer clinical questions from speech, outperforming baselines built on handcrafted acoustic features. Reasoning ALMs generate a chain of thought that refers to properties of the speaker's voice before predicting. Each statement the model makes about the voice needs to be checked against clinicians' perceptual ratings of the same recording. On clinical speech, existing evaluations score only the final answer. We introduce Speech Language Pathologist Bench (SLP-Bench), a benchmark grading each acoustic claim in the chain of thought against clinicians' perceptual ratings of the same recording. It covers five clinician-rated datasets and 25 perceptual dimensions, and assesses claims for factuality, stability under resampling, and consistency across reworded and different questions. Across ten open-weight reasoning ALMs evaluated zero-shot, claim balanced accuracy ranges from 0.52 to 0.58, claims change under resampling and rewording, and the most consistent models are not the most factual. Fine-tuning a 7B ALM with GRPO on a reward for claims that agree with clinicians raises its claim balanced accuracy from 0.54 to 0.60 and its mean kappa from 0.39 to 0.61, while preserving answer accuracy on per-dimension questions. SLP-Bench is available upon request, subject to approval by the providers of each dataset.
papers.summary: Reasoning audio language models (ALMs) describe properties of a speaker's voice in their chain of thought before answering clinical questions, yet existing evaluations score only the final answer. Speech Language Pathologist Bench (`SLP-Bench`) grades each acoustic claim against clinicians' perceptual ratings of the same recording across five datasets and 25 perceptual dimensions, checking factuality, stability under resampling, and consistency under rewording. Across ten open-weight reasoning ALMs evaluated zero-shot, **claim balanced accuracy ranges only from 0.52 to 0.58**, and the most consistent models are not the most factual. Fine-tuning a 7B ALM with `GRPO` on a reward for clinician-agreeing claims raises claim balanced accuracy from 0.54 to 0.60 and mean kappa from 0.39 to 0.61 while preserving answer accuracy.

papers.title: Redesigning Neural Networks to Not be Confidently Wrong even to Strong Adversarial Attacks
papers.abstract: Early deep learning models attempted to simulate visual perception using a neural hierarchy that alternated between two types of layer: one modelled on cortical simple cells (that was designed to increase selectivity), and one modelled on cortical complex cells (that aimed to increase tolerance). We show that such a neural network (NN) architecture, when implemented with novel components that are better able to learn selective and tolerant representations, is capable of accurate and robust image classification and improved alignment between the behaviour of the model and the perceptual abilities of humans. Firstly, the proposed models are shallow, fewer than ten layer-pairs, which is more consistent with the rapid feedforward object categorisation performed by the biological visual system. Secondly, they are far less prone to producing classification predictions with high confidence for samples from unknown classes or for image consisting of pure noise, and hence, like humans are not easily fooled into perceiving objects that are not present in the image. Thirdly, for the proposed NNs adversarial samples cause predictions with low confidence, enabling them to be accurately identified. In contrast to humans, our networks still do not correctly classify adversarial samples. However, the behaviour of our networks is a significant step towards human-like behaviour compared to standard DNNs that produce highly confident, but incorrect, classification predictions for adversarial samples. The increased robustness to adversarial and unknown samples is achieved while maintaining competitive performance in terms of generalisation to novel samples from the training categories. This enables models of this type to be competitive with state-of-the-art DNNs across multiple different evaluation metrics and benchmark tasks.
papers.summary: Standard deep networks give highly confident wrong predictions on adversarial inputs, unknown classes, and pure noise. The authors revisit early architectures that alternate layers modelled on cortical simple cells (for selectivity) and complex cells (for tolerance), implementing them with new components in shallow networks of fewer than ten layer-pairs. These networks are far less prone to confident predictions on unknown-class or noise images, and **adversarial samples produce low-confidence predictions that allow them to be identified**, although the networks still do not classify those samples correctly. The authors claim this robustness comes with generalisation competitive with state-of-the-art deep networks across multiple metrics and benchmarks.

papers.title: Autonomous quantum machine learning via Riemannian gradient-based optimization
papers.abstract: Quantum machine learning models typically rely on repeated quantum measurements and classical optimization during training, making the quantum-to-classical information-extraction process a fundamental bottleneck for scalability. We propose a framework for autonomous self-training quantum machine learning, based on Riemannian gradient optimization, in which the optimization proceeds entirely within the quantum domain without requiring quantum measurements or classical feedback. We derive the Riemannian gradient update rules for a broad class of learning tasks and identify sufficient conditions under which the resulting training dynamics can be realized fully autonomously. Within this regime, we establish an exponential convergence guarantee, in the training iterations, for sufficiently small step sizes, and further analyze the training cost in terms of the growth of the circuit depth. Importantly, we further show that the trained model can automatically discover symmetries hidden in the training data without $\textit{a priori}$ specification. For the canonical examples of quantum phase classification and unitary learning with a hidden symmetry, our numerical study indicates that learning can be achieved at low circuit depths with only a few distinct training examples. Our results thus establish autonomous quantum machine learning as a promising paradigm that removes the classical optimization loop while retaining strong theoretical guarantees and practical performances.
papers.summary: Training quantum machine learning models normally requires repeated measurements and a classical optimization loop, which limits scalability. The authors propose a self-training framework based on Riemannian gradient optimization in which the update proceeds entirely within the quantum domain, deriving update rules for a broad class of learning tasks and sufficient conditions for fully autonomous training dynamics. In that regime they prove **exponential convergence in training iterations for sufficiently small step sizes**, analyze how circuit depth grows, and show the trained model can discover symmetries hidden in the data without prior specification. Numerical studies on quantum phase classification and unitary learning suggest learning at low circuit depths from only a few distinct training examples.

papers.title: Sampling non-abelian lattice gauge theories with diffusion models
papers.abstract: We present gauge-equivariant diffusion models as samplers for lattice gauge theories (LGTs). Using lattice gauge-equivariant convolutional neural networks (L-CNNs) and the Metropolis-adjusted annealed Langevin algorithm (MAALA), we are able to accurately sample two-dimensional U(2) field configurations and show first promising results for four-dimensional SU(3). Our two-dimensional models extrapolate remarkably well to larger inverse couplings than originally trained on. We confirm this by comparing observables to analytically known values and to hybrid Monte Carlo results.
papers.summary: Gauge-equivariant diffusion models are presented as samplers for lattice gauge theories, the discretized field theories used in particle physics. Combining lattice gauge-equivariant convolutional neural networks (`L-CNNs`) with the Metropolis-adjusted annealed Langevin algorithm (`MAALA`), the authors accurately sample two-dimensional U(2) field configurations and show first results for four-dimensional SU(3). The two-dimensional models **extrapolate well to larger inverse couplings than those seen in training**, as checked against analytically known observables and hybrid Monte Carlo results.

papers.title: Mixture of Latent Recursions for Low-Rank Adaptation
papers.abstract: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) performs task-specific adaptation using a fixed low-rank architecture, whose expressiveness is typically increased by enlarging or adding learnable modules with a proportional parameter overhead. We introduce Mixture of Latent Recursions (MoLR), an adaptive recursion framework that enhances adaptation expressiveness while preserving parameter efficiency. MoLR recursively refines the down-projected latent representation of each input using a shared transformation. A lightweight threshold-based router independently determines whether each token should undergo further refinement, while dynamically adjusted thresholds encourage balanced utilization across recursion depths. Extensive experiments across diverse language and vision tasks demonstrate that MoLR consistently outperforms representative LoRA variants with negligible parameter overhead over LoRA. Further analyses show that MoLR learns input-dependent recursion-depth allocation and enables a controllable inference-time compute-performance trade-off without requiring retraining. Code will be publicly available.
papers.summary: Low-Rank Adaptation (`LoRA`) uses a fixed low-rank architecture, and making it more expressive usually means adding modules and parameters. Mixture of Latent Recursions (`MoLR`) instead repeatedly refines each input's down-projected latent representation with a shared transformation, while a lightweight threshold-based router decides per token whether to recurse further and dynamically adjusted thresholds balance usage across depths. Across language and vision tasks the authors report that it **consistently outperforms representative `LoRA` variants with negligible extra parameters**. The learned recursion depth is input-dependent and can be adjusted at inference time to trade compute for performance without retraining.

papers.title: Graph Signal Generation via Graph-Aware Diffusion Models
papers.abstract: Many signals are defined on the nodes of a graph, such as traffic flow at road sensors or user purchases of related products. They are often partly observed, and learning their distribution enables imputing missing values and forecasting future ones. Diffusion models learn such distributions, but their forward noise is independent across nodes and does not depend on the graph. We introduce graph-aware diffusion (GAD), whose forward process is a heat diffusion on the graph driven by Gaussian noise. In the graph Fourier basis, the forward transition is a scalar Gaussian channel at each frequency. With a shared diffusion rate, high graph frequencies are attenuated faster than low ones. We propose Mode-Adaptive SNR Scheduling (MASS), which assigns each graph frequency its own diffusion rate and keeps all of them at the same SNR. For graph-stationary signals, MASS equalizes the normalized error of the optimal linear denoiser across frequencies. We bound reverse-SDE stiffness as a function of the (shifted) Laplacian's condition number, with a logarithmic upper bound for MASS and a linear lower bound for shared rates. GAD with MASS improves recommendation accuracy by 5-19%, reduces traffic-imputation RMSE by up to 7.8% with half as many reverse steps, and improves forecasting MAE and RMSE using only 3 reverse steps.
papers.summary: Diffusion models for signals defined on graph nodes, such as traffic sensor readings or user purchases, normally add noise independently per node and ignore the graph structure. Graph-aware diffusion (`GAD`) uses a forward process that is heat diffusion on the graph driven by Gaussian noise, and Mode-Adaptive SNR Scheduling (`MASS`) gives each graph frequency its own diffusion rate so all stay at the same signal-to-noise ratio, with a logarithmic bound on reverse-process stiffness versus a linear lower bound for shared rates. `GAD` with `MASS` **improves recommendation accuracy by 5-19%**, reduces traffic-imputation RMSE by up to 7.8% with half as many reverse steps, and improves forecasting error using only 3 reverse steps.

papers.title: DistDNA: Language Model Fingerprinting under Stochastic Decoding
papers.abstract: Behavioral fingerprints identify a large language model (LLM) from its responses to a shared set of prompts, enabling applications such as verifying whether a deployed model corresponds to the checkpoint it claims to be. Deployed models, however, are commonly served with stochastic decoding, under which the same model may produce different responses to an identical prompt, depending on an unknown temperature and top-$p$ setting. Existing representations such as LLM DNA provide limited treatment of this variation. A natural remedy is to characterize models by their response distributions, which, however, raises two challenges. First, each distribution must be estimated from only a small number of sampled responses. Second, a change in decoding setting can alter responses to the same extent as a change of checkpoint. Consequently, fingerprint distances alone provide an incomplete basis for model identity, and identification typically relies on a classifier trained jointly on fingerprints from many checkpoints. We propose DistDNA, which represents a model by its prompt-conditional response distributions and compares models by promptwise maximum mean discrepancy (MMD). The model under examination is assigned to the known checkpoint whose reference fingerprints, collected at several decoding settings, lie nearest to its own, without training a classifier. We show that finite sampling adds variance-dependent terms to the expected squared fingerprint distance, with these terms decreasing as $O(1/R)$ for equal response counts, where $R$ is the number of responses per prompt. Experiments across 115 model checkpoint entries demonstrate that DistDNA improves identification accuracy over the strongest baseline, LLM DNA, by 10.36%.
papers.summary: Behavioral fingerprints identify an LLM from its responses to a shared prompt set, for example to verify that a deployed model is the checkpoint it claims to be, but stochastic decoding with unknown temperature and top-p makes responses vary as much as a change of checkpoint would. `DistDNA` represents a model by its prompt-conditional response distributions, compares models by promptwise maximum mean discrepancy (MMD), and assigns a model to the known checkpoint whose reference fingerprints at several decoding settings lie nearest, with no trained classifier. The authors show finite sampling adds variance terms to the fingerprint distance that shrink as O(1/R) in the number of responses per prompt R. Across 115 checkpoint entries it **improves identification accuracy over the strongest baseline, `LLM DNA`, by 10.36%**.

papers.title: Auditable Financial Knowledge Graphs: Schema-Driven Construction and Intrinsic Quality Evaluation
papers.abstract: Financial documents combine narrative disclosures, accounting metrics, corporate structures, management commentary, and time-dependent facts, making them difficult to represent using conventional chunk-based retrieval-augmented generation systems. This paper presents an auditable, schema-driven methodology for constructing temporal financial knowledge graphs from page-delimited documents parsed using a general purpose document intelligence service. Overlapping document windows undergo phased large language model extraction of structural entities, quantitative observations, and domain-specific relationships. Candidate graph elements are validated against predefined schemas and consolidated through scope-aware exact, normalized, fuzzy, embedding-based, and LLM-assisted entity resolution. Temporal merge constraints, deterministic edge deduplication, conflict-aware property management, and fine-grained provenance preserve issuer identity, reporting-period validity, and traceability to source evidence. The contributions of this work comprise the proposed methodology for financial knowledge graph construction, the creation of an evidence-grounded temporal knowledge graph from heterogeneous financial documents, and an intrinsic framework for evaluating the quality of the resulting graph. The evaluation framework assesses seven weighted dimensions, two hard validation gates, and structural diagnostics. By separating graph-quality assessment from downstream retrieval and answer generation, the framework supports systematic diagnosis and iterative refinement of the constructed graph.
papers.summary: Financial documents mix narrative, accounting metrics, corporate structure, and time-dependent facts in ways that chunk-based retrieval-augmented generation represents poorly. The authors describe a schema-driven method for building temporal financial knowledge graphs: overlapping document windows go through phased LLM extraction of entities, quantitative observations, and relationships, which are validated against schemas and merged through exact, normalized, fuzzy, embedding-based, and LLM-assisted entity resolution with temporal constraints and fine-grained provenance. They also propose an intrinsic evaluation framework with **seven weighted quality dimensions, two hard validation gates, and structural diagnostics**, designed to assess the graph separately from downstream retrieval and answer generation. The abstract reports no quantitative results.

papers.title: Beyond Self-Critique: Epistemic Convergence Control for Multi-Agent Research Verification
papers.abstract: Multi-agent systems for scientific claim verification increasingly rely on role-structured LLM debate to pressure-test hypotheses. However, when debating agents are instantiated from the same underlying base model, they share identical latent representations, making self-critique bias structurally inevitable. Static fixed-iteration protocols compound this by either halting prematurely before evidence stabilizes or wasting inference compute after convergence. We present \sys{}, a multi-agent research verification framework that addresses both failure modes. First, we introduce an asymmetric role architecture comprising an Advocate, Skeptic, and Arbitrator with opposing epistemic directives, producing significantly lower role-embedding similarity (0.852 vs.\ 0.918 for symmetric Multi-Agent Debate [MAD], $p = 5.82 \times 10^{-8}$) and surfacing more contested claims (22.0\% vs.\ 15.4\%). Second, we propose the Belief-Delta ($\DB$) convergence criterion, an evidence-grounded stopping rule that eliminates over-iteration (0.0\% vs.\ 62.5\% for Fixed-$3$) while cutting LLM calls by 2.4$\times$. Third, each supported claim is anchored to a verbatim literature snippet audited by an independent NLI classifier, achieving a 21.7\% hallucination rate (comparable to 25.9\% for a Self-Refine critic, $p = 0.61$) while establishing auditable evidence grounding. Across 200 runs on 40 research hypotheses evaluated with DeepSeek-R1-32B, \sys{} balances compute efficiency with rigorous epistemic verification.
papers.summary: LLM debate systems for verifying scientific claims suffer from self-critique bias when all agents share one base model, and fixed-iteration protocols either stop too early or waste compute. The proposed framework uses asymmetric Advocate, Skeptic, and Arbitrator roles with opposing directives, which lowers role-embedding similarity (0.852 vs. 0.918 for symmetric multi-agent debate) and surfaces more contested claims (22.0% vs. 15.4%). Its Belief-Delta stopping rule **eliminates over-iteration (0.0% vs. 62.5% for a fixed three rounds) while cutting LLM calls by 2.4x**.
