Supported claims are anchored to verbatim literature snippets checked by a separate natural language inference classifier, giving a 21.7% hallucination rate that is statistically comparable to a `Self-Refine` critic's 25.9%, across 200 runs on 40 hypotheses with `DeepSeek-R1-32B`.

papers.title: Anchors That Move Without Collapsing: Exclusive-Region Anchor Routing for Vision Transformers
papers.abstract: Anchor tokens let a vision transformer exchange global information through a few summaries, but nothing forces different anchors to summarise different things. On one shared backbone we show that a Perceiver-style pathway and an AnchorFormer pathway collapse to a single summary, the latter despite its mass normalisation (pooling-map similarity 0.99), while other soft pathways, including Representative Attention, stay partly redundant (0.59-0.79). These results concern the routing modules inside our block, not the full published models. An exclusive partition of the patch grid cannot collapse by construction, and matched component by component it is 2.4-3.6 points more accurate than Representative Attention on CIFAR-100. We then propose focus anchors, which place most anchors at the peaks of a learned importance map while all anchors keep one exclusive Voronoi partition. Focus anchors beat a fixed partition on a cluttered canvas (+1.5 points, 95% CI [0.5, 2.6]) but not on full-HD traffic-sign recognition. There, both variants match dense attention with local windows at about a fifth of its FLOPs, and the fixed partition also trains 1.5x faster per step than dense attention with FlashAttention, though both use more memory; a ViT on a downsampled input loses half its mean average precision. Hard exclusive assignment is the only region assignment we tested that is both stable and most accurate: softmax and Sinkhorn relaxations diverge, and Gumbel-softmax trains but is less accurate. We also report the limits: a ResNet-18 is more accurate on every task we trained it on in this from-scratch regime, and anchors train faster than FlashAttention only from about 1536x1536 pixels and never use less memory.
papers.summary: Anchor tokens let a vision transformer share global information through a few summaries, but nothing forces different anchors to summarise different content; on a shared backbone, `Perceiver`-style and `AnchorFormer` routing pathways collapse to a single summary and other soft pathways stay partly redundant. An exclusive partition of the patch grid cannot collapse by construction and is 2.4-3.6 points more accurate than `Representative Attention` on `CIFAR-100`, and the proposed focus anchors place most anchors at peaks of a learned importance map while keeping an exclusive Voronoi partition. On full-HD traffic-sign recognition both variants **match dense local-window attention at about a fifth of its FLOPs**, though focus anchors only beat a fixed partition on a cluttered-canvas task. The authors also report limits: a `ResNet-18` is more accurate on every task in this from-scratch regime, and anchors never use less memory than `FlashAttention`.

papers.title: Who Grades the Agent? Privilege Separation for Coding-Agent Benchmarks
papers.abstract:
Benchmarks for AI-based coding agents are a staple of the current AI landscape, because they are the leading way to measure the performance of LLMs. Their scores guide business and research decisions. Evaluating coding agents is challenging, since they are able to manipulate their evaluation infrastructure to artificially achieve better scores. Grading an agent's solution often requires running its code, which can then manipulate the evaluation process. BenchJack, an automated benchmark auditor, recently reached near-perfect scores on nine of ten popular agent benchmarks without actually solving their tasks. Agents already do this unprompted, as OpenAI's July 2026 Hugging Face incident showed.
  Building on secure systems design, we introduce SplitBench, a privilege separation framework for evaluating coding agents and the first in the scientific literature to separate running a task's tests from judging their results. Even an agent whose code takes over the entire test environment cannot forge a pass, because a trusted grader holds the expected answers. We show that real-world benchmarks (e.g., Terminal-Bench, DeepSWE) can be ported to the SplitBench framework with minimal effort and high fidelity: 180 of 202 tasks convert, and SplitBench agrees with the native graders on 98.7% of agent attempts. We attack the converted tasks in the worst case, where adversarial agents can read all the grading code but not the expected answers. SplitBench blocked 75% of their attempts; the rest mostly reveal weaknesses in the original tasks' tests rather than flaws in SplitBench.
papers.summary: Coding-agent benchmarks usually grade a solution by running the agent's code, which lets that code tamper with the evaluation and forge a passing score. `SplitBench` applies privilege separation from secure systems design: tests run in an environment the agent may fully control, while a separate trusted grader holds the expected answers and judges the results. Porting `Terminal-Bench` and `DeepSWE` converted 180 of 202 tasks, and the new grader agreed with the native ones on **98.7% of agent attempts**. Against adversarial agents that could read all grading code but not the expected answers, 75% of attacks were blocked, with most of the rest attributed to weak tests in the original tasks.

papers.title: SLICR: Strategy Logic-Guided Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Specification-guided reinforcement learning (RL) translates formal specifications of desired behavior of agents into shaped rewards. This paper introduces SLICR, a significant paradigm shift that advances the state of the art to specification-guided RL in adversarial settings under partial observability. We employ Strategy Logic (SL), which allows explicit quantification over agents' strategies and uses the linear temporal logic (LTL) to specify the agents' objectives and constraints. This enables reasoning not only about how agents should act to satisfy a specification, but also about how they should respond to the strategies and behaviors of other agents. We evaluate SLICR on three popular benchmarks: Predator-Prey, Google Research Football, and our home-grown extension of SMAC-HARD, demonstrating its effectiveness, scalability, and ability to adapt to diverse adversarial strategies.
papers.summary: Specification-guided reinforcement learning (RL) turns formal descriptions of desired behavior into shaped rewards, but has mostly not covered adversarial, partially observable multi-agent settings. `SLICR` writes specifications in Strategy Logic, which quantifies explicitly over agents' strategies and uses linear temporal logic (LTL) for objectives and constraints, so that **rewards can encode how agents should respond to the strategies of other agents** rather than only how to act alone. The method is evaluated on `Predator-Prey`, `Google Research Football`, and an extended version of `SMAC-HARD`, where the authors report effectiveness, scalability, and adaptation to varied adversarial strategies without giving headline numbers in the abstract.

papers.title: Integrating Generative Artificial Intelligence with Learning Style Models: Opportunities, Challenges, and Future Directions
papers.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (Generative AI) has emerged as a powerful tool for transforming learning. This review examines how Generative AI can be integrated with established learning style models (VARK, Kolb, Felder-Silverman, and Honey & Mumford) to support student engagement in large online classes. Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, we searched Scopus, IEEE Xplore, and Google Scholar (2015 to 2026) and included 41 studies that met the eligibility criteria. The review maps Generative AI capabilities to learning style preferences, synthesizes existing implementations, highlights benefits and challenges, and proposes pathways for future research and practice. Despite ongoing debates regarding the empirical validity of learning styles, Generative AI enables flexible, multimodal, and real-time adaptation. This study offers practical insights for educators and developers seeking to build more effective, learner centered learning systems
papers.summary: A systematic review following PRISMA 2020 guidelines examines how generative AI can be combined with established learning style models (`VARK`, `Kolb`, `Felder-Silverman`, and `Honey & Mumford`) to support student engagement in large online classes. Searching Scopus, IEEE Xplore, and Google Scholar for 2015 to 2026 yielded **41 included studies**, which the authors use to map generative AI capabilities to learning style preferences and to summarize existing implementations, benefits, and challenges. The review acknowledges the ongoing debate over whether learning styles are empirically valid, while arguing that generative AI allows flexible, multimodal, real-time adaptation.

papers.title: Beyond Visual Fidelity: Comparing Categorical and Continuous World Models
papers.abstract: Visual world models can now generate compelling interactive worlds, but visual realism does not guarantee faithful dynamics. We systematically compare how categorical and continuous prediction shape learned dynamics under both next-token and iterative whole-frame generation. These choices are often bundled in approaches such as autoregressive token models and whole-frame flow matching. We design controlled 2D and 3D environments and evaluate dynamics validity, calibration, and visual quality. In 2D with lossless visual encoding, categorical models achieve higher rollout validity with less training compute, particularly for stochastic entities. Among categorical models, greedy decoding produces the highest rollout validity, while sampling from a next-token model yields the best-calibrated stochastic predictions. Failures in continuous models, such as disappearing game characters, echo those seen in more complex environments. Here, known dynamics let us measure their impact. In 3D, categorical models also achieve stronger long-horizon performance with less training compute. Even models with lossy tokenization remain competitive on semantic accuracy and FVD, despite lower next-frame RGB accuracy. Together, these findings make a strong case for categorical prediction as a compute-efficient route to learning world dynamics.
papers.summary: Visually convincing world models can still get the underlying dynamics wrong, and design choices such as categorical versus continuous prediction are usually bundled with next-token versus whole-frame generation. A controlled comparison in purpose-built 2D and 3D environments with known dynamics separates these choices and measures dynamics validity, calibration, and visual quality. **Categorical models reach higher rollout validity with less training compute**, especially for stochastic entities in 2D and over long horizons in 3D, while continuous models show failures such as disappearing game characters. Among categorical models, greedy decoding gives the most valid rollouts and sampling from a next-token model gives the best-calibrated stochastic predictions.

papers.title: From Gist to Verbatim: The Controllable Path of One Image Through a Diffusion Prior
papers.abstract: Modern generative models are typically studied for their ability to generalize, while memorization is treated as a failure mode. We invert this perspective and ask how a generative model can recall a single datum. We frame memorization as a control problem: a learned conditioning signal steers a frozen diffusion model toward a target image, and we follow the formation of this memory throughout training. Before converging to exact reproduction (verbatim), memory passes through a regime of abstraction: samples preserve the target's semantic content (gist) while remaining diverse in appearance, leaving predictable detail to the generative prior. This semantic organization emerges despite the absence of labels, captions, or any explicit semantic objective. In the abstraction regime, the learned memory approaches ordinary text conditioning and supports editing, one-shot recognition, and retrieval more effectively than in the near-perfect reconstruction regime. These results suggest that memorization can serve as a probe of the relevance structure encoded by a generative model: what must be stored about a datum, what can be reconstructed from prior knowledge, and how learned memories interpolate between reconstructive recall and literal data storage.
papers.summary: Memorization in generative models is usually treated as a failure, but here it is studied as a control problem: a learned conditioning signal steers a frozen diffusion model toward one target image, and the formation of that memory is tracked during training. Before reaching exact reproduction, **the memory passes through an abstraction regime in which samples keep the target's semantic content but vary in appearance**, even though no labels, captions, or semantic objective are used. In that regime the learned signal behaves much like ordinary text conditioning and supports editing, one-shot recognition, and retrieval better than it does once reconstruction is near perfect.

papers.title: LesionAgent: Training-Free Agentic Tumor Tracking and Response Assessment in Longitudinal CT
papers.abstract: Every few months, a cancer patient's CT scans decide whether treatment continues. 3D foundation models can now detect, segment, register and track lesions, yet none of them reads the scans as a radiologist does. A radiologist decides which findings are lesions, which are the same lesion months later and whether a new spot means progression, and checks each decision against the extensive rules of a clinical guideline. We introduce LesionAgent, an LLM agent that performs this read end to end without task-specific training. It operates frozen 3D models as tools, acts in 3D through coordinate-labelled views, remembers every lesion across visits in a registry, verifies every model output it relies on, and leaves every number to a deterministic guideline engine. On four public longitudinal CT datasets, LesionAgent tracks more lesions and measures them more accurately than every automatic baseline, and where the same 3D models chained by fixed rules call progression falsely at 33 of 56 follow-ups, it does so twice. On clinical follow-up CTs, it agrees with the radiologists' response at 20 of 23 follow-ups, including every change in response, and without training on DeepLesion, it retrieves more of its lesions than every tracker trained on it (89.0% vs. 87.4%). Its harness, not its LLM, makes the difference: given the same LLM and 3D models but not the harness, Claude Code reaches a detection F1 of 41% and LesionAgent 78%, and an open-weight LLM that can run inside the hospital rises from 6% to 73%. LesionAgent and a napari reading app for any LLM are available at https://github.com/MIC-DKFZ/LesionAgent.
papers.summary: Assessing cancer treatment response from repeated CT scans requires deciding which findings are lesions, matching them across visits, and applying a clinical guideline, which existing 3D foundation models do not do end to end. `LesionAgent` is an LLM agent that needs no task-specific training: it calls frozen 3D models as tools, views the volume through coordinate-labelled slices, keeps a registry of lesions across visits, verifies model outputs, and hands all numeric calculations to a deterministic guideline engine. On four public longitudinal CT datasets it falsely called progression at 2 of 56 follow-ups versus 33 for the same models chained by fixed rules, and it matched radiologists' response at 20 of 23 clinical follow-ups. The authors attribute the gains to the harness rather than the LLM: with the same LLM and 3D models, `Claude Code` reaches a detection F1 of 41% against 78% for `LesionAgent`, and **an open-weight LLM that can run inside a hospital rises from 6% to 73%**.

papers.title: Renormalized Entropy from Symmetries: Simplicity Bias and Neural Heat Death
papers.abstract: Neural networks have parameter symmetries: parameter transformations that do not affect the represented function. How do these symmetries affect the functions that neural networks ultimately learn? We study the implicit bias arising from these symmetries by calculating the equilibrium distribution over represented functions under Langevin dynamics with Gaussian regularization. To isolate the effect of symmetries on this distribution, we study the limit in which the strength of the regularization is taken to zero. In certain cases, we show that the zero-regularization and infinite-time limits commute. In the low temperature limit, we recover known effective regularizations. At positive temperature, a renormalization procedure allows us to derive a novel entropy which predicts symmetry-induced preference for certain functions. For linear networks, we obtain explicit entropy terms that favor singular and low-rank functions. For networks with homogeneous activations, we find entropy terms that favor inactive neurons, which can lead to neural "heat death" in which equilibrium mass concentrates on networks with vanishing output. We interpret these results through the neural tangent kernel, as a simplicity bias selecting for functions that vary slowly under variations in the parameters.
papers.summary: Parameter symmetries, meaning transformations of a network's weights that leave its function unchanged, are analyzed for the implicit bias they create over learned functions. The authors compute the equilibrium distribution over functions under Langevin dynamics with Gaussian regularization, take the regularization strength to zero, and use a renormalization procedure to derive an entropy term at positive temperature. For linear networks this entropy favors singular and low-rank functions, and for networks with homogeneous activations **it favors inactive neurons, which can produce a neural heat death where equilibrium mass concentrates on networks with vanishing output**. Through the neural tangent kernel, the results are interpreted as a simplicity bias toward functions that change slowly as parameters vary.

papers.title: Speculative Decoding Is Less Speculative Than You Think
papers.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates language-model inference by preparing candidate continuations before the target model generates them. Its efficiency depends on how well limited drafting computation anticipates the path the target will actually follow. Anticipating this path involves two sources of uncertainty: the target model's predictions and the randomness of sampling. Yet the former requires a target-model forward pass, while the latter can be fixed before drafting. Building on this observation, we introduce DICE (Draw-Informed Candidate Selection), which pre-samples and synchronizes verification randomness across drafting and verification. By combining these known draws with predictions from an existing drafter, DICE allocates computation toward continuations more likely to be used in the current sampling run. This principle guides node selection throughout draft-tree construction and extends to asynchronous prefetching, where DICE predicts which next-round drafts to prepare. Without additional drafter training or changes to the target sampling distribution, DICE achieves state-of-the-art decoding throughput across diverse settings, with speedups of up to 24.6pp over strong baselines.
papers.summary: Speculative decoding speeds up language-model inference by drafting candidate continuations ahead of the target model, and its efficiency depends on how well the draft anticipates the path the target will take. The authors observe that part of the uncertainty is sampling randomness, which can be fixed before drafting, and introduce `DICE` (Draw-Informed Candidate Selection), which pre-samples the random draws and shares them between drafting and verification. Combining those known draws with an existing drafter's predictions guides which nodes to add to the draft tree and which next-round drafts to prefetch asynchronously. Without retraining the drafter or changing the target's sampling distribution, the method reports **speedups of up to 24.6 percentage points over strong baselines**.

papers.title: FairITR: Fairness-Aware Learning of Multicategory Individualized Treatment Rules
papers.abstract: Individualized treatment rules (ITRs) recommend treatment decisions based on individual characteristics and can improve treatment outcomes beyond traditional one-size-fits-all strategies. However, similar to other commonly used algorithmic decision-making methods, ITRs without considering model fairness may result in unfair decisions across groups defined by sensitive attributes, such as race or gender. Although extensive methods have been developed for ITR estimation, most focus solely on optimizing treatment outcomes, while research on fairness-aware ITRs remains limited. Moreover, the practical scenario of multicategory treatments is rarely considered in existing fair ITR studies. To address these gaps, we introduce a fairness notion for multicategory ITRs that requires treatment decisions to be independent of sensitive attributes, and then formulate the corresponding problem of estimating fair ITRs. To solve this problem, we further propose FairITR, a fairness-aware learning framework that jointly optimizes treatment outcomes and fairness. FairITR builds on angle-based classification for multicategory ITR learning and integrates adversarial learning with covariance-based regularization to mitigate unfairness in treatment decisions. A theoretical justification for the fairness properties induced by the adversarial debiasing mechanism is also provided. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets show that FairITR substantially reduces unfairness in ITRs while maintaining competitive treatment values relative to existing baselines.
papers.summary: Individualized treatment rules (ITRs) recommend treatments from patient characteristics, but rules optimized only for outcomes can produce decisions that differ unfairly across groups defined by sensitive attributes such as race or gender, and the case of more than two treatment options is rarely studied. The authors define a fairness notion for multicategory ITRs that requires treatment decisions to be independent of sensitive attributes. Their framework `FairITR` builds on angle-based classification and combines adversarial learning with covariance-based regularization, with a theoretical justification for the adversarial debiasing step. On real-world datasets it is reported to **substantially reduce unfairness while keeping treatment value competitive with existing baselines**.

papers.title: TEA-Bench-BR: Can Coding Agents Turn a Branching Clinical Specification into Correct Code?
papers.abstract: Coding agents increasingly implement rules written by domain experts, and bugs in such code are silent: it runs and returns a plausible answer. We introduce TEA-Bench-BR, a benchmark built on the Brazilian pathway for early autism (TEA) screening: three fictitious instruments with the structure of real ones, a multi-professional referral flow, and export to FHIR R4 with the national RNDS profiles, all specified in Portuguese. A generator samples each task's parameters (144 tasks, 6,798 hidden cases), and the hidden cases kill all 1,955 non-equivalent mutants of the reference. With Gemma 4 as the agent, the 12B solves 38.0% of single-instrument tasks and none at the FHIR level; the 31B solves 77.8%, 85.2% and 78.7% at levels 1 to 3 and passes over 99% of the hidden cases, its remaining failures mostly in input validation rather than clinical decisions. With the same tasks in English, the 31B solves 57.4% at level 3, as its code validates an identifier less often; the 12B's, more often. The 12B misses 10.10% of the cases that call for referral; the 31B, 0.02%. A contamination probe on a modified PHQ-9 finds no error that follows the original rules.
papers.summary: Code that implements rules written by domain experts can fail silently, running and returning a plausible but wrong answer. `TEA-Bench-BR` tests coding agents on the Brazilian pathway for early autism (TEA) screening, specified in Portuguese: three fictitious screening instruments, a multi-professional referral flow, and export to FHIR R4, with 144 generated tasks and 6,798 hidden test cases that kill all 1,955 non-equivalent mutants of the reference. With `Gemma 4` as the agent, the 12B model solves 38.0% of single-instrument tasks and none at the FHIR level, while **the 31B model solves 77.8%, 85.2%, and 78.7% at levels 1 to 3**, failing mostly on input validation rather than clinical decisions. With the same tasks in English the 31B model drops to 57.4% at level 3, and the 12B model misses 10.10% of cases that call for referral against 0.02% for the 31B.

papers.title: The Dual-Tier Sentiment Framework: Scalable Multimodal UX Attribution in Web Search
papers.abstract: Sustaining user experience (UX) quality in large-scale web search requires scalable evaluation. Traditional surveys are slow and bottleneck rapid A/B testing, while automated metrics often lack the granularity to diagnose visual-spatial UX anomalies. To address this, we introduce the Dual-Tier Sentiment Framework, a novel industrial architecture for automated UX attribution. Tier 1 (Macro System) acts as a scalable user sentiment regression detector, utilizing a fine-tuned encoder-decoder LLM (based on Gemini XS) on telemetry features. Through multi-task regularization and contextual feature engineering, this tier achieves a +9.8% PR-AUC gain on over 500,000 held-out records, matching baseline recall on all validated regressions with $\sim$20% relative precision gain among the 12 held-out experiments. In production, it reduces measurement latency from weeks to hours and cuts survey overhead by over 40%. Tier 2 (Micro System) provides granular diagnostics by employing a Multimodal LLM (Gemini 3.0 Pro) to natively assess visual renderings and spatial layout of web result blocks, quantifying "User Toil" as the estimated effort required to reach a satisfactory result. Enhanced by RL-based automated prompt optimization and an AI judge for win/loss patterns, the MLLM yields a $>$6.5% F1 score improvement, offering deep insights into content quality and layout friction. Ultimately, this framework enables scalable, accurate, and diagnostic UX attribution, processing O(100k) live experiment queries daily.
papers.summary: Evaluating user experience (UX) in large-scale web search with surveys is slow, and automated metrics often cannot diagnose visual or layout problems. The described industrial system has two tiers: a fine-tuned encoder-decoder LLM based on `Gemini XS` that detects user sentiment regressions from telemetry, and a multimodal LLM, `Gemini 3.0 Pro`, that inspects rendered result blocks and estimates the effort a user needs to reach a satisfactory result. The first tier gains 9.8% in PR-AUC on more than 500,000 held-out records and, in production, **cuts measurement latency from weeks to hours and survey overhead by over 40%**. The second tier, with reinforcement-learning-based prompt optimization and an AI judge, improves F1 by more than 6.5%.

papers.title: Communication-Efficient Federated Learning of Latent Patient Representations from Multi-Institutional EHRs
papers.abstract: Electronic health records (EHRs) contain rich health information for uncovering latent patient representations and clinically meaningful subgroups. Learning from EHR data across institutions is valuable because representations learned at a single site may reflect local data patterns and lack generalizability, yet pooling patient-level records across institutions is often impractical because of privacy constraints and communication costs. We propose a communication-efficient, non-iterative federated spectral method for learning shared latent representation components from multi-institutional EHRs, in which each institution shares aggregate marginal frequencies and a low-rank spectral summary while keeping patient-level records local. A central server aggregates these summaries with the pooled marginal frequencies to recover both the shared low-rank structure and the canonical row-normalization direction required for interpretable representation recovery. We prove row-wise recovery guarantees and error bounds, with a leading federated variance term matching a corresponding lower bound under explicit regularity conditions. Simulations show that our method closely matches pooled analysis in estimating latent representation components, improves as more sites contribute summaries, and outperforms single-site and existing federated benchmarks across a range of data settings. Applied to real-world multi-facility EHR data for stroke patients, the method learns interpretable patient representations that highlight clinically distinct subgroups and could help inform subgroup-specific care.
papers.summary: Learning patient representations from electronic health records (EHRs) across institutions improves generalizability, but pooling patient-level records is often blocked by privacy constraints and communication costs. The proposed federated spectral method is non-iterative: each institution shares only aggregate marginal frequencies and a low-rank spectral summary, and a central server combines them to recover the shared low-rank structure and the normalization needed for interpretable representations. The authors prove row-wise recovery guarantees with a leading variance term matching a lower bound under stated regularity conditions, and simulations show the method **closely matches pooled analysis** while beating single-site and existing federated baselines. Applied to multi-facility EHR data for stroke patients, it yields representations that separate clinically distinct subgroups.

papers.title: Decision Columns as an Index: Interpretable Embeddings for Explainable Entity Matching and Search
papers.abstract:
Business data systems must determine whether records refer to the same entity and retrieve records satisfying requests whose decisive properties are implicit. As agents act on these records, both tasks require auditable reasons. Dense embeddings perform well but offer opaque coordinates, cannot be filtered by meaning, and require corpus re-encoding to add new properties. We propose interpretable embeddings built from decision columns: each column stores a decision model's calibrated answer to a natural-language question, with outcomes yes, no, or not stated. A record's embedding is its answers across an ordered set of questions. Similarity decomposes exactly into per-question contributions, and new questions add coordinates without altering existing ones.
  On public product benchmarks, question-space retrieval matches dense candidate generation statistically in a retrieve-then-verify entity matcher, while providing exact explanations for accepted matches. Questions derived from retrieval failures triple mean reciprocal rank without re-encoding prior answers. For search, inferring the attributes of a suitable result outperforms encoding only the literal request, and combining question-space and dense scores improves retrieval, though not at our prespecified confidence threshold. A single small neural network predicts the full interpretable vector from an existing dense embedding, enabling corpus backfilling from a few thousand labeled rows at roughly 1/200 the cost. We position interpretable embeddings as a complementary, readable retrieval channel for explaining matches, filtering on attributes, and extending indexes as failures expose missing facts.
papers.summary: Dense embeddings work well for entity matching and search over business records but cannot explain a match, be filtered by meaning, or gain new properties without re-encoding the corpus. The proposed interpretable embeddings are built from decision columns, each holding a model's calibrated yes, no, or not-stated answer to a natural-language question, so similarity decomposes exactly into per-question contributions and new questions add coordinates without changing old ones. On public product benchmarks this question-space retrieval statistically matches dense candidate generation in a retrieve-then-verify matcher, and **adding questions derived from retrieval failures triples mean reciprocal rank** without re-encoding earlier answers. A small neural network can also predict the full interpretable vector from an existing dense embedding, allowing a corpus to be backfilled from a few thousand labeled rows at roughly 1/200 of the cost.

papers.title: Functional Depth Is Learned: Isolating the Computation That Layers Produce Only Together
papers.abstract: Transformer performance scales with depth, but layer count merely counts the opportunities for sequential computation: layers could still behave as nearly independent refinements that barely depend on one another. We study how transformers develop functional depth during pretraining, introducing an exact inclusion-exclusion decomposition that isolates the connected component, i.e., the computation that appears only when a specified set of layers acts together under identity ablation. Tracking this quantity across public checkpoints of Pythia, OLMo, and Amber yields three findings. First, write-relative connected coordination strengthens from its initialization or earliest-checkpoint baseline as pretraining proceeds, across all measured interaction orders. Second, these connected components are behaviorally consequential under direct intervention: deleting them damages perplexity more than deleting a norm-matched random direction at the same site in all 35 measured model-order cells. Third, pairwise representation similarity is consistently negatively correlated with pairwise connected coordination across seven models, yet the two signals are not interchangeable: similarity- and coordination-based block-removal criteria often agree in Pythia but diverge on Amber. Together, these results suggest that architectural depth provides the opportunity for sequential computation, while pretraining progressively organizes cross-layer dependencies within that depth.
papers.summary: Layer count measures only the opportunity for sequential computation in a transformer, since layers could act as nearly independent refinements. An exact inclusion-exclusion decomposition is introduced to isolate the connected component, the computation that appears only when a given set of layers acts together under identity ablation, and it is tracked across public pretraining checkpoints of `Pythia`, `OLMo`, and `Amber`. This cross-layer coordination strengthens as pretraining proceeds at every measured interaction order, and **deleting the connected components hurts perplexity more than deleting a norm-matched random direction in all 35 measured model-order cells**. Pairwise representation similarity is negatively correlated with coordination across seven models, yet the two signals give diverging block-removal choices on `Amber`.

papers.title: Star Panoptic Quality: Selectively Evaluating Split and Merged Instances
papers.abstract: Detecting individual instances is crucial for many segmentation problems. However, expert instance annotations are often unavailable, so instances are approximated heuristically (e.g., as connected components of semantic maps), which can merge touching objects or split fragmented ones. Even when expert annotations exist, expert disagreement or structural delineation biases can yield split or merged reference instances, corresponding to over- or under-segmentation, respectively. Panoptic Quality (PQ) and related metrics capture both segmentation and detection quality while weighting all instances equally, regardless of size. Yet when the references are biased, these metrics can neither detect split or merged instances nor distinguish valid from invalid overor under-segmentation. We present Star Panoptic Quality (StarPQ), a novel evaluation ramework, which closes this gap in two steps: First, we construct a so-called star forest in the bipartite graph whose clean, merge, and split stars isolate different failure modes. Second, we calculate the final metric by individually weighting each failure mode, allowing practitioners to account for instance delineation biases. Across various experiments, we demonstrate that StarPQ not only enables targeted penalization or eniency towards specific failure modes, but also serves as a diagnostic tool to reveal their prevalence.
papers.summary: Instance segmentation metrics such as Panoptic Quality (PQ) assume trustworthy reference instances, but references built heuristically or by disagreeing experts often merge touching objects or split fragmented ones. `StarPQ` builds a star forest in the bipartite graph between predicted and reference instances, whose clean, merge, and split stars isolate distinct failure modes, and then computes the final score by weighting each mode separately. Experiments show that this **lets practitioners selectively penalize or tolerate split and merged instances** and also serves as a diagnostic of how common each failure mode is.

papers.title: StereoVLM: Binocular Vision-Language Models for Metric 3D Spatial Reasoning
papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) exhibit strong semantic understanding but remain limited in their ability to reason about metric 3D space in the physical world. Existing VLMs typically infer 3D scene structure from one or more images without known camera calibration or cross-view geometric constraints. This makes metric 3D inference inherently ambiguous and leaves it unclear whether their spatial predictions are grounded in visual evidence or driven primarily by semantic priors. In contrast, calibrated stereo provides explicit cross-view geometry that resolves this ambiguity and offers a more reliable foundation for metric 3D perception and geometric generalization. We investigate how VLMs can learn transferable 3D representations directly from calibrated binocular observations. To this end, we introduce StereoVLM, the first geometry-aware binocular VLM for metric 3D spatial reasoning. StereoVLM follows a hierarchical learning paradigm spanning from cross-view correspondence and disparity estimation to calibration-conditioned metric depth perception and semantic spatial reasoning. We further find that disparity supervision generalizes substantially better than direct binocular depth supervision on unseen environments. To evaluate these capabilities, we introduce Stereo3D-Bench, a comprehensive benchmark across three levels, from point-level geometry to object-level spatial reasoning. StereoVLM-8B achieves 95.17% depth accuracy ($\delta_1$) and a 66.98 average object-level score on Stereo3D-Bench. Intervention results further indicate that the model's performance on Stereo3D-Bench benefits from valid cross-view geometry and cannot be explained solely by additional visual tokens or semantic priors. Hierarchical geometric supervision also yields average gains of 3.54 points across five spatial benchmarks and 4.3 percentage points in RoboCasa manipulation success.
papers.summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) struggle with metric 3D reasoning because they infer scene structure from images without camera calibration or cross-view geometric constraints, leaving distances ambiguous. `StereoVLM` takes calibrated binocular input and is trained hierarchically, from cross-view correspondence and disparity estimation to calibration-conditioned metric depth and semantic spatial reasoning, with disparity supervision found to generalize better to unseen environments than direct depth supervision. On the new `Stereo3D-Bench`, the 8B model reaches **95.17% depth accuracy** on the delta-1 metric and a 66.98 average object-level score, and intervention tests indicate the gains depend on valid cross-view geometry rather than extra visual tokens or semantic priors. The same supervision adds an average of 3.54 points across five spatial benchmarks and 4.3 percentage points of manipulation success in `RoboCasa`.
papers.highlight_summary:
Vision-language models usually infer metric 3D structure from uncalibrated images, so it is unclear whether their spatial answers come from visual geometry or from semantic priors. `StereoVLM` instead feeds a calibrated stereo pair to a VLM and trains it on a hierarchy of tasks running from pixel correspondence and disparity up to metric depth and language-grounded 3D object reasoning.

- Built on `Qwen3-VL-Instruct` at 2B and 8B scale, the model is fully fine-tuned with interleaved (not staged) instructions in which stereo tasks make up 25% of the mix, and the focal length and stereo baseline are written into the prompt for metric questions.
- In a geometry-only 2B ablation, supervising disparity and converting it to depth generalises far better to unseen scenes than supervising depth directly, with out-of-domain δ1 of **74.92%** versus 45.89% for direct binocular depth, which falls below even the monocular baseline at 51.00%.
- On the new `Stereo3D-Bench` (eight tasks, 94,546 question–answer instances), `StereoVLM-8B` reaches **95.17%** depth δ1 and a **66.98** object-level average, against 75.96% and 47.61 for `GPT-6 Astra`, the strongest general-purpose baseline.
- Right-view interventions on the 2B model show that the gains depend on a correctly paired second view, since depth δ1 drops from 94.51% to 80.82% with the left image alone and to 7.40% when the left image is duplicated as the right.
- Compared with a matched 2B model trained without stereo instructions, the average over five spatial benchmarks rises by **3.54 points** and `RoboCasa` manipulation success goes from 38.1% to **42.4%**, though the authors note the study is limited to controlled benchmarks and simulated kitchen tasks and requires calibrated, synchronised cameras.

papers.title: SUAF: Spectral Universal Advantage Features for Zero-Shot Policy Improvement
papers.abstract: Reward-independent representations enable reinforcement learning agents to reuse knowledge across tasks, but limited representation capacity raises three fundamental questions: what statistical dependence should these representations capture, which components of that dependence should be retained for policy improvement, and how does discarding the remaining components affect decision-making? We address these questions through canonical dependence analysis. For a reference policy, we construct an action-centered, positive-lag canonical dependence matrix (CDM) that isolates the additional predictive contribution of the current action beyond the current state. Its singular value decomposition yields Spectral Universal Advantage Features (SUAF), paired features that recover delayed advantage through linear reward projections. We show that the spectrum quantifies mutual information between current action and future state-action visitation conditioned on current state and determines reward specific approximation errors. Retaining the leading modes gives optimal rank-constrained approximations under both isotropic average-case and reward-uniform minimax criteria. Separating the immediate reward contrast also avoids the spectral floor arising from direct compression of the full advantage operator. To learn SUAF from reward-free data, we develop an action-centered Soft-HGR objective with bidirectional temporal-difference estimation. We further connect spectral approximation errors to sufficient conditions for policy improvement. Finite-state experiments validate the spectral predictions and feature-learning method, while zero-shot evaluations on discrete tasks and continuous-control benchmarks demonstrate the utility of the learned representations across rewards.
papers.summary: Reward-independent representations let reinforcement learning agents reuse knowledge across tasks, but with limited capacity it is unclear which statistical dependence they should capture and what is lost by truncation. The authors build an action-centered canonical dependence matrix (CDM) for a reference policy that isolates what the current action predicts about the future beyond the current state, and take its singular value decomposition to obtain `SUAF` features that recover delayed advantage through linear reward projections. They show that the spectrum quantifies the relevant conditional mutual information and that **keeping the leading modes is the optimal rank-constrained approximation under both average-case and minimax criteria**, and they link the approximation error to sufficient conditions for policy improvement. A reward-free learning objective based on `Soft-HGR` with bidirectional temporal-difference estimation is validated in finite-state experiments and in zero-shot evaluations on discrete and continuous-control tasks.

papers.title: BioEmu2: Scalable Emulation of Biomolecular Dynamics
papers.abstract: Despite major advances in structure prediction, modelling the motions and interactions that drive biomolecular function at scale remains a central challenge. We introduce BioEmu2, a generative model for atomically resolved biomolecular structures combining static structure prediction, equilibrium sampling and time evolution, that samples orders of magnitude faster than molecular dynamics (MD). Trained on experimental and synthetic structures and extensive MD data, it supports multi-component systems containing proteins, nucleic acids, modified residues, ligands and ions. Structure-prediction accuracy is comparable to top open-weight biomolecular folding models, and a context parallel mode enables prediction of megadalton complexes. Equilibrium distributions approximate MD references with free-energy errors near 1 kcal/mol across tested proteins and complexes. Time propagation predicts long-timescale dynamical trajectories and kinetics of binding and conformational changes. Generated structures can be controlled by conditioning on residue contacts or steering with user-defined bias potentials. Enhanced sampling enables free energy calculation involving rare states. BioEmu2 makes the study of biomolecular ensembles and dynamics scalable.
papers.summary: Structure prediction has advanced, but modelling the motions and interactions behind biomolecular function at scale is still out of reach for molecular dynamics (MD) simulation. `BioEmu2` is a generative model of atomically resolved structures that combines static structure prediction, equilibrium sampling, and time evolution, and covers multi-component systems with proteins, nucleic acids, modified residues, ligands, and ions. It samples orders of magnitude faster than MD, with **equilibrium distributions matching MD references to free-energy errors near 1 kcal/mol** across tested proteins and complexes and structure accuracy comparable to top open-weight folding models. It also predicts long-timescale trajectories and binding kinetics, and its outputs can be steered by residue-contact conditioning or user-defined bias potentials.
papers.highlight_summary:
Structure predictors give a single static answer while molecular dynamics (MD) is too slow to sample function-relevant motions at scale; `BioEmu2` is one all-atom diffusion model that does static structure prediction, equilibrium ensemble sampling and long-timescale time propagation for complexes of proteins, nucleic acids, ligands and ions, sampling orders of magnitude faster than MD.

- A `PairMixer` sequence trunk (4 MSA layers, 48 pair layers) feeds a 16-block dual-stream atom/token diffusion module, with a mode flag switching between structure prediction and equilibrium sampling, optional residue-contact conditioning, and an optional starting structure plus time lag τ that turns sampling into an MD-like propagation step.
- Structure-prediction accuracy on `FoldBench` and `Runs N' Poses` is reported as comparable to open-weight baselines such as `Boltz-1`, `Protenix` and `OpenFold3` (not better, and `AlphaFold3` and `Boltz-2` were excluded), while context parallelism over 16 GPUs scales inference to about **16,000 residues** and a single supplied contact cut RMSD on the 4,020-residue complex 8WY8 from **71.2 Å to 5.0 Å**.
- In equilibrium mode the model reproduces MD free-energy surfaces with errors of **0.7–1.2 kcal/mol**, but covers only around **50%** of MD-visited states for single proteins and protein complexes (over 100% for protein–ligand systems), and the single-protein-only `BioEmu1` remains better on single proteins.
- Time propagation yields trajectories in which **78%** of 500 PUMA–MCL-1 runs (391) reach the bound state within 6.53 ms and about **40%** of 50 adenylate kinase runs close within 50 μs only when ligands are present, while physicality steering cuts the unphysical-sample fraction for DNA monomers from **70.0% to 1.4%**.
- The authors state that slow kinetics are not established as quantitatively accurate, with dynamics sometimes relaxing faster than MD, energy barriers slightly too low, and branched components absent from the training data.

papers.title: The Optimal Sample Complexity of Agnostic PAC Learning for Partial Concept Classes
papers.abstract: Let $\mathcal H\subseteq\{-1,+1,\star\}^{\mathcal X}$ be a partial concept class of finite VC dimension $d$. We construct a deterministic agnostic PAC learner that, for every $\varepsilon,\delta\in(0,1)$, uses $O((d+\log(1/\delta))/\varepsilon^2)$ i.i.d. examples from an arbitrary distribution $\mathcal D$ over $\mathcal X\times\{-1,+1\}$ and returns a total concept $\hat h:\mathcal X\to\{-1,+1\}$ satisfying $\text{er}_{\mathcal D}(\hat h)\leq \min_{h\in\mathcal H}\text{er}_{\mathcal D}(h)+\varepsilon$ with probability at least $1-\delta$, where $\text{er}_{\mathcal D}(h)=\mathbb P_{(x,y)\sim\mathcal D}[h(x)\neq y]$. This establishes the optimal sample complexity, matching the lower bound of Alon et al. (FOCS 2021).
papers.summary: Partial concept classes allow hypotheses to be undefined on some inputs, and the exact number of samples needed to learn them in the agnostic PAC setting had not been settled. The authors construct a deterministic learner that, for a partial class of VC dimension d, uses **O((d + log(1/delta)) / epsilon^2) examples** to return a total concept whose error is within epsilon of the best hypothesis in the class with probability at least 1 - delta. This matches the lower bound of Alon et al. from FOCS 2021 and so establishes the optimal sample complexity.

papers.title: Topology Hub Optimal Transport: Eliminating Long Context Dilution at Flash Speed
papers.abstract: Long-context models use sparse or structured attention to avoid quadratic cost, yet retrieving a small set of relevant facts embedded among hundreds of thousands of distractors degrades as normalization mass disperses with length. Hub-and-spoke optimal transport (OT) replaces the dense $L \times L$ matrix with a linear-size graph over local windows and $K$ shared hubs balanced by Sinkhorn scaling. Building on block-wise tail refinement and fixed-support transport topology (arXiv:2605.08123, arXiv:2609.07954), we introduce Topology Hub Optimal Transport (THOT): (1) bounded-support capacity gating via simplex sparsemax ($O(L\log L)$) or sorting-free token-local thresholded ReLU ($O(L)$), driving excess distractor mass to zero; (2) a three-sweep $1+2$ annealed row-closed Sinkhorn schedule that damps bipartite residuals; (3) an exact rank-$(D+2R+1)$ One-Reference-Tile adjoint in batched split-factor Triton kernels (BF16 Tensor Cores, FP32 potentials); and (4) a chunked exclusive-prefix causal variant with verified zero future leakage. On NVIDIA L4, sparsemax THOT trained at $L=128$ reaches 97.40% zero-shot recall of fixed bindings at $L=262{,}144$ under pure task loss ($\alpha=0$) and 98.83% at $\alpha=0.05$ (matched by $O(L)$ thresholded ReLU at $\alpha=0.05$, vs. 80.60% at $\alpha=0$), while softmax-gated hub OT drops to 3.52%. In bidirectional operator microbenchmarks, our kernel runs forward+VJP in 100.1 ms at $H=8, D=64, L=262\mathrm{K}$ (2.2x faster with 4.0x smaller compiler temporaries than latent softmax) and 1.34 ms vs. 4.37 ms for cuDNN FlashAttention at $L=4{,}096$; multi-layer LM runs use the unfused path. Zero-shot WikiText-103 multi-needle retrieval hits 100.00% (128/128 queries at $L=65\mathrm{K}$) vs. 0.78% for short-trained RoPE FlashAttention, and compact 4-layer WikiText-4K runs show modest causal and masked LM gains.
papers.summary: Sparse or structured attention for very long contexts tends to lose a few relevant facts among hundreds of thousands of distractors because normalization mass spreads out with length. `THOT` replaces dense attention with a linear-size hub-and-spoke optimal transport (OT) graph over local windows and shared hubs, adding bounded-support gating through sparsemax or a thresholded ReLU, an annealed three-sweep Sinkhorn schedule, custom `Triton` kernels, and a causal variant with no future leakage. Trained at length 128 and run on an NVIDIA L4, the sparsemax version reaches **97.40% zero-shot recall of fixed bindings at a length of 262,144**, where softmax-gated hub OT falls to 3.52%. Operator microbenchmarks show the kernel running faster than a `FlashAttention` baseline at length 4,096, while language-modeling gains on compact 4-layer `WikiText` runs are described as modest.

papers.title: Ranking-Preserving Coreset Selection for Efficient Evolutionary Hyperparameter Optimization
papers.abstract: Hyperparameter optimization (HPO) is essential for high predictive performance, but its computational cost becomes prohibitive when candidate configurations require repeated training on large datasets. This paper proposes a ranking-preserving coreset (RPC) selection framework for accelerating evolutionary HPO. The method constructs a compact coreset that preserves the relative ranking of hyperparameter configurations observed on the full training data. Coreset selection is formulated as an evolutionary optimization problem that maximizes Spearman rank correlation between full-data and subset-based configuration rankings while penalizing subset size. The selected coreset is then used for HPO with three evolutionary algorithms: Genetic Algorithm (GA), Cross-generational elitist Selection, Heterogeneous Recombination and Cataclysmic Mutation (CHC), and Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO). Experiments on seven tabular, two text, and two image benchmark datasets show that RPC substantially reduces HPO time while maintaining test accuracy comparable to full-dataset HPO across decision tree, text classification, and image classification tasks. Across datasets and optimizers, HPO-stage speedups range from approximately 1.14x to 8.80x, while the one-time coreset construction cost is accounted for separately through end-to-end runtime and break-even analysis. On 20 held-out configurations excluded from coreset construction, RPC achieves higher ranking correlation than same-size random sampling on 8 of 11 datasets (dataset-level Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p = 0.014). These results show that ranking preservation extends beyond the configurations used during selection. The one-time construction cost can be amortized when the coreset is reused across HPO runs.
papers.summary: Hyperparameter optimization (HPO) becomes prohibitively expensive when every candidate configuration must be trained on a large dataset. The proposed ranking-preserving coreset (`RPC`) framework uses an evolutionary search to pick a small training subset that maximizes the Spearman rank correlation between full-data and subset-based rankings of configurations while penalizing subset size, and then runs HPO on that subset with `GA`, `CHC`, and `PSO` optimizers. Across seven tabular, two text, and two image datasets, the HPO stage runs **roughly 1.14x to 8.80x faster** with test accuracy comparable to full-dataset HPO, with the one-time coreset construction cost reported separately through break-even analysis. On 20 held-out configurations, `RPC` preserves rankings better than same-size random sampling on 8 of 11 datasets.

papers.title: Model Carving: Training Transformers That Optimize Their Own Topology
papers.abstract: Machine learning has largely kept separate the choice of architecture and the process of training. A classic Transformer, for instance, trains a fixed set of attention and MLP sublayers at every layer, in the same order, and optimizes the weights within. This uniformity is a convention rather than a principled design choice, and it is likely suboptimal: the best architecture for a given task may be smaller, more efficient, and far from uniform. We believe that, ideally, training itself should shape the model's topology. To this end, we introduce Model Carving, which learns both a Transformer's weights and its architecture in a single run. By applying learnable, scalar gates to each sublayer, we allow the training loss to remove the model's own components during training -- freeing a smaller heterogeneous network inside. We evaluate Model Carving by pre-training standard Transformers from 140M to 2.7B parameters and looped Transformers from 140M to 1.3B. At equal training compute, carved models reach a lower validation loss than dense models trained with up to 1.7 times more compute. Furthermore, carved models also outperform size-matched models produced by pruning or distillation, suggesting that the best way to obtain small models for edge devices is to carve them during training, not to compress a large one afterwards. This advantage both grows with scale and carries over to downstream tasks such as few-shot evaluation and generation. Because the removed sublayers no longer run, carved models also cost up to 34% fewer FLOPs per token and decode up to 1.6 times faster without cost in quality. Our results show that architecture, like weights, should be learned and not fixed in advance, and that inside every large transformer is a smaller, faster, stronger one waiting to be carved out.
papers.summary: Transformer architectures are normally fixed before training, with the same attention and MLP sublayers repeated at every layer. `Model Carving` attaches a learnable scalar gate to each sublayer so the training loss can remove components during a single run, leaving a smaller, non-uniform network. In pre-training runs on standard Transformers from 140M to 2.7B parameters and looped Transformers up to 1.3B, carved models at equal compute reach **lower validation loss than dense models trained with up to 1.7 times more compute**, and they outperform size-matched models obtained by pruning or distillation. Because removed sublayers no longer run, carved models also use up to 34% fewer FLOPs per token and decode up to 1.6 times faster, with the advantage reported to grow with scale and carry over to downstream tasks.

papers.title: Non-penetrating World Models
papers.abstract: We study a new problem of preventing object penetration in interactive video world models. To understand how existing models handle this, we introduce NoPeBench, a benchmark that evaluates how world models respond to physical obstacles. Our evaluation reveals that none of the open-source models can reliably prevent such failures. Surprisingly, however, these models already encode the information needed to predict such violations. We find that the hidden states of diffusion transformers (DiTs) can predict whether a candidate action will penetrate an obstacle. Building on this, we introduce NoPeWorld, a lightweight framework that detects and prevents penetration. Specifically, we train a small prediction head on top of a frozen DiT's hidden states to read out if a candidate action is safe or not. Unsafe actions are then replaced with safe ones that best preserve the original intent. Despite its simplicity, NoPeWorld substantially reduces the physical violation rate, averaged over six video world models, from 74% to 16%. Remarkably, our method shows zero-shot generalization to open-domain imagery, third-person viewpoints, and moving obstacles. We publicly release our code, the NoPeBench benchmark, and model weights. Project Page: https://nopeworld.github.io .
papers.summary: Interactive video world models often let the camera or agent pass straight through solid obstacles, and a new benchmark, `NoPeBench`, shows that no open-source model tested reliably avoids this. The authors find that hidden states of diffusion transformers (DiTs) already encode whether a candidate action will penetrate an obstacle, so their `NoPeWorld` framework trains a small prediction head on a frozen DiT to flag unsafe actions and swaps them for safe ones that best preserve the original intent. Averaged over six video world models, this cuts the physical violation rate **from 74% to 16%**, and the method is reported to generalize zero-shot to open-domain imagery, third-person viewpoints, and moving obstacles. Code, benchmark, and weights are released.
papers.highlight_summary:
Interactive video world models follow user commands straight through solid obstacles, yet the hidden states of their frozen diffusion transformers already predict whether a commanded action will penetrate one. `NoPeWorld` reads that signal with a small head and swaps unsafe actions for the safe stop or wall slide closest to the user's intent, and `NoPeBench` is introduced to measure the problem.

- A cross-attention head of **under 2M parameters** on mid-to-deep DiT blocks scores 34 candidate motions for safety, clearance and intent, trained on 729 Unreal Engine videos from 44 `UnrealZoo` scenes, and runs either on the first denoising pass of the current chunk (collision mode) or on the previous chunk's cached commit pass (prediction mode).
- On closed-loop rollouts scored against ground-truth geometry, the violation rate averaged over six frozen generators falls **from 74% to 16%** in collision mode, and on `LingBot-World 2.0` prediction mode cuts it **from 89% to 4%** while raising the Safe-Intent Score from 5 to 56.
- A halt-only external depth guard reaches fewer violations on four of the five pose-driven generators, but `NoPeWorld` has the best Safe-Intent Score on all five (up to **3.1×** the guard's) because it preserves wall slides, and it costs less: on `LingBot-World 2.0` prediction mode adds about **1%** to route time and collision mode 18%, against 27% for the guard.
- Trained only on first-person walks through static scenes, the heads transfer zero-shot to open-domain images, third-person views and moving obstacles, for example cutting static-obstacle violations on `LingBot-World 2.0` from 67% to 19% as judged by VLMs.
- Gains are uneven: on keystroke-driven `WorldPlay2` the Safe-Intent Score drops below the raw model's (36 versus 25–29), `Hy-Nomas` still violates on 40–45% of routes with 31–49% of its safe inputs altered, and the method handles only stops and slides, leaving pushing or carrying objects to future work.

papers.title: On the Complete Feature Set for ADHD Classification in Children and Adolescents Based on EEG Signals
papers.abstract: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder is a neurodevelopmental condition that can affect attention, activity and impulse control. Electroencephalography (EEG) records brain activity as children and adolescents perform cognitive tasks. However, comparing features derived from these recordings requires consistent signal preparation, shared analysis windows and documented quality decisions. We curated 669 existing BALLADEER recordings from 156 participants across five task conditions so that researchers can compare seven EEG feature families on the same time intervals for each participant and task. The dataset links continuous signals to precomputed measurements from 115 feature definitions or templates and records the quality decisions made for each recording. Analyses must still account for repeated measurements within participants, residual artefacts and differences between acquisition systems. Technical validation covered signal integrity, numerical checks on feature estimators and completeness of the released files. In every task, the median proportion of recording time retained after preprocessing was 100%. To illustrate reuse, we report saved participant-held-out evaluations comparing XGBoost using all seven families on eight-second windows with a predictor based only on recruitment-group prevalence in the training fold. Recruitment-group discrimination was stronger in Robots than in the three Slackline conditions. These descriptive results from overlapping cohorts do not establish diagnostic validity. The dataset, curation software and aggregate results for the predictive example are publicly available.
papers.summary: Comparing electroencephalography (EEG) features for studying attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) requires consistent signal preparation, shared analysis windows, and documented quality decisions. The authors curate **669 existing `BALLADEER` recordings from 156 children and adolescents across five task conditions**, linking continuous signals to precomputed measurements from 115 feature definitions spanning seven feature families, along with per-recording quality decisions. As an illustration of reuse, a participant-held-out `XGBoost` evaluation on eight-second windows is compared against a prevalence-only predictor, with recruitment-group discrimination stronger in the Robots task than in the three Slackline conditions. The authors state that these descriptive results do not establish diagnostic validity; the dataset, curation software, and aggregate results are public.

papers.title: MemOnce: A Scalable Memory Architecture for Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Deploying large language models (LLMs) in long-horizon and continual interactions requires maintaining reusable memory states for future inference, posing challenges for existing architectures. Standard Transformers accumulate layer-wise, token-level KV caches, incurring linear GPU memory growth and quadratic computational complexity as the context expands. In contrast, linear-time architectures compress history into fixed-size states, but struggle to retain fine-grained details. We introduce MemOnce, a foundation architecture that learns scalable memory states for language models. MemOnce is based on two core designs: (a) Memory encoder-decoder: it caches only a small subset of final-layer hidden states as compact memory representations and dynamically decodes them back into KV caches for attention layers; (b) Memory sparse attention: for each continual input, MemOnce adaptively retrieves relevant memory representations, with the sparse indices computed only once across layers. Coupling these two designs enables efficient on-the-fly memory loading and KV cache decoding, drastically reducing the GPU memory footprint and achieving linear-time complexity. We conduct extensive experiments to show that MemOnce outperforms Transformers and other architectures across varying model sizes, context lengths, and training paradigms (pretraining and post-training adaptation). In particular, adapting Qwen3.5-4B with MemOnce reduces memory state cache by 1313$\times$ and prefill latency by 6.9$\times$ at 1M context, and improves throughput by 3.5$\times$ and overall memory performance by +5.77%. Finally, MemOnce generalizes zero-shot to downstream representation tasks, achieving competitive results against specialized models.
papers.summary: Long-horizon use of large language models (LLMs) is limited by per-layer, per-token key-value (KV) caches that grow linearly in GPU memory and quadratically in compute, while fixed-state linear-time architectures lose fine-grained detail. `MemOnce` caches only a small subset of final-layer hidden states as compact memory and decodes them back into KV caches on demand, and it uses a sparse attention scheme that retrieves relevant memories for each new input with indices computed once and shared across layers. Adapting `Qwen3.5-4B` with `MemOnce` at a 1M-token context **shrinks the memory state cache by 1313x**, cuts prefill latency by 6.9x, raises throughput by 3.5x, and improves overall memory performance by 5.77%. The architecture is also reported to outperform Transformers and other architectures across model sizes, context lengths, and both pretraining and post-training adaptation.
papers.highlight_summary:
Long-running LLM sessions force a choice between Transformer KV caches that grow with every layer and token, and fixed-size linear states that lose detail. `MemOnce` stores a small slice of final-layer hidden states as compact memory, retrieves the relevant ones once per input, and decodes them into per-layer KV caches on demand.

- The memory encoder keeps only the trailing 1/r (default r=8) of each segment's final-layer states in a single bank that can be offloaded to CPU or SSD, and lightweight layer-specific MLPs project the retrieved states back into keys and values for every attention layer.
- Retrieval picks the top-K (K=64) long-term states by cosine similarity, adds a short-term window, and reuses that selection across all layers and decoding steps, so the active GPU state stays constant while the offloaded bank still grows with context.
- Adapting a frozen `Qwen3.5-4B` with LoRA and small projections scores **60.07** on average across five memory benchmarks from 4K to 1M tokens, **+5.77 points** over the full-context baseline (54.30) and well ahead of `M+` (41.39) and `Metis` (27.80), though it still trails full context on `LoCoMo` (67.01 vs 69.55).
- At 1M tokens the memory state cache shrinks by **1313×** (about 25 MB versus more than 32 GB), prefill is **6.9×** faster than the hybrid backbone, and decoding throughput is **3.5×** higher, while general reasoning on `MMLU`, `GSM8K` and `GPQA` is preserved (65.98 vs 65.88 average).
- Trained from scratch on `FineWeb-Edu`, it is only marginally ahead of `GDN` and the Transformer on zero-shot accuracy (52.35–52.63 vs 52.31 and 51.85), pretraining was validated only up to **1B parameters**, and agentic tasks such as long-horizon coding and tool use remain untested.

papers.title: A Methodologically Rigorous Benchmark of Linear Regression,RNN, and LSTM for S&P 500 Forecasting:Identifying Sources of Performance Inflation in Financial DeepLearning
papers.abstract: This study examines one-day-ahead forecasting of the S&P 500 closing level using a 2006-2025 dataset that includes fundamental price data, macroeconomic indicators, and engineered technical features. We benchmark three model families, namely linear regression, vanilla recurrent neural networks (RNN), and long short-term memory networks (LSTM), within a unified preprocessing and chronological evaluation pipeline. A central contribution of this work is a methodological audit of common practices in the deep-learning-for-stock-prediction literature. We identify three sources of result inflation that frequently appear in published methodologies: wavelet-denoised evaluation targets, the absence of a naive persistence baseline, and best-of-N replicate reporting. We then re-evaluate all model families under a corrected protocol that controls for each. Performance is reported using root mean squared error, mean absolute percentage error, and the Pearson correlation coefficient, averaged across N = 30 independent replicates per configuration. We compare models on accuracy, stability across replicates, and architectural depth sensitivity, using the naive persistence forecast (predicting today's close as tomorrow's close) as a primary baseline against which all candidate models must demonstrate improvement.
papers.summary: One-day-ahead forecasting of the S&P 500 closing level is benchmarked with linear regression, vanilla recurrent neural networks (RNN), and long short-term memory networks (LSTM) on 2006-2025 data combining prices, macroeconomic indicators, and technical features. The core of the work is an audit of common practice in deep-learning stock prediction, which identifies **three sources of inflated results: wavelet-denoised evaluation targets, no naive persistence baseline, and best-of-N replicate reporting**. All models are then re-evaluated under a corrected chronological protocol, averaging error and correlation metrics over 30 independent replicates and using the forecast that tomorrow's close equals today's as the baseline every model must beat. The abstract does not report the resulting numbers.

papers.title: Optimal Linear Regression Without a Variance
papers.abstract:
We study high-probability linear regression in the infinite variance regime, wherecthe regression noise has only a finite conditional $\alpha$-moment $\nu$ for some unknown $\alpha\in(1,2)$, and the covariates may only have finite moments up to a given order (e.g., 4th moment). We give a black-box reduction that converts finite-variance regression procedures into weak-moment procedures. The reduction is based on empirical residual pruning and is agnostic to the moment exponent, the noise scale, the covariance, and the design moment. Under a finite fourth-moment condition on the covariates, any finite-variance subroutine attaining the sub-Gaussian rate yields the following when the number of samples $n$ is above a suitably defined threshold: Without knowing $\alpha$ or $\nu$, we have with probability at least $1-\delta$ that $ \|\widehat\theta-\theta^*\|_\Sigma
  \lesssim_\alpha
  \nu^{1/\alpha}
  \big(\frac{d+\log(1/\delta)}{n}\big)^{\frac{\alpha-1}{\alpha}}, $ where $d$ is the dimension, $\Sigma$ is the covariate covariance matrix, and $\|v\|_\Sigma:=(v^\top\Sigma v)^{1/2}$. We further prove a matching minimax lower bound that holds under the same conditions. The reduction is computationally efficient whenever the finite-variance subroutine is. We also obtain a distribution-free prediction guarantee under a bounded raw $\alpha$-moment assumption on the response, and give an analogous $\alpha$-agnostic reduction for mean estimation.
papers.summary: Linear regression is studied with high-probability guarantees when the noise has infinite variance, having only a finite conditional moment of some unknown order alpha between 1 and 2, and the covariates have only a few finite moments. The authors give a black-box reduction based on empirical residual pruning that converts any finite-variance regression procedure into one for this weak-moment setting, without needing to know the moment exponent, noise scale, or covariance. Given a finite fourth moment on the covariates and enough samples, the resulting estimator's error **scales as ((d + log(1/delta))/n)^((alpha-1)/alpha) times the noise scale, matching a minimax lower bound** proved under the same conditions. The reduction is computationally efficient whenever the subroutine is, and analogous results are given for distribution-free prediction and mean estimation.

audio.title: cmHC: Balancing Stream Mixing in Hyper-Connections via Geometric Contraction
audio.script: Today's pick from the AI Paper Digest. Some language models carry several parallel streams of information between layers. Often the streams just get shuffled, not blended. Blend too much, and they all look the same. The authors nudge the mixing gently toward an even blend, only in the earliest layers. It adds no new parameters. In tests, loss dropped slightly, while strong blending everywhere made things worse. The gains are tiny, close to run-to-run noise. Still, it is a free tweak for training large models.
